Version 3.0, February 2026

Executive summary

Men and women are equal before the law, with some exceptions in customary law. Gender-based violence (GBV) in most of its forms is prohibited. Successive governments have adopted and implemented policies to promote, support and protect women. Women’s socio-economic status as compared to men has significantly improved though they are under-represented in the political sphere. Despite progress towards equality, Botswana remains a patriarchal society with women having a secondary role to men in family and community life, increasing their vulnerability to abuse.

GBV is widespread. The most up to date comprehensive data (from 2017) indicates that more than one in three women experience some form of GBV at least once in their lifetimes.

The government considers tackling GBV a priority. The Botswana Police Service has established a Gender and Child Protection Branch to improve the handling of GBV cases. The judiciary has established courts specialising in GBV cases and treats these as a priority. Although the UN and others have raised concerns about the effectiveness of the criminal justice system, GBV offenders continue to be arrested, prosecuted, convicted and imprisoned.

Women are able to move freely within Botswana. Essential public services, including education and healthcare, are available in places of relocation. Lone women do not face discrimination or stigma, their main challenge is having the financial means to relocate.

A woman who fears GBV from a rogue state actor or a non-state actor:

  • does not belong to a particular social group within the meaning of the Refugee Convention
  • is unlikely to face persecution or serious harm
  • is likely to obtain protection from the state
  • is likely to be able to relocate

Where a claim is refused, it is likely to be certified as ‘clearly unfounded’.

All cases must be considered on their individual facts, with the onus on the woman to demonstrate they face persecution or serious harm.

Assessment

Section updated: 29 January 2026

About the assessment

This section considers the evidence relevant to this note – that is the country information, refugee/human rights laws and policies, and applicable caselaw – and provides an assessment of whether, in general:

  • a woman is likely to face a real risk of persecution/serious harm by non-state actors because of her gender
  • can obtain effective protection from the state (or quasi state bodies)
  • can relocate within a country or territory to avoid persecution/serious harm
  • if a claim is refused, it is likely to be certified as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

The note considers risks of gender-based violence and discrimination faced by women including domestic and from strangers generally. It does not, however, specifically consider risks resulting from trafficking or modern slavery or those faced by lesbian, bisexual or trans women.

Decision makers must consider all claims on an individual basis, taking into account each case’s specific facts.

2. Convention reason(s)

2.1.1 Women do not form a particular social group (PSG) in Botswana within the meaning of the Refugee Convention. This is because while they do share an innate characteristic, or a common background that cannot be changed, or share a characteristic or belief that is so fundamental to identity or conscience that a person should not be forced to renounce it – their sex and/or gender – they do not have a distinct identity in Botswana because the group is perceived as being different by the surrounding society.

2.1.2 Women have the same civil, legal and political rights as men, albeit they face some discrimination in customary law. Women have parity to men in education and health outcomes and have made progress in other public and private areas of life. Although patriarchal attitudes persist and there is some societal discrimination this is not to the extent that as a group they are perceived as being different by the surrounding society (see Legal rights; Policy, programmes and campaigns; Social, economic and political status; and Social and cultural attitudes).

2.1.3 In the absence of a link to one of the 5 Refugee Convention grounds necessary for the grant of refugee status, the question is whether the particular person will face a real risk of serious harm sufficient to qualify for Humanitarian Protection (HP).

2.1.4 For further guidance on the 5 Refugee Convention grounds see the Asylum Instruction, Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status and Gender issues in the asylum claim.

3. Risk

3.1.1 A woman is unlikely to face gender-based violence (GBV) that amounts to persecution or serious harm from non-state actors.

3.1.2 While just over one in three women reported to have experienced some form of abuse in their lifetimes at least once, it varies in frequency and nature ranging from public shaming to rape and murder. Not all such treatment will by its nature and/or repetition amount to persecution or serious harm. The onus will be on the woman to demonstrate such a risk.

3.1.3 The Government of the Republic of Botswana (GOROB) is party to the principal international and regional instruments that support gender equality and protect women from discrimination and GBV (see International instruments). The Constitution provides for equality between women and men, although there remains a clause that allows exemptions from this for customary law and personal law (see Constitution). The Penal Code criminalises various forms of physical and sexual violence, including rape but not spousal rape (see Penal Code). The Domestic Violence Act 2008 protects women and girls from this form of GBV and includes provision to issue a range of protection orders although the Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs (MYGA) acknowledged gaps in this legislation. The Children’s Act protects girls from abuse including cultural practices such as child marriage and female genital mutilation (FGM). Other laws protect women from discrimination, including in the workplace, and from being trafficked. The GOROB has also introduced legislation creating a sexual offenders registry and to ensure women have equal access to land ownership (see Gender-specific legislation and Protection and maintenance orders).

3.1.4 Botswana has a dual legal system encompassing common law (see above) and customary law, which is based on tribal practice and commonly applied in rural areas. Some customary law discriminates against women, for example with regard to property rights or by allowing child marriage. Discrimination can also include treating married women as minors within a marriage and using corporal punishment against wives and children. The World Bank suggested that there had been some developments that strengthened women’s rights under customary law, and an official of the Ministry of Labour and Internal Affairs thought that the customary judicial system had become more progressive (see Customary law).

3.1.5 While the government has made progress in adopting laws that protect women’s rights and person, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women commented in July 2025 that the country lacks a comprehensive legal framework on GBV (see Gender-specific legislation). In response, the GOROB states it is developing gender equality and anti-GBV bills to address gaps in existing legislation (see Gender-based violence (GBV) and gender equity bills).

3.1.6 President Doko, elected in October 2024, has stated that combating GBV is a government priority (see Government position). The MYGA has the principal responsibility for mainstreaming gender equality across government and ensuring that priorities such as GBV are adequately resourced and addressed. Other public bodies including the Inter-Ministerial Committee on GBV and the National Gender Commission assist in co-ordinating activities on gender issues including GBV from the national to district levels (see Departmental responsibility and other public bodies).

3.1.7 Successive governments have adopted and implemented policies to promote, support and protect women. These include the National Policy on Gender and Development and the National Gender-Based Violence Strategy first published in the 2010s, which are both under review at the time of writing (see Policies, strategies and programmes). There have also been a series of awareness raising and educational campaigns run by the government at a national and community level against GBV involving various stakeholders, including the First Lady (the president’s wife), dikgosi (tribal leaders), religious groups and civil society organisations (CSOs). The police, Legal Aid Botswana, and CSOs also run regular educational campaigns about women’s rights and GBV (see Awareness raising, Legal aid and Civil society organisations).

3.1.8 Botswana has made significant progress in addressing socio-economic inequalities faced by women but falls short in achieving equal representation in the political sphere. Positive achievements include parity in school and university enrolment, the broad uptake of family planning, high rates of female entrepreneurship, wage equality for similar work and strong female representation in leaderships roles in the public sector. However, female-headed households account for a disproportionate number of the country’s poor, while women are more likely to be unemployed, earn less and work in the informal sector than men. Women also have a low representation in politics with only 6 out of 69 seats in parliament, 14% of cabinet positions and 15% of local government positions. Traditional leadership structures are also male dominated, with 2 women out of 33 sitting tribal leaders in the Ntlo ya Dikgosi (the House of Chiefs which advises parliament on tribal law and custom) (see Economic context and Social, economic and political status).

3.1.9 Societal attitudes generally support equality between men and women. In a study undertaken by Afrobarometer in 2022, the large majority of Batswana agreed that women should have the same rights as men to own or inherit land, in hiring for jobs and in voting. Around 60% of people consider GBV the most important issue related to women’s rights that the government must tackle. Despite the progress in law and attitudes towards equality, Botswana continues to be a patriarchal society with women having a secondary role to men in community and family life. Practices such as ‘bogadi’ (also ‘lobola’) or ‘bride price’, where a man’s family will pay a dowry to a woman’s parents to marry her (and bring expectations of matrimonial obedience), continue. These cultural inequalities increase women’s vulnerability to abuse (see Social and cultural attitudes).

3.1.10 There is limited current, comprehensive and reliable statistical data on the prevalence of GBV. The most recent systematic study is the Botswana National Relationship Study 2018 (BNRS 2018), largely based on information gathered in 2017. The BNRS 2018, however, may no longer reflect the current occurrence of GBV. Factors such as changes in the law and policy, women’s increased awareness of their rights and greater focus on GBV in the criminal justice system may have altered this. There are also police reports of GBV, Statistics Botswana data of magistrate and high court cases, data gathered by CSOs which engage with victims of GBV, and media reports. But this data does not provide a comprehensive description of the current levels of GBV. Sources expressing a view of the level in GBV in 2025 are basing this on a mixture of the BNRS 2018, police reports, media reports, small scale CSO studies or records, and their own experience, rather than systematic population studies (see Limited statistical information, Levels of GBV, Police reports, Convictions and sentencing and Civil society organisations). Additionally, women are likely to under-report GBV for a variety of reasons. These include stigma linked to patriarchal norms and expectations, family pressure, lack of access to first-responders, police not providing a separate space from the perpetrator to report the abuse, lack of trust in the criminal justice system, and economic dependency on the perpetrator of abuse (see Under-reporting).

3.1.11 GBV includes physical, sexual, emotional (psychological) and economic harm in public or private life. Such violence as documented by sources can range from making a woman ‘feel bad’, belittling her in front of other people, or withholding money for household use, to beating, threatening her with a weapon, rape, or murder/femicide by her partner. The severity and frequency of such violence is likely to vary (see Definitions of GBV).

3.1.12 Sources refer to GBV being pervasive, widespread, or having a high prevalence. The BNRS 2018 puts this into numbers, finding that 37% of women surveyed had experienced some form of GBV in their lifetimes at least once (slightly higher than the global average). Of the women surveyed 37% of women experiencing some form of intimate partner violence (IPV), 11% of women reporting sexual harassment either at school or work, and 5% stating that they had been raped by a non-partner. The most common form of IPV was emotional (30.8% of women experienced this), followed by physical (20.5%), economic (11.4%) and sexual (5.4%). Violence was most commonly committed by intimate partners, family members and then strangers. Sources interviewed by the Home Office (HO) in July 2025 generally agreed GBV was widespread but varied on whether they thought it was increasing. Some noted that women’s increased awareness of their rights and willingness to report may account for the rise in reports of GBV (see Levels of GBV).

3.1.13 The Botswana Police Service (BPS) publishes annual statistics of the number of reported crimes, including those defined as GBV offences and affecting children. The number of offences reported in 2024, the latest available at the time of writing, was 13,802, a 30.3% fall from 2023. Of the GBV-linked offences, these included 172 murders (a 30.3% rise on 2023), 2,018 cases of rape (a 12.1% fall), 3,773 cases of common assault (a 55.2% fall) and 1,162 cases of common nuisance (a 167.7% increase). However, BPS officials interviewed by the HO in July 2025 considered GBV cases were increasing in 2025 (see Police reports).

3.1.14 Factors that affect the likelihood of GBV include:

  • age (women between 18 and 24 appear most vulnerable)
  • having been abused in childhood
  • whether the partner drinks alcohol
  • having more than one sexual partner
  • quarrelling with partners
  • level of education (see Factors affecting likelihood of violence)

These are individual / relationship level factors which were found by Botswana National Relationship Study, 2018.

3.1.15 Sources interviewed by the HO in July 2025 agreed that traditional harmful practices, such as FGM or ritual killings, are unlikely to occur in present day Botswana (although they may have occurred in the past). No source was aware of a verified case (see Traditional harmful practices).

3.1.16 For further guidance on assessing risk, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status and Gender issues in the asylum claim.

4. Protection

4.1.1 A woman who fears a rogue state actor and/or a non-state actor is likely to obtain protection from the state.

4.1.2 The GOROB has taken reasonable steps to protect women by operating an effective legal system for the detection, prosecution and punishment of acts constituting persecution or serious harm and which is accessible to them. This includes:

  • establishing a legal and policy framework to protect women from discrimination and GBV (see Legal rights and Risk above). Although a number of sources indicated that the DVA 2008 needs to be updated, sources also indicated that laws and policies have not been effectively implemented (See State protection).
  • establishing, maintaining control over and adequately funding a competent law enforcement agency – the Botswana Police Service (BPS) – which is present throughout the country, including in small settlements and rural areas (see Botswana Police Service and Access to the police)
  • mandating that GBV cases cannot be withdrawn from police investigation to counter withdrawals that may arise for various reasons including pressure from a woman’s family or economic dependency on the perpetrator (see Botswana Police Service)
  • developing BPS standard operating procedures for handling GBV cases and training all police officers on gender-sensitive approaches to policing (see Gender-specific guidance and training and Gender and Child Protection Branch)
  • conducting GBV public awareness and outreach exercises, and developing community-led prevention programmes (see Gender and Child Protection Branch)
  • establishing a Gender and Child Protection Branch (GCPB) within the BPS to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of how GBV cases are handled. GCPB officers are posted in all 84 police stations across the country (but not in all police posts, of which there are over 380). GCPB officers are specifically trained to deal with GBV cases and work collaboratively with CSOs to support victims. CSOs interviewed by the HO in July 2025 noted that police stations with the GCPB officers have improved how GBV cases are handled (see Gender and Child Protection Branch)
  • establishing 8 child-friendly police centres which are also able to handle GBV cases and can provide additional services, such as counselling (Gender and Child Protection Branch)
  • introducing a toll-free number for victims of GBV to ring for assistance (see Gender and Child Protection Branch)
  • issuing protection orders and maintenance orders to support victims of domestic violence, although a number of sources note that restraining orders (a type of protection order) are not effectively or consistently implemented (see Implementation of protection orders)
  • arresting and prosecuting perpetrators of GBV. While there are no official figures for the number of arrests and prosecutions of offenders, sources interviewed by the HO in July 2025 acknowledge that perpetrators (who are almost always men) are arrested, detained and prosecuted. The US State Department (USSD) observed that in 2023 the authorities effectively enforced the law in rape cases when victims pressed charges (the USSD does not comment on women’s rights in its report for 2024) (see Arrests and prosecutions and Directorate of Public Prosecution)
  • operating an independent and effective judicial system with most GBV cases handled in the lower (magistrates’) courts. However, sources note that the time taken for a case to be disposed of - including convictions and acquittals - can be lengthy, in some cases several years (see Structure and jurisdiction; Fair trial and independence; and Convictions and sentencing)
  • establishing courts specialising in GBV cases, albeit sources are unclear if this pilot, originally set up during the COVID pandemic specifically in Molepolole, continues. The MYGA observed that the Chief Justice has instructed magistrates to prioritise GBV cases (see Gender-specific courts)
  • convicting and sentencing GBV offenders. Although there are no recent statistics on the number of GBV cases handled by the courts, the latest published by Statistics Botswana relate to 2020. During that year, over 7,000 cases of all types of offences were recorded mainly in magistrates’ courts, about half the number processed in 2019. The fall in the number of cases was because of the suspension of hearings during lockdowns imposed to control the spread of COVID. Of the 7,000+ cases,
    • more than 40% were withdrawn, reasons are not identified
    • 9% related to sexual offences, of these about 33% resulted in a conviction
    • 11.9% for attempts/threats to murder, assaults and harassment, of these about 23% resulted in a conviction
    • 6% for homicide, of these about 26% resulted in a conviction
    • the remainder of cases were variously disposed including being withdrawn, resulting in acquittal, referrals to the High Court, not heard, referrals back to another magistrate (NB an allegation of GBV reported to the police does not mean that offence has occurred (see Convictions and sentencing).
  • working collaboratively with CSOs which provide support to GBV victims, including referring cases to secure shelters, 2 in Gaborone and Francistown operated by the Botswana Gender Based Violence Support Centre (BGBVC) and one in Maun run by Women Against Rape (WAR) (see Shelters)
  • making legal aid and advice available to the poor provided by LAB, the accessibility of legal aid was highlighted as a challenge by several sources (see Legal aid)
  • maintaining oversight of the government by establishing the Office of the Ombudsman with the remit to investigate allegations of public sector maladministration and human rights abuses. However, sources note that while the Office investigates complaints it lacks staff (see Office of the Ombudsman)
  • operating an effective prison system in which there is specific provision to rehabilitate GBV offenders (see Prison system)

4.1.3 The UN and various CSOs have raised concerns about the effectiveness of the implementation of protection for women. Sources note:

  • the slowness of the police to respond to crimes generally and their lack of resources. Attitudes, which sometimes justify GBV, under react, or blame the victim, police sometimes try to reconcile a victim and perpetrator (see Effectiveness)
  • inconsistency in how GBV cases are handled by the police, with a lack of private spaces for victims to report abuse at police stations and posts (see Effectiveness)
  • difficulties in accessing police assistance, particularly for women in remote rural areas (see Access to the police)
  • the ineffectiveness of restraining orders at preventing perpetrators of GBV contacting further and abusing their victims. (see Implementing protection orders)
  • Police indicated that they are not always aware when a restraining order is in place (see Implementing protection orders)
  • weaknesses in the bail system with GBV suspects reportedly often released on bail. These suspects then go on to abuse their female victims including sometimes killing them. The government, in response, introduced the Bail Act in March 2024 which tightened the criteria for releasing suspects on bail. This included giving victims an opportunity to provide evidence to a court as to why a suspect should not be released. The full impact of the act remains unclear, with sources stating that test cases are needed to set precedence for how the law is to be applied (see Bail Act, 2024 and Implementation of bail)
  • cases that are handled by the customary courts often result in attempts at reconciliation rather than prosecution. The government has changed the law to allow any person the right to transfer GBV cases from the customary courts to the magistrates’ courts. The BPS officials interviewed by the HO in July 2025 observed that GBV cases are usually heard in the magistrate courts (see Customary law)
  • low prosecution and conviction rates (see Arrests and prosecutions and Convictions and sentencing)
  • the length of time taken to process cases through the criminal justice system (see Convictions and sentencing)
  • the high number of GBV cases withdrawn from the criminal justice process. There are a variety of reasons for this, including difficulties in investigating and identifying the perpetrator, pressure from families and economic dependency on the perpetrator of abuse. However, the BPS state that they no longer allow GBV cases to be withdrawn once raised with them (but these case may be withdrawn in the court system) (see Botswana Police Service and Withdrawal of cases)

4.1.4 Botswana has a well-developed civil society ecosystem which is able to provide various forms of support to women including GBV victims. The government provides funding and is generally co-operative with and responsive to these organisations. CSO resources are, however, limited and some organisations, such as the Botswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS (BONELA), have experienced a significant drop in funding following cuts in overseas aid introduced by the US administration in 2025 (see Overview of organisations and services).

4.1.5 The 3 main CSOs providing support to women are BGBVC, BONELA and WAR. The organisations provide a variety of services including counselling, psychosocial support, medical assistance, legal advice and referrals, empowerment programmes and community education (see Botswana Gender Based Violence Support Centre; Botswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS; and Women Against Rape). Other CSOs operating nationally and locally providing assistance to women include Gender Links, the Ratong Centre, Men and Boys for Gender Equality, Love Botswana and the Botswana Christian Health & AIDS Intervention Program. CSOs are not able to protect women but they are able to help them access protection from the state and provide them with secure spaces to stay temporarily (see Overview of organisations and services and Shelters).

4.1.6 There are weaknesses in the location, organisation, operation and administration of the criminal justice system which reduce its effectiveness and accessibility for some women. However, there is also clear and robust evidence that the state does not tolerate serious discrimination or other offensive acts against women and is both willing and able to provide protection.

4.1.7 For further guidance on assessing state protection, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status and Gender issues in the asylum claim.

5. Internal relocation

5.1.1 A woman is likely to be able to relocate to avoid persecution or serious harm from a non-state actor.

5.1.2 This is because in general there are parts of Botswana - such as Gaborone, Francistown or Maun - where it will be reasonable to expect a woman to relocate.

5.1.3 Botswana is about the twice the size of the UK but with a relatively small population of around 2.3 million. Gaborone, the capital, has a population of around 250,000. Other significant urban areas are Francistown (with a population of just over 100,000), Mogoditshane (88,000), Maun (85,000) and Molepolole (74,000). The population is largely young (under 35), mostly urban and dominated by the Tswana ethnic group. Around 44% of households are headed by women, most of whom are not married (see Geography).

5.1.4 Botswana is an upper middle-income country. Successive governments have used the country’s diamond wealth to improve the economy and living conditions, putting significant resources into education, healthcare and social protection. However, high rates of unemployment, poverty and inequality persist (see Economic context).

5.1.5 People are legally free to move within Botswana (see Legal right to move). Many people, including women, migrate to the cities and towns, such as Gaborone, seeking employment and economic opportunity (see Lone women). Women are able to access free public services, such as education and healthcare, throughout the country (see Accessing public services). Single female or female headed households do not face stigma or discrimination in urban areas, but attitudes might be different in conservative smaller settlements and rural areas (see Lone women).

5.1.6 Sources interviewed by the HO in July 2025 generally agreed the main barrier to a woman relocating within the country was financial – whether a woman would be able to support herself. As long as a woman has the means to support herself, relocation is possible (see Lone women). However, a couple of sources noted that it might be difficult for a woman to ‘disappear’ if an abuser was intent on finding her because Botswana has a small population (see Tracing and locating people).

5.1.7 For further guidance on internal relocation and factors to consider, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status and the Gender issues in the asylum claim.

6. Certification

6.1.1 Where a claim is refused, it is likely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002. This is because a woman is able to obtain effective protection and internally relocate within the country.

6.1.2 For further guidance on certification, see Certification of Protection and Human Rights claims under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 (clearly unfounded claims).

Country information

About the country information

This section contains publicly available or disclosable country of origin information (COI) which has been gathered, collated and analysed in line with the research methodology. It provides the evidence base for the assessment which, as stated in the About the assessment, is the guide to the current objective conditions.

The structure and content follow a terms of reference which sets out the general and specific topics relevant to the scope of this note.

This document is intended to be comprehensive but not exhaustive. If a particular event, person or organisation is not mentioned this does not mean that the event did or did not take place or that the person or organisation does or does not exist.

The COI includes information obtained during a Home Office fact-finding mission (FFM) to Botswana conducted between 5 and 17 July 2025. Background about the FFM including its purpose, methodology and terms of reference, as well as notes of interviews with sources, are included in the annexes. While the focus of the FFM was the treatment of women generally, the mission also obtained information about situation of LGBT+ people which is documented in the notes in the annexes.

The COI included was published or made publicly available on or before 29 December 2025. Any event taking place or report published after this date will not be included.

Decision makers must use relevant COI as the evidential basis for decisions.

8. Geography

8.1 Demography

8.1.1 Botswana is just over 580,000 square kilometres, about the twice the size of the UK[footnote 1].

8.1.2 Statistics Botswana, a public body which collects and shares official statistics in Botswana[footnote 2], in its ‘Population and Housing Census 2022 Population Distribution, Structure and Density in Botswana’, noted the country has a population of:

‘… 2,359,609 … comprising of 1,150,615 males (48.8%) and 1,208,994 females (51.2%) … Botswana … tends to have a youthful population, with 1-in-3 people … under-15 … The national population density has risen to 4.1 in 2022 compared to 3.6 people per sq. KM in 2011 … The Southeastern region, including [Gaborone] … boasts the highest density. The West remains the least populated ... The Eastern region continues to hold the largest share of the population.’[footnote 3]

8.1.3 Around two-thirds of the population live in urban areas (cities, towns and urban villages), one-third in rural areas[footnote 4].

8.1.4 Based on the 2022 census, the largest urban areas including ‘large villages’ are (in brackets - name of area and population):

  • Gaborone City – the capital city (246,325)
  • Francistown City (103,417)
  • Mogoditshane (88,004)
  • Maun (85,350)
  • Molepolole (74,861)[footnote 5]

8.1.5 Around 80% of the population are ethnic Tswana. Other ethnic groups include ‘Kalanga 11%, Basarwa 3%, other, including Kgalagadi and people of European ancestry 7%’.[footnote 6]

8.1.6 The census 2022 provided data that specifically relates to or is about women, including noting:

  • 44.4% of households were headed by women
  • 16.4% of people were married, 70.4% never married, 9.4% were living together
  • 9.7% of women aged 20 to 24 had been married before the age of 15
  • 12.5% of women aged 20 to 24 had been married before the age of 18[footnote 7]

8.1.7 Professor Neil Parsons in an entry updated 27 December 2025 in the Encyclopaedia Britannica (Parsons 2025) noted: ‘The national language, Tswana (Setswana, Sechuana), is widely spoken. The official language is English. The Khoisan speak languages characterized as Khoe, or Khwe, and San. Several other languages are also spoken in the country, including Kalanga, Sekgalagadi, Herero, Mbukushu, and Yei.’[footnote 8]

8.2 Map

8.2.1 The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) produced a map of the country in 2014 showing the country’s districts, main cities and towns, roads, and rivers[footnote 9]:

9. Economic context

9.1.1 The World Bank noted in an undated entry:

‘Once among the world’s poorest nations, well-managed diamond wealth has improved [Botswana’s] … economy and people’s living conditions … it is now an upper-middle-income country (UMIC). However, poverty and inequality persist at levels higher than in comparable middle-income countries … [gross domestic product per person was estimated to be US$7,695 (about £5,590) in 2024[footnote 10] [footnote 11]] Living conditions have steadily improved since independence as the wealth from diamond discoveries has helped lay the foundations for growth and development and fund major advances in social service delivery, expanding broad access to clean water, electricity, and sanitation. Basic education and health outcomes have also steadily improved. However, the extractives-driven growth model is reaching its limits and ability to further sustain poverty reduction and inclusive growth.

‘The government has invested significant resources in human capital development through education, health, and social protection. Government spending as share of GDP on health is 4.8%, education 7.1%, and social protection 2.6%, very high compared to neighbours in the region. Nevertheless, human capital outcomes are not consistent with spending levels.’[footnote 12]

9.1.2 The World Bank also stated:

‘Botswana’s economy faced significant challenges in 2024, contracting by 3%, due to a slump in the diamond sector, which dominates export earnings and government revenue. Growth forecasts for 2025 remain subdued, with expectations of negative growth as diamond demand stays low ... Inflation eased to about 2.1% in 2025 … Employment remains skewed toward low-productivity sectors, with unemployment at 27.6% reflecting structural labour market issues and limited private sector opportunities and extreme inequality … Inequality is persistent, and human capital outcomes require enhancement through better education, healthcare, and social protection reforms.’[footnote 13]

9.1.3 A World Bank press release of 15 July 2025 referring to an assessment of gender dynamics in Botswana dated March 2025 provided an overview of the economic disparities between men and women in the country:

‘“Women now account for 57% of university graduates, and Botswana has significantly expanded access to maternal health services, with most births taking place in health facilities. However, persistent gaps in women’s economic participation limit the country’s growth potential,” says World Bank Country Director for Botswana, Satu Kahkonen …

‘The assessment identifies gender disparities in three key areas: human capital (health, education, social protection), economic inclusion, voice and agency. Boys face higher rates of childhood stunting and lower early childhood education access [than girls], while 1 in 10 girls becomes pregnant before the age of 20, making it the leading cause of school dropout for young women … HIV continues to disproportionately affects [sic] women, with a 26% prevalence - nearly twice that of men.

‘Despite educational gains, women in Botswana have lower labour force participation (63% vs 73% for men), earn less, and are concentrated in informal, vulnerable jobs. The COVID-19 pandemic worsened these disparities, with women accounting for over half of all job losses. Rural and informal women workers are especially vulnerable to climate and economic shocks, underlining the need for inclusive, resilient economic systems. Despite advancements in the legal framework for gender equality, social norms and informal barriers still limit women’s full economic inclusion. Women are more likely to run informal businesses, have less access to finance …’[footnote 14]

9.1.4 The World Bank and International Monetary Fund provide statistics on the economy and society including gender specific data:

  • Economy | Botswana | World Bank Data360
  • Botswana | World Bank Gender Data Portal
  • Botswana and the IMF

10. Legal rights

10.1 International instruments

10.1.1 The Government of the Republic of Botswana (GOROB) has ratified the following UN conventions which include provision to protect equality generally and women’s and girls’ rights specifically:

  • International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
  • Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW)
  • Convention on the Rights of the Child
  • Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities[footnote 15]

10.1.2 The GOROB also acceded to the UN International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in October 2025. This convention has provision to protect and promote social and cultural rights without discrimination on various grounds including sex[footnote 16] [footnote 17].

10.1.3 The UN Botswana website in an undated entry noted ‘… the Government and the UN in Botswana pledge to work closely together … [to achieve] national implementation of the [UN’s] 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.’[footnote 18] This includes goal 5 on gender equality which aims to ‘Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls.’[footnote 19]

10.1.4 Botswana is also party to regional instruments which promote and protect women’s rights. The GOROB in their national review of implementation of the Beijing Platform for Action, a programme to assess progress on women’s rights, submitted to UN Women in June 2019 (GOROB national review 2019) stated: ‘Botswana is … Party to … the Southern African Development Community Protocol on Gender and Development (SPGD) among others.’[footnote 20]

10.1.5 A GOROB representative in discussions with the CEDAW on 27 June 2025 about the GOROB’s reports submitted to the committee (CEDAW discussions report 2025), dated 8 August 2025, stated: ‘In December 2023, Botswana had ratified the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (Maputo Protocol), demonstrating the Government’s ongoing commitment to promoting women’s rights and gender equality. Steps had been taken to enact gender-sensitive laws to promote the rights of women and other vulnerable groups.’[footnote 21]

10.2 Constitution

10.2.1 Article 3 of the Constitution protects the fundamental rights of all citizens. Article 15 protects people from discrimination including on grounds of sex[footnote 22]. However, subsection 4 of article 15 allows for exemptions from equal treatment for customary law, marriage, divorce and others matters of personal law[footnote 23].

10.2.2 The UKHO FFM 2025 interviewed officials from the Ministry of Justice and Correctional Services on 9 July 2025 (MOJCS officials 2025) who noted:

‘… the constitution promotes equality and non-discrimination. However, [comments] from the [UN] human rights treaty body reviews with regard to women [have noted that] we have a discriminatory element in section 15 of the BWA Constitution. The President has said that his government will be human-rights-centric. He has explained that human rights should be placed at the centre of development. One of the ways this will be realised is through a constitutional review which commenced in 2022, but this government is going to ensure is finalised. Therefore, we are sure that section 15(4) [of the Constitution] will be looked into.’[footnote 24]

10.3 Penal Code

10.3.1 The Penal Code criminalises rape (of either sex), ‘defilement’ of persons under 18 years and various non-gender specific acts of harm[footnote 25]. The Code was amended in 2021 to ‘enhance and make stiffer penalties for sexual offences’[footnote 26].

10.3.2 The US State Department’s 2024 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices: Botswana (USSD HR report 2024), covering events in 2024, does not comment on the rights or protections of women specifically[footnote 27]. However, the USSD HR report for 2023 which covered a broader range of human rights issues noted that the law criminalised rape (under the Penal Code) but did not recognise spousal rape[footnote 28]. Similarly, Freedom House in their report covering events in 2024 (FH report 2024) noted ‘Spousal rape is not considered a crime’[footnote 29].

10.3.3 The GOROB’s Botswana 2022 Voluntary National Review Report dated June 2022, submitted to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) (BVNRR 2022), noted ‘the Penal Code was amended to align it with the Children's Act towards protecting children from sexual offences. The amendment increased the age of consent from sixteen (16) to eighteen (18) years while introducing a close-in age provision to protect consenting and experimenting adolescents …’[footnote 30]

10.4 Gender-specific legislation

10.4.1 The BVNRR 2022 noted: ‘Botswana has extensive laws … that constitute an enabling environment for elimination of all forms of discrimination against women and girls including … the Criminal Procedure and Evidence Act, the Public Service Act, Marriage Act and abolition of Marital Power Act.’[footnote 31]

10.4.2 The USSD HR report for 2023 noted that amongst other things the law:

  • prohibited domestic and other violence against women and girls
  • prohibited discrimination in work based on gender[footnote 32]

10.4.3 Generis Global, an international legal service provider, noted in an article dated 9 November 2024:

‘Botswana has established a legal framework aimed at combating domestic violence, most notably through the enactment of the Domestic Violence Act of 2008 [DVA]. This legislation represents a significant commitment to addressing the pervasive issue of domestic violence within the nation. The Act defines domestic violence comprehensively, covering not only physical abuse but also emotional, psychological, and economic forms of violence. This broad definition ensures that various facets of domestic violence are recognized and can be acted upon under the law, thereby facilitating effective intervention measures.

‘The Domestic Violence Act emphasizes the importance of protection for victims, outlining various remedies that can be sought. It empowers individuals to apply for protection orders, which serve to restrict the actions of the perpetrator and safeguard the victim’s personal safety … Furthermore, the law mandates that police and other authorities take domestic violence complaints seriously by ensuring prompt investigations and appropriate actions, which underscores the critical role of law enforcement in protecting victims.

‘This legal framework also reflects an understanding of the socio-cultural dynamics surrounding domestic violence in Botswana. It recognizes the need for a victim-centric approach, offering support services such as counseling and shelters for those affected. Additionally, the Act promotes public education about domestic violence, aiming to change societal attitudes and increase awareness about the repercussions of such behavior. By fostering an environment where victims feel empowered to report incidents of violence, Botswana’s legal structure works towards dismantling the stigma associated with domestic abuse.’ [footnote 33]

10.4.4 However, the UN Committee for the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) in their concluding observations on the fifth periodic report of Botswana, based on submissions and discussions between 2023 and 2025, dated 11 July 2025 (CEDAW report 2025), noted a ‘… lack of alignment of the Domestic Violence Act with the Convention [on the Elimination of All Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW)] and its limited implementation, particularly regarding protection orders and access to victim support services, as well as the reliance on mediation by customary courts in domestic violence cases …’[footnote 34]

10.4.5 The UKHO FFM interviewed representatives of the Botswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS, a Botswanan NGO focussing on health and human rights including GBV, on 16 July 2025 (BONELA representatives 2025). The representatives commented they ‘would like the DVA to have more punitive measures or provision to prosecute from a criminal perspective [the Act defines domestic violence and provides for various orders to help protect victims but does not set out penalties for acts of domestic violence].’[footnote 35]

10.4.6 For more information on the various protection orders, see Protection and maintenance orders below.

10.4.7 The Children’s Act, 2009 makes ‘provision for the promotion and protection of the rights of the child; for the promotion of the physical, emotional, intellectual and social development and general well-being of children; for the protection and care of children; for the establishment of structures to provide for the care, support, protection and rehabilitation of children’[footnote 36]. This includes protecting male and female children from:

  • being encouraged, allowed or forced into cohabiting with any person in a sexual relationship
  • torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment
  • being subject ‘to social, cultural and religious practices which are detrimental to his or her well-being … A child shall not be subjected, by any person, to —
    • ‘(a) a forced marriage;
    • ‘(b) a child betrothal;
    • ‘(c) genital mutilation or female circumcision; or
    • ‘(d) any other cultural rite, custom or tradition which may inflict physical, emotional or psychological pain or harm to the child, or otherwise violate or endanger his or her bodily integrity, life, health, dignity, education or general well-being.’[footnote 37]

10.4.8 The UN CEDAW report 2025 ‘… welcomed … the following legislative reforms [which relate directly to women] …

  • ‘The Anti-Human Trafficking (Amendment) Act in 2024;
  • ‘… The Sexual Offenders Registry Act, in 2021;
  • ‘… The Revised Land Policy, granting married women and men equal access to land ownership, in 2020.’[footnote 38]

10.4.9 An article in the Botswana Gazette, a Botswanan newspaper, of 30 May 2025 noted: ‘The primary objective of the Sex Offenders Registry Act is to establish a centralised and secure database of individuals convicted of sexual offences … The registry will serve as a tool for law enforcement agencies, schools and childcare institutions, allowing them to conduct background checks and safeguard vulnerable groups – particularly women and children – from known sex offenders.’[footnote 39]

10.4.10 However, the UN CEDAW report 2025 observed there was a ‘lack of information on the effectiveness of the Sexual Offenders Registry’[footnote 40]. The UKHO FFM interviewed officials in the Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs on 11 July 2025 (MYGA officials 2025) who ‘explained that there is an act [Sexual Offenders Registry Act, 2021] which is yet to be operationalised, but it has been assented into law ... the debate had been that the police are the ones to implement it, and the police say they would rely on judgments from the courts [in order to flag a sex offender’s conviction for a particular offence] ... they were still trying to work out an end-to-end system that could facilitate that.’[footnote 41]

10.4.11 The UN CEDAW report 2025 was also concerned by ‘[t]he lack of a comprehensive legal framework … on gender-based violence [and] … the absence of legislation specifically criminalizing sexual violence …’[footnote 42]

10.5 Gender-based violence (GBV) and gender equity bills

10.5.1 The GOROB delegation noted in the CEDAW discussions report 2025 ‘… the Government was considering drafting a bill on gender equality that would incorporate all the standards established in the [CEDAW] … and institutionalize gender mainstreaming across all sectors.’[footnote 43]

10.5.2 The MYGA officials 2025 noted ‘… users of the Domestic Violence Act [2008] have pointed to a number of gaps in the act. We are currently [working on] a GBV [bill] to keep closing the gaps to ensure that people are safe and that perpetrators are adequately dealt with.’[footnote 44]

10.5.3 The MOJCS officials 2025 when asked about the GBV bill noted:

‘… the MoJCS could not comment on the full scope of the bill as it is the purview of the … MYGA. The general objective of the Bill is to make concrete the various measures discussed: shelters, education [public campaigning against GBV], the roles of stakeholders – government and civil society – to domesticate international human rights instruments BWA is party to – including the UN Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol), and the Southern African Development Community’s (SADC) Protocol on Gender and Development – to ensure that there is adequate protection [for women].’[footnote 45]

10.5.4 An article by Africa Press, an African media platform, dated 11 October 2025, reporting on comments made by the minister of the MYGA to parliament, noted: ‘A Gender-Based Violence Bill is currently in development, focusing on prevention, protection, care, and support. The bill targets [the] root causes of gender-based violence and provides comprehensive measures for addressing these challenges.’[footnote 46] Another Africa Press article dated 14 November 2025 reported the comments of the MYGA’s permanent secretary, who ‘explained that the legislation will enhance survivor protection, strengthen law enforcement responses, and improve access to healthcare, psychosocial support, and safe shelters.’[footnote 47]

10.6 Customary law

10.6.1 The USSD HR report 2023 noted that ‘under customary law based on tribal practice … restricted women’s property rights and economic opportunities, particularly in rural areas.’[footnote 48] Similarly the FH report 2024 noted ‘customary law, commonly applied in rural areas, often discriminates against women … Child and forced marriages [of girls and women] still occur under customary law.’[footnote 49]

10.6.2 The World Bank, Botswana: Trends and Opportunities to Advance Gender Equality, dated 31 March 2025, which assessed gender gaps in the economy (WB report 2025), noted:

‘Under Botswana’s pluralist legal system, customary and common law can come into conflict in the area of the protection of women’s rights. Both the Customary Law Act (1969) and Customary Courts Act (1961) prioritize the application of customary law for most civil cases within tribal groups. Customary law is not codified, and its content varies between tribal groups within Botswana. Although the Customary Law Act requires that customary law should be compatible with the Constitution, in practice customary courts do not always interpret the law so as to protect women’s rights (United Nations Botswana 2021). For instance, under the customary law of some tribal groups, women are treated as legal minors within marriage, unmarried women are considered under the guardianship of their fathers, husbands may use corporal punishment against their wives and children (who are considered a father’s property), and inheritance has traditionally been conferred through the male lineage (Botswana Court of Appeal 2012; Nkhata and Kalunga 2015). However, there have been some encouraging legal developments strengthening women’s rights under customary law. For example, in the case of Mmusi and Others v. Ramantele and Another, the High Court of Botswana ruled that customary law provisions restricting women’s inheritance rights were unconstitutional, and the case was subsequently upheld in the Court of Appeal.’[footnote 50]

10.6.3 The GOROB’s reply to the CEDAW dated received 28 April 2025, document dated 13 May 2025, stated: ‘The Customary Courts Act was amended in 2017 to confer to any person the right to transfer a case from [a] Customary Court to [a] Magistrate Court. On this note, Legal Aid Botswana in partnership with Non-Government Organisations (NGOs) continue to provide legal assistance to women who desire to transfer their matter from Customary Courts to Common law courts.’[footnote 51]

10.6.4 The UKHO FFM 2025 interviewed an official in the UN Population Fund on 8 July 2025 (UNPFA official 2025) who noted,

‘… that [there] are [equal rights] on paper [for women], but there is a dual legal system: customary law and modern [statutory or common] law. The customary law is where the chiefs preside over matters … [The dual system] has its own challenges. When there's an issue, let's say in the family, it would usually start at the customary setting, where it goes to the chiefs. It may end there, and [when] cases [do] end there – maybe it's a case of GBV – the family or the husband and wife would in most cases be told to reconcile. That’s the customary side. They tend to prioritise [reconciliation].’[footnote 52]

10.6.5 The UNFPA official 2025 also noted:

‘… modern [statutory/civil] law recognises that women have equal rights to property, [including in matters of] inheritance … customary law is in most cases trying to conform to that as well, in terms of recognising that women have equal rights. But in practice, you still find cases where, for example, there’s a fight over inheritance or [over who should become] the next chief if a chief [dies leaving only daughters]. It's not always a very smooth transition to say the eldest daughter automatically becomes the chief [even though] it’s recognised on paper now that daughters of chiefs can be chiefs. In practice, it’s not always that easy; it’s always contentious.’[footnote 53]

10.6.6 The UNFPA official 2025 also noted ‘… customary law leads more to [a victim being told] that it’s a family matter and they should go and talk to their uncles and so forth … customary law has no power to enforce a restraining order.’[footnote 54]

10.6.7 The UKHO FFM interviewed representatives of the Feminist Alliance Botswana, a ‘gender-centred organisation’, on 9 July 2025 (FAB representatives 2025). The FAB representatives 2025 noted:

‘… it's important to highlight that because of the way BWA society is structured, more of the population only have access to traditional courts than civil courts, so unless tradition and traditional law change, women will continue to be disenfranchised in terms of enforcing their rights. This is because whereas civil law prohibits discrimination, in traditional courts judgments are made with clear gender biases.

‘… explained that it costs money [to go through the civil courts], and it's multi-layered because you start off with a small mediation court, which is the traditional setting, before you go to a major customary court, and then after the customary court, they need to take it to the customary court of appeal. And if you're still not happy with it, that's when you take it to the High Court, which is governed by civil law. But all of that involves money, time and frustration.’[footnote 55]

10.7 Protection and maintenance orders

10.7.1 The Domestic Violence Act, 2009, provides for the issuance of 4 types of protection order by a court to victims of domestic violence depending on the circumstances and needs of the case. These are:

  • an interim order
  • a restraining order
  • a tenancy order
  • an occupancy order[footnote 56]

10.7.2 An application for a protection order to a court is accompanied by an affidavit (a written statement of facts for use as evidence in court) from the applicant (the victim of domestic violence). An ‘application may be brought on behalf of the applicant by a counsellor, health service provider, member of the Botswana Police Service, Local Police, social worker, teacher, District Commissioner or any other person, with leave of the court.’[footnote 57]

10.7.3 An interim order may be issued by a court ‘where it is satisfied that -

‘(a) domestic violence has occurred;

‘(b) there is a serious risk of harm being caused to the applicant or child; or

‘(c) the order will ensure immediate protection of the applicant.’[footnote 58]

10.7.4 The MOJCS officials 2025 noted: ‘There are restraining orders, and if these are violated a perpetrator can be imprisoned. [T]he Domestic Violence Act … provides for safety measures for incidents [in] the home. The court can be approached to issue a restraining order.[footnote 59]

10.7.5 The UKHO FFM interviewed the chief executive officer of the Legal Advice Board on 9 July 2025 (LAB CEO 2025). The CEO noted:

‘The forms for restraining orders are built into the [Domestic Violence] Act. The police will assist the victim to go to the magistrate’s court and be assisted by the office of the Registrar to complete the necessary forms and get [the relevant order] without the need for counsel … [but] it would be the person who actually submits [the restraining order] ... [the police may also sit] there with [the victim] … and the form is busily being filled in, or the police escort (protect) the person to the court so that they can fill in the form at the registrar's office and get it all signed.’[footnote 60]

10.7.6 The FAB representatives 2025 confirmed that restraining orders are issued by the authorities, adding ‘… there is an act called the Deserted Wives and Children Protection Act. Under that you can get speedy maintenance orders [which provide] financial support for the spouse and children.’[footnote 61]

10.7.7 The executive director War Against Rape, a non-government organisation based in Maun which supports victims of GBV, interviewed by the UKHO FFM on 14 July 2025 (WAR executive director 2025) noted a woman can obtain a restraining order by going to a court, which the police have to enforce. The police also notify the perpetrator of violence of the restraining order. The executive director considered that if the terms of a restraining order were breached the police should enforce this by, for example, by arresting the offender. However, the executive director did not know whether the police enforced restraining orders[footnote 62].

10.7.8 See also Implementation of protection orders below.

10.8 Bail Act, 2024

10.8.1 The FH report 2025 noted: ‘In March 2024, [the Bail Act] … introduced stricter bail regulations and granted victims of rape and other serious offenses a say in bail proceedings came into effect.’[footnote 63]

10.8.2 The MYGA officials 2025 observed:

‘The Bail Act was amended [in 2024] to ensure that if a perpetrator applies for bail, the survivor should have a say before the decision is taken as to whether or not bail is granted ... [adding] that the reason why the Bail Act was adopted last year [2024] was because there was an outcry from the public that people who are released on bail tend to re-offend, particularly for GBV where they have threatened to kill … they are arraigned, and they will eventually be released on bail and go on to commit the offence.’[footnote 64]

10.8.3 The MYGA officials 2025 agreed with the UKHO FFM’s summary of the interview discussions that the Bail Act 2024 tightened the criteria for releasing a suspected ‘but there's no case law [yet] to determine how it's going to be applied [by the courts].’[footnote 65]

10.8.4 The WAR executive director 2025 commenting on the Bail Act 2024 explained that law had been changed so that ‘… the victim should have a say, should come to court and convince the court why they shouldn't give this person bail. So, if the person is [the victim’s] … husband or … partner and has threatened to kill [her] …, and now they are going to apply for bail, then [the victim] … ha[s] … to go to court and convince the court why they shouldn't be. That’s the change. So, it's not that they can't get it, but the victim has to come and plead.’ The UKHO FFM questioned whether by giving the victim the opportunity to provide evidence this would improve the process by increasing the likelihood that the GBV offender would not get bail. The executive director hoped it was an improvement but ‘thought no one had tested it yet and … hadn’t yet heard of a case [of the new measures being applied].’[footnote 66]

10.8.5 The UKHO FFM interviewed senior officers in the Botswana Police Service on 11 July 2025 (BPS officers 2025). The officials noted,

‘… the issue of bail is a big concern for all residents … Citizens generally praise the police for arrests in GBV offences however they complain that unfortunately following the arrest, the perpetrators are then let out on bail.

According to Botswana laws, one is presumed innocent until found guilty in court, hence the reason why bail is given whilst awaiting trial. This unfortunately leads to a lot of reoffending in GBV. The issue is being discussed in many platforms in attempts to find a lasting resolution. Furthermore, the Bail Act 2024 has also narrowed the existing gaps … with GBV, it depends on the seriousness of the offence. If it’s common assault, normally the police would arrest [the suspect] and detain them for 48 hours, then they’d release them on what’s called police bail. For serious offences, they might be held until [the case was heard before a] court. In the past, there used to be that problem of bail being granted. Now there’s a new Bail Act, which is [tougher] … there was no such Act before.’[footnote 67]

10.8.6 See also the Implementation of bail below.

11. Policy, programmes and campaigns

11.1 Government position

11.1.1 The MOJCS officials 2025 noted: ‘The police are mindful of GBV; government is mindful of GBV … the government is now very much aware of the problem of GBV. The president, Duma Boko, has gone on record that [Botswana] BWA cannot countenance GBV, and interventions are being put in place … The President has said that his government will be human-rights-centric. He has explained that human rights should be placed at the centre of development.’[footnote 68]

11.1.2 The UKHO FFM interviewed officials at the Ministry for State President on 9 July 2025 (MSP officials 2025), who observed:

‘GBV is a priority for government … [it is an issue] that needs to be dealt with very seriously and [is] now reflected in resourcing. The police [are] resourced to ensure that child friendly centres … protect [children] and that within the police … we are developing strategic partnerships with the other organisations - civil society organisations - that take care of the victims of GBV. Measures have been put in place by the police to ensure safety generally, which is an issue … We are trying to, especially as we work with churches and civil society, to ensure that as a government [GBV] is a very high priority.’[footnote 69]

11.1.3 A GOROB representative told the UN CEDAW in June 2025:

‘The Government was committed to promoting gender mainstreaming in policies and programmes and to eliminating harmful gender norms in order to empower women. In that connection, the Human Rights Strategy and National Action Plan had been developed, and a commitment had been made to establishing gender parity in the legislature by 2030. A committee responsible for overseeing the implementation of the Human Rights Strategy and National Action Plan had been established …

‘The Government was developing a broad range of measures to prevent and combat gender-based violence. At the grassroots level, community leaders campaigned against gender-based violence and civil society organizations provided practical training. The Government had committed to establishing one-stop centres that would provide a comprehensive range of services relating to gender-based violence, including law enforcement and judicial services, healthcare and psychosocial services, and shelters. A national action plan to combat gender-based violence was being developed on the basis of the regional strategy established by the Southern African Development Community (SADC) for the period 2020–2030. Under the plan, coordinated psychosocial, legal and shelter services would be provided for survivors.’[footnote 70]

11.2 Departmental responsibility and other public bodies

11.2.1 A GOROB representative told the UN CEDAW in June 2025:

‘… the Government had established a ministry of youth and gender affairs [MYGA] as part of its efforts to build a supportive and protective system of governance that respected the rights of all citizens, irrespective of their socioeconomic, cultural or political status. Recognizing that gender inequality impeded development, the Government had intensified its efforts to mainstream gender across all sectors and to institutionalize gender-responsive budgeting to ensure that priorities, such as efforts to combat gender-based violence, were adequately resourced.’[footnote 71]

11.2.2 The GOROB in its submission to the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights that covers the period from 2018 to 2023, dated September 2023 (GOROB ACHPR submission 2023), noted the ‘… Government established the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Gender Based Violence in 2020 to provide strategic direction and coordination of the national response to GBV. The committee comprises Ministers of Youth, Gender, Sport and Culture [now the MYGA], Local Government and Rural Development, Defence, Health, Justice, Education and Skills Development, Labour and Home Affairs and … [the] Minister for State President. The committee is supported by a multi-sectoral team of experts at technical level.’[footnote 72]

11.2.3 The GOROB in its submission to the CEDAW dated 1 November 2023 (GOB CEDAW submission 2023) noted

‘… [The] Government reconstituted membership of the National Gender Commission in 2022 to strengthen gender mainstreaming across all sectors. An Inter-Ministerial Committee on GBV was also established in 2020 to provide strategic guidance on the national response to Gender Based Violence as well as put in place mechanisms for monitoring the implementation of these efforts. At [a] local level, 28 District Gender Committees were established and trained to lead implementation of the National Policy on Gender and Development.’[footnote 73]

11.2.4 The MYGA officials 2025 noted,

‘… the government has also established oversight institutions … the National Gender Commission, which looks broadly at gender issues in the country, including GBV. Above that, we also have a high-level structure, the Inter-Ministerial Committee on GBV, which is now … a sub-cabinet committee because it comprises of 8 ministers, and that body is chaired by the minister responsible for youth and gender affairs … there are also District Gender Committees, which are responsible for coordinating the gender response at district level. There has been keen interest [in this]: [some] districts have cascaded it to village gender committees.’[footnote 74]

11.2.5 The MSP officials 2025 observed the ‘core mandate and co-ordination of gender-related matters lies with the Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs (MYGA) … in every ministry there will be a liaison person with the MYGA, with programmes that are trying to stop GBV mainstreamed through the ministries.’[footnote 75]

11.3 Policies, strategies and programmes

11.3.1 Bertlesmann Stiftung, a German private foundation, in its Transformation Index 2024, Botswana country report based on the views of country experts, covering events between 2021 and January 2023 (BTI 2024), stated: ‘… [the previous] administration has intensified efforts to promote youth and women’s empowerment through targeted policies and programs. These initiatives include substantial investments in tertiary education financing, a national service scheme, a youth development fund, and an internship program.’[footnote 76]

11.3.2 Afrobarometer, a non-profit company conducting research across Africa, noted in its survey about gender equity in Botswana based on a nationally representative sample of 1,200 adult Batswana between July and August 2022, published 12 January 2023 (Afrobarometer findings 2023):

‘The government of Botswana has shown commitment to ending gender-based violence (GBV) and discrimination by formulating policies, strategies, and programmes such as the National Policy on Gender and Development [in March 2015] (with a National Gender Commission to monitor implementation), the National Gender-Based Violence Strategy 2015-2020, and the Women’s Economic Empowerment Programme (Republic of Botswana, 2017; UN Women, n.d.).’[footnote 77]

11.3.3 The GOROB national review 2019 noted:

‘… the Government of Botswana adopted Vision 2036 [in September 2016] … [this] … calls for the elimination of gender discrimination and gender-based violence in Botswana society … Working towards this Botswana has developed the National Strategy towards ending Gender Based Violence in Botswana (2010-2020). This strategy has articulated the guiding goals and objectives of the national multi sectorial approach to GBV response. [The] Government in Botswana GBV Strategy focuses on (i) GBV prevention, (ii) protection, Care and Support of GBV victims and survivors, (iii) National capacity development for the GBV Response, (iv) GBV Strategic information and knowledge management and (V) Coordination and management of the national Response.’[footnote 78]

11.3.4 The GOROB ACHPR submission 2023 noted:

‘[The] Government adopted the National Policy on Gender and Development which has amongst its five (5) priorities: Access to Justice; Protection of Human Rights and Freedom from Violence. The National Towards Ending Gender Based Violence (GBV) on the other hand provides concrete guidance on the National GBV Response. The Strategy is multi-sectoral and multi-pronged, and it mainly focuses on Prevention, Protection, Care and Support with clear actions for each development sector.’[footnote 79]

11.3.5 The GOROB’s (then named) Ministry of Nationality, Immigration and Gender Affairs (MNIGA) Botswana National Relationship Study, a comprehensive study of GBV published in 2018, (BNRS 2018). The study including the following infographic[footnote 80] showing the structure and relationships of multi-sectoral mechanism introduced as part of the NSTEGBV to enhance co-ordination:

11.3.6 The GOROB CEDAW submission 2023 noted:

‘… [the] Government [has] intensified efforts to mainstream gender through active engagement of various sectors as evidenced by the Gender Strategy in Agricultural Sector; development of Climate Change Policy and the current mainstreaming of gender into the Justice System … To facilitate effective implementation and strengthened monitoring of the National Policy on Gender and Development, the second National Gender Commission was appointed in 2022. In addition, the Inter-Ministerial Committee on GBV was established in November 2020 to provide strategic direction on the National Response on GBV.’[footnote 81]

11.3.7 The GOROB CEDAW submission 2023 also noted:

‘The National Policy on Gender and Development continues to guide Gender Mainstreaming across sectors which has resulted in the improvement of the quality of life for vulnerable groups. Botswana has made notable progress in mainstreaming gender in the economic and social sectors, and these include land ownership by married women and youth, access to Agricultural Programmes such as Livestock Management and Infrastructure Development (LIMID) which has a deliberate window to promote increased women’s access to productive resources including small stock and boreholes. The Citizen Economic Development Entrepreneurial Agency has also developed a programme designed for improved financial access to women. There is also preferential treatment for women, youth and people with disability on Government procurement. In 2021 Botswana adopted the Citizen Inclusion Act which aims to promote effective participation of targeted citizens in the economic development of the Country. The Industrial Development Policy also establishes industries in rural areas which are mostly women owned small scale businesses.’[footnote 82]

11.3.8 Africa Press reporting on the minister of the MYGA’s comments to parliament in October 2025, noted: ‘The National Policy on Gender and Development as well as the National Strategy Towards Ending Gender Based Violence are both under review …’[footnote 83]

11.3.9 The UKHO FFM interviewed a on 8 July 2025 International diplomatic source- 2. The source noted,

‘… the new government and the Ministry of Gender and Youth Affairs which is supposed to focus primarily on building policies protecting women. But … [the policy officer] hadn’t seen in practice any of these [policies] institutionalised in an efficient way. Not able to speak on their current status … [laws and policies were not] … sufficient but only because their implementation hasn't been effective. It is hard to give credit to policies that are not actualized in in an efficient way. [The official] … did not mean policies were not working but instead putting in place more policies perhaps work needs to be done in improving their efficiency.’[footnote 84]

11.3.10 The MYGA officials 2025 noted:

‘After the 2012 study, we then decided [to come up with] a strategy to address GBV. Those documents we can readily share. We then adopted a GBV strategy, which was a 5-year strategy. That strategy was looking at prevention, protection, and care and support, trying to holistically address GBV. Also, after the 2012 study, we wanted to address perceptions, which are mostly culturally based. In 2012, we started engaging our traditional leaders, the dikgosi, because we believe they are fundamental to addressing issues of GBV, particularly as they also play a mediation role. So 2012, we engaged them; 2015, they developed their action plan in terms of how they are going to deal with gender-based violence. That's the one part.

‘The second layer of that is that we developed a training manual for the same leaders because they are very close to the people, and also some tools that they can use to track gender-based violence cases within their communities. There has also been engagement with civil society organisations, who are critical [in addressing] gender-based violence, in [recognition] of the fact that they reside in communities.

‘The third layer again was also to train the faith-based sector. Every religion has its own sacred text and we had also realised that sometimes they are gender-biased. So we trained the faith leaders, and I would say all religions in Botswana have been reached. That exercise continues, of course, with the civil society organisations [CSOs]. Beyond that, we also acknowledge the CSOs who are capacitated regularly on GBV, and we also track the emerging complications around gender-based violence and we have dialogues around those and how we can actually adjust our programmes to address those specific cases … from the study, GBV manifestations differ per locality. What would … [pertain] in the North would not … [pertain] in the South because of the diversity of the groups. So our programming is community-specific because it targets a particular community based on the issues that prevail in their communities.’[footnote 85]

11.3.11 The MYGA officials 2025 also noted,

‘… they were currently reviewing the gender policy and that they had recently appointed a consultant. There is the gender strategy, and the World Bank is helping with that. We are very alert to ensure that we keep up with the unfolding situation. Another thing we are looking into is coming up with a gender equality bill because some of these things are really emanating from stereotypes.

‘So, there’s a need to intensify education and change norms that may be harmful so that increasingly everybody, starting from a young age – formation – should just understand that women have all equal opportunities in life. That way, we feel respect and recognition that no one is entitled to end anyone's life or harm anyone.’[footnote 86]

11.4 Awareness raising

11.4.1 The GOROB national assessment 2019 noted,

‘… Measures have also been put in place to intensify GBV prevention through awareness raising and educational campaigns at national and community levels through cultural and community dialogues, television and radio discussions, seminars and campaigns including international commemorations. Government has led national consultative fora for Dikgosi/Chiefs and for leaders of faith-based organisations as partners in the fight against GBV.’[footnote 87]

11.4.2 The GOROB ACHPR submission 2023 noted:

‘The First Lady of the Republic of Botswana prioritises the empowerment of women and adolescent girls especially those living in rural areas. To this end, the First Lady is working in close collaboration with the public and private sector, as well as civil society to raise awareness on GBV, sexual reproductive health and HIV/AIDS prevention.

‘As a member of the Organisation of African First Ladies for Development (OAFLAD), the First Lady in May 2021 was awarded a grant for a project aimed at promoting advocacy on GBV related issues. The First Lady’s campaign is currently being carried out in six (6) Districts, where incidences of GBV are most prevalent. The intervention is meant to increase knowledge and skills on GBV prevention and to intensify the involvement of men in mitigation efforts. The project targets community leaders, including Dikgosi (Traditional Leaders), Bahumagadi (Spouses of Traditional Leaders), Religious Leaders, People with Disability, Orphans and Vulnerable Children, Women and Girls, Men and Boys as well as Civil Society Organisations.

‘There is continuous awareness raising on gender-based violence through community outreach through kgotla meetings. Including commemoration of the 16 Days of Activism Against Violence on Women and Children.’[footnote 88]

11.4.3 The GOROB CEDAW submission 2023 noted:

‘In an effort to address gender stereotypes and negative cultural practices, there are ongoing programmes geared towards mobilising male involvement into family and societal matters such as the Men Care Programme, Men in the Kitchen and Monna Tia. These are implemented by Government and Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) and aimed at promoting positive male masculinity, role models and to curb absent fathers. In addition, different sectors continue to implement Abolition of Marital Act which abolishes men as the head of the family as well as restrictions which the marital power places on the legal capacity of a wife. Furthermore, Botswana continues to strive for promotion of positive aspects of culture through the engagement with relevant actors, including tribal chiefs, religious and community leaders on the negative impact of discriminatory stereotypes on the enjoyment of women's human rights. Government recognises the importance of traditional leaders (Dikgosi) as custodians of culture and continues to engage them. In November 2020, Government in partnership with UNDP developed a Training Manual on GBV to standardise capacity building of Dikgosi on GBV.’[footnote 89]

11.4.4 The MOJCS officials 2025 noted:

‘… the MYGA has undertaken public awareness campaigns. Last year, for example, there were workshops, through focus group discussions, through commemoration, and the media is also engaged, especially on gender sensitive reporting. We have a dual legal system [customary and secular courts], the nearest place of safety will [often] be the dikgosi (tribal chiefs).
