There are customary courts in every village, so there have been workshops for traditional / community leaders as well as for faith-based organisations and women themselves. Faith and religion have had an impact - in some religions people have been told that women should be submissive which can sometimes be misconstrued to mean women can be treated anyhow.’[footnote 90]

11.4.5 The MYGA officials 2025 noted

‘… there has been engagement with the wives of chiefs, the Bahumagadi, who are also leaders, so that they also participate in the GBV response. The Former First Lady also had a programme around addressing GBV where she has engaged with different community leaders. The targeting of the programme considered the results of the surveys mentioned [above] plus statistics from the police, so that the interventions were specific to communities that presented a high prevalence of rape.’[footnote 91]

11.4.6 The MYGA officials 2025 also

‘… explained that mostly there are CSOs in different districts, but we also have gender offices and the Ministry of Local Government and Traditional Affairs, where we have social workers, and also the Ministry of Health. They also raise awareness on GBV. So really, we have stakeholders in collaboration with the faith-based organisations, with the traditional leaders, the dikgosi, that have been trained on GBV. They're also doing something because they have an extra plan that they’re implementing. At the village level, you’ll find it’s more about awareness raising.’[footnote 92]

11.4.7 The BPS officials 2025 noted,

‘… there is an organisation called the Organisation of First Ladies of Africa. All of our first ladies belong to that organisation – the previous one and the current one – and they've been targeting GBV. The police work with the First Lady together with other stakeholders across the country, and generally what we see is that as soon as we have been doing a campaign in a certain place, the reporting goes up.

‘… [The BPS] have intensive campaigns that are specific to GBV coming up. In November every year, there's an annual 16 days of activism against GBV, where it’s just the BPS. There's also an annual 60-days of action on Crime and Road Safety Campaign Coded Operation Pabalesego where GBV is among the targeted crimes. Both operations are held across the country.

‘… The police collaborate with village leadership in what they call Pitso where they call all stakeholders to come and talk about GBV … they just had a Commissioner’s Run against GBV in March [2025], and many others yet come.

‘… [The] BPS also conducts operations with neighbouring countries, operations that are co-ordinated: Operation Thunder, Operation Basadi – an operation that was led by police officers in the region. These operations target specific offences such as human trafficking, drug trafficking, GBV related offences and so on

‘… [The regional campaigns] are held annually in some cases more than once a year.’[footnote 93]

12. Social, economic and political status

12.1.1 For background on the economic situation of women, see Economic context above.

12.1.2 The BTI 2024 noted:

‘Despite government efforts to achieve gender parity in education and employment, gender inequality remains a significant issue in Botswana’s economy. A 2021/2022 Afrobarometer study revealed that fewer than half of Batswana approve of the government’s performance in promoting equal rights and opportunities for women, with a majority calling for more action. Moreover, the 2021/2022 Human Development Report indicates that Botswana’s Gender Inequality Index stands at 0.468, with the country ranked 117th in the world in this regard [Botswana was ranked 127 out of 172 countries in the 2023 index with a value of 0.490[footnote 94]]

‘… citizens are granted equal access to educational and employment opportunities …

‘The female literacy rate is at 88.01%, while males have a slightly higher rate of 88.93%. The Gender Parity Index [for education], as reported by the World Bank in 2021, stands at 0.98159 [0 = no gender parity; 1 = gender parity], further indicating a relatively balanced gender distribution in education. Additionally, World Bank data shows that in 2021, women made up 47.7% of the labour force in Botswana. This aligns with the government’s commitment to women’s empowerment, as is reflected in the increasing number of women occupying senior public positions.’[footnote 95]

12.1.3 The World Economic Forum, an international advocacy non-government organisation and think tank, in its Global Gender Gap Report 2025 (GGG 2025) ‘based on a methodology integrating the latest statistics from international organizations and a survey of executives’[footnote 96], dated June 2025, looked at women’s ‘Economic Participation and Opportunity, Educational Attainment, Health and Survival, and Political Empowerment’ compared to men in 148 countries[footnote 97]. Botswana was ranked 60th overall (a high ranking indicating greater gender parity). This was, however, primarily because of being ranked 129th in the category of political empowerment and 80th in the sub-category of healthy life expectancy. In the categories of economic participation and opportunity and educational attainment, and the sub-category of sex ratio at birth, the country was ranked top in the world[footnote 98].

12.1.4 The GGG 2025 included the following infographic[footnote 99] of Botswana’s performance in the index including values and rankings for all categories and sub-categories:

12.1.5 The WB report 2025 citing other sources noted:

‘Botswana … continues to struggle with high rates of inequality and persistent gender gaps. Inequality in the distribution of wealth has increased over time and Botswana is now one of the top 10 most unequal countries in the world, as measured by the Gini index … Less than half of all households in Botswana are headed by women but female-headed households account for more than half of the poor …

‘There has nonetheless been significant progress in addressing several gender challenges in Botswana, notably parity in school enrollment, broad uptake of family planning, high rates of female entrepreneurship, and strong leadership of women in the public sector … However, important challenges remain, including low levels of women’s political representation in the National Assembly, a significant gender gap in labor force participation, and high rates of maternal mortality … While Botswana performs well on several gender-related human development indicators relative to the averages for Sub-Saharan Africa, it generally ranks poorly in comparison to the averages for upper-middle-income countries … Inequalities in key poverty and human development indicators between language groups and regions result in significant marginalization of some groups. These groups tend to reside in the poorest and most rural areas of the country. In general, women and girls in rural areas have lower levels … [of] education and experience higher levels of unemployment. Those from marginalized groups, women and girls living with disabilities, and lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, and other gender diverse (LGBTQI+) persons face additional challenges.’[footnote 100]

12.1.6 The GOROB CEDAW submission 2023 noted:

‘[The] Government made deliberate efforts to address low representation of women in political office … [and the president] made a conscious decision to appoint 67% of the specially elected Members of Parliament as females [there are 6 indirectly elected members[footnote 101]]. Furthermore, His Excellency the [then] President appointed the first female finance Minister, first female President of the Court of Appeal, First Permanent Secretary to the President and the Deputy Permanent Secretary to the President are also females. The Commissioner of Prisons and Commissioner General for Botswana Unified Revenue Service (BURS) are also females. At local level 34% of women were appointed as Councillors.’[footnote 102]

12.1.7 The BTI 2024 stated ‘… women continue to encounter obstacles when seeking political representation due to various constraints that hinder their participation in politics. Notably, the absence of quotas reserving a proportion of seats for women remains a challenge in advancing the agenda of women’s empowerment.’[footnote 103]

12.1.8 A GOROB representative told the CEDAW in June 2025: ‘Despite the progress made, women’s representation in political life remained limited. In the National Assembly, women currently held only 6 out of 69 seats, which was fewer than in previous years. Women occupied 14 per cent of positions in the cabinet and 15 per cent of positions in local authorities.’[footnote 104]

12.1.9 The WB report 2025 citing other sources also noted:

‘Traditional leadership structures are heavily male dominated. In addition to the National Assembly, Botswana also has the Ntlo ya Dikgosi (House of Chiefs), made up of 35 traditional leaders, which acts as an advisory body to Parliament. Although it has no legislative or veto powers, all bills affecting tribal affairs, customary law, and the administration of customary courts must go through the Ntlo ya Dikgosi [the House of Chiefs, which advises parliament on tribal law and custom[footnote 105]] before being discussed in the National Assembly. The House of Chiefs must also be consulted when the Constitution is being reviewed or amended. Of the 33 chiefs currently sitting in the Ntlo ya Dikgosi, only two are women after a third recently stepped down to allow her brother to take her seat … At the local level, tribal chiefs and community councils (kgotla), which have significant influence over community life, are also heavily male dominated …’[footnote 106]

12.1.10 The UKHO FFM 2025 interviewed an official in the UN Population Fund on 8 July 2025 (UNPFA official 2025) commented on the position of women:

‘Economically, it's been challenging, but … there were areas where progress has been made. We have a lot of women in the informal sector. That's a sector that they find it easier to operate in because there's a lot they initiate – starting an enterprise, running a project. The informal sector generally has less bureaucratic processes and requirements and often has the flexibility that allows women to run their businesses and still do family care work. There are also limited employment opportunities with the employment rate at around 28%, which further pushes women to the informal sector. That's where most of women are. We've seen some improvements over time with women getting access to positions of leadership in the private sector, namely management, leadership and being [chief executive officers] CEOs, and [serving] on some boards of directors and so forth. But in the political space, we're seeing regression right now. We only have 6 women in Parliament, which is a drop from 11 [in the last Parliament]. So in terms of the targets we've set ourselves on gender equality as far as women's representation and leadership is concerned, [the situation is] not so great. And then, of course, women are still also doing a lot of the care work when it comes to raising children, and even in some of the roles that involve a lot of care work, like teaching, day care, nursing … [with regard to the public sector] there weren’t many issues there. She explained that she didn’t have the exact numbers but that a number of women hold the position of permanent secretary [in government departments]. But [representation] varies according to the sector. We still have some male-dominated sectors like mining, which is still very much male-dominated from lower positions all the way up …’[footnote 107]

12.1.11 The FAB representatives 2025 noted:

‘… more girls are doing better than boys in school and are finishing school in larger numbers. In [small and medium enterprises] SMEs or small businesses, there are a lot of women, yet in more established businesses, there are a lot of men [in leadership roles]. So, where there’s structure, it's men, and when there's less structure, it's mostly women-led businesses. Recent studies have also shown that even in corporates [large companies], there are more women in management positions. If you were to look currently at the banks’ structure, Absa [Bank Botswana], the CEO is a woman and then there was a woman at Barclays [Botswana], and the other 3 are men. More women are advancing to senior management positions. However, it is important to note that only 6 members of Parliament are women [out of 69], of the 6 female MPs, 3 were elected by the electorates, whilst 4 are specially nominated by the President, which means they weren't elected by the people. In fact, we’ve regressed in terms of numbers as regards representation of women in political office.’[footnote 108]

13. Social and cultural attitudes

13.1.1 The BNRS 2018 undertook a comprehensive survey of, amongst other things, the prevalence of GBV and gender attitudes based on qualitative and quantitative research. This included interviews with 4,224 women and 3,696 men (a total of 7,920) over 18 undertaken between June and September 2017. The BNRS 2018 noted:

‘Men generally held less gender equitable views than women. For example:

  • ‘More than half of the men and only 43% of women think that a woman should obey her husband.
  • ‘Fifty-two percent of men and a third of women agreed that if a woman works, she should give her money to her husband.
  • ‘Fifty-nine percent of men and 36% of women believe that a man should have the final say in all family matters.
  • ‘Fifty-three percent of men and 36% of women professed that a woman needs permission from her husband to do paid work.
  • ‘Almost equal proportions of men (41%) and women (43%) expressed that a woman cannot refuse to have sex with her husband.
  • ‘Forty-five percent of men and 24% of women equate paying of lobola [‘bride price’ or dowry to their wife’s family] to wife ownership.’[footnote 109]

13.1.2 The BNRS 2018 also documented male and female attitudes towards rape:

  • ‘Forty-one percent of men compared to only 16% of women expressed that in any rape case there is need to ask if the victim was not promiscuous
  • ‘Thirty-four percent of men and 19% of women affirmed that in some rape cases women want it to happen
  • ‘Forty-one percent of men and 17% of women believe that if a woman does not fight back, it is not rape
  • ‘A fifth of men and 9% women blame the rape victim for putting themselves into the situation’[footnote 110]

13.1.3 The Afrobarometer findings 2023 noted:

  • ‘… more than three-fourths (77%) of Batswana endorse gender equality in hiring, rejecting the idea that when jobs are scarce, men should be given priority … Men are less likely than women to support gender equality in hiring (72% vs. 82%). Support for women’s equal right to a job increases as respondents’ education level rises, ranging from 58% among citizens with no formal schooling to 86% among those with post-secondary qualifications.
  • ‘An even greater majority (91%) of Batswana “agree” or “strongly agree” that women should have the same rights as men to own and inherit land … Men (91%) and women (92%) are about equally likely to support this attitude …
  • ‘[There is] overwhelming popular support for gender equality at the ballot box. Almost nine out of 10 Batswana (86%) “agree” or “strongly agree” that women should have the same chance as men to be elected to public office; only 13% say that men make better political leaders and should thus be elected instead of women … Women are somewhat more likely than men to endorse equality in politics (89% vs. 84%), while 26- to 45-year-olds express the highest levels of support (88%-89%) for this view …
  • ‘Fewer half (42%) of Batswana say the government is doing “fairly well” or “very well” in promoting equal rights and opportunities for women, while a majority (56%) disapprove of its performance on this issue …
  • ‘When asked what they consider the most important issue related to women’s rights and gender equality for their government and society to address, six in 10 Batswana (59%) cite gender-based violence … Far fewer would prioritise the lack of women in influential government positions (14%), unequal opportunities or pay in the workplace (13%), unequal property rights (6%), and unequal access to education (4%). Women and men offer the same prioritisation of these issues.’[footnote 111]

13.1.4 The UN CEDAW report 2025 noted:

‘The Committee positively notes some initiatives aimed to engage men and boys in challenging patriarchal attitudes and stereotypes, and the partnership of the Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs with Ntlo ya Dikgosi (traditional leaders) and representatives of faith-based movements to address gender imbalances in power relations and structural barriers to gender equality. However, it remains concerned at:

‘(a) Persistent discriminatory cultural norms, including in customary law, which negatively affect women and girls, promote male dominance and female subordination, reinforce unequal power relations and unequal access to economic opportunities and legitimize gender-based violence against women and girls.

‘(b) The lack of effective targeted outreach programmes for religious leaders, youth, men and boys and community leaders to challenge gender stereotypes and foster non-violent masculinities.

‘(c) The need for a comprehensive strategy to engage the private sector, including the film industry and creative arts, in addressing and countering gender stereotypes, the culture of silence around and the underreporting of gender-based violence against women.’[footnote 112]

13.1.5 The UKHO FFM interviewed an International diplomatic source- 1 who noted: ‘Women have come a long way in terms of [legal] … recognition … but culturally, BWA is a patriarchal society and there's a conservative element … The main human rights situation threat to women in BWA is GBV… In Botswana’s traditional system - the Kgotla - which is like the traditional gathering point for every tribe in every village, women are still discriminated in terms of how they're allowed to show up. For example, they're not allowed to wear pants [trousers] to the traditional gathering, which puts off some women. There are legal protections, but the conservative nature of the society puts women on the back foot.’[footnote 113]

13.1.6 The international diplomatic source 2 – 2025 noted:

‘Botswana is a patriarchal society - women are socialised to behave in a certain way, men are dominant. For example, marriage is an institution in which women are expected to be obedient and respectful; there is still a ‘bride price’. Women’s place in society frames how they are treated, their experience of gender-based violence. Women are not all treated horribly – too general a statement. But they face discrimination in the home and in the workplace. They are paid less. The law prescribes equality of men and women but in practice it does not occur.’[footnote 114]

13.1.7 The UKHO FFM interviewed managers at the Botswana Gender-Based Violence Prevention and Support Centre (BGBVC), a non-profit organisation which aims to respond to and raise awareness about GBV, on 10 July 2025 (BGBVC managers 2025). The BGBVC managers 2025 noted:

‘Botswana has a relatively good legal framework to address the rights of women. However, there is still a need for a mindset change to appreciate these from the traditional and cultural perspectives. Culturally, women lack power compared to men, so they are usually on the lower receiving end of anything that protects them. There have been efforts [to address this] for quite some time now … women are still treated as a minority, or they are subservient to men generally because of cultural beliefs and practices. We can have beautiful rules like we have but when you get home, you don’t pull out a [legislative] act and say, “This is how you're supposed to treat women according to the law.” At home, people mostly live according to the customary practices.’[footnote 115]

13.1.8 The BGBVC managers 2025 also noted ‘… there’s a culture of silence in BWA because all of these things [abuses of women] happen, but some are not reported … there's also the stigma that’s attached to GBV because it's always, “Why did he do this to you?” If it goes there, it means it’s [the woman’s] fault. So, there's a stigma that comes with intimate partner violence, with [being expected to] stay in a marriage that is dysfunctional. leaving is associated with a number of things, including “being a failure”.’[footnote 116]

13.1.9 The FAB representatives 2025 noted:

‘… our culture is based on a patriarchal system where men are more elevated. That permeates how we treat and ascribe rights, whether it's socioeconomic rights - not in terms of the civil law - but culturally. For example, if you're born to a local chief and your father passes away, it’s more likely that instead of a female first-born child succeeding, the [chieftainship] will probably be given to a male child, and in the absence of a male child the father's brother will then take over.

‘However, … more and more women, especially in that space [tribal chiefs], have been enforcing their rights, their rights to inherit and succeed their fathers’ thrones.’[footnote 117]

13.1.10 The International diplomatic source 1 - 2025 noted: ‘There's a distinct difference between rural and urban areas [in attitudes]. The majority of the population lives in urban areas, but there are still some tribes – because BWA is divided according to tribal territories – that are much more liberal than others. But in some places, you'll see that women are still very far behind in how they're recognised and how they're treated.’[footnote 118]

13.1.11 The WAR executive director 2025 noted:

‘… in Botswana, traditionally, women – like women in the Old Testament in the Bible – are considered minors to men, and it’s considered that they should listen to men. [‘Minor’] … meant “less than a man”. It's only nowadays that the young generation, the current generation, is talking about equality and doing things in a manner that whether you are a woman, whether you are a man, whether you are LGBT+, you are a person, full stop.

‘… her generation and those older than her who are still in the workplace are from that crop of traditionalists. So even when you go to the police and you find an elder person who reports that [her] husband is beating [her], they will ask you, “Have you talked to your uncles? Have you talked to your aunts?” But you're coming to the police to help you. The police will ask, “Have you talked to them?” because that's the culture, that's the tradition. And the victim has been abused so many times before they go to the police because they've been going around the village to their uncle, to their aunt, who have been saying, “No, we'll talk to him. It will be fine.” By the time they go to the police, they’ve been to all these people, so that also delays and escalates the violence. So the community as well needs to get that education, needs to understand that they need to be protecting this woman.

‘… when you're in the rural areas, you are more vulnerable because of the vulnerabilities that you are living under.’[footnote 119]

13.1.12 The BONELA representatives 2025 commenting on martial rape noted:

‘… as a woman who is raped in a marriage faces a lot of challenges in reporting such an incident and dealing with the issue. There’s one’s own stigma and external stigma. Also, we have something called “bride price” – “lobola” – which a family pays [for a wife], say 8 cows, 12 cows, that instils the idea that when somebody has paid – that token - then they own you. When people count their properties, a woman is included … this was an issue behind GBV because men have a sense of entitlement for women. This is a challenge for a woman because the family has paid lobola so in her mind she has an obligation to provide conjugal rights regardless of what the context is. We cannot then say existing laws will help us deal with that [the traditional practice of bride price/lobola or how women are traditionally perceived].’[footnote 120]

13.1.13 The UKHO FFM interviewed members of Mosaditia Women in Tourism, a non-government organisation in Maun focussing on women in the tourist industry, on 14 July 2025 (MWT representatives 2025). The representatives noted ‘In rural areas, women are being oppressed as the culture they still believe in won’t allow women [to be equal to men/do the same work as men].’[footnote 121]

13.1.14 On the reasons why a woman may not report an incident, the MWT representatives 2025 ‘thought [women] cannot express [what happens]. For example, maybe my husband is violating my daughter, I’ll know. Because he is the provider, I'll decide to keep [quiet] … because of the economic situation. [Other reasons] … maybe culture. Some cultures don’t allow women to have a say. Even some churches don’t allow women to have a say. Women should just keep quiet when a man talks. A woman should just follow what a man says.’ The MWT representatives 2025 added that they did not consider women were aware of their rights in rural areas[footnote 122].

13.1.15 See also subsections on Under-reporting and Withdrawal of cases for discussion of the societal pressures and cultural reasons why women do not report incidents of GBV or withdraw cases of GBV from the criminal justice system.

13.1.16 The LAB Communications, media and public relations officer noted, ‘…[women in rural areas] don’t have access to where they could report, for instance, WAR. The first responders aren’t close to them. There’s also a community mindset, so if someone’s abused by their uncle or their parents, they don’t disclose it.’[footnote 123]

14. Prevalence of GBV

14.1 Limited statistical information

14.1.1 There are 2 comprehensive studies of GBV:

  • the Gender Based Violence Indicators Study Botswana 2012 (GBVISB 2012), Women’s Affairs Department, Ministry of Labour and Home Affairs, and Gender Links, published September 2015
  • The Botswana National Relationship Study 2018 (BNRS 2018). This
    • ‘… measured GBV experience and perpetration, gender attitudes, selected health-related behaviour and exposure to prevention campaigns among women and men.
    • ‘The study used a mixed method approach that includes both qualitative and quantitative methodologies.
    • ‘A cross sectional household survey measured GBV prevalence, HIV risk behaviour, pregnancy history, mental health, and help seeking behaviour after experiences of GBV. [This consisted of interviews with a total of 7,920 people over 18 - 4,224 women and 3,696 men - between June and September 2017]
    • ‘Researchers analysed administrative data from the police, shelters, health, and courts to triangulate survey data.’[footnote 124]

14.1.2 Various sources noted the lack of recent or current statistics on GBV. The USSD HR report 2024 does not comment on GBV[footnote 125] but the USSD HR report 2023 stated: ‘Although statistics were unavailable, media widely reported on cases of violence against women, including several high-profile murder cases.’[footnote 126] The UN CEDAW report 2025 similarly noted the lack of statistics on GBV[footnote 127].

14.1.3 The World Bank report 2025 stated:

‘Recent and gender-disaggregated data are lacking in several key areas. Updated demographic household survey data are needed, as the latest available information comes from the 2017 Botswana Demographic Survey and the 2018 National Relationships Study. Furthermore, these surveys do not provide the full range of information collected through a standard Demographic and Health Survey … which would provide updated information on adolescent pregnancy, GBV attitudes and behaviors, family planning, women’s health-seeking behavior, women’s decision-making within the household, and other indicators. Gender analysis of data collected in the 2023 Enterprise Surveys (World Bank 2023) is needed as there is a general lack of disaggregated data on firm productivity, growth, and access to financial services. More gender-disaggregated data on time use, agricultural productivity, and climate change impact would enable closer gender analysis in these areas. Finally, gender disaggregation of data by region, language group, disability, and other dimensions of vulnerability are not readily available, making it challenging to assess the gender gaps and barriers facing these populations.’[footnote 128]

14.1.4 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 noted ‘… the only authority [to publish statistics] would be the police [see Police reports below] and they're quite inconsistent in what they release, what the information documents. But there was a study [the BNRS 2018], from 2018, that's the one referred to a lot. That’s the one that says that 67% of women [experienced GBV].’[footnote 129] NB the GBISB 2012 refers to 67% of women experiencing GBV, the BNRS 2018 refers to 37% of women reported some form of GBV, see Levels of GBV below.

14.1.5 The UNPFA official 2025 confirmed that the BNRS 2018 was the most recent comprehensive study of GBV noting that the ‘UNFPA had been trying to support [the government] … to update it because it’s quite dated, but it’s the latest national study [adding] … there may be smaller ones – [the] Botswana Gender-Based Violence Prevention and Support Centre also recently did something but on a smaller scale.’[footnote 130]

14.1.6 The MYGA officials 2025 ‘noted that [the government] … hadn’t done any new study [since the BNRS 2018], but that there were systems [for checking] occurrence … data … from civil society organisations ... from shelters and … crime statistics from Statistics Botswana. So, in the interim, those are our reference [data for GBV].’[footnote 131]

14.1.7 The MYGA officials 2025 also noted:

‘… people don't always report to the authorities, but they report to different organisations. The Ministry receives a few walk-in GBV clients who are often referred to Service Providers based on their needs. These include District Commissioners, Counsellors, the Police, Legal AID and Shelters. So, you will have, for example, the Ministry of Local Government and Traditional Affairs because that's where social workers are and those mostly deal with children's matters, plus other civil society organisations that deal with children's matters, so they will have statistics of the cases they handle. It could be per week, it could be per month, per quarter. The Shelters also receive walk-in clients who report their cases. The Social Workers at the Shelters assess them to determine whether they can be referred to appropriate service providers or whether they need to be housed for their protection. The Shelters can also assist clients to apply for a Restraining Order where their life is at risk. And then we also have the CSOs. Those are the people that would share data in terms of the cases they have dealt with and [documented].’[footnote 132]

14.1.8 The WAR executive director 2025 noted:

‘Botswana doesn’t have a central point where all this data [about GBV] can be entered, so that if [WAR] … sees a person, Love Botswana [a Maun-based NGO] sees them and the police see them, they don't count the person three times. They see that this person went there and there and there. Now she needs to go to the hospital or somewhere, but there is no central record … The only figures are the 2018 relationship study and the 2012 [Gender Based Violence Indicators Study - Botswana] survey. The 2012 survey said 67% of women had been abused … Then the numbers were released [for the 2018 study], and then it came to 37% [in the BNSR 2018], which is … almost what the global picture looks like. But those figures are only for the survey that was done. There is no daily administrative collection from different service providers, and no central point where the data is collected.’[footnote 133]

14.2 Definitions of GBV

14.2.1 The World Health Organisation in its factsheet on violence against women of March 2024 (WHO VAW factsheet 2024) referred to the UN’s definition of GBV as ‘“any act of gender-based violence that results in, or is likely to result in, physical, sexual, or mental harm or suffering to women, including threats of such acts, coercion or arbitrary deprivation of liberty, whether occurring in public or in private life”’[footnote 134].

14.2.2 The BNRS 2018 defined GBV as:

  • ‘Physical, sexual, psychological [emotional] and economic intimate partner violence.
  • ’Rape and sexual assault by a partner, stranger, acquaintance or family member, experienced by adults and in childhood; and
  • ‘Sexual harassment.’[footnote 135]

14.2.3 The BRNS study 2018 provided further explanations of the different forms of intimate personal violence (IPV) committed by a partner or former partner:

  • emotional IPV identified by acts classed as ‘… controlling, frightening, and intimidating, or those that undermined the participant's self-esteem. Researchers asked participants if a partner had ever insulted them or made them feel bad; belittled or humiliated them in front of other people; threatened to hurt them; stopped them from seeing friends; done things to scare or intimidate them; or boasted about or brought home girl/boyfriends. To assess perpetration of violence, researchers asked them if they in turn had done any of these things to their partners …
  • ‘Acts of economic IPV … include withholding money for household use, prohibiting a partner from earning an income, taking a partner's earnings or forcing a partner and children to leave the house in which they live ...’
  • ‘Researchers assessed physical IPV by asking five questions about whether participants had been slapped, had something thrown at them, had been pushed or shoved, kicked, hit, dragged, choked, beaten, burnt or threatened with a weapon. Similarly, researchers asked them if they had perpetrated any of these acts ...’
  • ‘The study assessed sexual IPV experienced using three questions … if their current or previous partner had ever physically forced them to have sex when they did not want to; if they had had sex with him or her because they feared what he or she might do; and whether they had been forced to do something sexual that they found degrading or humiliating.’ [footnote 136]

14.3 Under-reporting

14.3.1 See also Social, economic and political status and Social and cultural attitudes for context on the societal status of women generally.

14.3.2 The BNRS 2018 found that of women who had reported some form of GBV in their lifetime:

‘26% of women … physically abused and injured by an intimate partner sought medical attention because of the injuries. Twenty-seven percent of women physically injured reported the abuse to the police … Three percent of women reported rape to the police … The extent of reporting of rape to the police was even lower than that of physical IPV implying that women … do not report rape cases more often than they do physical abuse cases. A slightly higher proportion (4%) of women compared to 2% men sought medical attention after rape.

‘Different stakeholders interviewed including the police cited the following potential reasons why women and men do not report:

  • ‘The response and support services do not deal with women experiencing violence in a sensitive manner and worse for men who often face ridicule when they come to report.
  • ‘Culturally it is a taboo for women to expose their husbands. Women who experience violence do not want to jeopardise their relationships.
  • ‘Women view men as weak if they report abuse by a woman.
  • ‘Women do not want to lose their homes and support.
  • ‘Communities and families often handle relationship matters and few women and men report cases.’[footnote 137]

14.3.3 The BNRS 2018 also found that for women who had experienced GBV in the 12 months prior to the survey:

‘Generally reported rape less than they reported physical IPV. This could point to the stigma attached to rape in the community. One in six of the women reported experiencing physical IPV injuries and reported this to the police … Nineteen-percent of women reported physical abuse or threats to the police … As is in the lifetime experience of violence, few women (2%) … reported rape to the police. Less than one percent women … sought medical attention in the past 12 months for rape related problems.’[footnote 138]

14.3.4 The UN CEDAW report 2025 was concerned about: ‘The stigmatization of women who report gender-based violence, particularly rape, due to deeply entrenched patriarchal norms that seek to legitimize domestic violence and the underreporting of cases due to stigma, family pressure or lack of trust in the justice system …’[footnote 139]

14.3.5 The BGBVC managers 2025 noted: ‘GBV is mostly underreported … because of the fear of being exposed … we've been in communities [where] … there are lots and lots of cases that don't get reported.’[footnote 140]

14.3.6 The UKHO FFM interviewed representatives of Love Botswana, a faith-based NGO based in Maun which provides support to communities in the local area including women, on 14 July 2025 (LB representatives 2025). The representatives explained that ‘for example, with emotional abuse, not all cases are reported. Some of the individuals who have been wronged will say that they have forgiven the person, and they are no longer interested in pursuing the case, so cases might be dropped.’ The representatives also noted ‘that [women in rural areas] don’t have access to where they could report, for instance, [the NGO War Against Rape] WAR [in Maun]. The first responders aren’t close to them. There’s also a community mindset, so if someone’s abused by their uncle or their parents, they don’t disclose it.’ [footnote 141]

14.3.7 The WAR executive director 2025 noted: ‘there are a number of issues why people don't report, because there’s poverty and this person is the only one who's looking after me. I live in his house. He's looking after my children. If he goes to prison, what am I going to do? So it's also mixed with bread-and-butter issues.’[footnote 142]

14.3.8 The FE officials 2025 noted that they see ‘a lot’ of censorship, self-censorship (women not speaking out/reporting an incident). ‘We also hear that there is the tradition of fixing household problems in private, at the Kgotla, which is the local village. So, before things escalate, they gather at the Kgotla and try and sort it out without it being everyone's business.’[footnote 143]

14.3.9 The MWT representatives 2025 noted: ‘In rural areas where there are high numbers of GBV [cases], people don’t report. Some women suffer in silence, because they are being oppressed.’[footnote 144]

14.3.10 The UKHO FFM interviewed the acting Deputy Commissioner of North-West District (Ngamiland) on 15 July 2025 (ADC 2025), who noted ‘Many people are victims, but they don’t come out, there are many unreported issues about GBV. Women who depend on a man, if they report they lose a source of income.’[footnote 145]

14.3.11 The UKHO FFM interviewed representatives of the Botswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS (BONELA), a Botswanan NGO focussing on health and human rights, on 16 July 2025 (BONELA representatives 2025), who noted the GBV being reported in the media ‘is only the tip of the iceberg because many of these issues are not reported, some happen in rural areas which are not reported or do not reach mainstream media.’[footnote 146]

14.3.12 The BONELA representatives 2025 further noted that in Botswanan

‘… culture, when a woman gets married there is a tradition of older women providing counsel, asking the bride to put a blanket over her shoulders and telling her that everything that happens in your household must stay under this blanket. So, this is socialising a woman not to say anything if she has issues [problems within the marriage]. That's exactly what happens, people experience GBV and don't tell anyone …[but] the main reason [women do not report issues] is the economic situation of women [their economic reliance on men].’[footnote 147]

14.4 Factors affecting likelihood of violence

14.4.1 The BNRS 2018 found that

  • ‘… age is a significant factor in both experience and perpetrating GBV in lifetime by women and men: for women the highest incidence is 18 to 24; for men, 25 to 34.
  • ‘Abuse in childhood was a significant determinant of both GBV experience and perpetration by women and men …
  • ‘… having a partner who did not drink alcohol reduced the odds of experiencing IPV.
  • ‘Having more than one sexual partner increased the risk of experiencing IPV.
  • ‘Quarrelling within intimate relationships was significantly associated with perpetration of IPV.’[footnote 148]

14.4.2 The table below from BNRS 2018[footnote 149] shows the societal level gender attitude towards women

14.4.3 The International diplomatic source 1 - 2025 commented when asked about factors that affect treatment of women:

‘… education … [is] the top [factor] … and then of course economic background … if a woman comes from a well-off family, then the prospects of her rising up in society are much higher and how they're treated also corresponds to that. But the Official did not think … [relatively wealthy women] can avoid gender-based violence, it affects all women – but [they] didn’t think economic background matters that much. The Official had heard and seen examples of women who are well-educated still experiencing GBV.’[footnote 150]

14.5 Levels of GBV

14.5.1 As context, GBV affects about one in 3 women globally (see also Definitions of GBV above). The WHO VAW factsheet 2024 noted:

‘Population-level surveys based on reports from survivors provide the most accurate estimates of the prevalence of intimate partner violence and sexual violence. A 2018 analysis of prevalence data from 2000–2018 across 161 countries and areas, conducted by WHO on behalf of the UN Interagency working group on violence against women, found that worldwide, nearly 1 in 3, or 30%, of women have been subjected to physical and/or sexual violence by an intimate partner or non-partner sexual violence or both …’[footnote 151]

14.5.2 A number of publicly available sources stated that GBV was widespread in Botswana but these statements either rely on the GBVISB 2012 and BNRS 2018 or do not refer to specific data sets to support these statements. These include:

  • The USSD HR report 2023 stated:

‘According to the World Population Review, the incidence of rape was extremely high, at 92.93 per 100,000 persons (2010 data). According to a 2022 report by the Women’s Affairs Department in the Ministry of Labour and Home Affairs, 67 percent of women experienced some form of gender-based violence in their lifetime including partner and nonpartner violence. A smaller, but still high, proportion of men (44 percent) admitted to perpetrating violence against women … domestic violence remained a serious problem during the year.’[footnote 152] [CPIT was not able to find this report. The data, however, appears to be from the GBVISB 2012]

  • The FH Botswana report 2025 which stated ‘[g]ender-based violence, including domestic violence and rape, is pervasive … Women can experience harassment for not dressing conservatively.’[footnote 153]
  • Amnesty International in its annual report for 2024 noted:

‘Gender-based violence remained widespread and continued to rise. Women Against Rape [based in Maun, Ngamiland] … reported an increase in cases from 2023 … In June, the UN Population Fund identified violence against women as a major public health concern in Botswana. In September, Tonota District Council reported a rise in sexual abuse cases. The police service recorded 47 threats to kill, 25 murders, 30 sexual abuse cases, and 93 rapes and attempted rapes against women over the Christmas holiday period.’[footnote 154] The source does not however provide context to the rise – from when, over what time period and if there were particular reasons that may explain it.

  • The UN CEDAW report noted ‘with concern the high prevalence of gender-based violence against women and girls …’[footnote 155]

14.5.3 As noted above, the BNRS 2018 is the most recent comprehensive and systematic study of the prevalence of GBV. It found:

  • ‘Thirty seven percent of women reported experiencing some form of GBV [including economic, emotional, physical and sexual violence] at least once while 30% men conceded to perpetrating GBV in their lifetime …
  • ‘Thirty seven percent of ever-partnered women … experienced some form of intimate partner violence.
  • ‘Eleven percent of women … experienced sexual harassment either in school or at work or in public places.
  • ‘Five percent of women … reported experiencing rape at the hands of a non-partner.
  • ‘The most commonly experienced form of IPV is emotional IPV followed by physical, economic, and sexual IPV.
  • ‘Fourteen percent of women and 17% of men reported perpetrating some form of abuse against their partner in the past 12 months.
  • ‘Fifteen percent of women who had ever been pregnant reported experiencing abuse at some point during their pregnancy.…’[footnote 156]

14.5.4 The BNRS 2018 created the following table of prevalence of GBV amongst men and women in their lifetimes and 12 months prior to the survey[footnote 157]. This includes IPV, sub-categories of IPV, non-partner rape, abuse in pregnancy, sexual harassment, sexual harassment at school, sexual harassment at work and sexual harassment:

14.5.5 The BNRS 2018 also presented the data on IPV experienced by women and perpetrated by men broken down by emotional, physical, economic and sexual IPV plus abuse in pregnancy in the bar graph below[footnote 158]:

14.5.6 The BNRS 2018 additionally provided information on the socio-demographic characteristics of people who had experienced and those who had perpetrated intimate partner violence (IPV) over a person’s lifetime:

  • ‘Experience of IPV in women decreased with increase in age.
  • ‘Age was significantly associated with both experience and perpetration of IPV except in perpetration by women (p>0.05).
  • ‘Although not statistically significant it is worth noting that most (59%) of the IPV perpetration was recorded by women aged 29 years and below. (This could point to increased assertiveness).
  • ‘Men aged between 18-39 years recorded the highest levels of both IPV perpetration and experience while in women these were observed among women aged 18-29 years.
  • ‘Women between the ages of 18-29 reported experiencing more violence (8%) than any other women aged 30 and above.
  • ‘There are more men (5%) than women perpetrating IPV below the age of 34.
  • Women and men aged 40 and over reported experiencing lower levels of IPV in their lifetime compared to younger women and men.
  • Men aged 45 and over reported perpetrating lower levels (3%) of IPV in their lifetime compared to the younger men.
  • ‘Women with a secondary education reported experiencing higher levels (20%) of IPV than women with lower levels (4%) of education.
  • ‘Similarly, men with higher levels of education reported perpetrating higher levels (13%) of IPV than men with lower levels (3%) of education.
  • ‘In the 12 months prior to the survey, 15% of the women in the sample were employed as compared to a fifth of the sample who were unemployed but reported experiencing violence.
  • ‘In the same period, 17% of men and 7% of women in the sample who were employed reported perpetrating violence compared to 10% and 11% of men and women respectively who were unemployed.’[footnote 159]

14.5.7 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 noted:

‘The main [type of GBV] … would be intimate partner violence (IPV). That's resulted in a lot of cases. Murder … [although the official] did not have the numbers off [hand] but there was a particular period during the festive season [Christmas 2024] … when the police reported the number of cases of murder, incest or molestation were in their hundreds nationally in that period alone. [The government has released statistics on GBV] … more recently, but it's not consistent. It will be attached to a particular period. For example, they report a lot during the holiday period.’[footnote 160]

14.5.8 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 was also aware of rape:

‘Where the woman is walking on the street and raped by a stranger, for example. That happens quite a lot, especially in rural areas … The International diplomatic source had heard of traditional doctors assaulting their purported patients or clients, like a client for a consultation. And they're sexually assaulted by the traditional doctor … [but] [i]t's not as prevalent as other forms of violence.

International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 also indicated it is not documented like other forms of GBV: ‘… Also, because of the stigma associated with people going to traditional doctors, people don't tend to report it. And then in addition to that, a lot of assault that's been reported is from religious leaders, for example, especially the more modern type of churches. The pastors would occasionally lure [victims] them into private spaces. There has been a proliferation of these new churches, they are called “fire churches” or “prosperity gospel churches”.’[footnote 161]

14.5.9 The International diplomatic source 2 – 2025 ‘was not able to give specific numbers but observed that every week the source gets Botswana (BWA) newspapers and reads about incidents of GBV, not a week has passed that an incident is not reported. For example, there was report from 2 weeks ago about the murder of a female employee at the University of Botswana (UofB) who was stabbed during the day in her office at the university by her partner.’[footnote 162]

14.5.10 The UNPFA official 2025 noted the most prevalent form of GBV is sexual assault, noting:

‘… rape statistics for BWA are the second highest in the world, so [the number of] sexual assaults is quite high – physical [violence], like beating, which is quite high; and economic [violence]. Economic [violence] is particularly in cases where the man is working but the woman isn’t, [so] she’s dependent on the partner. Sometimes [the man withholds funds] because the women are dependent on them. That also leads to the pattern that has been observed [where] a lot of reported cases of GBV are withdrawn because the woman says that this person is the breadwinner and the caretaker, and if you take him to prison then the family has no means of sustenance.’[footnote 163]

14.5.11 The UNFPA official also noted that men are the main perpetrators of GBV and most violence ‘is intimate partner violence, but when you look at the data, there's a lot perpetrated by family members – a brother having raped his sister or an uncle having raped a niece. It’s intimate partners, then family members, then others – just general strangers.’[footnote 164]

14.5.12 The BGBVC managers 2025 noted:

‘[Types of GBV include] … sexual violence, physical violence, emotional violence and economic violence … this mostly happens within the domestic arena, so it's mostly domestic violence. There’s a high [prevalence] of domestic violence and intimate partner violence … [but] it’s a disadvantage that we don't have data. Usually, we rely on police data, but GBV is mostly underreported. The situation might be higher. We’ve been getting a lot of reports of GBV, including femicide. There are frequent reports of GBV/femicide cases in media …

‘… Now that the police have a special unit that deals with GBV (Gender and Child Protection Branch) we want to believe that reporting has increased a lot. Police statistics show that the total number of reported cases to the police in 2024 only was 32,172. This is the total number of all cases of all types [of crime] reported to the police. Out of that, the total number of what the police say was recorded as GBV is 11,287. What is important is that this is just what is reported … BGBVC cannot confidently say cases [of GBV] are increasing …’[footnote 165]

14.5.13 The BGBVC managers 2025 also noted that technology ‘is playing a role, especially in intimate relationships, especially ex-partners where one is trying to move away from the other and they don’t want to explicit details to be shared, whatever they shared during the relationship, either videos or pictures. [Their ex-partner says,] ‘It's either we get back together, or I share this material in public.’ It has happened a lot so that people end up living in this situation. SOCIAL CARE OFFICER explained that he had read that, and that some people actually end up committing suicide or contemplating it because of the shame.’[footnote 166]

14.5.14 For more detail on police reported GBV, see Police reports below.

14.5.15 The BGBVC managers 2025 commenting on changes in the levels of reporting, noted:

‘… when you look at the trends, it shows that … [GBV is] increasing … [but] what has increased is mostly the reporting. More people, as they become aware [of GBV], are starting to talk more than they used to. But what we can confidently say is that GBV is [at its] highest now … [reporting of GBV had] especially increased with [the creation of the police’s Gender and Child Protection Unit, see Gender and Child Protection Unit (GCPU) below] … but also BGBVC are going out and explaining what GBV is [to communities]. When [BGBVC] started some years ago, people didn’t know, but even now there are still people that think that it's only GBV if it's physical. So [BGBVC] are trying to create awareness as to what GBV looks like, because a lot of times it can present itself in different ways. If my boyfriend or my husband keeps calling me every 30 minutes, I might interpret it as love, when it's actually control. So, they’re trying to get people to understand things like that.’[footnote 167]

14.5.16 The BGBVC managers 2025 further noted: ‘… there is a clear suspicion that [GBV] cases are increasing, but what they mostly see is that people are [bringing cases to light] because of greater awareness. They keep on seeing an increase in the number of cases they deal with every year, but they cannot confidently conclude that this is because there’s an increase in prevalence.’[footnote 168]

14.5.17 The BGBVC managers 2025 on whether social media helps with the reporting of GBV considered that it did, noting: ‘… culturally, people stay [in relationships where there is GBV]. It's normal; some things have been normalised. As we create awareness through social media, through media, through workplace presentations, people begin to say, “Oh, so this is actually not normal. Actually, there are people who are talking about it. So that means that I can also talk.”’ They also noted: ‘BGBVC has centres in urban areas, and that this may also go to the fact that in urban areas, there’s more sensitisation and awareness of GBV.’[footnote 169]

14.5.18 The FAB representatives 2025 acknowledged that data on the prevalence of GBV is limited and referred to police reports of GBV as indicating a rise (see Police reports). The representatives claimed:

‘GBV is on the rise in BWA – [it includes] femicide by intimate partners, whether current or previous intimate partners, sexual assaults ranging from homosexual assaults to defilement, rape, physical abuse, financial abuse, emotional abuse and verbal abuse. But there’s a lack of awareness of what constitutes verbal abuse, so you find that it's under-reported … with financial abuse, you'll find the most vulnerable women are those who are unable to find employment and/or earn less than their partner in the relationship. Because they end up needing to come to the man to say, ‘We are short of this’, then they experience financial abuse in that way.’[footnote 170]

14.5.19 The LB representatives 2025 considered that women were mostly affected by physical and sexual violence, which affected many women and was a ‘pandemic’. They also noted that the main perpetrators are partners, husbands and parents. Some cases of GBV by strangers but they are rare[footnote 171]. However, the LB representatives 2025 acknowledged that they did not have statistics on the numbers of GBV cases. The representatives provided data from LB’s cases ‘… in the last quarter [source did not confirm but likely to be April to June 2025], they had 13 women coming for counselling sessions … the problem with the numbers is that most of [the GBV victims] come and then they don't go to the police station, so it's hard for us to track them. But the previous quarter [January to March 2025], we had 18, so it’s dropped … they deal with different [types of] cases and that there were 213 cases [of people supported for any type of reason] overall.’[footnote 172]

14.5.20 The LB representatives 2025 explained that they came across GBV cases ‘through self-referrals; [people] come to [LB’s] offices. LB hasn’t had agency referrals. Most of them are just members of the community or self-referrals.’ On whether they had referred GBV cases to the police, the representatives noted ‘that they had referred them to [War Against Rape] WAR, but then once they end up in WAR, most of the women go to the police.’ The LB representatives 2025 thought that 2 women had been killed in the previous months, 5 in the previous 6 months in the Maun area[footnote 173].

14.5.21 The WAR executive director 2025 noted:

‘Gender-based violence against women … it’s quite rife today … if [they] … gave the FFM team her numbers, they would be much, much lower than what they would get from the police, and the police numbers would be much lower than what they would get from the hospital. Each stakeholder has their customers, has their numbers. People will go to the hospital, and they know that the hospital will not go to the police. Those who go to the police are the ones who feel threatened that this person might kill them. But if they feel it's something that you can put a bandage on or look after, then they'll go to the hospital. Those who come here [to WAR], they also want WAR to take them through the system. So, everyone gets their people. If you go to, say, faith-based organisations, they will get people who believe in God and want to be prayed for or pray for the perpetrator. So, each one of us gets their own kind of people.’[footnote 174]

14.5.22 The WAR executive director 2025 noted that the organisation collected data on the numbers of cases it handled but could not identify a pattern over the previous 4 to 5 years,

‘… that they had looked but there is no pattern. Some years it goes up, then it comes down, then it goes up, then it comes down … the numbers are high because people are now aware that GBV is wrong. It's like talking about child marriages. In Botswana, if you search anywhere, you'll find that Botswana doesn't have child marriages because we're not reporting child marriages, we are not even defining them as child marriages. It's just that this child is living with this man. But there's no certificate that says they're married, so technically they're not married because the chief didn't marry them. The magistrate didn't marry them. Nobody married them, even though they're in a marriage set-up. So, we can easily hide child marriages because the chiefs will tell you, “I never marry anyone below the age of 18,” which is true. You go to the records, you won't find anything, but the children will be there.

‘… similarly, with GBV, people choose when to report and when not to report, so you can't really say the numbers are low or they're increasing. If people are resorting to violence, others in similar situations will also resort to violence because they hear it. [Another reason is that] Batswana are [now] more aware of their human rights. They are more aware of the laws that are there to protect them, like the Domestic Violence Act, the Penal Code, the sexual assault register. There's more publicity when the laws come out. There are a lot of NGOs coming up. There are a lot of lawyers … coming up to say, “We want to help.” When we publicise the law, when an act comes up, it will be discussed on the radio … So there's more access to information now. People are now recognising, “This is wrong. There's something I can do about this.” So it's quite hard to tell if it's changed since the 2018 study. We don't know if it's gone up or down. We can't know until we do a survey.’[footnote 175]

14.5.23 The UKHO FFM interviewed 2 officials at the French Embassy who led on gender related programmes on 10 July 2025 (FE officials 2025). They noted ‘women die every day, we know it happens quite often [but do not have the numbers].’ The FE officials were not aware of statistics on levels of domestic violence. They also noted ‘since the new current government [came to power] there has been more talk about GBV in the press as people are urging the government to pass an anti-GBV law and to declare a national state of emergency. So, there is more [reporting and commentary on GBV] in the press but no data on it.’[footnote 176]

14.5.24 The UKHO FFM interviewed representatives of Bana Ba Letsatsi, a non-government organisation that assists children in Maun and surrounding areas, on 14 July 2025 (BBL representatives 2025). While BBL did not focus on GBV, the representatives noted ‘that the number of GBV cases in Maun is high. Kids are being abused by their caregivers, the people who are supposed to protect them. Most of it is where the parents work on safaris in the deltas. Their uncles take care of them and there are some cases of rape, defilement, teenage pregnancy, usually because of the absence of the parents.’ However, the representatives did not have any data to support this observation[footnote 177].

14.5.25 The BONELA representatives 2025 noted:

‘We have reached crisis levels looking at the numbers that are reported on a daily basis ... It is a national crisis for us, a national problem. We are seeing skyrocketing cases of sexual violence

‘… there is evidence of an increase in number [of GBV cases]. [But they] wouldn’t say the awareness raising doesn't have an impact in getting people to report. The sad reality is that the cases which are mostly documented are those which have reached a vital stage, where somebody has lost their life. It’s not like we are seeing more people in GBV relationships reporting more because we only see GBV cases at the end, when nothing can be done.’[footnote 178]

14.5.26 The ADC 2025 noted that they did not have statistics on the number of GBV cases reported to the district Gender Committee but ‘thought the number of cases was going up.’ The data reported to the Gender Committee was provided by the police (including the Gender and Child Protection Branch), the Directorate of Public Prosecutions, the government social and welfare office and Women Against Rape. The cases included assault, rape and other forms of violence[footnote 179].

14.5.27 The UKHO FFM interviewed representatives of the Lesbians, Gays and Bisexuals of Botswana, a non-government organisation that advocates for and supports lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people), on 16 July 2025 (LEGABIBO representatives 2025). The representatives focussed on the experiences of LGBT+ people but thought GBV generally was getting ‘worse’, noting ‘there's been a rise in violence and the law is not doing anything to hold people accountable.’[footnote 180]

14.6 Police reports

14.6.1 The BPS Annual Crimes Statistics Report 2024 covering the period 1 January to 31 December 2024 (BPS 2024 annual report) noted:

‘Over the past eight years, crime has shown a slight but consistent downward trend, with an overall decrease of 0.6%. In 2024, the BPS registered 146,529 offences, representing a significant reduction of 13,151 cases (8%) compared to the previous year. A further analysis revealed that Penal Code offences accounted for the majority of recorded crimes, among which, offences against property were the most prevalent, constituting 50% of the total … The report further analysed 5,929 victims under offences with which the person was targeted such as robbery, murder, threat to kill, rape and defilement of persons under the age of 18 years. The analysis generally proved that women were disproportionately affected, representing 85% (5,040) of the victims. Conversely, a total of 5,766 individuals identified as perpetrators were analysed in regard to all the selected offences, with 98% of them being male. Worthy of note is that the perpetrator numbers relate to only those were dealt with by the time of reporting.’[footnote 181]

14.6.2 The BPS 2024 annual report also noted:

‘The data highlights a strong correlation between unemployment and victimisation, with 65% of victims and the majority of perpetrators being unemployed and unmarried. The most common victim-perpetrator relationships involved romantic partners, strangers, and acquaintances, while a few incidents involving friends and relatives were registered.

‘A distinct analysis of cases shows that jealousy (33.8%) and arguments (26.4%) were the most common motives in murder cases. Also, the most frequently used weapons in aggravated offences, such as murder and robbery cases, are knives. Geographically, most incidents of rape, threats to kill, defilement, murder, and motor vehicle theft occurred within the victims’ residences. However, defilement was most prevalent in perpetrators’ homes, while human trafficking incidents predominantly happened on the streets.’[footnote 182]

14.6.3 The BPS 2024 annual report, the most recent report available at the time of writing, noted:

‘The prevalence of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) and offenses involving children has been a significant concern, highlighting various forms of abuse, including physical, sexual, and psychological violence, as well as deprivation. Notably, there has been a commendable reduction in overall cases, decreasing by 30.3%, from 19,440 cases recorded in 2023 to 12,490 in 2024.

‘Specifically, incidents of physical harm, which constitute the majority (54.0%) of cases, experienced a significant decline of 46.5%. Similarly, sexual harm, the second most prevalent category (at 29.2%), saw a reduction of 8.5%. However, it is concerning to note that the category of deprivation increased dramatically by 97.2%, alongside a rise of 13.0% in psychological harm cases.

‘These trends indicate both progress in certain areas and the urgent need to address rising issues, particularly in deprivation and psychological harm, to ensure continued improvement in safeguarding the well-being of vulnerable populations.’[footnote 183]

14.6.4 The BPS 2024 annual report included the following table of cases involving GBV and child abuse[footnote 184] (the report does not distinguish between the 2):

14.6.5 Detailed data on GBV offences are provided in the BPS’ annual statistics reports covering 2022 to 2024. Summaries of the GBV offences are available in the BPS’ annual reports from 2016 to 2024.

14.6.6 The BGBVC managers 2025 explained that: ‘Police statistics show that the total number of reported cases to the police in 2024 only was 32,172. This is the total number of all cases of all types [of crime] reported to the police. Out of that, the total number of what the police say was recorded as GBV is 11,287.’ The BGBVC managers 2025 explained that: ‘Now that the police have a special unit that deals with GBV (Gender and Child Protection Branch) we want to believe that reporting has increased a lot.’[footnote 185] See also the Gender and Child Protection Branch (GCPB) for discussion of the activities and impact of this specialised police unit below.

14.6.7 The WAR executive director 2025 noted: ‘[reporting of GBV had] especially increased with … [with the GCPB’s creation], but also BGBVC are going out and explaining what GBV is [to communities].’[footnote 186]

14.6.8 Africa Press, in article dated 14 November 2025, noted: ‘The Botswana Police Service recorded 31,975 cases against persons last year, of which 10,747 were GBV-related, highlighting the urgent need for stronger prevention and response measures.’[footnote 187]

14.6.9 The BPS officials 2025 noted that GBV offenses,

‘… are documented. Every year, the police compile reports. The recent GBV statistics indicate an increase in GBV statistics. This, however, does not in itself indicate an increase in GBV crime. Factors that could explain this trend include increased reporting resulting from increased awareness creation. Another possible reason is the improvement in the handling of GBV victims thus leading to victims generally feeling safer within the police stations. Therefore, generally speaking, the numbers are going up, but this doesn’t necessarily indicate a worsening crime situation.’[footnote 188]

14.6.10 The FAB representatives 2025 noted ‘… that there has been an increase in terms of cases being reported … to the police. And sometimes, there are some victims who feel uncomfortable reporting to the police, so they report to shelters or organisations that specifically work with GBV. [The NGOs] … are the link between [the victims] and the law enforcement agencies.’[footnote 189]

14.6.11 On the reasons for the rise, the FFM team asked if this was because the population is increasing, and women are aware of their rights so are reporting more. The FAB representatives 2025 noted it is,

‘… also, because there is knowledge now, knowledge of the interventions where people feel like they’ll get justice, which is a very important step … people are now leveraging the power of social media. A lot of cases, just like the MeToo movement, are talked about and people are bravely posting their stories online. That is how other people get the courage to come forward with their stories. And sometimes those are not reported. It's just somebody coming out and saying, “This is also my story.” It’s a form of healing just to speak about it.’[footnote 190]

14.7 Traditional harmful practices

14.7.1 The FAB representatives 2025 noted ‘… that there haven’t been a lot of [cases of ritualised abuse or traditional harmful practices] recently ... culture had been dynamic in terms of trying to eliminate abusive practices such as genital mutilation. [FAB] … haven't [seen any cases]. They’re just seeing an increase in more modern types of abuse that you would get anywhere else. Also, there is online abuse [harassment].’[footnote 191]

14.7.2 The LAB CEO 2025 noted:

‘… cases where body parts are used for traditional medicine [ritual killings] are really not rife in the country – they are in fact few … thought that in the year before the general elections [2023] and the year of the general elections [2024], it appeared from the newspapers – … [but] personally [the CEO] had no specific knowledge of this – that there were a number of people who disappeared, and when they were found, they had body parts missing. But it was not such a number as to raise a hue and cry … it would therefore be irrational for people to leave Botswana seeking asylum because of ritual killings … there used to be a lot [of these cases] when [the CEO was a child, now in their 50s], so it’s a long time ago … more of normal parlance [then], but not so now. [In the past], they were typically the cases that would attract capital punishment.’[footnote 192]

14.7.3 The LAB CEO 2025 did not consider female genital mutilation (FGM) occurred in Botswana and was not a national tradition. The CEO also noted:

‘… not sure about the issue of incest. Again, it would be notorious in certain areas more than other areas, and that's where it is one of the customs of a particular tribe. People practise these things without necessarily knowing they are wrong in terms of the law, and that's where public education has to come through and is very important in making sure that people move away from some of these practices. [Asked if such practices would not occur Gaborone or other main towns but may still in rural areas, the CEO agreed.] … incest is an offence under the Penal Code.’[footnote 193]

14.7.4 The BGBVC representatives 2025 noted: ‘… you hear about [ritual killings and traditional harmful practices] … but … couldn’t say how many cases there are … confirmed that it’s not [in] urban [centres] … a person will disappear or not be found, and suspicion is generally directed towards someone, but it’s never substantiated.’ With regard to FGM, the representatives noted ‘that it’s not a tradition that’s documented. It’s not a traditional practice in BWA. Maybe up north, maybe some communities, but even if it was there … thought it had been lost, or that maybe we don't know.’[footnote 194]

14.7.5 The LB representatives 2025 noted ‘… that there are ritual practices that go on in the country as well …[but] that would be more a matter of perception. There are not many of those … more hearsay and … more speculation and rumours than fact-based examples.’[footnote 195]

14.7.6 The UKHO FFM 2025 interviewed officials from Ministry of Labour and Internal Affairs, Botswana, on 10 July 2025, (MLIA officials 2025), who ‘… explained that there are a lot of myths around witchcraft … witchcraft was highly unlikely to be a reason for a person to flee to the UK … Bowono was known as the centre of witchcraft [in Botswana]. [If a person needed to leave], it would be best to go to Gaborone or Francistown. They did not need to go to the UK …’[footnote 196]

14.7.7 The MWT representatives 2025 did not consider there were incidents of witchcraft or ritual killings. ‘Can’t say it doesn’t happen but not aware of cases … this may have happened in the past, maybe in 1960s and 1970s but now this doesn’t happen. We have stories of this happening, but we haven’t seen cases. Christianity was not as practised as much as today, ritual practices were there but most people are now Christian, so we don’t see this happen.’[footnote 197]

14.7.8 The BBL representatives 2025, commenting on cases of witchcraft or ritual killings among children, noted ‘these happened in the old days, but not nowadays, or if they do happen, there are only a few [cases].’ The representatives had not heard of or witnessed such activities[footnote 198].

14.7.9 The BBL representatives 2025 also noted that female genital mutilation ‘happened back in the day [but] thought that this doesn’t happen in [towns …], but it did for … girls in the bush … a group of girls were called. They would go. It was not in the community, but they were taken to a place.’ However, this ‘had [stopped] because of the rights in … the 2009 Children's Act, which … recognises that the lives of children are precious. [The Act also criminalises FGM – see Gender-specific legislation above.]’[footnote 199]

14.7.10 The BPS officials 2025 noted ‘… that there are no [reports of] mutilations [FGM] in BW[A] ... definitely not [FGM] … if [FGM] happens here, we’re not aware of it. There’s definitely no case reported to the police.’[footnote 200]

14.7.11 On witchcraft and ritual killing including where some of the victims’ body parts are removed, the BPS officials 2025 noted:

‘… calling someone a witch is an offence … regarding ritual killing … didn’t know whether it's a perception [that body found with parts missing was a victim of a ritual] by Batswana because at times, maybe the person will be reported as missing, then they'll later be found dead, maybe in the bush with some body parts missing. The assumption by the Batswana might be that it’s a ritual killing, whereas [it might have been] scavengers [animals] … it is not completely unusual for body parts to go missing. This, however, in many cases is attributed to other factors such as anger by the perpetrator, scavengers, etc, rather than ritual killings.’[footnote 201]

15. State protection

15.1 Botswana Police Service

15.1.1 The Overseas Security Advisory Council (OSAC), ‘a public-private partnership between the U.S. Department of State’s Diplomatic Security Service (DSS) and security professionals from U.S. organizations operating abroad’[footnote 202], noted in its security report for US citizens travelling to Botswana dated 4 April 2025 (OSAC report 2025): ‘The Botswana Police Service is responsible for providing law enforcement service. The Botswana Police College outside of Gaborone hosts the U.S.-led International Law Enforcement Academy (ILEA), a focal point for education and development for law enforcement agencies across Africa … The Botswana Police Service is professional, although limited in numbers and essential services to lessen crimes occurring in and around populated and rural areas.’[footnote 203]

15.1.2 The BPS officials 2025 noted:

‘[The] Botswana Police Service is mandated to ensure the safety and security of the people of Botswana and the residents of Botswana by section 6 of the Botswana Police Act … The mandate of the Botswana police is to prevent and detect crime, repress internal disturbances, maintain security and public tranquillity, apprehend offenders and bring them to justice, and to enforce all written laws with which it is directly charged to generally maintain peace. Therefore, as a result, the Botswana Police Service has prioritised the fight against gender-based violence in its policing agenda …’[footnote 204]

15.1.3 The BPS officials 2025 noted that there about 12,200 police officers of whom approximately 30% are women adding that they are now recruiting an equal number of men and women. The officials noted that the police are divided into 5 divisions and 17 districts across the country, with 84 police stations and 384 police posts[footnote 205].

15.1.4 However, the BPS’ annual report 2024 provided slightly different data from the BPS officials on the number of staff, stating: ‘The BPS has a total labour pool of 13,892 officers, encompassing 11,553 police officers, 1,732 Special Constables and 607 civilian cadre. A decision has been taken to discontinue.’ Additionally, the BPS annual report 2024 provided different figures for the number of police stations and posts, referring to 83 police stations and 412 police posts[footnote 206].

15.1.5 The government in its submission to the UN Human Rights Committee as part of Botswana’s Universal Periodic Review (UPR), dated 17 March 2023, (government UPR report 2023) set out:

‘The following measures are implemented by the Botswana Police Service in the fight against GBV:

  • Developing competencies of police officers in handling cases.
  • Provision of psycho-social support and counselling to victims.
  • Collaboration with other stakeholders and referral systems.
  • Use of informers.
  • Appointment of Gender Focal Point Persons.
  • Community Policing (bringing on board the community to assist in policing.
  • Community out-reach programmes (public education).
  • Anti-GBV campaigns.’[footnote 207]

15.1.6 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 noted when asked about police resourcing ‘… They're not underfunded. When you look at the budget allocation every year for government, the security sector gets probably the second biggest or the third biggest … though, there will be issues of no accommodation for police officers or pay issues. But in terms of resources, I think they’re relatively good.’[footnote 208] While the BPS officials 2025 noted: ‘we can never say we have enough resources, but we do … the government puts a lot of resources into supporting the police to do their work.’[footnote 209]

15.1.7 The BPS officials 2025 explained that police operate
