‘… the CCRS, the Crime and Criminal Recording System. However, the Gender and Child Protection Branch has also developed their database which they use to record GBV, and child involved offences. There’s a lot of other communications that is shared between police stations on criminals including digital platforms on criminal/wanted person particularly those that are on the run thus increasing police capability to catch criminals … in addition to the CCRS and the manual recording in the registers, there is an office at police headquarters responsible for the collation of statistics. On a quarterly basis, they do the crime returns and that is done online. We also have the strategy department and monitoring branch, which produces the annual reports. So that's where you get all the statistics for all reported cases … if you file [a case] at the central police station in Gaborone, then it’s in an automated data centre and you can find it in that database …’[footnote 210]

15.1.8 The GOROB ACHPR submission 2023 also noted:

‘To reduce the rate of withdrawal of GBV cases, Botswana Police Service undertakes the following actions: bringing charges against any person who is obstructing the cause of justice either through intimidation or coercion; and conducting public awareness on consequences of GBV case withdrawals. In order to ensure that gender-based violence cases are handled in a timely manner, with effect from 1st December 2020, all GBV cases are treated as urgent applications and given expedited management and disposal.’[footnote 211]

15.1.9 The BPS officials 2025 similarly noted ‘… we’ve taken a stance to say that we will not withdraw any GBV cases. But they can still be withdrawn at the magistrate level in court ... So, the police made a decision to disallow withdrawal of GBV cases at investigation (police) level and register all GBV cases with the courts.’[footnote 212] The MOJCS officials 2025 also commented on the withdrawal of cases, noting:

‘… Maybe in the past the handling of GBV cases may not have been effective but nowadays these cases are prepared for trial. Where a person alleges [a GBV offence] their case is facilitated because they have to prove that case before a court of law. But there are instances where a person who has registered a case chooses to withdraw their case … with regard to effectiveness, the country realised that cases were being reported to the police, then due to a variety of situations victims would withdraw their cases, saying they had reconciled their situation, or the family advised them to step down. But following reconciliation the GBV would escalate, sometimes leading to the death of the victim. So, it was decided that the police will no longer accept the withdrawal of cases. It can only be done at court.’[footnote 213] (see withdrawal of cases for more information)

15.1.10 The GOROB ACHPR submission 2023 noted: ‘In an effort to promote reporting, the Botswana Police Service undertakes continuous improvement of investigations to secure convictions and thereby win public trust. Furthermore, public awareness and outreach on GBV have been intensified. The community policing approach to promote participation of the public in identifying potential threats/ crime, and community dialogues on Gender Equality and GBV prevention continue to be implemented.’[footnote 214]

15.1.11 The GOROB ACHPR submission 2023 further noted, ‘The Botswana Police Service (BPS) continues to employ science and technology in strengthening its response and interventions to GBV and its emerging complexities, through the introduction of Standardised Forensic Evidence Collection Kits in Sexual Assaults, Use of DNA and DNA databases for cold cases, Use of Digital Forensics for online sexual exploitation cases.’[footnote 215]

15.1.12 The BPS officials 2025 noted:

‘Over the years, the BPS has continually employed various measures and interventions to ensure prompt response to GBV reports, safety of parties involved and protection of the vulnerable ... during the Covid era, we recorded an increase in the number of GBV cases. There was a very sharp increase in the number of GBV-related offences during the lockdowns imposed from April 2020 as well as offences against children. This has not only raised awareness on the prevalence of GBV issues but also served as an urgent demand for a change in the BPS responsiveness towards combatting GBV and child-related offences.’[footnote 216]

15.1.13 The BPS officials 2025 also noted:

‘In terms of prevention, the BPS mission is to provide professional policing services and partnership with the community. This was formulated in the quest to bring the community on board to assist in policing and prioritising prevention. So, we have got the promotion of community-led prevention programmes or strategies. There are also programmes geared towards empowerment of men, as we believe that men are the agents of change. There is also use of science and technology in GBV investigations. Furthermore, it is important to coordinate and cooperate with partners, therefore the BPS continues to collaborate with key stakeholders in the fight against GBV and child abuse.

‘The BPS has also benefited from development partners such as UNICEF, SADC [Southern African Development Community] Debswana, who continuously support our efforts in providing quality and comprehensive services for all victims of GBV, including children. Future efforts to improve our operational efficiencies include promoting community-led prevention programmes, enhancing reporting and support systems, and prioritising the establishment of the GBV one-stop service centre. We're also developing the caring for the carers programme to support officers that are involved in the investigation of GBV and child involved offences. We are also going to expand the victim- and child-friendly spaces that we already have and lastly integrate the restorative and reformative approach to policing.’[footnote 217]

15.1.14 The BPS officials 2025 noted:

‘… adults are generally attended in normal police stations but in what are called victim-friendly spaces. The police haven’t always had them; they’re a new development. All the new police stations that are being built come with victim-friendly spaces. But the thing they feel is more important is the knowledge within the police officers themselves in terms of what the victim needs, in terms of privacy, in terms of proper risk assessment. That’s why they concentrate on the police officers, so that even if there's no space to hold an interview, they realise that the victim still needs privacy. So even if there's no office, the victim can be taken aside somewhere, and they’ll still be able to have a private space where they can be interviewed.

‘… it’s possible that some victims may not have been afforded privacy because many of these victim friendly efforts are a new development. However, the BPS is doing its best to close the gaps. A lot of effort is put into training police officers to understand victim centred approaches so as to provide sensitive handling and response to GBV ... wouldn't be surprised if at one or 2 stations there could be a situation where somebody may not have been given the right treatment, but in general, police officers are trained to understand that if somebody – anybody – comes into a police station and needs to be attended to, they will be afforded the necessary assistance.’[footnote 218]

15.1.15 The BPS officials 2025 additionally noted:

‘… the issue of affording victims privacy dates back to 2001. Police officers have been instructed to afford [victims] the privacy that they need. So, if a rape victim comes to the office, they'll not be interviewed in a Community Service Centres (CSC) where there are lots of complainants. They will be taken out of the CSC to a safe private room, so they are not interviewed in the presence of other complainants. This has been in place since 2001. But we can’t dispute that someone could say, “I was interviewed in the presence of so many officers.” The other arrangement that we practise is for female victims to be interviewed by female police officers so that they are comfortable. But sometimes a rape victim might feel more comfortable to be interviewed by a different gender and if that aids the case, they are afforded that choice.’[footnote 219]

15.2 Gender-specific guidance and training

15.2.1 The GOROB ACHPR submission 2023 noted:

‘… The Botswana Police Service (BPS) has deployed trained Gender and Child Protection Focal Persons to deal with Gender Based Violence matters in a gender sensitive manner. To date, a total of 2248 police officers have received training on GBV and human rights through the BPS in-service programmes ... To ensure professional response to GBV issues, the Government, through BPS also developed a set of guiding principles aimed at ensuring that officers are committed to gender mainstreaming into their work and adequately skilled to do so. The following have been carried out in that regard, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) were developed as a standard tool for dealing with GBV and child related cases, to ensure comprehensive, coordinated, and synchronised interventions.’

15.2.2 An article in Botswana youth, a Botswanan online magazine, dated 2 April 2025 reported:

‘In a significant step towards addressing Gender-Based Violence (GBV), the Botswana Police Service (BPS) and the Directorate of Public Prosecutions (DPP) have commenced a three-day “Training of Trainers” workshop in Gaborone. The training, which began on April 1, 2025, is organised by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) to enhance the capacity of law enforcement officers in handling GBV cases effectively.

‘… [The BPS] Commissioner Marathe expressed gratitude to UNODC for its ongoing support, acknowledging the importance of multi-sectoral training initiatives in strengthening case referrals and streamlining case management. She also recognized past contributions from partners such as UNICEF, SADC, and the EU, which have led to the establishment of Child-Friendly Centres and the development of Standard Operating Procedures. Additionally, she stated that such training programs would contribute to the development of a localized multi-sectoral training framework within the BPS.’[footnote 220]

15.2.3 The MYGA officials 2025 noted ‘… that Botswana Police Service is aware of GBV that affects persons with disabilities, and they have trained officers that deal with such cases. However, we note that there are still gaps in terms of specifics looking at the particular disability of an individual, but it’s an issue that they are very much alive to.’[footnote 221]

15.2.4 The BPS officials 2025 noted:

‘In term of training or capacity of police officers, the BPS has developed some training programmes in achieving best evidence-based practice in interviewing children. Officers have been and continue to be capacitated with appropriate competencies and skills for preventing acts of violence and providing the needed care to survivors of violence and abuse. Hence developments brought by the organisation facilitated effective and comprehensive provision of medical and psychological care to GBV survivors and children exposed to any form of abuse or harm. In order to protect victims, we also have the virtual juvenile courts. The BPS collaborated with the Ministry of Justice and Correctional Services, and they have adopted video teleconferencing. Equipment is fitted in the child-friendly centres to enable virtual hearings in children’s cases. The new model is being heralded as a groundbreaking, making court more accessible and convenient for the children. The BPS in its efforts has a strategic approach for promoting gender equality across all sectors and levels of policymaking, development and organisational practices. This is to ensure the integration of the gender perspective into the design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of all the policies, programmes and processes within the BPS.’[footnote 222]

15.2.5 The BPS officials 2025 further noted:

‘… all police officers are trained on gender-sensitive approaches to policing. There are a select few officers who are then deployed to the Gender and Child Protection Branch, and those officers are given even more specialised training and investigative tools to deal with GBV as a whole. That includes human trafficking and child protection issues. But all police officers are trained to adequately be able to provide assistance should there be an issue of GBV.’[footnote 223]

15.2.6 The BPS officials 2025 also explained that ‘… they work closely [with customary courts] because there are some cases that are handled by the customary court, and the police officers take those cases to the court. In some instances, the police are housed at the customary court; they have an officer at the customary court in the same building where their offices are.’[footnote 224]

15.2.7 However, the CEDAW report 2025 was concerned by ‘The absence of comprehensive capacity-building for law enforcement officers on gender-sensitive investigation and interviewing methods in gender-based violence cases …’[footnote 225]

15.3 Gender and Child Protection Branch

15.3.1 The BPS officials 2025 noted:

‘… in April 2021, the Gender and Child Protection Branch [GCPB] was established as a strategic initiative towards efficient and effective tackling of [GBV] … crimes. The mandate of the branch is to provide investigative support in cases of GBV and crimes involving children in all environments they are in, including offences which are facilitated by the use of the Internet. The formation of this branch was necessitated by a number of factors, such as the prevalence of GBV-related offences and also compliance with international and regional instruments and protocols … Furthermore, recommendations from various studies and reports … and the 2004 CRC reports placed a demand on the police for specialised and focused services, specifically tailored on GBV victims and vulnerable groups such as children. Since its inception, the branch has been working progressively towards improving response and handling of GBV cases, integration of child-friendly policing concepts to our processes, strengthening partnerships for a seamless and comprehensive service, improving the experience of victims on reporting cases and ensuring that police officers are equipped with the necessary training to respond to GBV and all crimes against children.’[footnote 226]

15.3.2 The BPS officials 2025 noted: ‘The Gender and Child Protection Branch has officers across all the 84 police stations in the country.’ They added that ‘there are more female than male officers deployed in the GCPB, to deal with such issues surrounding cases of GBV.’[footnote 227]

15.3.3 The BPS officials 2025 also noted:

‘… after the establishment of the branch itself. We have seen improved access to services. We have the GBV toll-free number [0800 600 144] where victims can call from the comfort of their homes at any time. We also have created safer spaces for reporting. Furthermore, we make case follow-ups from social media platforms. There[’s] … also the integration and child-friendly policing concept. The BPS established victim- and child-friendly spaces as a measure to eliminate disparities in accessing of justice for all victims, including key populations and those in vulnerable situations. We have 8 child-friendly centres across the country. These centres were developed to strengthen child-friendly and age-sensitive procedures for children in contact with the law. The objective of establishing these facilities was to create a justice system which is more aligned with children's specific and development needs and to facilitate child participation. This is a step in the right direction to attain improved access to justice. The BPS has also developed a set of guiding principles aimed at ensuring that officers are committed to integrating GBV into their work and are adequately skilled to do so. We have also developed the standard operating procedures [SOPs] for the reception, interviewing and referral of cases involving children at police stations. These are the tools that deal with GBV and child-related cases to ensure that interventions are well-coordinated, comprehensive and synchronised.’[footnote 228]

15.3.4 The BPS officials 2025 explained that GCPB staff ‘receive, investigate and provide referrals [of GBV cases from healthcare or social workers], and look at the safety measures that are needed for the victims, like shelters in cases where you can't take the victim back to the same environment that they come from … officers are from different professional backgrounds such as social work, psychology, investigations, early child development, counselling, etc.’[footnote 229]

15.3.5 The BPS officials 2025 confirmed that GCPB officers operate the standard operational procedures and train other officers in handling GBV cases. ‘GCPB is responsible for cascading all of its training, all the specific techniques that are needed to attend to GBV cases, to all police officers, so that at any point in time when somebody comes with an issue, they'll be attended to.’[footnote 230]

15.3.6 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 noted:

‘… the police have established the Gender and Child Protection Unit; this is a department that's mandated to deal with GBV cases and issues of child abuse. The unit was established in 2021 - it was a big thing. The president announced it as a way for them to deal with issues of domestic violence. They train every police officer [on handling GBV cases] because you'll find that a police officer or some of them will be first responders. They'll sit at the reception desk. So, they make sure that they train that one, they make sure they train the sergeant, the station commander. And from what we understand, since we've been supporting them with this work, they've incorporated that within the police college curriculum. Every new police officer that comes into the force is trained on how to deal with GBV and child abuse … [the official] did not know how many police officers are in the unit, but they're around the country … [the official] did not think every single police [officer] has been trained so far. But there's been efforts to incorporate it into the retraining of police officers who are already in service and then training of the new ones as well.’[footnote 231]

15.3.7 The UNFPA official 2025 commented that it was too early to tell if the GCPU was effective, noting:

‘… It's a relatively new unit, which is a step in the right direction towards recognising that we have a problem that needs a specific response, but it's still too new. It's not even countrywide ... some police stations … have specific GBV units, with resources, with training, police officers and cars and everything to respond to cases like that. So, it's still too new to see the impact, but we see the effort, one of them being that at least nowadays where such units are in these police stations when a woman comes to report, we've seen a difference in the way the case is handled. Initially, we'd come in and somebody would be shouting, “How can we help you?” But this thing has had a positive change even just in the way the reporting is being handled. The big question is beyond the reporting because you have the report and then you do an investigation and then the person goes to court … We now have the police saying they’ve done their job; they’ve investigated and handed [over] the evidence [to the Directorate of Public Prosecutions and the courts]. But then the magistrate is saying to grant bail or not – the loopholes – or if there’s insufficient evidence, they’ll still have to investigate better. Those are some of the challenges.’[footnote 232]

15.3.8 The UNFPA official 2025 also noted:

‘The GBV [unit] in the police station is under the police. They are in charge of GBV cases reported at the Police station. They are provided with specific training to handle GBV cases. The training is done as part of their police training, but then we also have specialised training where different organisations come and train them and so forth. Just a few weeks ago we had a session with the traditional leaders we are collaborating with, the [Directorate] of Public Prosecutions and the police. So, they'll have that as part of their pre-service training and then have specialised training specifically [provided by] that unit, but not necessarily [given] by the unit. I think the unit mainly does service provision [handling GBV cases] within police stations.’[footnote 233]

15.3.9 The BGBVC managers 2025 noted:

‘[The police] have about 8 child-friendly police stations, or child-friendly centres, which are trying to facilitate children to go [to the police]. Whether that’s working is another story, but they have developed those, they have created those in 8 districts so far, in collaboration with UNICEF. In Gaborone, at least, we do refer to them if we have cases of children, and they also refer cases to us … that BGBVC has a good relationship with the child friendly centre[s] and the police in general in Gaborone. They are usually responsive when we call for them.

‘… the branch is responsible for GBV cases plus children. In the past, the reporting system was stigmatising. There were issues of confidentiality in receiving cases, which deterred people from taking action. Now they’ve allowed for confidentiality, and that’s one of the reasons GBV cases are now not reported in the normal setting of the police station. The 8 branches have a separate space for GBV cases. They mostly hire psychologists, social workers and those who are trained to provide counselling as well. So, they’re not just dealing with cases; they can also provide counselling. [The BGBVC managers confirmed a lone woman could go to the child-friendly centres as well as children] … [and were aware of centres in] Kasane, Ghanzi, Francistown and Gaborone.’[footnote 234]

15.3.10 The BGBVC managers 2025 commenting on the impact of the GCPB noted:

‘… the feedback they got from people is that, particularly generally on the police around GBV, there’s still a lot to be done. What the police have now done is that at the police college itself they have a module where they are trying to teach the police about GBV and sensitive reporting and such things. But BGBVC still gets people that come and say they went to the police, but they weren’t assisted or that this and that happened. [The police] should actually be sensitive and have a clear understanding of GBV. Recently, the police also attended online training on working with perpetrators [of GBV]. They attended in large numbers.’[footnote 235]

15.3.11 The LB representatives 2025 agreed with the UKHO FFM that there was more reporting of GBV cases to the police. On whether this increased reporting indicated that the police had improved their handling of GBV cases, the representatives noted ‘… that the improvement had resulted from the creation of the GBV unit, so that the people dealing with these cases are trained and know how to improve them ... [The police] are not yet at a place where they are sufficient, but they are at a place where they can handle cases and make referrals.’[footnote 236]

15.3.12 The BGBVC managers 2025 noted:

‘… the police have the gender units for children, and then in the police stations, they have what they call gender desk officers or gender-focal persons. If that gender-focal person is not there, that means any other police [officer will deal with the matter]. In the Domestic Violence Act there are provisions [to the effect that] when someone comes into report [a GBV case], they cannot be assisted in the community service centre [of the police station]. But a lot of people just come in and [report in front of everyone], and no effort is made [to provide a private space] … that there's a lot that compromises the safety and the security of people who are experiencing GBV, coupled with the attitude of the community.’[footnote 237]

15.3.13 The WAR executive director 2025 commenting on the GCPB noted:

‘… it's a very good initiative, something that, if they had resources, would work. But what we see now is, like the one in Maun specifically, they only deal with children. It’s their children's unit, it's not gender-based violence. We still go to the main police office. There's a child-friendly unit. Only that is separate from the main place, separate from the main police station. So, from that [perspective] of looking after children, it's fine. There’s GBV-specific [support] at the police station; you still have to queue. I take people, then I have to sit and wait while they are attending other issues … [the police] say [they have specially trained officers], yes. Specially trained officers are probably there … GBV is now part of … [the police training] curriculum … [the police station in Maun] do[es] have private rooms because GBV is attended by CID, the Criminal Investigation Department. Those CID officers are the ones who work on GBV … [but] when you go to the police anytime, you'll be handled by the police or any police officer. The CID work during the day, but after hours, any police officer would be there to help. Officers in the special unit are there, they are trained, but they do other things as well. They’re in the CID, criminal investigation. So, they're part of that system, and they only work during the day. If I go to the police after hours, I will be assisted by the person who's there, not – or not necessarily – a GBV person … [but a woman would regardless of who was working be taken into a private room].’[footnote 238]

15.3.14 The WAR executive director 2025 also acknowledged the police had improved. ‘[T]here had been more training, more interaction with WAR and more interaction from government as well. Setting up the Gender and Child Protection Unit [in Maun] had helped, even though they're still working on children, not everyone. But at least it's something that's there. There’s intent.’[footnote 239]

15.3.15 The MWT representatives 2025 noted that the GCPB, set up around April 2025 in Maun, makes a difference. Women ‘are free to speak, [previously] when people coming and going [a woman] would not be able to express themselves [at a police station]. When indoors [in private] a woman is able to say anything. It's safe, definitely it's good.’[footnote 240]

15.3.16 The BONELA representatives 2025 noted:

‘… what the police have done, which is innovative, it just needs to be scaled up, is create gender desks in police stations [the GCPB]. These help in terms of expediting access to justice for victims and in terms of dealing with cases from a gender lens, which is critical. Unfortunately, not every police station has these desks, but it's long overdue that each police station should have such a desk … when we know there is a gender desk [at a police station] we report cases directly to them and it makes life very easy. The officers don't take GBV issues lightly. They act on the cases fast, more so than other police officers.’[footnote 241]

15.3.17 The UKHO FFM observed that the police had said cases would he handled sympathetically, that if an officer from GCPB was not present other police trained to handled GBV cases are, and a woman would be offered a private space to report an incident. The LB representatives 2025 noted there are ‘… some survivors of violence who will testify to that. But the majority of them would say that is not how it is. The improvement is not the standard way. But the police are doing their best with GBV cases.’[footnote 242]

15.4 Access to the police

15.4.1 The BPS annual report 2024 provided a map showing the police divisions and police stations across the country:

243

15.4.2 An undated entry on the BPS website lists the districts, the police stations in those districts and the addresses of the police stations244.

15.4.3 The police operate:

  • a general emergency telephone line – 999[footnote 245]
  • a toll-free telephone line for GBV cases – 0800 600 144[footnote 246]

15.4.4 The BPS officers 2025 noted ‘accessibility to police services is quite good in Botswana. Even the smallest villages would have access to at least a Police Post … even in posts, they try as much as possible to have the representation of both female and male officers … there are also customary courts, and that at every customary court, there’s a police office. Customary courts are in almost every village.’[footnote 247]

15.4.5 The UNFPA official 2025 considered,

‘… it would be relatively easy [to contact the police]. You can pick up the phone and call. But the question would be whether they’d be there when you needed them, because sometimes you call in the middle of the night – a woman has been beaten, or sometimes you even call as a neighbour when a woman has been beaten next door, or your colleague – but the police tell you to come back [later], right now they don’t have a car. So, the reporting part is easy; you just call 999 or you can physically go to the police station. The response is a different matter.’[footnote 248]

15.4.6 The WAR executive director 2025 agreed with the UKHO FFM observation that in a rural area, a police station might be small, people know each other, but in a city, there may be younger police who are better trained and the person is not part of the local community meaning more access to justice. The director added ‘that greater accessibility in the cities even included access to information – just knowing where you can go, who can help you.’[footnote 249]

15.4.7 The FE officials 2025 also considered it was ‘probably hard, but did not know, for women in a rural area as there is less infrastructure to go to a police station but assume [this is the case]. The women on our projects, for instance, had difficulties in going to a place as there's no transport and it was hard for them to move around the city. This would be an obstacle when trying to reach out for help. Economic means are very dire - complicated. There is a lot of poverty in the villages.’[footnote 250]

15.4.8 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 indicated that

‘Women feel more able to seek assistance from the police than a few years ago, but stated: ‘it's relative. Depends on which part of the country. [Think it is better] in more urban areas, the police are much more proactive in terms of encouraging women to consult them. Whereas in rural areas, I think they would be much more hesitant because they are in smaller communities. If you go to a police officer, they most likely know you or your family… The first avenue would probably be the village chief, because they also play a role in mediation of family conflicts in most instances. Actually, people would prefer to go to the chief than the police because the chief would just be mediation. There's no punishment.’[footnote 251]

15.5 Directorate of Public Prosecution

15.5.1 The GOROB website in undated entry noted:

‘The Directorate of Public Prosecutions is headed by the Director of Public Prosecutions appointed in terms of Section 51A of the Constitution. Our primary mandate is the prosecution of criminal cases before all courts of the land, criminal applications and appeals arising from criminal litigation.

‘The Directorate operates from the main office in Gaborone and also has satellite offices in Francistown, Maun, Palapye, Lobatse and Selibe Phikwe.

‘Primary Statutes – The primary penal statutes used by the Directorate in criminal prosecution are the Penal Code, Criminal Procedure and Evidence Act which gives guidance on general matters of procedure in criminal litigation. However, the prosecutorial mandate extends broadly to all such other legislation except where statute provides for trial by court martial. In executing his/her mandate, the Director is constitutionally obligated to consult with the Attorney General on matters considered by the latter to be of national importance.’[footnote 252]

15.5.2 However, the Botswana Guardian Sun, a Botswanan newspaper, in an article dated 7 February 2025 noted:

‘The Office of the Director of Public Prosecution (DPP) continues the process of taking over the prosecutorial functions from the Botswana Police Service as directed by Presidential Directive of 2006 … since the inception of the project, the DPP has extended its offices to Maun, Selibe Phikwe, Palapye, Kasane and Tsabong.

‘[However, the Attorney General Mmako Abram said] … we still need to have [DPP] footprints in other parts of the country and as a result require more resources to do so … We have however, noticed that the project has brought about additional workload as it uses the existing resources … In this connection, we have been discussing this with the Minister as well as Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Justice and Correctional Services and have agreed to request Cabinet that we put the Project on hold until it is properly resourced” …

‘[The Attorney General] … pointed out that the provision of IT equipment and access to reliable internet facilities is essential for purposes of research when officers within the justice ecosystem carry out their respective mandates, be it investigation, prosecution or adjudication … revealing that the DPP has been engaged … in the process of digitising its processes. Abram said as a primary step, the electronic Case Management System has been rolled out to all DPP offices for utilisation.’[footnote 253]

15.5.3 An article in Botswana youth, a Botswanan online magazine, dated 2 April 2025 noted ‘… the Director of Public Prosecutions, Ms. Nomsa Moatswi, acknowledged the challenges faced by the DPP, including case withdrawals, victims’ reluctance to report, and failure to follow court procedures. To address these issues, she noted that a strict policy has been implemented, preventing the withdrawal of certain cases, including GBV-related matters, without the complainant’s written consent.’[footnote 254]

15.5.4 The BPS officers 2025 noted ‘police officers take cases to the customary courts. In [the] higher courts, [the] Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) takes charge. A police officer may be delegated responsibility to prosecute at Magistrate’s Court by DPP.’[footnote 255]

15.6 Effectiveness

15.6.1 The OSAC report 2025 stated:

‘The police are well-intentioned and active in their efforts to prevent and combat crime. However, personnel and resource shortages limit operational effectiveness. Vehicle and foot patrols in residential and commercial areas are infrequent. Mobile response capability is limited ...

‘The Botswana Police is [sic] responsive to emergency calls, but response time to the scene of the incident is slow compared to the United States. In response to shortfalls, there are community policing programs in many neighbourhoods in Gaborone and other major cities such as Maun and Francistown. Community Policing programs have been effective at deterring criminal elements when there is active support of private citizens, who report crimes through social media platforms, the Botswana Police Service monitor. The Botswana Police Service also uses CCTV to monitor neighbourhoods and major intersections through a program called the “Safe City Project.” The government has installed more than 500 surveillance cameras in Gaborone and Francistown to supplement police services. The program is effective, and the Government of Botswana has called for additional surveillance cameras to be installed.’[footnote 256]

15.6.2 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 noted when asked by the UKHO if the police would intervene in a GBV case:

‘[The police will] … take a sworn statement from the victim, and then they'll open a case, investigate the perpetrator, and they'll ask the victim, “Do you want to press charges?” Then if they say yes, then they’ll press charges, they’ll detain them, and the perpetrator will have to wait for a date to see the magistrate. And if they want to apply for bail, they'll apply for bail. Then they’ll wait for a court date and the trial will start. Sometimes, especially if it's married people or long-term partners, the woman will drop the charges or the family will intervene and say, “We'll deal with this at a family level”, and then they'll drop the charges. But yes, if the prosecutor tried, they'll get the punishment (usually a fine if found guilty).’[footnote 257]

15.6.3 The International diplomatic source 2 – 2025 noted

‘… [the police] are active in implementing the law but there is a gap in terms of their capacity and their ability to intervene, a lot to be learned. There's some training in police stations to allow them to handle GBV cases, but they do interviews in an open space … it was police structures that perhaps are not equipped enough to handle sensitive matters in a proper way. If the police do not [handle these cases sensitively] this might disincentivise victims from approaching law enforcement.’[footnote 258]

15.6.4 The International diplomatic source 2 – 2025 considered that the police were willing to assist but

‘… recounted how [they] … had asked the police about GBV during the field trip and that most of them had said sometimes it was OK to understand where the man, the perpetrator, was coming from, and that because most GBV related to infidelity, they felt it was justified. There's still a lot of unlearning to be done so that the police don't have bias in situations like that.

They tend to personalise it, thinking “if I was in this situation and I found that my partner was cheating and the child raised wasn't mine, I don't blame the guy for doing that”. So, because that's already a mentality that exists it is problematic in terms of whether or not they can sufficiently help a victim if they come reporting and access these services. ‘[footnote 259]

15.6.5 The UNFPA official 2025 considered:

‘… there are a lot of [loopholes in protection] … Just recently, about 2 to 3 weeks ago, we had a woman murdered at the University of Botswana [UB] in broad daylight at work. She had a restraining order against [the perpetrator]. Half the time, when a woman has a restraining order, no one knows about it. There are no first responders or anything to [step in to protect] her if the person who is subject to the restraining order violates it by approaching her. So, there are loopholes in the protection system.

‘[The FFM team queried of the UB case was a single example or representative of other women’s experiences] … it is very common, particularly with repeat offenders. People on bail, people with restraining orders are very common. That's why currently there's a bit of an uproar around bail. People feel like people perpetrate violence, they go to court, they are given bail, they come back, and they commit the same crime – or even worse, to the point of killing – because they're out on bail. We have repeat offenders who've been out on bail multiple times.… The first weakness is the investigation part because judges rely on the evidence presented before them. [The decision whether] to grant or refuse bail is dependent on what evidence they are dealing with. The second [weakness] is the protection mechanism, for instance, [implementation in the case of bail and restraining orders]. While the law can guarantee somebody whose life is under threat protection by means of a restraining order, the implementation of that is a problem because it seems like it's just a piece of paper that somebody's carrying around and enforcement is a big problem in terms of protection.’[footnote 260]

15.6.6 The UNFPA official 2025 added that the police

‘… have power in theory, on paper [to provide protection]. When people see the police, when I’m walking around at midnight and I see the police, I might get a sense that the police are here for protection. We have the police arresting somebody who is perpetrating violence. They do investigations and so forth. The whole process will go to a point where there’s a woman being given a restraining order. One then wonders where the police come in to make sure that that restraining order is enforced. Can a woman just call and say that the person I have a restraining order against is violating it, they’re following me or they’re in my vicinity? Half the time, the police are challenged – “We don’t have a car, we don’t have resources.” So, they may have the power, but are also limitations, particularly in terms of resources and other things.

‘… [the official] couldn’t confidently say [the police] have the willingness [to provide protection]. If you call to report, you get multiple interrogations [questions by the police] and things like that. One’s life is under threat [from the perpetrator] … therefore not sure about the willingness [of the police to provide protection]. Maybe some [police officers are willing], but not all … they weren’t all on the same page.’[footnote 261]

15.6.7 The FAB representatives 2025 also noted in regard to the police’s approach to GBV cases:

‘… there is an underreaction to the approach to abuse that often leads to either rape and/or murder by a partner. For example, if you say to the police, “I fought with my man or somebody on the street and they said they would kill me,” they tend to underreact to that, or if you fought and it was almost physical, they'll tell you, “Go and talk it out.” People don't just wake up and kill somebody; there’s usually a lead-up to it, especially where intimate partners are concerned. But because the police tend to underreact to the lead-up, it begs the question again of just how effective is the training that they are getting? If I left my house to come and tell you somebody said to me, ‘I will kill you,’ you must take that seriously. There's a reason why I thought I’d report it.

‘[Asked if it was a weakness in their training or investigatory processes the representatives agreed] … and that it’s personal, cultural. Even cat-calling is normalised, when you're walking down the street. [Men] don't usually go as far as to grab you, which apparently happens in some countries, but just somebody saying unsavoury words as you walk by as an indicator that they could gain access to you without your permission, in the form of rape.’[footnote 262]

15.6.8 The MOJCS officials 2025 commented on the University of Botswana murder and when asked by the UKHO FFM team if it was representative of other cases noted:

‘… thought it was subjective, also gave an example of a case of a female police officer who was stabbed by her partner outside of the police station. These cases are shocking and there has public discussion on how to make sure these don’t happen again. But although not the first of its kind [this type of violence] is not prevalent. So, [this will be achieved] through the GBV bill [see Gender-specific legislation above], continuing with the death penalty [to act as deterrence] but there is a need to find the root cause. Even if [electronic] tags were used for restraining orders, if the woman is out at the mall or at work it will not be possible for the police to monitor these situations. As the president noted, it is not possible to monitor people in their home. Laws need to be made to work but there is also a need to change peoples’ mindsets.’[footnote 263]

15.6.9 The FAB representatives 2025 noted the University of Botswana case of June 2025 referred above:

‘… brought to the fore the weaknesses in both the judicial system and the police investigating system. If I commit a crime in Gaborone and I leave Gaborone with the case being opened against me and I've been charged in the magistrates’ court here [in Gaborone] and then I go to Francistown and I commit a similar offence or a different offence, the police and the magistrates’ courts in Francistown will not be able to pick that up because our systems operate in siloes. There is a lack of connectivity or systems that support magistrates courts, the DPP [Directorate of Public Prosecutions] which is the prosecuting arm [of the state criminal justice system], and the investigating unit of the Botswana Police Service. So in this instance, the restraining order … was obtained in Mochudi, which is outside of Gaborone, but not far. When systems don't speak to each other, there's no way of knowing that this person has a restraining order against them or has been accused of a similar offence. It is something that the Administration of Justice [the judiciary] has spoken about and the police service has thought about, but they need to meet to develop a system that would then allow them to interlink with each police department.’[footnote 264]

15.6.10 The FAB representatives 2025 also noted that there was

‘… [a lack of a national database of reported crimes] … it's also a resource issue, because [the police’s] resources are limited … although … the police are being trained, when you speak to individual station commanders of various police stations, they will tell you that it's very difficult to manage the resources. Transfers of police officers are not done by them, so you'll find that, [for example], in 2023, you have 10 police officers who were trained in GBV and gender mainstreaming, etc, and then in 2025, 10 of them are transferred to different units and your staff complement is not replaced with people who've undergone the training, so there's a lack of continuity in education of police officers and judicial officers.’[footnote 265]

15.6.11 The FAB representatives 2025 also had the view ‘… a GBV survivor … [is] often not protected from intimidation by the perpetrator and his family, which is a situation that one of their colleagues had faced. Even … the lawyer, was being harassed by the perpetrator and his family, and there was no protection.’ One agreed that there was no witness protection system[footnote 266].

15.6.12 The LAB CEO 2025, in response to the UKHO FFM team observation that some sources had told them that the police’s investigatory processes could be improved, agreed this was the case:

‘This observation was also made by one police officer at a certain conference, that not only in matters of GBV but in a lot of cases where the investigation is prosecutor led, the police are more likely to know what evidence to collect and how to collect it properly to ensure that the prosecution is successful … the police prosecute in the name of the DPP [Director of Public Prosecutions] or on behalf of the state … – a legacy situation. There was a project previously for the DPP to take over all prosecution to provide quality prosecution and ensure things were done in the best interests of the judicial system … However, there were obstacles. The police have a footprint in every corner of the country, and in most areas there’s a magistrate. But there will not be a DPP [office in all areas] because the DPP was predominantly in the big cities and towns. Expanding in order to take over the function of prosecuting means you need a presence there. When you’ve been detaining someone and 48 hours elapses, a DPP representative ought to be there to go to court about the person’s detention, and there were just not enough lawyers to do that. There was not enough budget to hire that many lawyers. They had to amend the scope of the project of taking over prosecution from the police, so the police are still prosecuting and the DPP is prosecuting in areas where it has a footprint and resources.’[footnote 267]

15.6.13 The LAB CEO 2025 in reference to whether a victim of GBV in Gaborone would be assigned a lawyer from the DPP explained:

‘… they would not: a GBV case will have aspects of civil law and aspects of criminal law, so where the matter is under the DVA the DPP would not be involved and an entity such as LAB or certain NGOs, if approached by the victim, might represent them to access remedies under the DVA. But if somebody has been physically harmed criminal law would come to play and the DPP would be involved to represent the State in prosecuting the accused and where allowed by its precepts, LAB might represent such an accused person. Cases must be disposed quickly otherwise there is a negative impact on the victim, having to relive their experience over a protracted period of time and their healing process disrupted.’[footnote 268]

15.6.14 The BGBVC managers 2025 noted ‘… what they know is that the whole criminal justice system needs to do better. It’s not just the police, because it starts with the police, but it goes to the Directorate of Public Prosecutions (DPP), it goes to the courts and then the prisons, because prisons have a different role. For them, it's when somebody has already been convicted, or when someone is waiting to go for trial.’[footnote 269]

15.6.15 The BGBVC managers 2025 also noted

‘…as regards safety, there is an issue they are trying to address: it’s confrontation, which is traumatic to survivors… They're trying to improve it for the children to not have it face to face… But for adult survivors and victims, there’s still confrontation in front of the police. It's complicated because the police say if they don’t do that, they won’t have heard the other side of the story in the presence of the other person. But the other person who is being asked to come and confront [the alleged perpetrator] is obviously already traumatised. How are they going find courage in the presence of [the perpetrator]?[footnote 270]

15.6.16 However, the Love Botswana representatives acknowledged they did not have statistics for the GBV cases generally. LB had assisted 213 cases between January and March 2025 of which 13 involved some form of GBV. The representatives added that ‘the problem with the numbers is that most of them [GBV victims] come and then they don't go to the police station, so it's hard for us to track them. But the previous quarter [October to December 2024?], we had 18, so it’s dropped … [The cases handled were … through self-referrals; [people] come to [LB’s] offices. LB hasn’t had agency referrals. Most of them are just members of the community or self-referrals.’[footnote 271]

15.6.17 The Love Botswana representatives 2025 also noted, referring to the GCPB over the previous 3 to 4 months, that the police have ‘… tried to mediate [in GBV cases] because they've been very prepared in mediation. But with the recent outcomes [the police have] … seen with GBV, the danger that women are facing, they’ve come from mediation to questioning whether what they typically do in this situation is working, and they’ve tried to move more towards action.’ The representatives ‘thought [the GCPB] … was making a difference but very slowly because the culture has already been instilled around GBV. [The change] is not immediate even once the laws are in place.’[footnote 272]

15.6.18 The LB representatives 2025 also thought

‘… things were improving in terms of legislation, but that the impact is not there. Even cases that are reported, that are legitimate, will stay [in the criminal justice system] for a very long time without being judged. There are a lot of loopholes within the system itself. If there are 10 cases of rape, only one case will have been tried in 3 months and the other cases will still be under investigation or information will still be missing. The system is there, but because this system is not utilised fully … whether this is because of the people that are dealing with the system or the community that utilise the system – there are a lot of gaps within the system itself. Even when legitimate cases are admitted to the system, the system is just not dealing with them to bring out the result.’[footnote 273]

15.6.19 The LB representatives 2025 in comparing the effectiveness of the criminal justice system in handling criminal cases generally and GBV cases specifically, considered

‘… less time and effort goes into GBV. Compared to common murder cases or theft, she thought GBV had less priority, although more of a spotlight had been shone on it now … explaining that with cases of GBV, the justice system is not responding as it should. In Maun, there is only the High Court, and it’s not handling most of the cases. There is a massive crisis, and the justice system is just not that responsive. For some time, they [the government] have wanted to improve the justice system. There were mobile courts, but they weren’t really the answer … confirmed that there are [mobile courts] but explained that [they] … had never experienced one ...’[footnote 274]

15.6.20 The LB representatives 2025 considered that there was more reporting of GBV incidents to the police than in the past, noting ‘that the improvement [in handling cases] had resulted from the creation of the GBV unit, so that the people dealing with these cases are trained and know how to improve them. They are not yet at a place where they are sufficient, but they are at a place where they can handle cases and make referrals [to healthcare and social services].’[footnote 275]

15.6.21 On how the police handled GBV cases, including if a woman who had experienced GBV could report this in a private room, at the police station in Maun the LB representatives 2025 noted ‘it is still a challenge in that regard because … the [GCPB] … is outside the police station, some distance away. It’s not always that you will find an appropriate person from the GBV unit in the main police station, only in their satellite office. When you go to the main police, what you will find are just general police and they may still investigate in front of everyone … people come [to the main police station] without knowing about the [GBV] unit.’[footnote 276]

15.6.22 The LB representatives 2025 added ‘… when you go to the police, you find nice GBV billboards [outside the police station explaining how cases will be processed]. But the system itself within [the station], when you go there with a GBV case, is not quite a scandal but is nowhere near the way it should be even at a district level.’[footnote 277]

15.6.23 In response to the UKHO FFM’s summary that the police had shown some willingness to provide protection and there was a general government willingness to make things better, but implementation could be better, the WAR executive director 2025 ‘confirmed that yes, it could be better.’[footnote 278] The WAR executive director went on to describe the negative impact of tradition on the ability of the police to provide protection.

15.6.24 The FE officials 2025 noted ‘that women can report [incidents of GBV] to the police, but they were not separated [from the perpetrator or other people in the police station] when disclosing information about what happened to them. This does not encourage them to report if they cannot ensure safety and privacy.’[footnote 279]

15.6.25 The MWT representatives 2025 noted ‘normally if a woman is sexually molested/harassed/beaten, they go to the police who take them to the shelter [in Maun].’ The representatives further noted the police ‘do protect [women] but they do not have enough resources, to go to rural areas. If ask, they may come after 2 hours or say they do not have a car by which time the incident has happened … [a woman] would be treated fairly [at a police station] although did not know that much [about this]. Had not come across any woman who said that [they had not been treated fairly] but it takes forever to solve [cases].’[footnote 280]

15.6.26 The MWT representatives 2025 commented on the experiences of women. ‘It depends on the type of … police officer [they report their case to]. Some are willing to help but others might [blame the woman], saying she [spent the perpetrator’s money on alcohol]. Most of the cases where women are killed, they reported to the police once or twice. The police don’t follow up or question the perpetrator but let him go free.’[footnote 281]

15.6.27 The BBL representatives 2025 noted ‘the police have youth-friendly, child-friendly policies. BBL don’t refer them to the main police; they take them to a special police station … the police there wear ordinary clothes, and there are TVs … [There are] about 4 [police officers].’ The child friendly police station is not open 24hours a day but ‘BBL work with WAR [Women Against Rape]. If there’s a case that requires urgent attention, they refer it to WAR, and WAR refers it to the police in the morning, or you can refer it to the main police.’[footnote 282]

15.6.28 The LEGABIBO representatives 2025 agreed with the statement put them that ‘there are quite strong anti-GBV laws to protect women, but implementation is the problem’[footnote 283].

15.7 Implementation of protection orders

15.7.1 See Protection orders above for information on their legal basis and the different types of orders including restraining orders.

15.7.2 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 noted that women can get restraining orders ‘… but recently we found that the police are not very effective at enforcing restraining orders. I think 2 or 3 weeks ago there was an unfortunate incident [at the University of Botswana where a female employee was murdered by her former partner] where this woman got a restraining order against her partner, and a few days later, the man followed her to work at the university [of Botswana] and stabbed her in open space … Not a lot of people take out restraining orders. That's when the case has escalated …’[footnote 284]

15.7.3 The UKHO FFM observed that the University of Botswana case of June 2025 referred to by the official may not be representative of all cases. The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 noted ‘Yes, true. But the magistrate who presided over the case was quite vocal in criticising the police about how they let the deceased woman down … Well, I don't think [the case referred above reveals how effective the police are] … that would be unfair on the police. I don't think it paints a bad picture of the police. I think the police, of course, do the best that they can to enforce restraining orders and so.’ [footnote 285] The FAB representatives 2025 confirmed that the police can arrest people (men) who breach restraining orders, noting ‘it does happen and that there have been cases where restraining orders were breached and people were arrested, but that after about 7 days they were released.’[footnote 286]

15.7.4 The LAB CEO 2025 noted when asked about the police’s willingness to be involved in restraining orders ‘… she’d got the sense that there had been great improvement in this space over time. Times past, the police used to encourage the parties to resolve the matters between themselves but with the increase of advocacy for women rights and against GBV, with the incidence of GBV increasing over time, particularly during the COVID era, the police responsiveness and treatment/interaction with victims vastly improved …’[footnote 287]

15.7.5 The LAB CEO 2025 ‘explained that the police out of mere practice would then help the person enforce [a restraining order] … although it is not their duty to do so.’[footnote 288]

15.7.6 A BPS officials confirmed that the police is not always aware when restraining orders are in place, stating ‘we have to realise that the issue of restraining orders is outside the police because the police are not necessarily involved in getting the restraining order.’[footnote 289]

15.7.7 The MYGA officials 2025 noted: ‘The other gap we have identified is that when restraining orders are issued, enforcement can be problematic because [the woman] who has applied for the restraining order is the one who has to sound the alarm when the perpetrator is within her radius. If he [, the perpetrator, approaches] unnoticed, that is dangerous. So we see the need to start using technology and modernising our services for effectiveness.’[footnote 290]

15.7.8 The FE officials 2025 commenting on the murder of the woman at the University of Botswana in June 2025 ,

‘… thought it [had gained public interest] because the woman had taken [several] measures to protect herself – she had gone to the police, had got a restraining order …had talked about [her concerns] with colleagues, and that it happened inside the university where there's security at the entrance and people around (it's not just a domestic case) – but it still happened. It's a perfect case study of a [woman doing everything she could to protect herself but still being murdered].’[footnote 291]

15.7.9 The FE officials 2025, on being asked if they were of similar cases, noted ‘there [was the case of the woman murdered] inside BGBVC in 2023. A similar case [to the UofB incident] of a woman reaching out for help from specialists and it happened inside the [woman’s] shelter.’[footnote 292] This case was also referred to by the BGBVC managers 2025[footnote 293] and the WAR executive director 2025[footnote 294].

15.8 Implementation of bail

15.8.1 See also the Bail Act, 2024, for discussion of the changes to the bail process for the introduction of the law.

15.8.2 The UNFPA official 2025 noted:

‘… there's a public outcry around the bail system. We have a lot of these repeat offenders out there. Bail is part of the legal system. You can't necessarily deny people bail simply because the public is saying these are repeat offenders. [Courts] say to grant or not grant bail, they consider the evidence that is presented before them, and the facts and merits of the case. In some cases, you hear that the investigators will be saying they’re still investigating, and in that case then the magistrate will say they can't keep somebody incarcerated while [the investigations are ongoing] … the fact that there are a lot of perpetrators of GBV, particularly repeat offenders, who are out on bail because the investigations are still ongoing, says a lot. These are some of the things we're observing, but we don’t have data from the police or the courts. But if you speak to the police and ask them how many perpetrators of GBV are repeat offenders, how many of them have been granted bail and committed similar or even worse offences while out on bail, [it would be] quite a lot. Even the perpetrator of the [University of Botswana] UB murder [referred above] was out on bail. So, a lot of them are repeat offenders and they commit most of these while they're out on bail.’[footnote 295]

15.8.3 The MWT representatives 2025 commented ‘… sometimes [the government does] fail us. Most women who are killed, they will have reported the case to the police, the perpetrator is arrested but later is released and kills the woman … there are many cases … they knew the women. On that, the government has failed us. Some perpetrators are given bail then [kill a woman]. Some perpetrators kill one person then, after bail, will kill the witness.’[footnote 296]

15.8.4 The LAB CEO 2025 noted:

‘LAB … assist in getting restraining orders and protection orders and we work closely with NGOs, particularly WAR [Women Against Rape] in Maun. We're actually in the same compound as WAR, leasing one of the offices there, so we get a lot of referrals from them and are singing from the same hymn book in terms of the Maun area … in Gaborone, informally we also work with BONELA, but they deal with the demographic [victims of GBV] within their mandate whether there's indigence [state of poverty] or not. But they will talk about it further on their side and if [an indigent] is coming to them and has an issue that doesn't fall within their focus area – for instance, you are gay, but the issue that you're coming for help for, from BONELA is inheritance which they do not deal with – they will refer such person to us because our focus includes succession and inheritance laws or property issues ... They have their objectives and demographics that they're focused on, so we complement each other.’[footnote 297]

15.8.5 The BGBVC managers 2025 noted:

‘There are lots of people on bail for murder, and then they commit crimes again. Even when there are restraining orders, they break them. BGBVC knew “a whole lot of cases” where a person hadn’t been arrested again for [violating] a restraining order. It’s a serious problem and it means that the victims, the survivors, their families are suffering and are not safe at all.

‘… [Also] noted that in the case where the woman was murdered at the University of Botswana [in June 2025], one of the things the magistrate said was that the police failed in their duty because the man was subject to a restraining order. He had defiled the woman’s daughter years ago. They had withdrawn the case but the woman had a restraining order against him. They had been to court that day, the same day that he murdered her. He followed her afterwards because he was given bail even though there was a restraining order. So cases go through the criminal justice system, but another thing the High Court judge said – and this magistrate also – is that it's very important that when you bring a case [before the court], you bring the history. Where a person has repeatedly committed crimes, it cannot be [just] a single incident … this showed that there is negligence – either negligence or a certain level of ignorance, but she suspected more likely negligence.

‘[Asked if this was negligence, the CEO] … confirmed this, noting that the magistrate had been very frustrated – how had the restraining order been missed, and how could we find ourselves granting bail when we shouldn’t have, to someone who was already in our system? And then he leaves and goes and commits murder the same day.’[footnote 298]

15.8.6 On whether the University of Botswana case was representative of GBV cases generally, the BGBVC managers 2025 noted:

‘… it’s very recent, and very sensational [but] …it's [not] the only one. The week before, another woman had just been murdered, and that same week, a man had driven a truck into a house and killed a child of his ex-girlfriend. So maybe it's because of the sensitisation around the case, but there are other cases … that BGBVC have their own case of a woman who was murdered here [at BGBVC in Gaborone]. It has not even made its way to court. It happened in May 2023. She was murdered by her husband in our office, our counselling room … he wasn’t given bail. He's still in prison. But just a few weeks later, a man murdered his wife and girlfriend, and he was given bail. Security and safety of survivors is a big problem. BGBVC have bars on their windows and there are people where they need to say to their security guard, ‘Here's a picture. When this person comes, it's not safe.’[footnote 299]

15.8.7 The LB representatives 2025 noted:

‘… they had heard [of the Bail act 2024 which had tightened requirements for the release of individuals suspected of committing crimes including GBV] … but that they hadn’t seen it at the community level. They hadn’t seen the strengthening of the system because the cases are there, the incidents are there. People don’t get it at the community level and survivors might not understand why this person isn’t being held in jail, but that is the law. The person can’t be kept in jail because they haven’t been found guilty. As service providers, they are still saying that even though the bail system has been strengthened, it is not actually serving the process.’[footnote 300]

15.8.8 The BONELA representatives 2025 noted: ‘We also think bail needs to be reconsidered for domestic violence cases - we do not consider bail should be given in domestic violence cases until the state has established there is no risk for victims. We are seeing perpetrators get bail and recommit offences.’[footnote 301]

15.8.9 The LEGABIBO representatives 2025 noted ‘you can do something [today] and get bailed tomorrow. The bail laws are really lenient to perpetrators. You could kill someone today and then tomorrow you’d be out on bail … the other thing is that laws were being passed [such as the Bail Act 2024] but were not being implemented, so you could have a bail law passed by Parliament but not effectively put into place.’[footnote 302]

15.8.10 The BPS officials 2025 acknowledged:

‘… the issue of bail is a big concern for all residents of BW. Citizens generally praise the police for arrests in GBV offences however they complain that unfortunately following the arrest, the perpetrators are then let out on bail. According to Botswana laws, one is presumed innocent until found guilty in court, hence the reason why bail is given whilst awaiting trial. This unfortunately leads to a lot of reoffending in GBV. The issue is being discussed in many platforms in attempts to find a lasting resolution … the Bail Act 2024 has also narrowed the existing gaps.

‘[The criteria for releasing a GBV offender under the Bail Act 2024] … depends on the seriousness of the offence. If it’s common assault, normally the police would arrest [the suspect] and detain them for 48 hours, then they’d release them on what’s called police bail. For serious offences, they might be held until [the case was heard before a] court. In the past, there used to be that problem of bail being granted. Now there’s a new Bail Act, which is [tougher]. It passed last year [2024] … there was no such Act [legislating bail procedures] before.’[footnote 303]

15.8.11 The BPS officials 2025 confirmed that the Bail Act 2024 provided clearer guidelines on when to provide bail,

‘… they should be followed before the accused can be released. All necessary process should be followed involving the victim and the [police] station commander of the area, and any other person who is involved in the matter should also be involved. [They considered it had had an impact] because the accused in the University of Botswana case has been refused [bail] …[The suspect in that case] continues to be remanded in prison and that stakeholders were called to come and show why he should or should not be bailed, in accordance with the new Bail Act.

‘… on paper, as a country, there are lots of efforts to try and fix all these problems. However, in terms of effectiveness in cascading new initiatives such as this one [the use of bail], we have a challenge as a country because of resource limitations. The way the Bail Act is set, we shouldn't really see a lot of people being granted bail.’[footnote 304]

15.9 Arrests and prosecutions

15.9.1 There are no official figures for the number of GBV cases which are arrested or prosecuted in the sources consulted (see Bibliography). The UKHO FFM asked sources in Botswana, including the BPS, for this data but none had been provided at the time of writing (December 2025).

15.9.2 The GOROB ACHPR submission 2023 stated ‘The prosecution rate [of GBV cases] improved from 51% in 2021 to 68% in 2022.’ However, the submission did not provide the source of the information, what offences fell within the definition of GBV, what was the absolute number of cases prosecuted and through which courts[footnote 305].

15.9.3 The USSD HR report 2023 noted: ‘Authorities effectively enforced laws against rape when victims pressed charges, although police noted victims often declined to press charges against perpetrators.’[footnote 306] However, the FH report 2024 stated without referring to underlying evidence or statistics that ‘Perpetrators are rarely prosecuted.’[footnote 307]

15.9.4 The UNFPA official 2025 was not aware of data on arrests or prosecutions[footnote 308].

15.9.5 The FAB representatives 2025 referring to the GOROB’s representations to the CEDAW in May 2025 ‘… a man from the Ministry of Justice mention[ed] how a few cases that were reported were successfully prosecuted in terms of abuse, and the number was just appalling. [FAB] … recalled him saying 3 were successful, but there was no context of 3 out of how many.’[footnote 309]

15.9.6 The MOJCS officials 2025 stated that GBV cases do not go through the customary courts, noting

‘… There is no longer mediation [by the police] because people used to reconcile at the Police stations after which the other party will kill the other, and the Police were blamed for not doing their mandate. Whenever a case is brought to the police, it is investigate[d] and submitted to the Directorate of Public Prosecutions for consideration to prosecute … However, with customary law, the person is not marrying an individual, they are marring the whole family. So, whenever there's a conflict, the family considers it is in the best interests of the parties to mediate. But of course, the couple can make whatever decisions they feel are necessary in the circumstances.’[footnote 310]

15.9.7 The MOJCS officials 2025 also noted ‘… the police are very effective at receiving cases and preparing these for trial but the challenge they face is that sometimes the couple reconciles. There is also the issue of economic livelihoods, especially for women. Sometimes the man is the caregiver and the provider, so a woman has to consider the economic costs/benefits [of pursuing a case]. That’s when cases are closed – unfortunately the police cannot force a victim to give evidence.’[footnote 311]

15.9.8 The MOJCS officials 2025 also suggested there are social and cultural pressures why a couple might stay together rather than for the victim to press charges:

‘… there is still customary law. Parents are guardians of a marriage and often by virtue of customary law the expectation is for the couple to fight for the marriage even in tough situations. Sometimes the man can be the monster, but in spite of that, the couple cannot just walk away. There is also the practice of bogadi - dowry - where a man provides a ‘gift’ [of cattle, for example, to the wife’s family]. So, if there is a marriage breakdown the wife's family has to return the cattle [the gift]. So [there] sometimes [is the expectation] to hold on to the marriage and walk the course even if it's uncomfortable.’[footnote 312]

15.9.9 The LB representatives 2025 provided the following views on the BPS’ handling of GBV, but this information was anecdotal and not supported by empirical data and statistics:

  • The LB representatives 2025 further noted ‘… that there had been a problem recently – or in fact as an ongoing culture – where the victim would go and report the case, then the police would oversee a meeting between the victim and the perpetrator and say that it was a family matter. Instead of filing a report … [the police] mostly try to resolve it, so it tends to die out before it becomes a case. The rare times when the victim insists that they want to take it further, the perpetrator does get apprehended and there’s a trial, and then after a few months they get released on bail or get early release and they go out and perpetrate the same thing. In most cases, this leads to the death of victims.’
  • The LB representatives were of the view that ‘even if the culprit [who had committed GBV] gets apprehended, they are released back to the community again and they repeat the same thing.’
  • The LB representatives 2025 also thought there was a high reoffending rate, noting ‘… there’s a high number [of such cases] but that the FFM team would need to check that with Statistics Botswana. It’s a high number, like a pandemic of re-perpetrating.’[footnote 313]

15.9.10 The LB representatives 2025 expressed the view on the effectiveness of the police’s investigations, ‘… that they write up the investigation, [and sometimes the people involved in the investigation processes do not provide the police with enough information] but when it goes to the [Directorate of Public Prosecution] DPP, the cases carry little or no weight to proceed to the courts and end up taking a long time to be resolved … something [the representatives have heard] … from the DPP in the District Gender Committee.’[footnote 314]

15.9.11 The LB representatives 2025 also noted that they thought the local District Gender Committee, which included a variety of government and non-government stakeholders, had reported ‘5 cases brought into the [criminal justice] system in the last quarter, from January to March [2025], but only one was being tried [in court]. The other cases lacked information and were still being investigated [by the police].’ However, there no other information was stated to provide context such as the total number of reported incidents of GBV or how this compared to previous quarters[footnote 315].

15.9.12 The WAR executive director 2025 noted ‘… it takes time for a GBV case to be heard. WAR have had cases that have taken up to 2 years before they appear in court.’[footnote 316]

15.9.13 The MWT representatives 2025 when asked if perpetrators of GBV had been arrested, prosecuted and put in prison noted ‘yes, some are. But many are on bail.’[footnote 317]

15.9.14 The ADC 2025 noted ‘the police file the cases and undertake investigations [but the ADC] could not say if these cases went to the court, the DPP would have this data. [Adding] the reason the various organisations come together in the Gender Committee is to discuss cases going to court. There is a trend for women to withdraw cases [from being investigated/go to court]. Currently, the ADC understood that [the police] no longer allow [GBV] cases to be withdrawn [from investigation].’[footnote 318]

15.9.15 The BPS officials 2025 noted that ‘all activities such as report, arrest, bail, investigation, and trial are documented.’ The BPS officials agreed to provide the UKHO with some or all of data but had not done so at the time of writing in December 2025[footnote 319].

15.9.16 The BPS officials 2025 also noted that there is a general problem in prosecuting and convicting rape cases:

‘It's an issue of … the general justice system in BWA. Conversion of cases from report to prosecution takes a bit long. But it's across all … cases, it’s not specific to rape cases. Now we are trying to move to electronic courts because most of our courts are still manual [paper-based]. If everything is being captured manually, it's tedious, so it takes a bit of time. So what we are trying to do is that process of digitalisation of everything, which includes the court system itself, so that even with the records, it makes the process more efficient. Then justice will be served, on time.

‘… there are different kinds of rape: gang rape, stranger rape, date rape. So depending on the type of rape that has been committed the difficulty of detection varies. For example, if it's stranger rape, it's not going to be easy to arrest the perpetrator. It will take time looking for the perpetrator, unless they’re habitual offenders. For example, in the recent past the Forensic Science Laboratory was able to link old rape cases with the offenders though DNA analysis. In all cases of rape, samples or specimens are taken to the lab, which are analysed to help detect the perpetrator.’[footnote 320]

15.9.17 The BPS officials 2025 also explained that because the age of consent for sexual intercourse is 18 ‘the number of persons that experience defilement (statutory rape) will generally look higher in Botswana [than compared to, for example, the UK where consent can be given at 16] thus inflating the crime statistics in Botswana.’[footnote 321]

15.10 Withdrawal of cases

15.10.1 The BNRS 2018 based on police statistics from 2015 and 2016 noted that out of almost 24,000 reported GBV cases over 5,400 were withdrawn. The study noted:

‘… the number of cases withdrawn by women survivors is about twice as high as that for men. For both women and men, physical abuse constituted the highest number of cases withdrawn.
