A significant number of rape cases are also withdrawn. There are several push factors that compel survivors of abuse to withdraw cases …

‘During interviews, the Botswana Police cited the following reasons for withdrawal of cases:

  • ‘Insufficient evidence because cases are reported too late and without medical proof.
  • ‘Some withdraw cases when they feel they have been dragging for too long before the courts.
  • ‘Reconciliation between victim and perpetrators within intimate relationships.
  • ‘Some perpetrators show remorse and others promise to give victims compensation for withdrawing the case. Some victims prefer out of court resolutions. This may include dealing with the matter at home or before the Headman of Arbitration. Most parties have been reconciled at the Customary Courts.
  • ‘Fear of victimisation by the alleged perpetrator.’[footnote 322]

15.10.2 The UNPFA official 2025 noted ‘A lot of women tend to withdraw cases of GBV due to their economic dependence on the male perpetrators.’[footnote 323]

15.10.3 The International diplomatic source 2 – 2025 ‘considered families pressure women to [withdraw cases] [the official] … had attended 2 or 3 sessions run by … NGO where women have testified to being pressured to drop a case because it was with a family member - a cousin, an uncle - or with a neighbour.’[footnote 324]

15.10.4 The International diplomatic source 1-2025 noted ‘survivors eventually drop the charges. And there's a lot of interference from families - families of the perpetrators especially - especially if the perpetrator is considered to be a breadwinner.’[footnote 325]

15.10.5 The MOJCS officials 2025 noted ‘… cases were being reported to the police, then due to a variety of situations victims would withdraw their cases, saying they had reconciled their situation, or the family advised them to step down. But following reconciliation the GBV would escalate, sometimes leading to the death of the victim ...’[footnote 326]

15.10.6 The MOJCS officials 2025 also noted:

‘… there are socio-economic issues, when the breadwinner is the accused and if imprisoned the family will suffer. There are also cultural issues as previously mentioned. People may feel regret after reporting an incident or the abusers reconcile themselves with the victim by offering an apology, maybe giving flowers or chocolates … a victim becomes the state witness as required by the regulation of standards for GBV cases. So, when the case is in the court, it is the state vs the perpetrator [not the victim vs the perpetrator]. Victims whose request to withdraw the case at the Police Station, usually refuse to testify in Court, leading to low conviction rates.’[footnote 327]

15.10.7 The MOJCS officials 2025 commenting that the police no longer allow the withdrawal of GBV cases, noted: ‘So, all cases received go to the Director of Public Prosecutions and end up in court. But in court, prosecution depends on evidence submitted by witnesses for the state. There are situations where the victims refuse to give evidence, or they don’t attend court, which affects the outcome of the case.’ [footnote 328]

15.10.8 The MYGA officials 2025 noted:

‘… because GBV happens mostly between intimate partners, [a woman] could report [her partner] and be given a protection order [restraining order], but because of their intimacy and the dynamics of their relationship, they could still violate the protection order. For example, if I'm given a restraining order [against the male partner], then because of the manner in which we relate, I can choose to still have contact with him despite that order. In reported cases, we have noticed that [women who have reported a male partner] can choose to drop the charges and the prosecution cannot continue in their absence. It’s just one of the gaps we have realised, and it's mostly women who choose to drop the cases for various reasons. Some women drop cases at the police [station] thereby preventing them to continue with prosecution. This has been a major concern and efforts to educate and support women to stand for their rights continue … explained that the police attitude [protocol] is that they don’t allow any dropping of cases [brought by women against male partners/perpetrators], but even though the police refuse to drop the case, when it goes forward to the magistrates’ court, [the victim] can just choose [to drop the case]. I was the witness so I can just choose not to participate … She added that it’s a complex situation [between the couple].’[footnote 329]

15.10.9 The MYGA officials 2025 noted:

‘[A coupling separating is] … a complex issue because there's also societal pressure [in that] when you have reported your partner or husband, you have pressures from both [the woman’s and man’s] families. So sometimes we are dealing with that, but also economic pressures … Even if you have got a court order that says the man should be paying for the house and [the woman] can stay there, the man will stop paying rent and the landlord will chase you out because of the economic dependency of women, who are sometimes not working ... it’s sometimes easy to put the legal systems [in place] to address this, but when it comes to [the] social [situation], that’s another issue.’[footnote 330]

15.10.10 The LB representatives 2025 expressed the view that when ‘most of these cases get to the courts, the victims withdraw the cases and there’s no way you can stop them … [this] might be because of coercion at home or because of mediation, or [the victims] … get scared about leaving people [or because the majority of perpetrators are breadwinners]. It’s a number of factors.’[footnote 331]

15.10.11 The BONELA representatives 2025 noted:

‘… the perpetrator [of GBV] is in most cases the breadwinner, so a woman will drop the charges because they say to themselves “What am I going to do?”, “What is the family going to say?”. We’ve also had women say that the perpetrator is the father of my child/children, and she does not want to deprive them of their father. There are also issues relating to societal stigma. There's this phenomenon where people want to maintain a certain facade which is not necessarily true. This especially happens for families who have a link to religious or Christian backgrounds where there's concern about what people say …’[footnote 332]

15.10.12 The BPS officials 2025 noted ‘There are a lot of cases that are withdrawn … [and thought] these withdrawals are poverty related. So, there are many reasons that play into it. And it’s not specific to GBV, it’s across the board … [of] cases were being reconciled at family level so that the cases would be withdrawn.’[footnote 333]

16. Judiciary

16.1 Structure and jurisdiction

16.1.1 Botswana has a ‘mixed legal system of civil law influenced by the Roman-Dutch model, including customary and common law’[footnote 334].

16.1.2 The GOROB’s website in an undated entry noted: ‘The Judiciary is established by the constitution … Its pivotal role in the governance of the country is defined … as the adjudication of both civil and criminal cases involving citizens and the state. It comprises of the Court of Appeal and the High Court and the Magistrates Courts.’[footnote 335]

16.1.3 The GOROB website also noted:

‘The Court of Appeal is the highest court in the country and is the final arbiter of all legal matters …

‘The High Court is a superior court of record with unlimited jurisdiction … There are currently four locations of the High Court: Lobatse, Francistown, Maun and the headquarters in Gaborone. The High Court presides over matters beyond jurisdiction of the lower courts, and appeals emanating from the lower courts …

‘The Industrial Court is a Court of Law and Equity … the Court has exclusive judgments in all labour disputes and ranks equal to the High Court in its status and power …

‘The Magistrate court[s] are created by statute with power defined by the Magistrates Courts Act. They are subordinate to the High Court. Unlike the High Court, Magistrates Courts are not created by the Constitution. They are therefore controlled and supervised by the High Court, through reviews and appeals.’ [footnote 336]

16.1.4 The GOROB website further noted:

‘The Botswana Magistracy performs a very pivotal role in the judiciary of the nation. The Magistrates try the bulk of the offences committed and they handle the bulk of common disputes between ordinary citizens of Botswana.

‘The following services are available at the Magistrate Courts:

  • Family related cases such as paternity and alimony orders.
  • Adoption of children.
  • Restraining orders in domestic violence cases.
  • Civil suits ...
  • Criminal trials - Magistrates Courts hear the bulk of criminal cases.’[footnote 337]

16.1.5 The Statistics Botswana Crime Statistics Report 2020 dated December 2022 (SB CRS report 2020), the most recent published dataset on the number, type and outcome of magistrate and high court cases, noted:

‘Magisterial Courts are categorized into two regions as follows:

‘1. The Southern region which comprises of the Broadhurst Magisterial Court, Village, Extension II, Ramotswa, Lobatse, Jwaneng, Mochudi, Kanye, Molepolole, Hukuntsi, Tsabong, and Gantsi Magisterial Courts.

‘2. The Northern region includes the Francistown Magisterial Court, Selibe-Phikwe, Bobonong, Mahalapye, Serowe, Palapye, Letlhakane, Masunga, Maun, Gumare and Kasane Magisterial Courts.’[footnote 338]

16.1.6 Customary courts are recognised under the Customary Courts Act, which outlines their establishment, jurisdiction, composition, and appeal procedure[footnote 339].

16.1.7 The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention following a visit to Botswana in July 2022 published a report on 11 July 2023 (UN WGAD report 2023). This explained:

‘Botswana has a dual legal system encompassing common law and customary law. In addition to common law magistrate courts, there are customary courts, presided over by Dikgosi (chiefs), with jurisdiction over civil and criminal matters, which are regulated by the Customary Courts Act. Dikgosi are not legal professionals, although they are provided with basic training on statutes. There are two customary courts of appeal in the country. Customary Courts apply the Penal Code and other relevant law. Except for the most serious crimes, they may hear a number of criminal matters and impose penalties, including imprisonment.’[footnote 340]

16.1.8 The MOJCS officials 2025, when asked if GBV cases in the customary courts could be switched to the common law courts, noted ‘they can, ultimately [also they can go to] the customary court of appeal and then the [common law] High Court …’. The officials also noted ‘… there are customary courts in every village, but not every village has a police station. The customary courts have first contact with people. The police are usually stationed at customary courts.’[footnote 341]

16.1.9 The UNFPA official 2025 explained that sometimes GBV cases

‘… would go through customary law [courts], like in the case of people in a village. [Their] first point of contact with the legal system would be to go to the chief, the kgosi, who is the leader of the village and relies on customary law. But sometimes cases are removed from the customary [law system] to the [common law] magistrate[s’] [courts], and then it depends but maybe from the magistrate to the higher courts. Not all cases that are heard in the customary court will ultimately make it to the magistrates’ court.

‘… The customary law leads more to [a victim being told] that it’s a family matter and they should go and talk to their uncles and so forth. Even where somebody has gone to the courts, like the magistrates’ court, imagine being issued with a restraining order and then going back to the community. The customary law has no power to enforce a restraining order. If anything, a victim might face [comments from] people in the community about her having taken her own husband to court and obtaining a restraining order against him. So, the 2 [legal systems] are in a lot of conflict in terms of GBV cases.’[footnote 342]

16.1.10 A GOROB representative told the UN CEDAW in June 2025 that:

‘[GBV] … cases transferred from the customary courts were referred to a magistrate’s court or to the High Court. Any case involving assault required the involvement of the police to ensure that the victim received the protection of the law. The Ministry of Justice was responsible for training magistrates to take the gender perspective into account. Under the Bail Act [of 2024], victims of offences were interviewed by a magistrate, who could issue a detention order against the accused person, if necessary, in order to protect the victim.

‘… Court rulings were deemed sufficient to repeal discriminatory legal provisions even before the relevant legislation had been Officially updated. Rulings handed down by lower courts and customary courts could be appealed in the higher courts. Legal aid was available to persons who required it. Judges had been provided with training on how to make courts friendlier places for children and other vulnerable groups.’[footnote 343]

16.1.11 The BPS officials 2025 noted:

‘… the customary courts have 2 responsibilities: they try criminal cases as well as civil cases, the same as a magistrate [court] … Serious cases are taken to the higher courts and less serious cases are taken to the customary courts. Generally speaking, GBV cases go to the magistrates’ courts … the victim doesn’t decide [which court hears their case]; the determination is made on the basis of the nature of the case that’s been reported … The prosecution decides where the case goes. In terms of GBV, those cases don’t go to the customary courts.’[footnote 344]

16.1.12 The MLIA officials 2025 noted that ‘kgotlas [customary courts] are very progressive nowadays. It’s highly unlikely that someone would get away with GBV.’[footnote 345] However, regarding the traditional justice system, MWET representatives 2025 stated that ‘the traditional system is not that effective.

We have the dikgosi [traditional chiefs], we have their support.’[footnote 346]

16.2 Fair trial and independence

16.2.1 The BTI report 2024 noted:

‘Botswana is lauded for maintaining an independent judiciary capable of functioning and interpreting the law. The judiciary encompasses a range of courts, from lower-level ones to the High Court of Appeal.

‘Judges, for the most part, operate independently when carrying out their judicial duties and are not unduly influenced by external factors, including the executive branch. However, the appointment of judges, the chief justice, and the judge president (i.e., the head of the highest court in the country, the Court of Appeal) by the state president remains a point of concern as it can potentially compromise the judiciary’s independence. It’s important to note that while the government is responsible for appointing judges, this does not imply that they can be arbitrarily dismissed by the executive. Therefore, the judiciary’s independence is effectively safeguarded despite these appointment procedures.’[footnote 347]

16.2.2 The FH report 2024 noted: ‘The judiciary is generally independent and free from interference. Judges have ruled against the government in several high-profile cases in recent years.’[footnote 348]

16.2.3 While the USSD HR report 2024 does not comment on the competence of the judiciary[footnote 349], the USSD HR report 2023 noted:

‘The constitution and law provided for the right to a fair and public trial, and an independent judiciary generally enforced this right. Trials in civilian courts were public, although trials under the National Security Act could be held in secret. Defendants had the right to be present and to consult with an attorney in a timely manner. In capital cases, the government provided legal counsel or private attorneys to work pro bono for indigent clients. Courts tried those charged with noncapital crimes without legal representation if the defendant could not afford an attorney. As a result, many defendants were not aware of their procedural rights in pretrial or trial proceedings. Some NGOs provided free but limited legal assistance.

‘A customary or traditional court system existed in addition to the formal court system. According to traditional practice, a tribal chief presided over most small villages. While customary (traditional) courts enjoyed widespread citizen support and respect, they often did not afford the same due process protections as the formal court system. Defendants did not have legal counsel, and there were no standardized rules of evidence. The quality of decisions reached in the customary courts varied considerably, and defendants often lacked a presumption of innocence. Tribal judges applied corporal punishment, such as lashings on the buttocks, more often than did formal courts.’[footnote 350]

16.2.4 The MOJCS officials 2025 noted ‘BWA has a well-functioning judicial system and when cases occur, they are reported to the police who prosecute the perpetrator (most are male) and action is taken.’[footnote 351]

16.3 Gender-specific courts

16.3.1 The GOROB ACHPR submission 2023 noted ‘Botswana has also established specialised Courts dedicated to gender-based violence cases and set them up at all Magistrates Courts with a Chief Magistrate.’[footnote 352] The UN CEDAW report 2025 noted the positive ‘creation of specialized courts to expedite gender-based violence cases’[footnote 353].

16.3.2 The FAB representatives 2025 noted:

‘… there had been training [for the judiciary] … thought training had been provided by several entities: UNICEF … [United Nations Development Programme] and even with other organisations like LEGABIBO and BONELA, local [non-government organisations] NGOs that work in the gender space. However, in terms of it translating into sensitivity and seriousness and the speed with which justice for GBV is meted out, there hadn’t been any change.’[footnote 354]

16.3.3 The MOJCS officials 2025 noted: ‘The courts are GBV-friendly, and the government has also piloted child-friendly justice system - children are also affected by GBV and sometimes they have to give evidence as they are molested. There are now child friendly police stations and evidence can even be given in camera if a child has to come before the court.’[footnote 355]

16.3.4 The LAB CEO 2025 noted ‘… the government … saw fit to … have courts that were designated for GBV cases so that they were dealt with quickly … she believe[d] they are continuing, but that the Administration of Justice should have that information.’[footnote 356]

16.3.5 However, the BGBVC managers 2025,

‘… observed that following an upsurge of cases during Covid, the Chief Justice had announced that special GBV courts would be set up … [the representatives] thought these had been set up, but that it hadn’t been possible to continue with them because they weren’t necessarily planned; they were just a response to what was happening [at that time] ... [BGBVC] had received new information the week before the FFM interview [July 2025] confirming that these courts were no longer in existence, that they were tried but it was not happening again …’ [footnote 357]

16.3.6 The MYGA officials 2025 noted: ‘[During] Covid, specialised courts that dealt with GBV were established to speed up the GBV cases, and also to get them moving there has been some training for magistrates to actually equip them with the skills to be able to address gender-based violence cases.’[footnote 358]

16.3.7 The MYGA officials 2025 noted:

‘… since Covid [2020 to 2022] there had been a directive from the Chief Justice to all magistrates to prioritise GBV cases, so that is the attitude. In Botswana, all cases start at Magistrate level and are elevated to the High Court based on their gravity such as murder or where an individual appeals the decision of the Magistrate Court, hence the Directive was to the Magistrates, who are more spread in the country than the High Court. Maybe here and there, there could be slippages, but they know that such cases need to be prioritised … special courts doesn’t mean the facility, it doesn’t mean a building where GBV cases are heard because there are mobile courts that move to where the cases are. They are specialised courts in terms of prioritising. But by travelling, they [ensure] that hearings are done where they are closer to the people. Furthermore, many times, GBV cases are heard after [usual work] hours or at weekends.’[footnote 359]

16.3.8 The WAR executive director 2025 noted: ‘During Covid, the government piloted GBV courts … thought this was in Molepolole. In a 3-month pilot, they pushed so many cases, it showed that they really need a GBV court ... there are mobile courts for drinking and driving … but not for GBV. The executive director also thought that there are no longer GBV courts, ‘[i]t was just a pilot because GBV went up during Covid, so they piloted [in particular] spots (areas of the country – Molepolole) and they moved a lot of cases.’[footnote 360]

16.3.9 The BONELA representatives 2025 noted ‘there was an attempt to create GBV courts, a pilot project in Molepolole, one of the epicentres of violence. We are yet to see whether that really improves access to justice ... [BONELA] thought the pilot in Molepolole was ongoing but were not sure.’[footnote 361]

16.4 Convictions and sentencing

16.4.1 Statistics Botswana (SB) publishes crimes statistics which include the number of cases heard and disposed of at the magistrate and high courts. At the time of writing (December 2025) annual reports had been published covering the years 2009 to 2020 only – no more recent data was available.

16.4.2 On the quality of this data, SB included the following qualifier. It:

‘… analyses secondary data on criminal cases from all Courts in Botswana. The Administration of Justice (AOJ) department through the Case Information Management System (CIMS) collects the data. All Magistrate Courts in the country are connected to the system that is housed at the Gaborone High Court and information on cases is entered directly into the system in real time. The data needed for statistical purposes is then extracted and given to SB in electronic format for analysis … Since the information in the Case Information Management System (SIMS) is meant largely for administrative purposes, some variables, crucial for statistical purposes, such as sex and age of the accused, date of initial filing, date of judgement are at times omitted leading to lack of conclusiveness in the findings. In some instances, offences are not consistently entered into the system, leading to a lengthened and cumbersome process of data cleaning, classification and coding. Some variables which are used to calculate some key indicators such as disposal rates, conviction rates etc. are either not stated or not consistent with other entries making it difficult to calculate such indicators.’[footnote 362]

16.4.3 The SB CRS report 2020, the most recent dataset on case outcomes in the magistrates’ courts, noted:

‘[There was] … a steady increase [in court cases] from 6,830 cases in 2017 to 9,499 in 2019. This was followed by a huge decrease to 4,148 cases in 2020. The decrease can be attributed to the fact that in March 2020 [t]he World Health Organization (WHO) declared COVID-19 a global pandemic. In response, in April Botswana started to put measures in place to curb the spread of the virus; [sic] [t]he country went on Lock down in April and continued through May, as a result many activities including case hearings were suspended hence the decrease in cases disposed of in 2020.’[footnote 363]

16.4.4 The SB CRS report 2020 also noted:

‘Offences recorded in 2020 were lower (7,386) compared to (13,906) offences recorded in 2019 for reasons earlier enunciated.

‘The offence that ranked highest was theft and related offences accounting for 16.6 percent of all cases. The top four offences were sexual offences (9.0 Percent), Offences against Government, Justice Procedures and organizational crime (9.3 percent), Attempts/Threats to murder, assaults, Harassment and related offences (11.9 percent) and Theft and related offences. Cases involving use of force such as homicide, robbery, sexual offences were also high recording 6.0[%], 6.3[%] and 9.0[%] respectively. This is in the midst of a period when the country is grappling with a high prevalence of gender-based violence as well as femicide. The use of controlled drugs was also high accounting for slightly more than 5 percent of the offences committed.’[footnote 364]

16.4.5 The SB CRS report 2020 further noted that in the magistrates’ courts ‘a high proportion (42.6 percent) of the accused had their cases withdrawn, while about a quarter of the accused were found guilty and sentenced or fined. Only 14.5 percent were acquitted and discharged. About 5 percent of the cases were referred either to the regional office (1.2 percent) or committed to the High Court (3.8 percent).’[footnote 365]

16.4.6 The SB CRS report 2020 also stated that there were 116 cases heard in the 4 high courts of which:

  • 28 were acquitted and discharged
  • 6 were convicted but sentencing was postponed
  • 2 were found guilty and fined
  • 14 found guilty but were considered ‘insane’
  • 62 were withdrawn
  • 4 were not started[footnote 366]

16.4.7 The SB CRS report 2020 lists 16 offences including those against the person as well as those against property, broken down by age and sex of perpetrator where this is known. There is no GBV category, but the offences of ‘homicide’, ‘sexual’ and ‘attempts/threats to murder, assaults, harassments, and related’ include cases related to GBV. Each of these broad criminal offence types includes a range of specific offences. For example, ‘sexual’ offences include:

  • rape
  • defilement (of a minor)
  • sexual offences involving mentally impaired persons
  • aggravated sexual assault
  • sexual assault
  • incest
  • child pornography offences
  • child pornography – obstruction of warrant
  • gross indecency
  • attempted rape[footnote 367]

16.4.8 The tables below include information on the number of magistrate cases and their outcomes in total and by sex for the offences listed in the previous paragraph. Since the SB CRS report 2020 does not include data on the sex of the victims it cannot be assumed that, for example, in cases of homicide the victim was a woman (or targeted because she was a woman). However, as context, police statistics indicate that of reported crimes in 2024 around 85% of victims of all crimes were women, while 98% of perpetrators of all crimes were men (see Police reports).

16.4.12 The International diplomatic source 2 – 2025 stated ‘that conviction rates are not great [but did] not have the data [for these].’[footnote 371] Similarly, the UNFPA official 2025 ‘… did not have those exact numbers [on arrests, prosecutions and convictions] …’[footnote 372]

16.4.13 The FAB representatives 2025 noted:

‘Convictions are generally low … thought the last research that was done – … was a 2018 study [the BNRS 2018 – see above] – indicated a conviction rate in terms of these specific crimes of less than 0.5%. It is predominantly because of the manner in which cases are investigated, the manner in which evidence is obtained and handled, and kept and preserved. Also, in most instances, cases take about 5 years, from time of reporting to verdict / sentencing (if found guilty). So, you will report in 2025 and your case will most likely be heard or finalised – you’ll get a conviction or an outcome – in 2030.’[footnote 373]

16.4.14 The BGBVC managers 2025 referring to comments made by a high court judge at a conference the Chief Executive Officer had attended noted ‘… the High Court judge … had said cases of murder, for instance, if they reach his court, have been on the table somewhere between the police and the DPP for a minimum of 5 or 6 years … this means justice is delayed, and because of bail, the person could actually be out, not only walking the streets but threatening the survivor and her family. There are restraining orders, but they [perpetrators] don't care about restraining [orders].’[footnote 374]

16.4.15 The BGBVC managers 2025 also noted the number of cases disposed of in the courts is ‘very low, so there’s a backlog.’[footnote 375]

16.4.16 The WAR executive director 2025 acknowledged that they were aware of GBV cases being progressed through the courts and resulting in a disposal, noting ‘that the conviction rate is quite low in GBV [cases, including rape and femicide] but she thought that was a worldwide phenomenon.’ The director also noted ‘… that they had had cases at the shelter that were thrown out of court. The perpetrator was set free … [but] they had some success, not all doom and gloom … 10% success … [WAR had] consulted someone to come and do [a survey of conviction rates] … for them between 2007 and 2009 and the conviction rate then was below 10%. It's still below 10% now.’[footnote 376]

16.4.17 The BBL representatives 2025 thought the police were sometimes helpful, ‘perpetrators can be found guilty … getting prison sentences of] 10 to 15 years … [for] rape or defilement [abuse of a minor].’[footnote 377]

16.4.18 The BONELA representatives 2025 noted ‘the Children's Act, 2009 (CA) is a good piece of legislation for protecting children against violations but there is need for resources to implement it. Cases relating to children can take a long time to be handled. For example, where a child is raped, it takes 5 years for them to get justice and in some instances the child says they don’t want to deal with that, they just want to put the situation behind them.’[footnote 378]

16.4.19 However, the BONELA representatives 2025

‘… were aware of cases of convictions [of GBV offenders] … [but] noted that what is concerning is that GBV cases where a woman is killed are reduced from murder to manslaughter [for a killing of a woman] because the law recognises “a crime of passion”. There is a case we are using to raise this as an issue although we can do nothing about the case as it was decided by the Court of Appeal … A woman was killed by her boyfriend who was given a death sentence, but this was reduced to 25 years. The family came to us for help about this case and reduction in the sentence. So, we/our lawyer are looking at the case to see if there were loopholes that merited a reduction in sentencing.

‘… we need better handling of GBV cases in the way the victims are prepared for evidence, the way that the prosecution handles evidence. Women feel that justice is not working for them. Even the language we use – “passion killing” - it's almost as if we are unnoticed.’[footnote 379]

16.5 Delays in the judicial process

16.5.1 While commenting on the situation in 2022, the UN WGAD report 2023 noted that there were delays in the trial process because of insufficient number of court reporters for producing records of proceedings. Cases were also adjourned because of the failure of lawyers and sometimes magistrates and judges to attend hearings. This had reportedly led a to a backlog of 2,000 cases and contributed to lengthy pre-trial detention[footnote 380].

16.5.2 See also Prison system for information on the proportion of the prison population held on remand.

16.5.3 The BONELA representatives 2025 confirmed that male perpetrators of GBV including rape and sexual assault have gone through the courts and resulted in a disposal (either acquittal or conviction). However, the representatives also not that the timeliness of processing cases in the criminal justice system

‘… is a general problem … As there are many GBV cases it becomes even more evident that cases are taking longer than they should … [which is a problem for] the [criminal justice system] CJS more broadly. There is not a peculiar system for GBV cases, they follow the same route for being disposed as other cases … timeliness is a challenge. If GBV cases are handled in the same way as other cases, you create a bottleneck and that is when people are more likely to withdraw their case and thought this needed to be looked into. There is a propensity for victims to withdraw case[s] but the government should take these cases forward anyway, this would make a difference.’[footnote 381]

16.5.4 The LEGABIBO representatives 2025 commenting on GBV generally noted: ‘It’s taking a long time to litigate. If you were assaulted today, the litigation process of the case would be [concluded] after about 3 years.’[footnote 382]

16.5.5 The CEDAW report 2025 did not comment on number or rate of convictions and sentencing of GBV cases but was concerned by ‘the prolonged nature of criminal proceedings’[footnote 383].

17. Prison system

17.1.1 The Institute for Crime & Justice Policy Research, Birkbeck, University of London, noted in its World Prison Brief that as of December 2022 there were over 3,900 people incarcerated in the country’s 23 prison establishments/institutions. Over 20% were foreign nationals and 22.5% were pre-trial detainees/on remand[footnote 384]. However, there is no data available in the sources consulted indicating the reasons for prisoners’ incarceration, including how many or what proportion of the prison population was detained because of GBV-related offences (see Bibliography).

17.1.2 The USSD HR report 2023 noted:

‘There were no significant reports regarding prison or detention center conditions that raised human rights concerns … Authorities investigated credible allegations of inhuman conditions brought against prison officials … The government generally allowed international and local nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) to meet with prisoners, and it permitted independent human rights observers to visit prisons. The International Committee of the Red Cross visited prisons.’[footnote 385]

17.1.3 However, the GOROB ACHPR submission 2023 indicates some proportion of the prison population were GBV offenders, noting: ‘The Botswana Prisons Service has also initiated the GBV Perpetrators programme in September 2021. This is a character moulding programme geared towards behaviour change of the offenders. It also raises awareness on the integration of offenders to curb them from being re-offenders. More integration and community engagements continue to be conducted across the country.’[footnote 386]

18. Legal aid

18.1.1 The GOROB CEDAW report 2023 stated:

‘The Legal Aid Act of 2013 established Legal Aid Botswana (LAB) which has branches in Gaborone, Francistown, Kasane, Tsabong, Maun and Palapye to provide access to justice by indigent persons in Botswana. The initial support offered was in respect of civil matters. However, Government is currently piloting the expansion of support to criminal matters. In ensuring that legal aid is available and accessible to all particularly indigent women, a total of 6 521 persons were supported between April 2019 and December 2022. Of these beneficiaries, 56% were women of whom 21% were from rural areas. The legal aid services include matters on access to identity documents, child maintenance and support, GBV and medical malpractice cases. These services are delivered through the React program supported by the Global Fund, an intervention which trains community reactors and paralegals to document human rights violations of identified key and vulnerable groups and provide information, education and linkage to services including legal aid and health services.’[footnote 387]

18.1.2 The LAB CEO 2025 explained that legal aid is means tested to determine if the person is poor (an indigent) and cannot afford a lawyer. The test is ‘a very complex and complicated calculation’ based on the person’s tangible assets, ‘a person's moveable and immovable property as well as revenue and revenue-generating activities.’[footnote 388]

18.1.3 The LAB CEO 2025 noted that ‘… probably 99% of legal aid is provided to adults … when we were established, we were directed to provide civil legal aid … LAB ran a criminal legal aid services pilot project from November 2023, ending 31st March [2025] … the government has embraced the idea, and we have been given a healthy budget for this financial year 2025/2026 to roll out criminal legal aid.’[footnote 389]

18.1.4 The LAB CEO 2025 noted that LAB had 32 lawyers nationwide with an approximate budget in 2024 to 2025 of 55 million pula (around £3million[footnote 390]) increasing to 65 million pula (around £3.5 million) in 2025 to 2026. This included an additional 10 million pula (around £540,000) for the criminal legal aid roll out (LAB has focussed on civil cases to date). LAB handled around 2,500 cases a year to disposal: settlement, through the courts, mediation or withdrawal. This included legal advice if a case had no prosect of success in court. LAB has run campaigns advertising their services on TV and radio, including covering GBV[footnote 391].

18.1.5 The LAB CEO 2025 noted that LAB is head-quartered in Gaborone with service centres in Gaborone, Palapye, Francistown, Maun, Kasane and Tsabong. Adding, ‘[w]e are very few and so we can't do both representation of the offenders and representation of victims, which is why you see us working very closely with the NGOs as they are better positioned to champion victim rights … it also [enabled LAB to have] a referral system. If a person is rejected under the means test, LAB can turn to an NGO which has a mandate that can receive [a person and provide legal advice].’[footnote 392]

18.1.6 The LAB CEO 2025 added:

‘… people do just turn up [at LAB offices], but there is a Facebook page and a website, [on] both of which [you can] interact with [LAB] and make an appointment so that there's somebody to receive you when you arrive [at one of the offices]. A person can [also] phone in and be processed, means-tested and so on and then an appointment can be set up for them with counsel. The same thing would happen with those that reach out either via Facebook or the website – they would be processed by the same office, it's called Client Services Office[.] They are the bridge between those who reach out electronically, including [by telephone], and the actual centres throughout the country.’[footnote 393]

18.1.7 The LAB CEO 2025 noted:

‘… in terms of criminal legal aid, for adults – an adult is 18 plus – we don’t represent them at the lower courts, which are the magistrates’ courts. If they are an adult, such a person will not have representation [as an] accused person or offender from LAB at such lower courts. If it's a child, which is a person who's 17 years and below, we will represent such a child who’s in conflict with the law, even in matters of GBV at both lower and higher courts … If [the person is] an adult, we apply the means test and we do represent adults at the higher courts, meaning the High Court and the Court of Appeal. Most of these criminal matters are tried at the magistracy, which means that we rarely get involved at trial stage and only get involved at the appeal phase [at the High Court], from the convictions and/or sentencings or the judgments of the magistrate.’[footnote 394]

18.1.8 The UKHO FFM observed that LAB provided assistance to defendants (people who are accused of committing offences) but queried if victims of GBV would also get help. The LAB CEO 2025 noted:

‘[Victims] can come to us … if they came to us, we would assist. It is the nature of the assistance provided under the [Domestic Violence Act] … to a certain extent facilitates a victim to obtain remedies without the assistance of counsel. There are … various protective orders under the … Act, but if you are just a member of the public, you may not know. [GBV victims] do come, and LAB ascertains the facts and determines the correct order to apply for [a protection order]. If a woman has been cohabiting with an aggressor, the aggressor can be evicted from their home temporarily and the woman or partner is allowed to go on residing in that home. The orders include restraining order, tenancy order, occupancy order, eviction orders.

‘… [LAB] would facilitate whichever order needs to be made, but mostly people know only about restraining orders, which is regrettable because then you run away and the aggressor is stays in your house. There was a situation where a young lady was actually the owner of the property and the aggressor was in her house and wouldn't leave. This state of affairs carried on and on and she didn't know we could evict the person.’[footnote 395]

18.1.9 The LAB CEO 2025 provided data on the number of GBV cases they had assisted and could be directly identified for 2024 to 2025[footnote 396]:

18.1.10 The LAB CEO 2025 also noted that some NGOs refer cases to LAB:

‘BONELA is typically one that they work with as well as Stepping Stones [International], although Stepping Stones is more focused on children … [LAB] do have to work a lot more closely with civil society, because civil society is an extension of – is part of – the legal aid system of the country … [civil society] also provide advocacy and representation by instructing attorneys in private practice to take on their identified cases … observed that there is a growing requirement for government to also fund [NGOs] … LAB helps indigents, not helping women [per se] or providing special treatment for women. A poor woman will get the same [access to legal aid services] as a poor man in terms of their focus, but somebody else is focussing on women somewhere out there, whether they're poor or not.’[footnote 397]

18.1.11 The LAB CEO 2025 noted ‘[LAB is] … working very well with other stakeholders in the environment - civil society, Botswana Prison Service, Administration of Justice, DPP, Ombudsman, Tribal authorities etc. She thought their service provision could significantly improve if there was a closer working relationship with Botswana police and the social workers, but that it is “not all gloom and doom”.’[footnote 398]

18.1.12 The FAB representatives 2025 noted

‘... Legal Aid … is normally [for] enforcement of civil rights. So if I'm violated, it's treated as a criminal case and I need to put it through the criminal system. Legal Aid won't prosecute the matter on my behalf. It has been mentioned that because of the length that it takes from the start to finalise a criminal matter, countries sue under civil law against the perpetrator, but that hasn't yet been tested … the Legal Aid [means test] threshold leaves a lot of people out … thought the maximum someone could be earning was about 2,500 pula a month [approximately £130[footnote 399]]. But for a person who earns from zero to even 10,000 pula [approximately £520], it would be very expensive to afford the services of a lawyer [FFM team comment: Statistics Botswana estimated that average annual nominal gross domestic product (GDP) per person in 2024 was just over 104,000 pula (around £5,700[footnote 400]) , about 8,600 pula (£470) a month. However, GDP per person is not necessarily the same as actual income per person].’[footnote 401]

18.1.13 The International diplomatic source 2 – 2025 noted there is legal aid, but accessibility is an issue:

‘There are 2 parts to accessibility: 1) there is a lack of education or knowledge that the provision exists to some communities. They don't know they have a right to legal aid (assistance); 2) proximity to those amenities is also an issue. Need to rethink how to make legal aid (assistance) more accessible to all. Language can also be a barrier – people assume that everyone speaks 2 languages, English and Tswana, but that is not the case if you move towards the northern part of the country. Some people there do not speak either. This makes it difficult for them to articulate when harm has been done and is even more of a barrier for someone to provide them with the legal assistance.’[footnote 402]

18.1.14 The UNFPA official 2025 commenting on the provision of legal aid, noted:

‘… there is Legal Aid Botswana, which provides legal aid to people who may not necessarily have the means, and there’s also Botswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS, BONELA, an NGO, which provides legal aid support. And those who can would just get a lawyer, legal representation. And then there’s even the UB legal clinic, at the University of Botswana. In terms of legal representation, even the law provides that where somebody is not able to afford [a lawyer], one will be provided for them by the state.’[footnote 403]

18.1.15 On accessing legal aid and/or support, the UNFPA official noted:

‘We may have legal aid, but to access it could be a challenge. And then BONELA, the NGO, the headquarters are here [Gaborone] and then they have project sites but they do a whole range of projects: HIV/AIDS, TB and stuff like that. But at least where you have a BONELA office, they may be able to facilitate with their headquarters, but where they are not, then that would be a challenge in hard-to-reach areas where [these organisations] would not have their offices. But you could try to phone.’[footnote 404]

18.1.16 The MWET representatives 2025 noted that while there is legal aid in Maun ‘some people don’t know it is there.’[footnote 405]

19. Office of the Ombudsman

19.1.1 The GOROB website in an undated entry stated that the Office of the Ombudsman

‘… is part of the justice architecture with a focus on promoting administrative justice by investigating allegations of mal-administration within the public sector. As a dispute resolution mechanism alternative to the courts, the Office discharges its mandate by investigating complaints of improper administrative conduct and recommending remedial actions where, in the opinion of the Ombudsman, the complainant has suffered injustice arising from the administrative conduct.’[footnote 406]

19.1.2 The USSD HR report 2023 noted: ‘An ombudsperson within the Office of the President handled complaints of maladministration, including some human rights abuses in the public sector, and the government generally cooperated with the ombudsperson. The Office of the Ombudsman, however, lacked sufficient staff.’[footnote 407]

19.1.3 Africa Press, a pan African news service, noted in an article dated 15 March 2025, referring to comments made by the Assistant Minister of Justice and Correctional Services, that:

‘[The] Ombudsman was mandated by the law [Ombudsman Act, 2021] to investigate complaints of improper administrative conduct on the part of ministries, departments and government agencies … [as well as] investigating … human rights violations by ministries, departments and government agencies.

‘… since [the human rights mandate came into effect] … in July 2023, the office received 35 cases of human rights violations, which were still under investigation … during the financial year 2024/2025, the Ombudsman registered 1 330 new complaints as at end of January 2025, compared to 695 in 2023/2024.

‘Out of this total, 554 complaints were resolved … the Office of the Ombudsman continued to resolve cases, although it has not attained the desired high-resolution rate … a number of reasons were behind the shortcoming, including non-response and or delayed response by ministries, departments and government agencies.

‘… the office currently had 37 legal investigators delivering on [the] core mandate posing a challenge of delivery as the mandate had expanded not only in the area of investigation but also on other functions such as public education and advocacy as well as protection and promotion of the enjoyment of human rights.’[footnote 408]

20. Civil society organisations

20.1 Overview of organisations and services

20.1.1 The FH report 2025 noted: ‘Nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), including human rights groups, generally operate without restriction.’[footnote 409] Similarly, the USSD HR report 2023 noted: ‘The small number of domestic and international human rights groups generally operated without government restriction, investigating, and publishing their findings on human rights cases. Government officials were generally cooperative and responsive to domestic NGO views on most subjects. The government interacted with and provided financial support to some domestic organizations.’[footnote 410]

20.1.2 The GOROB ACHPR report 2023 noted:

‘Civil Society Organisations such as Botswana Association of Local Authorities (BALA) in collaboration with Gender Links also continue to play a significant role in addressing gender and GBV issues through local government Centres of Excellence programme, which encompasses the appointment of Gender Focal Points in District Councils. For the reporting period, Government committed a total of USD1.5 million to support the housing of GBV survivors.’[footnote 411]

20.1.3 The GOROB ACHPR report 2023 additionally noted ‘Civil Society also established Toll-Free lines for reporting GBV as well as offering on-line counselling.’[footnote 412]

20.1.4 The UNFPA official 2025

‘… explained that when she was working for BOCONGO [Botswana Council of Non-Governmental Organisations] [where the official served as executive director up between November 2023 and April 2025] they had around 300 individual members across the country, but these were working in a wide array of areas. Less than 20 worked specifically with GBV. Members are divided into 6 thematic groups: gender, human rights and youth; economic justice; arts and creative industry; the environment and nature management; democratic governance and … social protection. The gender NGOs were part of the gender and human rights thematic working groups. [They included] Emang Basadi [Women’s Association], Gender Links and BONELA. Because BONELA do law and a lot of human rights issues, they will take on GBV. So, [the number of] GBV [civil society groups]: about 20 to 30.’[footnote 413]

20.1.5 The UNFPA official 2025 also noted:

‘… there are some NGOs providing economic empowerment support to women, for women to start, sustain or even scale up enterprises. But when NGOs have a service like that, they are usually donor-funded, as with Women Against Rape in Maun or Cynthia Childcare Trust. The official noted that Cynthia Childcare Trust was supported by the French Embassy specifically to run women’s economic empowerment programmes. So a lot of these are donor-funded, but the government of BWA’s gender affairs department also has a women’s economic empowerment programme where there's usually a grant set aside so individual women can apply, those that are starting enterprises, those that are scaling up. It’s about 500,000 pula [circa £26,870[footnote 414]] when it's a group of women or 100,000 pula [circa £5,360[footnote 415]] for an individual.’ [footnote 416]

20.1.6 The UNFPA official 2025 added that:

‘… there are other NGOs [supporting women with economic empowerment], for example, Ratong Centre and Botswana Gender-Based Violence Prevention and Support Centre (BGBVC). BGBVC offers support for women who are victims of GBV, and the second part [of its work] are economic empowerment programmes for victims of GBV. Women Against Rape in Maun also provide shelter[s] and while the women are there [they provide] economic empowerment programmes to try and help them self-sustain, so that they don't go back to the perpetrators. The Ratong Centre was actually set up by a woman who was a victim of GBV, so from her own experience now she helps other women by providing economic empowerment programmes. They also do therapy through the projects they do, like beadwork and things like that.’[footnote 417]

20.1.7 The FAB representatives 2025 noted:

‘… there are various NGOs [that support women] …, for example Women Against Rape, an NGO in Maun. There is also the Ratong Centre, which is based in Gaborone, and Botswana Gender-Based Violence Prevention Support Centre, [also based in Gaborone]. They provide counselling and legal services, but not the full range [of services]. The services that one receives from the shelters is limited due to constrained resources. For example, though they can provide counselling services, this is not long-term counselling. If they provide you with legal services, it would be for immediate protection such as obtaining a restraining order, but unlikely that they will provide legal services to get a maintenance order or institute divorce proceedings, depending on the circumstances of the case. They'll probably start off with obtaining a restraining order and seeking a protection order (Protection Order is an all-encompassing phrase used to mean any of the orders listed under section 7 of the Domestic Violence Act, particularly restraining order, tenancy or occupancy order. It generally refers to orders given to protect the survivor and children if any and their interests against the perpetrator), enforcing maintenance orders, etc. They also provide a temporary shelter … thought the maximum stay [at a shelter] would be 3 months. However, [the NGOs] also [state] that they are not able to provide victims of GBV with start-up capital. More often than not, [victims] have to leave their homes and start life afresh, and for a lot of them, it's very difficult to do that.’[footnote 418]

20.1.8 The BGBVC managers 2025 noted:

‘… there are organisations such as Men and Boys for Gender Equality and others where their mandate isn’t really around GBV, but they are doing their best to also try and create awareness in communities on ethics, law and HIV/AIDS. There’s BONELA, there's the Human Rights Centre, there’s also LEGABIBO. There are also Tebelopele wellness centres, [Source confirms Tebelopele wellness centres is still operating (as of 25 Sept 2025) however other sources suggests it stopped operating in February 2025 see Gov't confirms Tebelopele nationwide shutdown:: Mmegi Online] their main mandate is HIV, but they've also integrated GBV. Even the Botswana Christian Health & AIDS Intervention Programme have integrated some community work on GBV. BGBVC and WAR are providing both prevention and response services, while the other organisations were mostly doing prevention (awareness creation) and referring to us for response.’[footnote 419]

20.1.9 The BGBVC managers 2025 explained that the organisation worked with other NGOs

‘… but that their collaboration in activities has reduced a little bit over the years. But they are all members of the Botswana Council of NGOs, BOCONGO, and under BOCONGO they are together within what is called the ‘gender and human rights thematic group’. So they have conversations once in a while where they talk about what to do about what is happening. But … it hasn't been really as it used to be. There's also another organisation called Molao Matters. Their main mandate is legal support. They’re also a member of the gender and human rights thematic group … they are in Francistown, but they have people in Gaborone. They mostly work with lawyers who volunteer their services, so wherever there’s a lawyer who is willing, anywhere in the country, they become part of it.’[footnote 420]

20.1.10 The MOJCS officials 2025 noted ‘…There are also psychosocial organisations which are not necessarily in the shelters, some of which are supported by the government, but there is need for improvement in this area. Most people would go to their church or their parents rather than go to [publicly available] psychosocial services. There is a need to encourage people to trust the services and let them know where they are.’[footnote 421]

20.1.11 The MYGA officials 2025 noted:

‘… several [NGOs/civils society organisations (CSOs)] and that they're doing different work, focusing on different areas. Most CSOs will be providing counselling. They will also be raising awareness [about] GBV … [BGBVC] also has other offices like Ghanzi where they are just providing services like other NGOs, raising awareness on GBV and [providing] counselling. There also faith-based organisations that are also providing the same, raising awareness and counselling, and may refer cases to the police. There are a lot of referrals, and people even go to the health sector, the Ministry of Health, those that need counselling, but those also who need care, medical care if they have sustained injuries. There's a lot of referrals between social workers, the police and the civil society organisations. You find that most of the work that is done is on raising awareness and then counselling, but there is really a need for more shelters … we’ve found that this is a critical need to make sure that people who need shelters can be provided within their own district, not far. Right now, we have 3 [shelters] and it's really limited.’[footnote 422]

20.1.12 The LB representatives 2025 noted:

‘… there are several organisations dealing with the issue of GBV, and their approach to GBV is one of prevention, which means you get messaging around GBV. There is an organisation called BOCAIP [Botswana Christian AIDS Intervention Programme, also known as Botswana Christian Health & AIDS Intervention Program (BOCHAIP)] dealing with issues around GBV, giving out messages. We also have BONELA … [which] deals with issues around GBV, and they’re dealing with it from a legal perspective, sending out legal organisations, dealing with barriers in the areas where people have no access to services. There’s also an organisation called Silence Kills, dealing with GBV for the lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people) community. They also come into contact with GBV cases. [Love Botswana (LB)] also provides support there. LB also helps as an organisation, Just Hope [Foundation] too. They’re dealing with counselling for people experiencing issues around GBV … BOCAIP is a national organisation, an NGO, and it has an office in Maun. BONELA also has an office here. Just Hope is a national organisation that has an office in Maun.’[footnote 423]

20.1.13 The FE officials 2025 noted:

‘[Civil society organisations] CSOs play a big role in [providing] protection in the social and health sectors. CSOs have been complementary to public service and definitely do a lot in [supporting] these women [who experience GBV], for example WAR’s shelter, and making sure they have a police officer to talk to. They provide the link between state services, like the police, and women in need/survivors [of GBV]. If they weren't there the situation would be very dire … [also thought CSOs provided legal advice] but not the CSOs’ main function. It's more health and social support.’[footnote 424]

20.1.14 The ADC 2025 noted that in Maun CSOs included ‘WAR, Red Cross – they provide psychosocial support – there are many [organisations]: LEGABIBO, Tshidilo Stimulation Centre, Love Botswana, Queen Esther. Also prisons and DPP, the tribal administration, the district health team, and the Department of Youth and Gender. These [address] GBV but also mainstreaming of gender.’[footnote 425]

20.2 Botswana Gender Based Violence Support Centre

20.2.1 The BGBVC managers 2025 explained:

‘[BGBVC is] an organisation that works on the prevention and response to GBV, their name sets out what they do: prevention and support. They work in 3 districts [across Botswana (BWA)] on 3 sites: the one they’re running here [in Gaborone], which is their head office, as well as Ghanzi and Francistown. BGBVC have existed for 27 years, working towards the prevention of GBV as well as response and protection, particularly of those that have experienced GBV. In the past, they have had conversations with UK organisations and even people leaving to go to the UK, to the US and other countries due to what they were experiencing … The organisation is run by a board of trustees that oversees everything they do. BGBVC is known by government and society [generally] because they mostly work in communities.’[footnote 426]

20.2.2 The BGBVC managers 2025 also noted:

‘… they have a support programme … providing care and support to survivors of GBV together with their families. They have drop-in centres in Gaborone, Francistown and Ghanzi where clients can just walk in and seek their services. They also have mobile outreach, where BGBVC go where the people are because some people are not comfortable coming to their centres and being seen as survivors of GBV. The main reason for the mobile outreach is mainly to take the services to the people; to make accessibility easier for those who cannot reach our centres or even are not aware of the available service.

‘… [the] BGBVC works with the police, government bodies and other entities. Under their support programme, there are different types of services that are provided, the first being counselling to deal with the trauma that comes with GBV and its effects. They have recently introduced [the option of] telephone counselling. Within the support programme, BGBVC provides legal support, some of it through legal volunteers. BGBVC is also able to provide clients with drafting of different [protective] orders, including restraining orders and protection orders, (‘(a) an interim order; (b) a restraining order; … a tenancy order; or … an occupancy order.’) or applications for divorce because of GBV. They introduce clients to the range of orders available and provide legal advice about other options open to them within the justice system.

‘… also have a clinic on this site [their head office] … specifically for survivors of GBV. They provide it with the purpose of clinical care because some clients come in having sustained injuries, so they treat injuries here. Some of them are survivors of rape, so they provide post-rape care – HIV prevention, preventing unwanted pregnancy, through emergency contraceptive. They also provide STI [sexually transmitted infection] screening and treatment, as well as mixed method contraceptives.’[footnote 427]

20.2.3 The BGBVC managers 2025 also noted that the organisation

‘… deploys different strategies to achieve the goal of making sure that people are aware of GBV, its prevalence and its context. They use the media space and the social media space – all the networks that are available, including Facebook and LinkedIn – to talk about the organisation. They use the mainstream media – TV, radio and newspapers – to disseminate information about GBV and for social marketing of services that are available at the organisation … they also do what they call mobile outreaches, where their community mobilisers accompany a nurse or clinical staff and counsellors to go to communities. [Those in the community] will be screened for GBV, and if they're eligible, they get referred to the counsellors to access the service. Currently, BGBVC has a school-based programme called ‘Connect with Respect’ to address respect in schools, especially issues of bullying and GBV. Through this programme, they are trying to identify students who are somehow susceptible to, or who have been through, GBV situations, especially at home or at school. The idea is to take the students through different GBV topics, but before that, they are pre-assessed for GBV – that is, they’re given a set of questions to share what they understand about GBV and their experiences. This is done in Ghanzi and Francistown only, for 7 schools in total.’[footnote 428]

20.2.4 The BGBVC managers 2025 added that they also do,

‘… capacity-building exercises for frontline workers or those who are at the forefront of responding to and addressing GBV: nurses, police officers, social workers, teachers and the like. They also capacitate tribal leaders and take them through GBV education to enable them to identify GBV and how to better handle cases. These are the people who actually deal with very sensitive cases, and much as BGBVC is aware of traditional norms and perceptions, they need these people to align that to the current situation. They promote the organisation [BGBVC], its services and, by extension, other services that are available out there.’[footnote 429]

20.2.5 The BGBVC managers 2025 explained that their funding was mainly from the government, but they have also received funding from ‘the US government, the Finnish Government and the European Union … [They own one property, but] for the 2 shelters that they are renting, [funding comes from] a private company, a private sector partner.’[footnote 430]

20.2.6 The BGBVC managers 2025 noted ‘… they … get support from the police, and some cases are referred to BGBVC by the police themselves. We’re one of the 2 organisations in the country that have emergency shelters [the other is provided by Women Against Rape in Maun], so whenever they have a victim that needs protection from the perpetrator, they bring them to us … they also have referrals from government social workers.’[footnote 431]

20.2.7 The BGBVC managers 2025 explained the process for entering the centre in Gaborone:

‘When [new clients] come here, the security officer checks them, and then they’re ushered to the clinic. Our approach is that we don’t know how critical it is for each of them to receive medical attention. So before they sit down with the counsellor, their [medical] vitals are taken, such as blood pressure. If they’re injured, they’re provided with medical attention. Then, with a counsellor, they do a screening to see whether they need the shelter or will be able to go home. If they need the shelter, they are transported to the shelter. It also depends on the counsellor because they will find out what’s important for the client. For example, if they want to report to the police, we ensure that they reach the police safely. If they want to see a legal adviser to work out their options, legal advisers can come and see them here … the lawyers don’t work for them; they are volunteers who are called in when needed. Also, we have a Memorandum of Understanding [MoU] [since the beginning of 2025] with Legal Aid Botswana, and they can provide legal support.’[footnote 432]

20.2.8 The BGBVC managers 2025 that women can come to the centre for support, not necessarily to be housed at the shelter. Noting, ‘we have the shelters particularly for those [women who need protection], and then there are those who come here for [other] services. They can come here for trauma counselling, come every week and then go home.’[footnote 433]

20.2.9 The chief executive of the BGBVC in an article in the Daily News, a Botswanan newspaper, summarised the services that the organisation provided in addition to operating a shelter in Gaborone. This included ‘provided counselling, psychosocial support, medical assistance, legal referrals, empowerment programmes, and community education to address harmful gender norms and practices.’[footnote 434]

20.2.10 The BGBVC annual report covering 1 January to 31 December 2024 provided statistics on the type of support and numbers of people assisted in the year:

  • tele-counselling to 69 people
  • shelter to 274 people
  • post GBV care to 717 people
  • psychosocial care to 917 people
  • prevention messaging against GBV and HIV to 5,152 people[footnote 435]

20.2.11 For information about the BGBVC shelter in Gaborone, see Shelters below.

20.3 War Against Rape

20.3.1 War Against Rape (WAR) is, as noted by its executive director, a non-government organisation established in 1993, Maun, Ngamiland, with a vision to end violence in Botswana. WAR supports women who fear GBV by

‘… providing psychosocial support, which is counselling, and public education. They do a lot of public education on prevention [of GBV], including prevention of re-victimisation for those who have experienced violence ... they provide services to those who have been affected, such as offering a shelter … Their first approach is to visit legal practitioners. They used to have their own legal practitioner but then because of funding they piloted [using] government [funded] legal aid … The government is renting space from WAR to run Legal Aid [through Legal Aid Botswana (LAB)] from their office, which is useful because WAR’s clients just refer straight to the office … They have published a number of research papers on GBV and alcohol, and on children's understanding of sexual and reproductive health. This they did with Amplify Change, a British non-governmental organisation (NGO), and they have worked with the University of Rutgers in New Jersey on the publication of findings from their work in schools. They also work with the University of Botswana. Their partners in the work they do are mostly government … the [Ministry of Youth and] Gender Affairs, social services, the dikgosi [traditional chiefs] and the police … WAR is also in a network of NGOs as a member of NCONGO [Ngamiland Council of Non-Governmental Organisations] in Ngamiland and BOCONGO [Botswana Council of Non-Governmental Organisations] in Gaborone.

‘Currently, WAR’s main funding comes from government, [the Ministry of Youth and] Gender Affairs, but they have had funding from a variety of funders including Oak Foundation, Raising Voices in Uganda, Amplify Change, Canada Fund for Local Initiatives, Stephen Lewis Foundation and embassies like the British [High Commission]. They worked with the British [High Commission] during Covid, just a short project with Men and Boys for Gender Equality. They have an ongoing relationship with the French embassy, which puts up calls for proposals and WAR responds. Currently, they are running a project with the French embassy, the [US] embassy and the [US] Peace Corps Volunteers. So WAR has a variety of donors and partners.

‘… they currently have 25 staff members as well as 3 volunteers – 2 German volunteers and one American … all of their counsellors have done a Bachelors [degree in] Counselling or have done social work ... there are 6 counsellors and the shelter manager also has a degree in social work. They don't have a clinical psychologist, so for clinical psychology they refer to Letsholathebe II Memorial Hospital [in Maun] …’[footnote 436]

20.3.2 The WAR executive director 2025 also noted

‘… they have a toll-free number and the WAR number, which is an emergency number that women can send a message or a WhatsApp message to. Women can ask for a “call me back” and the call is always with a counsellor or with the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR … They have to respond if a woman sends them an SMS [text message]. So women can contact WAR directly and at this centre [the WAR office], and that number is 24 hours. [The] Toll free number is 0800 600 387 and the 24hr emergency number is +267 71 311 244. The toll-free number diverts to the emergency number if not answered immediately. The Executive Director and the Head of Counselling alternate in taking the emergency phone after hours and at weekends.’[footnote 437]

20.3.3 The WAR executive director 2025 noted the organisation works with ‘work with the mohumagadi [wives of traditional leaders], counsellors, [social and community development officers] … social workers and other NGOs’ social workers. They are all in a network. The police can call … WAR after hours or call the WAR number after hours, and they are always available.’[footnote 438]

20.3.4 For information about the WAR shelter in Maun, see Shelters below.

20.4 Botswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS

20.4.1 Botswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS (BONELA), as noted by its representatives, was

‘… formed in 2002 with the primary role of integrating ethics, law and human rights in national response to the HIV/AIDS crisis but works on health holistically. BONELA works with marginalised and vulnerable groups including women; children; migrants; sex workers; lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+) people; rural area dwellers; and prisoners – specifically in health and HIV/AIDs.’[footnote 439]

20.4.2 BONELA depends on funding from the government, international organisations - primarily the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (Global Fund) - the European Union and overseas governments. However, the US administration’s cuts to USAID and the Global Fund in the first half of 2025 have significantly reduced the organisation’s income, leading it to reduce staff from 86 to 16 and close 11 offices outside of Gaborone[footnote 440].

20.4.3 BONELA’s services and work include:

  • free legal advice – one in-house lawyer (external lawyers kept on retainers)
  • advocacy including working with the government to ensure laws and policies protect marginalised communities
  • healthcare including HIV testing, provision of condoms and lubes, various service related to sexual and reproductive health
  • community education and mobilisation raising awareness of the rights of marginalised groups
  • research on marginalised groups - collecting information from community contacts[footnote 441]

20.4.4 The BONELA representatives 2025 noted it had:

‘… an emergency fund to assist sex workers, who experience a lot of violence. When they experience violence they could notify us, we provide support and connect them to the police. If they needed immediate shelter, we would provide this. We also provided toiletries and medical supplies. This was a 3-year project that ended in 2024, funded by Dutch government. The same is needed for victims of GBV as most needs are not met at the time of reporting an incident. For instance, victims spend a lot of time at a police station before there can be any form of incarceration. There needs to be rapid response support from that point which would help facilitate access to the justice system in a more dignified way. Some might go to the police station not properly dressed or needing medication.’

20.5 Shelters

20.5.1 The MOJCS officials 2025 noted ‘… there are no government shelters, but the government subvents civil society to provide shelters and support.’[footnote 442]

20.5.2 The GOROB ACHPR submission 2023 noted:

‘Government currently provides financial support to the two (2) shelters run by Non-Governmental Organisations. To strengthen support to GBV survivors, the shelters make referrals and provide transport to access services outside their facilities such as meetings with legal representatives and health care. Other support services include family counselling and reconciliation to ensure sustainability and lifelong benefits for survivors, involvement of men in violence prevention initiatives; and engagement of Religious Leaders in counselling services as preferred by survivors. Legal Aid Botswana in collaboration with shelters provides legal assistance.’[footnote 443]

20.5.3 The UN CEDAW report 2025 was concerned by limited access for survivors of gender-based violence to shelters and psychosocial counselling …’[footnote 444] The GOROB’s reply to CEDAW May 2025 stated: ‘Though Government does not operate and shelters, it continues to provide financial support to the ones run by [civil society organisations] CSOs. For the financial year 2024/2025, the shelters were allocated a total of USD580 thousand.’[footnote 445]

20.5.4 The MYGA officials 2025 noted there are 2 organisations that operate shelters:

  • Botswana Gender-Based Violence Prevention and Support Centre in Francistown and Gaborone
  • Women Against Rape in Maun[footnote 446]

20.5.5 The BGBVC managers 2025 noted:

‘[The BGBVC] … also have the emergency shelters for those in imminent danger. A counsellor does a risk assessment and screens the client for eligibility for admission [to the shelters]. The [shelters] are primarily for those whose lives are in danger because of physical violence, threats to kill or sexual violence, especially for women and children who [need to be] removed from their homes. While [police] investigations are going on, a child can be removed from their home environment if necessary. While in the shelter they also receive other services. The shelters are in undisclosed locations for security – for the protection of clients and the BGBVC staff. Clients are admitted for a maximum of 3 months while BGBVC work around a discharge plan for ensuring their security once they leave the shelter. Shelter clients are mostly referred by the police and social workers, and BGBVC works with [these agencies] on a sustainable plan for ensuring each client’s security beyond the shelter. If the intervention hasn’t been completed after 3 months, this work continues, and depending on the security issues in the case, a client can stay for a year or more. BGBVC’s shelters are only in Gaborone and Francistown, 2 in Gaborone and currently one in Francistown.’[footnote 447]

20.5.6 The BGBVC managers 2025 on the capacity of the shelter explained,

‘… they have 2 shelters in Gaborone. They can accommodate 16 to 18 people in one, and the other is for 8 people. The one in Francistown can also accommodate 16 to 18 people. There are many rooms inside that can accommodate families or individuals … they can never say they don’t need any more [shelters]. The reality is, at this time, they need more shelters. However, the rationale behind it is the number [of people] coming to the shelter, and that is mostly dependent on sensitisation. There are still a lot of women out there who don’t know that there [are] shelters despite the awareness [-raising efforts]. There’s still more that needs to be done because there are women who still would rather stay in an abusive environment and risk their lives. However, we still need more shelters.’[footnote 448]

20.5.7 In an article in the Daily News, a Botswanan newspaper, the chief executive of the BGBVC observed that the shelter in Gaborone ‘accommodates a maximum of 18 people, who typically stay for one to two weeks.’[footnote 449]

20.5.8 The WAR executive director 2025 noted that the organisation had one shelter in an undisclosed location in Maun, adding

‘… the shelter could accommodate up to 20 people, but they limit it to 16. They went up to 16 during Covid, but the facility is not big enough to take 20 people because of the need for showers and [for] cooking – the kitchen is not so big. It's just a house. There is food and a bed and psychosocial support and everything that you get in a house. As well as the manager, there are 3 members of staff there who work on a rotational basis, so it's covered 24 hours. There's always a member of staff there and sheltered abused women and children, boys up to the age of 14 years. WAR doesn’t know if that age limit will go down, but it's 14 for puberty, and before this age WAR considers that boys are not sexually active. Up until then, they can keep the boys with the girls, but once the boys are over 14, they can't take them in the shelter. Then either the boys are sent to SOS villages or social workers will find alternative housing for them.

‘[On how long women may stay at the shelter] when WAR started the shelter, they said 3 months, but 3 months is just on paper. The women can stay up to maybe 6 months and then they leave. But the children can stay up to 2 years or even more. It depends on when the case gets concluded. Sometimes the adults will leave the shelter before the case is concluded because they have a life outside of the shelter and they feel this has been put on hold; it's been like they're now in prison when the men are out. The adults’ way of thinking is different from children’s, and you can't hold an adult in a shelter.
