So, adults can choose to say that they would prefer to be outside the shelter while they wait for the case to be concluded, whereas with children, because they are admitted with a court order and a social worker report, it's only the court that can remove the child from the shelter. If, for example, a child was placed in the shelter for a 6-month period initially, but the case was still not concluded after 6 months, the social workers would go back to court and get another court order for WAR to do an extension, and then the social workers have to support WAR in looking after the child until then. If children in the shelter are of school age, WAR makes sure that they go to school and takes them to school and picks them up again.’[footnote 450]

20.5.9 The WAR executive director 2025 also noted:

‘The adult cases can be where a woman runs away and goes to the police and says, “My husband, my partner, is beating me. I’m scared of going home. There's nobody to talk to. Please help me.” And then the police, assessing the situation, feel maybe they don't have a car to find this person, or they have looked around, but they can't find him. Then they will say, “Women Against Rape, can you hold on to this woman until we find the perpetrator? And once we’ve found that perpetrator and understood the situation, then we can take her out [of the shelter], or she will stay in if there is a case to be investigated.” So, women can come in while the police are doing an investigation. They can also come in when there is a court case going on where they need protection, sometimes because of a threat to kill. If someone threatens to kill you in Botswana, you can be taken into protection. And then the perpetrator will be in a cell or they look for him and then they go to the magistrates’ court to get a restraining order or something.’[footnote 451]

20.5.10 With regards to shelter security, WAR executive director 2025 stated:

‘…if somebody was sitting here [pointing to one side of the desk] and she was sitting there [on opposite sides of her desk], it's a long way to go to that panic button. So, security is always an issue… at the counselling centre in Gaborone (at BGBVC in around 2023) … [a] perpetrator agreed to come for a counselling session but ended up stabbing [his wife]. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that there was a security guard, there were panic buttons, there was everything, so sometimes you don't know what you could have done to prevent that. Security is always at the forefront of what WAR does.’[footnote 452]

20.5.11 On whether the BGBVC shelters were full at the time of the interview in July 2025, the BGBVC managers noted ‘… you can stay in a shelter for a maximum of 3 months, or more based on circumstances. In terms of new applications, there may not be too many at a time, but there will be those who are already in the shelter, so they are usually fully occupied.’[footnote 453]

20.5.12 The BGBVC managers 2025 also noted ‘… [the shelters] are available to women nationwide so they can get a referral from anywhere.’[footnote 454] Similarly, the WAR executive director 2025 noted the organisation

‘… take[s] women from all over the country. They had a case of a couple where the woman was abused so much that she needed to be taken out of Maun. They felt that the husband knew where the shelter was and was capable of coming to threaten WAR or threaten WAR and the shelter, which he did. But they negotiated with the women's shelter in Gaborone to send the woman to Gaborone. She was assisted in … [Gaborone] and the man was here. Sometimes, [the women’s shelter in Gaborone has] … cases where they feel the woman will be safer far away from the perpetrator. So [WAR and BGBVC] … work together, they co-operate.’[footnote 455]

20.5.13 On access to support, the UNFPA official 2025 noted it was physically easy to access GBV support (where it is available): ‘You can just walk in and they don’t charge you anything. The challenge is that GBV is spread across the country, but BGBVC is only here in Gaborone with satellite offices and shelters. Women Against Rape is in Maun. In other places, particularly the remotest places, there are no shelters … But if a woman is able to get herself to a shelter, it’s quite easy. These are open centres but most have very limited capacity.’[footnote 456]

20.5.14 The MYGA officials 2025, when asked what long term support is provided to women who have to go into shelters, noted that there are

‘… several aspects to it, [the first being] that shelters themselves have training in terms of trying to equip [women] with skills to undertake income-generating activities – culinary, sewing, knitting, etc. And then there’s a social inquiry report which goes to the ministers responsible for social services, who say this person needs to at least to be enrolled [with social services] because of their inability to be employed at a point in time. So that is now at a bigger level. There are those measures.’[footnote 457]

21. Internal relocation

21.1 Legal right to move

21.1.1 The FH report 2025 noted: ‘Most citizens can move freely within Botswana and travel internationally …’[footnote 458] The USSD HR report 2024 does not comment on freedom of movement[footnote 459] however, the USSD HR report for 2023, which covered a broader range of human rights issues, noted ‘The law provided for freedom of internal movement … and the government generally respected these rights.’[footnote 460].

21.1.2 The WAR executive director 2025 noted ‘movement is not restricted, in the simple way of can you get on a bus’ and that there are no barriers to travel[footnote 461].

21.1.3 The MLIA officials 2025 noted when asked about freedom of movement: ‘Every person in this country has the right of freedom of movement. If movement is restricted, there's something they can do. They can approach the authorities and report it. The basis of these provisions and the law is really to protect individuals.’[footnote 462]

21.1.4 The BONELA representatives 2025 thought the only barrier to for a woman to move with Botswana was financial[footnote 463].

21.2 Accessing public services

21.2.1 The UNFPA official 2025 noted:

‘… you can access healthcare anywhere; you don't have to be a resident of that locality. Women’s economic empowerment programmes are usually tied to a district. There'll be a budget under the Ministry of Youth & Gender Affairs and then it will be allocated to the different gender offices across the district because they'll have a sense of roughly how many people qualify and anything like that. But they’re generally accessible, so you can apply and try your luck anywhere, because in Botswana you can live anywhere.’[footnote 464]

21.2.2 The WAR executive director 2025 commenting on access to public services ‘explained that [it also depends on] whether you are going to qualify for those government services, because it's not everyone who can. Even for poor people, it’s not everyone who receives support.’[footnote 465]

21.2.3 The MWT representatives 2025 noted ‘that education, health, everything is free, so everyone can access this. It's only [people’s mistaken] beliefs that might prevent [them from relocating], for example a belief that their children can’t go to school. [But] everyone has the right to education … the government takes responsibility for providing healthcare and education, including boarding schools.’[footnote 466]

21.3 Lone women

21.3.1 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 noted it was common for women to move within the country for jobs / employment adding ‘unless my view is biased, I think single women are not looked down on [in Gaborone].’ 467

21.3.2 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 also thought:

‘… the majority of households are female-headed … It's quite normal ... [Asked what the reaction would be if a woman left her partner] Well, it depends. Some men will accept it, but I would presume it's a small majority … If the man is a lost cause, they wouldn't really care. They would just continue on with their life and let the woman, if she wanted to, have the responsibility for their kids and bear the cost of raising the kids. Some men will just let them be, but in some instances, family are often the first people to intervene and say, “No, you can't do that. Come back to your husband or to your partner, raise the kids together.”’[footnote 468]

21.3.3 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 noted that ‘… in some instances nowadays, because men are becoming much more alive to their legal rights in terms of custody and stuff, they would challenge that to the courts and then in some unfortunate instances, we've heard of men following their partner, assaulting them and in some instances killing them or leaving them.’[footnote 469]

21.3.4 The International diplomatic source 2 – 2025 did not consider a woman, including a single woman or single mother,

‘… would face discrimination [from other people]. But if she was married and was being harmed within the marriage and she relocated with her kids there will be some backlash from her in-laws because there is a traditional belief you should work things out. That's what most women in abusive marriages explained to [the official]. The stigma [for moving away] might come from there. But … didn’t think people would generally [discriminate against a woman] or judge her or [not] accept them in society [for being a lone woman].’[footnote 470]

21.3.5 The UNFPA official 2025 noted ‘… that a lot of people come to towns seeking employment opportunities or economic empowerment opportunities and that there is a lot of internal migration. If you don't find them [economic opportunities], that's when the challenges begin.’[footnote 471] The official also noted:

‘…. [women] who have the economic means can [relocate], but it's tough because a lot of victims are economically dependent on their partners. The houses they live in were bought by their partners. If you need shelter, where are you going to go? [What is your] means of sustenance? That's why a lot of the cases are withdrawn, because they say these men are the ones who provide support, but those that have the economic means can [continue with a court case] … BWA is only small [in population]. There are cases in which perpetrators of GBV have travelled hundreds of kilometres [to find their victims] … even if a woman moves to a different village or town, it’s very easy for [the perpetrator] to find them if they're determined to do so. It may be easy for a woman to get on a bus and decide she’s moving from Gaborone to Francistown, but it's just as easy for the perpetrator to move and find her.’[footnote 472]

21.3.6 The FAB representatives 2025 noted ‘that there would perhaps be more prospects for work and finding work [in Gaborone] than in most places in the country because most development has been centred here. Most companies are [in the city] … you find the headquarters of most companies here.’ Also noting:

‘… [for a woman] choosing to move away from a spouse means you're relying on your financial [means] to protect yourself. Often support will be from family members and/or friends, not from the state, in terms of setting you up. There is an unemployment rate of approximately 37% (for youth up to 35 years of age), so if you're leaving a city, for example Gaborone, your probability of getting a job there [in the new location] as opposed to [Gaborone] is very low. So, if you're moving, it means you're leaving your work … If you're entrepreneurial, then you can start doing some entrepreneurial undertakings. … [but] you are sacrificing your financial stability for your physical safety.’[footnote 473]

21.3.7 The FAB representatives 2025 commenting on societal attitudes to a single woman noted:

‘… there would be no shame because … there is a high percentage of single female-headed households in BWA so [it would not be unusual]. She thought that despite everything, Batswana are accommodating and understanding. They still have a communal sense of responsibility to each other, especially when it comes to sensitive issues like this [GBV, break up of families]. So you'd be able to start a life. You'd be able to find support where you are. A majority of women tend to rely on churches and social clubs for communal support.’[footnote 474]

21.3.8 The LB representatives 2025 noted:

‘… relocation would be fairly easy depending on income and whether she’s able to move jobs. There’s a high level of unemployment, but … thought that in most cases, it would be very possible … there’s no stigma [for a single woman], and healthcare is free. They also have a temporary rescue centre for children aged 0 to 5. Where there’s been neglect or sexual abuse, the children are removed from their home and are sent to the centre while the case is before the courts. Cases can take a long time, so they do extended court orders.’[footnote 475]

21.3.9 The WAR executive director 2025 noted:

‘… it’s very, very difficult. You have to move from your place. To move from, say, Maun and go to Francistown, you must know somebody in Francistown, or you must have a job that you are going to that will sustain you. You first of all think, “Where am I going to stay? How am I going to sustain myself?” so that you must have found a job. There must be someone who says, “I will take you in.” That “I will take you in” must happen before you can move and just go, because you can’t just go into a shelter, you have to go through the police. They don't just come straight through the police, and you don't house them forever. The other option is going through social services. Social services have destitute programmes, and for you to qualify as a destitute we have to evaluate 1,2,3,4, and if you are found to be able to work, then you don't get that funding.’[footnote 476]

21.3.10 The UNFPA official 2025 on how society considers single women or mothers noted:

‘… depend[s] where the woman moved to. A city like Gaborone is multicultural and there are different people who are here for different business. But society is very traditional in people’s home villages because of the kgotla [customary court/community council] system, which means everybody knows everybody, everybody is tied to a kgotla and they have a traditional chief and they know each other by their family names. By moving from your home village to, say, another village, you're settling into an already established community, so obviously you're going to draw public attention. It depends on how traditional the place is that you're moving to, but ultimately people always get to know why you are there. In urban centres, it may not be so obvious.

‘[The official did not consider a woman moving to Gaborone or Francistown would face societal backlash] … not really in urban centres … probably a woman moving would have the means to sustain herself because otherwise she would struggle and become stranded, and people might then ask where she had come from and make the connection to her history if she had been missing. If she has the means to move to an urban centre and self-sustain, it should be easy. But again, the fact that it’s easy for a woman to move means it’s very easy for the perpetrator to follow her.’[footnote 477]

21.3.11 The WAR executive director 2025 confirmed that a single or lone woman

‘… can move and live in a rental. People have built houses. And if you've got children, the children will easily be admitted in a school because of the law that children must go to school. There's no school that can refuse your children going into a public school … Like the children who come to our shelter – when they come in, we insist that the social workers bring their school forms, they transfer them, then they come here, we find them a school as well, and there's no school that can refuse. So the issue is finding a place to stay and something to take care of yourself, and a job can do that.’ [footnote 478]

21.3.12 The WAR executive director 2025 did not consider there was stigma for single women ‘… anymore – there are so many such women. She thought that in Botswana, the marriage statistics are going down. Single families are now everywhere, so there's no stigma around them. She didn’t think so anyway.’[footnote 479]

21.3.13 The FE officials 2025 ‘thought there are multiple issues [for a woman relocating within Botswana]. There's still this big weight of community even if you have the economic means. There's a system around you - it wouldn't be seen in the right way by the family or the community, especially for women with kids.’[footnote 480]

21.3.14 The MWT representatives 2025 noted women ‘are free as long as their finances allow, they can move. Some won't move because of their financial status, their beliefs and their culture. BWA is a free country, people can leave when they want and live where they want.’[footnote 481]

21.3.15 The ADC 2025 noted for a woman to relocate ‘family may offer support, but there are not shelters to accommodate a large number. So, this is the challenge, the lack of shelters [but] … people can move anywhere [but] they will need money and somewhere to stay.’[footnote 482]

21.4 Tracing and locating people

21.4.1 The International diplomatic source 1 – 2025 also noted ‘BWA is a small country, and you can't disappear and live off the grid without somebody eventually finding you.’[footnote 483]

21.4.2 The UNFPA official 2025 noted:

‘There had been a case in which a woman had moved to the BGBVC shelter [in Gaborone] and [her husband] had followed her and killed her in front of others in broad daylight. Imagine if a woman moved to a different village and, instead of being in a shelter, she just lived on her own. Many women are financially dependent on their partners, but if a woman who [is financially independent] moves away, there are cases where the perpetrator follows her and ultimately either rapes her again or kills her.’[footnote 484]

21.4.3 The FAB representatives 2025 when asked if a person could ‘disappear’ noted: ‘… you can’t disappear … Given our small population it is difficult to disappear and start life afresh in another part of Botswana … [perpetrators] will always find ways. If a person is intent [on] killing you, they'll track you down and kill you. Because there is such a small population, it's very easy for a perpetrator to find where their partner is … [Even Gaborone is] still quite small. Everybody knows everybody's business.’[footnote 485]

21.4.4 See also sections on Geography, Economic context, Social economic and political status, and Social and cultural attitudes for discussion of factors relevant to considering internal relocation.

Annexes

Annex A - Botswana fact finding mission: background

Acknowledgement

The fact-finding mission (FFM) team are profoundly grateful to the British High Commission, Gaborone, our driver, and the many sources who spoke to them for their time, knowledge, support and patience. The FFM team returned to the UK with a much better understanding of Botswana and gender-based violence in the country.

Pula!

Purpose

Three officials from CPIT undertook a fact finding-mission (FFM) to Botswana between 6 and 17 July 2025 to gather information about gender-based violence (GBV) and the experiences of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people). The team were supported by officials at British High Commission, Gaborone (BHCG). The FFM team visited Gaborone and Maun.

See Annex V for the FFM’s Terms of Reference (ToR).

Research standards

The FFM was undertaken with reference to the EU [European Union] common guidelines on (Joint) Fact Finding Missions: a practical tool to assist member states in organizing (joint) Fact Finding Missions, November 2010 (EU Guidelines 2010), and CPIT‘s internal guidelines for conducting FFMs.

Identification of sources

The FFM team sought to interview a wide range of informed sources, including government officials, members of non-government organisations and international organisations, and western embassy officials. Sources were identified primarily by desk-based research and in consultation with the BHCG.

The sources contacted and interviewed are those that the FFM team and the BHCG identified as relevant to the mission’s ToR. But, as with any FFM, factors including time constraints and availability of sources meant that the list of sources-consulted and information provided are not exhaustive.

That a particular source was interviewed and the notes of the interview have been included are not endorsement of that source or the information provided. Rather, all the information provided needs to be critically assessed and considered against other publicly available material.

Arranging and conducting interviews

The FFM team conducted 19 face-to-face interviews, and one video interview over Microsoft Teams, meeting a total of 56 people.

All interviews and subsequent correspondence with sources were conducted in English.

At the start of each interview the FFM team explained the purpose of the mission and the how the information gathered would be used. This included that the notes of the interview may be published in a report on the GOV.UK website and the sources would be able to review the notes before publication.

Sources were also given an introductory note explaining this (see Annex W).

Notes of interviews/meetings

The FFM team recorded all meetings using Microsoft Teams on their work mobile phones as well as taking written notes. Agreed notes of the meetings were subsequently sent by email to the sources for review and approval. Covering emails explained that if a source did not respond within a specific deadline CPIT would assume the source was content with the notes as sent to them.

Of the 20 interviews:

  • Eleven sets of the notes were approved by sources with a number making amendments to the original drafts
  • Nine sources did not respond to CPIT’s emails but had given permission orally during the interview for the notes to be published

All sources are described/referred according to their preference as expressed at the interviews or subsequently in email correspondence.

The notes does not reflect the views or assessment of the Home Office. All opinions expressed are those of the sources interviewed only.

Terms of reference

A ‘Terms of Reference’ of the topics considered relevant to the FFM are at Annex U.

Annex B - Interview with an International diplomatic source 1

Date 7 July 2025
LocationGaborone
Attendees Diplomatic source 1; 3 Home Office (HO) officials

The FFM team as if the International diplomatic source could you summarise the situation of women in Botswana in terms of their social and political rights. The International diplomatic source noted that the Constitution recognises everyone, women enjoy legal protections, and they're recognised in society as equals to men. Women have come a long way in terms of that recognition; it wasn't always the case. But culturally, BWA is a patriarchal society and there's a conservative element. There's still some progress to go in terms of political participation of women: only 9% of MPs in Parliament [who are women]. Women also enjoy some recognition in law on inheritance. Women can benefit from their parents’ inheritance as much as their male counterparts. In the private sector, there's still low representation of women in senior leadership positions.

The main human rights situation threat to women in BWA is GBV, like that due to the lack of economic empowerment. They find themselves subject to mean[ness], whether it's their husbands, their boyfriends or their male relatives. So that puts them at a disadvantage economically and in terms of how society treats them. In Botswana’s traditional system - the Kgotla - which is like the traditional gathering point for every tribe in every village, women are still discriminated in terms of how they're allowed to show up. For example, they're not allowed to wear pants [trousers] to the traditional gathering, which puts off some women. There are legal protections, but the conservative nature of the society puts women on the back foot.

The FFM team asked if the new government has introduced any new legal protections for women, or had it shown intention to protection women further.

The International diplomatic source noted that there is strong rhetoric but not much political will and there haven't been any substantive changes to legislation, although the government has been in power for 7 months now so there have been limited opportunities. The government portray themselves as a human-rights based government, saying they want to put human rights at the centre of everything that they do. But BWA is still a patriarchal society which is quite conservative.

The FFM team asked if there is a difference in how women are treated Gaborone and Maun or for women in rural areas generally. The International diplomatic source said yes, very much. There's a distinct difference between rural and urban areas. The majority of the population lives in urban areas, but there are still some tribes – because BWA is divided according to tribal territories – that are much more liberal than others. But in some places you'll see that women are still very far behind in how they're recognised and how they're treated.

The FFM team asked if there are particular factors – age, tribe, where people live, education and the economic success of families – that affect treatment. The International diplomatic source considered yes, education, the top one and then of course economic background with the family. The FFM team clarified, if they have more money what does that mean. The International diplomatic source considered that if a woman comes from a well-off family, then the prospects of her rising up in society are much higher and how they're treated also corresponds to that. But the International diplomatic source did not think they [relatively wealthy women] can avoid gender-based violence, it affects all women – but didn’t think economic background matters that much. The International diplomatic source had heard and seen examples of women who are well-educated still experiencing GBV.

The FFM team asked how the government and society treat lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+) people generally and for lesbians in particular. While we’re on the topic we should address LGBT+ people and particularly lesbians and bisexual women. They're a subset of women. So first of all, how do government and society regard LGBT+ people and particularly that subset of women? What's their place and what's their experience? What's their protection first of all?

The International diplomatic source noted that the Botswana legal system approaches people as just being people. It does not draw distinctions between LGBT+ and other people. But of course, even though there are those legal protections how they're treated in law enforcement, for example, if they come in to report an issue and they say, ‘I've been assaulted by my partner. I'm a lesbian woman, and I've been assaulted by my partner’, the treatment that the official had heard of in these cases is quite different than that of a heterosexual woman. It will depend on the police officer that's handling the issue. The source had heard of male police officers, particularly, laughing at men: the man comes into the police station and they say they've been assaulted by a woman or by their gay partner and there was a slap, and they’ve (the police) undermined their complaint.

The FFM team asked whether the International diplomatic source had heard of cases where a gay man or lesbian has gone to the police, is it all negative? The International diplomatic source it's mostly been negative, from the reports that I've heard. The FFM team asked if these reports have been in the newspapers. The International diplomatic source noted that there’s a difference in how the media cover LGBT+ issues. Some [media] are more explicit - there are particular newspapers that are much more explicit how they cover issues, but some don’t report them at all. The International diplomatic source didn’t think lesbian women report as much that they've been assaulted - so there is under-reporting.

The FFM team asked what are the main types of gender-based violence? International diplomatic source: The main one would be intimate partner violence (IPV). That's resulted in a lot of cases. Murder. Asked if husband or boyfriend, The International diplomatic source thought mostly boyfriend, girlfriend.

Asked how many cases of murder, the International diplomatic source did not have the numbers off but there was a particular period during the festive season [Christmas] last year when the police reported the number of cases of murder, incest or molestation were in their hundreds nationally in that period alone. The FFM team asked if these were publicly available statistics. The International diplomatic source said yes, can pull the report from early January this year. The FFM team asked if the government generally released data on reports of domestic assault and murder, the International diplomatic source said yes, more recently, but it's not consistent. It will be attached to a particular period. For example, they report a lot during the holiday period.

The FFM team clarified what IPV equated to. The International diplomatic source physical and sexual assault. Did not hear a lot about emotional abuse, but it's mostly included as part of the physical assault. The FFM team asked if this has other forms too, like denying money, if the main is the main breadwinner. The International diplomatic source: agreed.

The FFM team asked what other types of GBV are there, non-intimate partner violence? The International diplomatic source: noted rape. Where the woman is walking on the street and raped by a stranger, for example. That happens quite a lot, especially in rural areas. The FFM team asked about other types, such as mentions of or links to traditional ceremonies and animist beliefs. The International diplomatic source had heard of traditional doctors assaulting their purported patients or clients, like a client for a consultation. And they're sexually assaulted by the traditional doctor.

The FFM team asked if that is media reports? The International diplomatic source: It's not as prevalent as other forms of violence. The FFM team clarified that it is not documented like other forms of GBV? International diplomatic source: No, not really. Also, because of the stigma associated with people going to traditional doctors, people don't tend to report it. And then in addition to that, a lot of assault that's been reported is from religious leaders, for example, especially the more modern type of churches. The pastors would occasionally lure [victims] them into private spaces. There has been a proliferation of these new churches, they are called ‘fire churches’ or ‘prosperity gospel churches’.

The FFM team asked of women who experienced GBV had a particular profile.

International diplomatic source: No, there's never a particular profile. It could be anyone.

The FFM team noted that there appears to be limited systematic documenting of GBV. Was this source’s understanding too - are there any other statistics, government Official studies or any other private or research studies?

International diplomatic source: the only authority would be the police and they're quite inconsistent in what they release, what the information documents. But there was a study [Botswana National Relationship Study], from 2018, that's the one referred to a lot. That’s the one that says that 67% of women [experienced GBV].

The FFM team asked if there is data on the levels of violence experienced by LGBT+ people. International diplomatic source: Not that I’m aware of. The FFM asked if the source knew what the general levels of violence and harassment are for that group at all? Is it documented? International diplomatic source: No, not really. Because again, this is very much under-reported because it doesn't come very much from the mainstream media. Of course, NGOs talk about it, but they talk about it from anecdotal references.

The FFM team asked if the source knew of the size of the LGBT+ community? International diplomatic source: I don't think it’s documented. The FFM team further asked if communities exist, is there a more urban/rural split? International diplomatic source: assumed they would be more concentrated in urban areas. And then there's an extension to that. The official thought there are specific LGBT+ healthcare services, for example, like for certain injuries. They're called drop-in centres for LGBT+ people. Those ones, I think, will probably have an idea of where the population is. These groups include LEGABIBO, Rainbow Identity Association, BONELA - the BWA network on ethics, law and HIV/AIDS, which is mostly public health. The FFM team asked if these were in certain areas or across the country. International diplomatic source: BONELA has different centres across the country, outside the city. The FFM team asked if these provide healthcare only, or there’s advice and treatment? International diplomatic source: Yeah, drop in centres provide counselling services as well SRHR services. For treatments, clients must go to clinics and hospitals.

The FFM team asked if women are completely equal in the law to men? International diplomatic source: I’d say so. The FFM team clarified this included inheritance rights? International diplomatic source: That changed a couple of years ago. It was a court case. The woman challenged [the law] because she was basically skipped over for her father's inheritance, and she went to the judiciary and challenged them. The FFM team asked about custody rights for children? International diplomatic source: in practice, custody cases are usually more in favour of women than men. The FFM team summarised: in general, the law and the government's policies are progressive and really equal. The issue is around implementation and the traditional position of women and that's manifest. International diplomatic source: Somewhat but still have some way to go to achieve true equality.

The FFM team asked if women feel able to go to police for assistance. International diplomatic source: Yes, more recently as opposed to a couple of years ago. But it's relative. Depends on which part of the country. [Think it is better] in more urban areas, the police are much more proactive in terms of encouraging women to consult them. Whereas in rural areas, I think they would be much more hesitant because they are in smaller communities. If you go to a police officer, they most likely know you or your family. So, they will be quite hesitant to report it. The FFM team asked of women in rural areas might feel able to go to the nearest big town and report it? International diplomatic source: I don't think so. The first avenue would probably be the village chief, because they also play a role in mediation of family conflicts in most instances. Actually, people would prefer to go to the chief than the police because the chief would just be mediation. There's no punishment.

The FFM team asked if traditional chiefs are they still present in, for example, Maun or Gaborone? Do they still have a place, a role to play? International diplomatic source: Yes. The FFM team asked even when people have moved? International diplomatic source: They do, but they’re much less visible in cities and urban centres than in the villages.

The FFM asked if somebody had moved from a village to Gaborone, would there be a village chief to consult? International diplomatic source: Yes, that's right. It depends on the location. For example, if you're living in Gaborone in the west, there would be a customary court or local authority. The FFM team clarified that the tribes are mostly Tswana. International diplomatic source: Yes, the country's predominantly Tswana speaking, and then there's different tribes: for example the Kalanga tribe, the Bamangwato, Bangwaketse etc. source didn't know how many there are. The FFM team asked if they are all Tswana speakers? International diplomatic source: No, there are tribes that speak Tswana as their first language and then tribes that have a different first language, but they do speak Tswana as well. So, Tswana would be their second language. For example, in the north in Francistown, because it’s near the border with Zimbabwe, they speak Kalanga, which is [similar to] Tswana. And then towards the west, near the border with Namibia, you find that they speak languages that are spoken in Namibia.

The FFM team asked if a person can go to any traditional chief or they have to go to their own tribe? International diplomatic source: noted that it depends on where you live. If you have moved, the majority of the time, you can go to the nearest chief [in Gaborone] [but who may be from a different tribe]. Tribal administrations fall under the Ministry of Local Government, so in essence, the public government service. The FFM team clarified, that this is part of traditional justice system, which is overseen by the government and any person can use this system to mediate irrespective of their tribal background. International diplomatic source, yes. Customary law exists in parallel with the common statutory law system, even though it doesn’t have the same effect as common law.

The FFM team asked, can a person be arrested or go to prison under customary law? International diplomatic source: Yes, customary courts have authority to issue arrest warrants for defendants. They’d arrest you and then transfer you to the police. So, they [tribal chiefs] give you a punishment and if it's beyond their remit then they will transfer you to the police, to enforcement, or to that magistrate system. For example, if I've stolen cattle or somebody's animal or pet, they report me to the chief and the chief has the authority to deal with that. If it's murder, the chief can't deal with that, it's common law. The FFM clarified, the chiefs could only had minor matters? International diplomatic source: More like simple things. They could deal with mediation with families, but if a woman had been beaten by a partner, they'd have to go to the secular support system, the police, they couldn't deal with violence. So, people have a choice - if you'd like to press charges, then you go to the police. If you want mediation between you and your husband or you and your partner, then you can go to the chief or to a social worker.

The FFM team asked if a woman goes to the police, would they then intervene. International diplomatic source: They'll take a sworn statement from the victim, and then they'll open a case, investigate the perpetrator, and they'll ask the victim, ‘Do you want to press charges?’ Then if they say yes, then they’ll press charges, they’ll detain them and the perpetrator will have to wait for a date to see the magistrate. And if they want to apply for bail, they'll apply for bail. Then they’ll wait for a court date and the trial will start. Sometimes, especially if it's married people or long-term partners, the woman will drop the charges or the family will intervene and say, ‘We'll deal with this at a family level’, and then they'll drop the charges. But yes, if the prosecutor tried, they'll get the punishment (usually a fine if found guilty).

The FFM team asked if the police trained in handling GBV cases; are they independent and fair in how they go about these cases; what’s their capability and training in managing these cases and how proactive are they? International diplomatic source: the police have established the Gender and Child Protection Unit, this is a department that's mandated to deal with GBV cases and issues of child abuse. The FFM team asked when the GBV unit was established? International diplomatic source: in 2021 - it was a big thing. The president announced it as a way for them to deal with issues of domestic violence. The FFM team asked if there police officers from this unit in most police stations? International diplomatic source: noted that they train every police officer because you'll find that a police officer or some of them will be first responders. They'll sit at the reception desk. Every new police officer that comes into the force is trained on how to deal with GBV and child abuse. But it's a new thing. Source did not know how many police officers are in the unit, but they're around the country. Source did not think every single police has been trained so far. But there's been efforts to incorporate it into the retraining of police officers who are already in service and then training of the new ones as well.

The FFM team summarised: the GBV unit’s role is to set standards on how to approach gender-based and child-based violence cases, to train and be a focus, but there aren't specialist officers for GBV or child violence cases? International diplomatic source: not sure if there are specialist officers that only deal with GBV cases.

The FFM team asked if there is similar guidance for the police in handling LGBT+ cases? International diplomatic source: the director of the Gender and Child Protection Unit told us that [the police] don't classify LGBT+. If a LGBT+ person goes into [a police station] to report [an incident], that's just the person. The FFM team summarised: there’s recognition that gender is an issue in itself, but not that sexual orientation and gender identity are an issue. International diplomatic source: Yes.

The FFM team asked if there is a parallel for LGBT+ people in the judicial process, where judges have been trained on gender-based violence cases and child-based violence cases? International diplomatic source: noted that magistrates and judges are more aware recently. But judges are not easy people to pull together in a training day or workshop, magistrates you can with luck. Magistrates, yeah, with some luck. You can finesse. Magistrates easier to convene and coordinate with than judges because judges tend to be busier. Recently, different international development partners, including the UK, have undertaken training sessions for magistrates, prosecutors and judges. I think international partners include the UNDP, UNICEF, and the UNFPA.

The FFM team asked if GBV training had been formalised into the judicial system. International diplomatic source: not sure how far they've gone to incorporate it because one of the things we encourage is ownership of training programmes.

The FFM team noted that during COVID in 2021 the judges had reportedly introduced fast track courts for GBV, was International diplomatic source aware of these? International diplomatic source: Yes, aware of these, they would prioritise GBV cases and have specialised spaces. [But] that implementation has been slacking.

The FFM team noted that there are lots of reported GBV cases but the actual number resulting in convictions and sentencing is quite small, why is that? International diplomatic source: The main reason is that people drop charges. The victims or survivors eventually drop the charges. And there's a lot of interference from families - families of the perpetrators especially - especially if the perpetrator is considered to be a breadwinner. They're quite powerful within their families because of financial muscle.

The FFM team summarised, that culture and family are the most influential in cases being dropped but asked if it was also because the police and the judiciary were not effective or resistant to handling these cases. International diplomatic source: noted that even when the police do a fair investigation, collect all the evidence that they need to, I don't think we're there yet in terms of the legal system, where if a victim drops the charges, the state can continue the case – there are loopholes. The FFM team queried what was meant by ‘loopholes?’. International diplomatic source: It's not strong enough in terms of enforcement. If a victim chooses to drop the charges, then the state won't continue. As in there’s no legal foundation for the state to continue the case if the plaintiff drops the charges. The FFM team queries whether that is a loophole or just how the justice system works [with investigations and evidentiary requirements]? International diplomatic source: I know in other jurisdictions the state has authority to continue with the cases even if the victim has dropped the charges.

The FFM team checked that International diplomatic source was not aware of data on conviction and sentencing - there’s no data on that, there's no surveys on that. International diplomatic source: No, not that I know of.

The FFM team asked if GBV victims and LGBT+ people are they able to get legal aid from Legal Aid Botswana, and support for the legal process? International diplomatic source: assumed they would. But there's that distinction that they [LGBT+ people] come to the legal system as just a human being. The legal system doesn't discriminate to say, ‘No, just because you're a gay person, you can’t access the legal system.’ As far as I'm concerned they do, and there are NGOs that offer legal assistance specifically to key populations including LGBT+ people. BONELA has lawyers in that team - actually they outsource private practice lawyers to do that on an [individual] basis.

The FFM team if Lesbians, Gays and Bisexuals of Botswana (LEGABIBO) offer a legal aid support service? International diplomatic source: not sure. I think they have, but they don't have in-house lawyers, they outsource. The FFM team asked if there many women’s groups that provide legal aid? International diplomatic source: Not that I’m aware of. Maybe the Botswana Gender Based Violence Prevention Centre (BGBVPC).

The FFM team asked if there was state support - financial, accommodation, shelters – for GBV victims? International diplomatic source: In fact, one of the issues that always comes up is severe lack of shelters. International diplomatic source: The state doesn't have any [shelters]. NGOs: I know the BGBVPC has one and I think Women Against Rape has one [in Maun]. I’m not sure if it's still there, I don't know. There are no state-run shelters. The FFM team asked if the state provided any other forms of support for victims - counselling, healthcare, could be financial, some sort of payments. International diplomatic source: No, the Botswana police is in the process of setting up one-stop centres for GBV. where you come into a one-stop for the police, to report. It's a police officer, doctor, healthcare worker and a lawyer, but they're yet to operationalise it. The FFM team asked if they have intention to operationalise the one-stop centres? International diplomatic source: We're not sure. They've mentioned lack of resources and funding. I know it's something they're working on. On the child protection front, they do have child-friendly centres. There's about 8 of them across the country that we've helped fund and support help with operationalisation. There's a separate room where a child can come in and spend a couple of nights. There's a bed. There's a bathroom. There's a kitchen.

The FFM team asked if girls could go to these centres and girls who’ve had violence at home and if the centres were in Gaborone, Maun, Francistown …? International diplomatic source: Yes, Gaborone, Francistown, Palapye, Maun, Ghanzi, Lobatse, Letlhakane and Shakawe.

The FFM team asked which NGOs not mentioned already that support women who have experienced GBV. International diplomatic source: I think that's all of them, BGBVPC, Women Against Rape in Maun, Feminist Alliance, but they are more like the policy side. BOCONGO does some work as well, which is like the umbrella body for NGOs, and there's Men and Boys that deals with engagement with men. The FFM team asked if this was to stop [men from] causing violence against women? International diplomatic source: Yeah. But they do engagement with NGOs.

The FFM team asked that if there may be other NGOs that International diplomatic source was not aware of? International diplomatic source: Yes, there might be others that are much smaller and based on communities, smaller communities as well.

The FFM team asked if civil society was strong in Botswana generally? International diplomatic source: Of course, they're free to operate and they enjoy freedom of expression and freedom of association. But they're not quite strong in terms of their voice because Botswana is an upper-middle income country that doesn't attract a lot of NGO funding, so that if you compare it to South Africa, they're very, very weak. The FFM team asked if funding was domestic, local. International diplomatic source: They rely on the good will of people, donors.

NGOs are allowed to raise the funding from outside the country, but of course they have to comply with anti-money laundering [laws]. Of course, there’s government funds [for] some portions of civil society, but it's mostly skewed towards public health.

The FFM team asked of the NGOs that support GBV cases if they all provide shelters, legal advice, counselling, healthcare support. International diplomatic source: The BGBVPC in Gaborone is the only one that has that sort of structure, like a one-stop centre. They have healthcare workers and volunteer doctors, so not there all the time. Legal [advice] is also outsourced, so it's not all days and times they have access to that.

The FFM team asked if International diplomatic source knew how many women the centre could accommodate? International diplomatic source: No, [don’t know].

The FFM team asked about NGO support for LGBT+ people – International diplomatic source mentioned LEGABIBO and Rainbow Alliance. Are there others out there? International diplomatic source: Rainbow Identity Association, Success Capital. They work on both LGBT+ right issues and also women's issues. I think they have a blend and then they also include intersex and transgender people. The FFM team clarified that LEGABIBO and the Rainbow Identity Association work with the whole of the LGBT+ plus community? International diplomatic source: LEGABIBO more than others. Rainbow Identity are more transgender focused. Then there’s a regional NGO, it's called the Southern African Litigation Centre (SALC). They have 2 people based here, but they mainly operate out of South Africa, more legal advocacy. SALC was the main NGO that funded the case in 2021 / 2022 that normalised same-sex relationship. Rainbow Identity Association focusses more on access to healthcare services for transgender and LGBT+ people. Success Capital are more policy advocacy. The FFM asked if any of the NGOs can provide shelters or healthcare assistance? International diplomatic source: not sure. I think they have some kind of patient space for people who need it for a short period.

The FFM team asked where the NGOs were located. International diplomatic source: Until recently, LEGABIBO had a small business outside of Gaborone. I think they have some presence in Francistown, but it wouldn't be a physical space - just people that work from there, doing outreach in those different communities. They were mainly USAID-funded, so that the aid pause has meant a drop in their funding. The FFM team asked if LEGABIBO were they solely reliant on US money? International diplomatic source: The majority I think, because they got funding from USAID and the Global Fund, which is also predominantly US-funded.

The FFM team asked if there been any Gay Pride events? International diplomatic source: Yes, there was a Pride march in June hosted by UNAIDS and LEGABIBO in Gaborone. The FFM team asked how big the event was. International diplomatic source: Not very big, mostly embassies, the UN and NGOs – less than 100 people. They marched from the LEGABIBO office to the UN building here. The FFM team asked if the police were present. International diplomatic source: Yes, a police presence is always there during peaceful protests and marches. That's because you have to apply for permission to march or protest from the police.

The FFM team asked if there was public reaction. International diplomatic source: They let them march peacefully. The only thing that you come across is snide comments on Facebook, Twitter, that's it. The FFM team if the comments were against the march specifically, or any LGBT+ activity? International diplomatic source: So, either people on social media generally or the Evangelical Fellowship of Botswana, a religious group, but they choose when they’re vocal. In the past, they were vocal when the state repealed the law that criminalised same-sex relationships. The courts ruled the existing law was unconstitutional and then the attorney general went ahead and removed that section from the penal code, but then it was supposed to be tabled in Parliament to be Officially debated, which was just a formality. But the Evangelical Fellowship went on radio, TV, print media and threatened MPs that if they tabled the bill in Parliament, there would be consequences for the elections. But that was it. There was no violence or anything.

The FFM team asked if International diplomatic source was aware of documented cases of violence against LGBT+ people? International diplomatic source: Not murder but physical assault. The FFM team asked if these were reported in the media? What kind of scale? And is it people being attacked and injured? International diplomatic source: In some cases it was people the victims’ family members. Some cases it was a person walking in a mall and somebody would just hobble them and beat them up. The FFM team asked how would the attacker know the person was LGBT+? International diplomatic source: assumed it was the way that the person was dressed.

The FFM team asked if a man and woman would hold hands in public? International diplomatic source: Yes, of course. The FFM team asked: So could 2 men or 2 women hold hands? International diplomatic source: Two women can, because people would assume they're best friends.

The FFM team asked if people knew they weren't best friends? International diplomatic source: If there was PDA [public display of affection] on the hand holding, then maybe that's when people would react. But I've seen at drinking spots lately in Gaborone, gay men are becoming very free to express PDA. The FFM team asked if there are other venues - is there a sense of community and spaces in Gaborone which are for LGBT+ people? International diplomatic source: Not explicitly for them, but I've seen that some spaces have become much more liberal and even hold fried food, drinking events, social events. I've seen that in Gaborone now people don’t really care. Just this past weekend I saw 2 men kissing. The FFM team asked if this was in public? International diplomatic source: Yes, in a nightclub. The FFM team asked if the experience of LGBT+ people was different in smaller towns, Maun or Francistown or the countryside. International diplomatic source: Yes, different.

The FFM teams asked if International diplomatic source had an idea of the number of attacks on LGBT+ people? International diplomatic source: No. The FFM team asked if these are reported in the BWA press? International diplomatic source: Some. There are 2 newspapers I would say would be the ones to typically pick that up: The Voice and the Midweek Sun. The FFM team asked if the newspapers were popular and what their position was on LGBT+ people? Yes popular. They're quite liberal in terms of how they report. The FFM team asked if the reporting was sympathetic or negative? International diplomatic source: Sympathetic. The FFM team asked about other parts of the press. International diplomatic source: There are some that are sensationalist, as opposed to trying to deliberately cause harm. It's just trying to sell a newspaper. It won't be explicitly anti-LGBT, but it would be like, ‘Gay man does 1,2,3’ just to sell a newspaper.

The FFM team asked about attacks on LGBT+ people, are these widespread and systematic or just random? International diplomatic source: Random. Especially in public places, nobody would just provoke anybody just out of the blue. I’ll give an example of taxi drivers or public transport operators because those are usually the ones that provoke, in a taxi rank, for example. If they see a man dressed in some type of way then they would heckle them, and then people have the courage as a group. Otherwise, it wouldn't happen, just one person standing up and assaulting a person out of the blue. They usually do it because they are surrounded by other men who would be like, ‘Let's beat him up.’ The FFM team observed that BWA does not appear to be generally a violent society. International diplomatic source: No, Botswana is famous for resolving issues through dialogue. It's considered to be the foundation of its democracy. If you compare how BWA got its independence compared to South Africa, Botswana didn't get its independence from uprising. The story is the 3 chiefs [dikgosi] went to the UK, met with Queen Victoria and asked for independence back and they got it.

The FFM team summarised: there aren’t particular venues or places or a part of Gaborone where LGBT+ people hang out? International diplomatic source: between 2011 and 2015 there used to be a nightclub that was considered to be a gay club, but it burned down by accident - it was just an electric fault. The FFM team observed even 10 years plus ago, before the legislation was repealed. So it's been building up for some time, this move to decriminalise the same sex law, but there are no positive laws to protect LGBT+ rights. International diplomatic source: Not yet.

The FFM teams asked if a LGBT+ person faced violence, which would often be from members of their family or community, or a random person, one option might be for them to move somewhere else within the country. How viable is that? Can a woman move from, say, Maun to Gaborone and get a job? Can they find accommodation? Can they get healthcare and other basic services? Are there any barriers to moving such as needing documents? International diplomatic source: People mostly move to have economic opportunities, employment. And some, I’ve heard, move to Gaborone because Gaborone is much more tolerant and liberal than, say, a random village in the north. So people do move to Gaborone because they feel like society is much more open-minded and accepting.

The FFM team asked if it is viable if the person is at school or a student, can they get into the education system, if they have a child, or if the woman is a single woman from a rural area? International diplomatic source: Yeah, it's quite easy, but of course Gaborone is much more expensive than other parts of the country. If they can move here, if they can get a job, they can afford rent, food, take their kids to school.

The FFM team asked if society accepts single women living by themselves? International diplomatic source: Yes. I would say the majority of households are female-headed. The FFM team queried, so women with no partners? International diplomatic source: Yes. It's quite normal. The FFM team asked what happens if it’s the woman who leaves? INTERNATIONAL DIPLOMATIC SOURCE: Well, it depends. Some men will accept it, but I would presume it's a small majority. The FFM team asked if a woman came to Gaborone from Francistown, how would other people react? International diplomatic source: It depends. If the man is a lost cause, they wouldn't really care. They would just continue on with their life and let the woman, if she wanted to, have the responsibility for their kids and bear the cost of raising the kids. Some men will just let them be, but in some instances, family are often the first people to intervene and say, ‘No, you can't do that. Come back to your to your husband or to your partner, raise the kids together.’ And in some instances nowadays, because men are becoming much more alive to their legal rights in terms of custody and stuff, they would challenge that to the courts and then in some unfortunate instances, we've heard of men following their partner, assaulting them and in some instances killing them or leaving them.

The FFM team asked if someone is a single mother, coming to Gaborone from a rural area or a smaller city, would it be possible for the man to follow her here? International diplomatic source: BWA is a small country and you can't disappear and live off the grid without somebody eventually finding you. The FFM team asked if that is because family links and communities are very strong? International diplomatic source: Yes, very much. The FFM team asked if the person could go to the police and get a restraining order? International diplomatic source: Yes, you can, but recently we found that the police are not very effective at enforcing restraining orders. I think 2 or 3 weeks ago there was an unfortunate incident where this woman got a restraining order against her partner, and a few days later, the man followed her to work at the university and stabbed her in open space. The FFM team observed that's one example, but how indicative is that of restraining orders generally and police involvement? International diplomatic source: Not a lot of people take out restraining orders. That's when the case has escalated. The FFM observed one case does not necessarily represent a pattern. International diplomatic source: Yes, true. But the magistrate who presided over the case was quite vocal in criticising the police about how they let the deceased woman down.

The FFM team asked what this reveals about how effective the police are? Is it illustrative of a wider concern? International diplomatic source: Well, I don't think it is because that would be unfair on the police. I don't think it paints a bad picture of the police. I think the police, of course, do the best that they can to enforce restraining orders and so.

The FFM team asked if the police are relatively well funded? And how big is the police force, do you know? International diplomatic source: Not sure, you have to ask this to the police. The FFM team asked can they provide protection to the public as a whole? What resources do they have? International diplomatic source: Yes, they can. They're not underfunded. When you look at the budget allocation every year for government, the security sector gets probably the second biggest or the third biggest. The FFM team clarified that the police and the armed forces? International diplomatic source: And the intelligence agency, and the wildlife rangers because poaching is an issue here. The police, though, there will be issues of no accommodation for police officers or pay issues. But in terms of resources, I think they’re relatively good. The FFM team suggested that effective law enforcement rated highly by the government? International diplomatic source: Yes, very much.

The FFM team asked is common for women to move/relocate? International diplomatic source: Yes. For jobs or employment options. The FFM team asked if it is not just for GBV, but for other reasons as well, they can move? International diplomatic source: Yes, of course. I think it’s quite easy. Also to be with family. The FFM team asked if it would be possible to move from Gaborone to Maun or Francistown if you had a problem in Gaborone with domestic violence? International diplomatic source: Yes, it's possible. The largest employer here is government, so if you feel like the city is too expensive, you can put in a request to be transferred to Maun or Francistown. The FFM team asked if you’re not a government employee? International diplomatic source: You can just get a job. The FFM team asked if those towns are not as tolerant socially as Gaborone? International diplomatic source: Unless my view is biased, I think single women are not looked down on there.

The FFM team asked if a lesbian woman or bisexual woman moved to Gaborone from the village where she was born, would she be able to rent a room and get work if she was open about her sexual orientation? International diplomatic source: People don't tend to be open about their sexuality, especially women. Generally, only a small proportion of women would be open. The FFM team as if someone found out that she was a lesbian? Would that be an issue? Would she be able to rent a place and get a job? International diplomatic source: It depends. I've heard of some landlords who are super religious refusing to rent property to the person just because they think the person is gay. But a person wouldn't volunteer their sexuality to just a random person or a stranger or a new person that they've just met. But it would mostly be on religious grounds that a person would respond. The FFM team observed there might be landlords who’d have a problem with that and they would kick them out if they knew. But might there be other landlords who would be more tolerant? International diplomatic source: Yes.

The FFM team asked in terms of healthcare, if the healthcare authorities found out about a person’s sexuality, would that be an issue? International diplomatic source: Gay people have specific healthcare needs. I have heard of some healthcare workers being rude to LGBT+ people. But generally, public opinion has shifted over time and that has translated to healthcare institutions. A couple of years ago, sure, you’d hear that a lot LGBT+ people face discriminatory attitudes. That's why LEGABIBO set up separate drop-in centres outside of the public healthcare system. But those with more authority and knowledge on this can speak more. I think it has changed over time.

The FFM team asked if public healthcare free? International diplomatic source: Yes, it’s free.

The FFM team summarised on education and public services generally, the government's position is neutral with regard LGBT+ people - except that all people are protected by the Constitution, regardless of race, sex or background

The FFM teams asked what is the presence of trans women in BWA and how are they viewed by the government? International diplomatic source: They’re increasingly coming up and being much more assertive in terms of their identity. The government is not accepting – or the government system is not accepting – of trans people, if somebody wants to change the gender marker on their ID document. There's one famous case where a person wanted to gender transition and they did it in South Africa. But when they came to Botswana and tried to change the ID document, the government refused outright to do that because they were born a certain way. So they challenged that decision through the courts. They won, so now the procedure is that if somebody wants to do the same change their sex on their ID document, the only avenue is to get a court order and undergo a medical examination or assessment. I think they also undergo some psychological assessment.

The FFM team summarised: a person cannot simply ask to change their gender marker but it is possible through the courts. International diplomatic source: That's the only way to do it. There's no section of Constitution that is for people to change that gender.

The FFM team asked what documents would someone need to settle in Gaborone, to show a landlord for example? International diplomatic source: It depends. If it’s private, somebody's ID and a surety that they'll be able to afford the rent, so people usually just ask for a payslip or bank statement. The FFM team asked the name of the national ID card? International diplomatic source: ‘Omang’, which is a Tswana word which in English translates to ‘why’. The FFM team asked if it is digital? International diplomatic source: No, it's a physical card. The FFM team asked how a card is obtained. International diplomatic source: You go to immigration when you turn 16. They're yet to make it digital, but they're talking about making it digital. Every citizen when they turn 16 can apply for this, using their birth certificate. The FFM team asked where a person goes to get a card. International diplomatic source: The Ministry of Labour and Home Affairs, Department of Immigration and Citizenship (DIC). There's an immigration office in almost every village. The FFM team asked if is straightforward to get an ID card? International diplomatic source: Yes, you just need your birth certificate. The FFM team asked if the card can be replaced if lost. International diplomatic source: Yes, you pay 100 bucks [pula], it gets printed right there and then and you can get that from any outpost of the DIC. it has a ‘D’ on it, which is a duplicate. If you move towns or cities or villages, you don’t really need one. You just pack your bag. But nowadays, because people register their properties as a company, if you have a bunch of apartments, for example, and somebody comes to you and they want to rent an apartment, they’d need a bank statement or pay slip, that’s it. And of course, your ID.

Annex C - Interview with an International diplomatic source 2

Date 8 July 2025
LocationGaborone
Attendees Diplomatic source 2; 3 HO Officials

Gender-based violence (GBV)

The fact-finding team (FFT) asked international diplomatic source to summarise the situation for women. International diplomatic source observed that to understand women’s position you need to understand their societal context. Botswana is a patriarchal society - women are socialised to behave in a certain way, men are dominant. For example, marriage is an institution in which women are expected to be obedient and respectful; there is still a ‘bride price’. Women’s place in society frames how they are treated, their experience of gender-based violence. Women are not all treated horribly – too general a statement. But they face discrimination in the home and in the workplace. They are paid less. The law prescribes equality of men and women but in practice it does not occur.

Asked about types of gender-based violence (GBV), international diplomatic source noted there is a lot of violence - every week a woman is killed. It’s also in the form of rape, physical and emotional violence.

Asked about data on GBV incidents, international diplomatic source was not able to give specific numbers but observed that every week the in Botswana (BWA) newspapers the source reads about incidents of GBV, not a week has passed that an incident is not reported. For example, there was report from 2 weeks ago about the murder of a female employee at the University of Botswana (UofB) who was stabbed during the day in her office at the university by her partner.

Asked about the profile of women affected by GBV, international diplomatic source said it affects women across society. Previously people would think that it affected women in privileged places but this is an elitist way of looking at the issue. Now it happens to women indiscriminately. Asked if there were differences between rural and urban areas, international diplomatic source thought it occurred in both. International diplomatic source referred to the UofB case as an example of this happening in urban areas.

Asked who are the perpetrators, mainly partners – husbands or boyfriends. It can be a ‘fight piece’, extramarital affairs. This takes away from the conversation because GBV shouldn't happen in general. Statistically it's partners. The FFM team asked if was correct to summarise - perpetrators are mainly men who know the victims? International diplomatic source noted, absolutely, it is seldom strangers.

Asked what laws and policies the state has introduced to protect women, international diplomatic source commented that she would not speak on the laws but observed that there's now the new government and the Ministry of Gender and Youth Affairs which is supposed to focus primarily on building policies protecting women. But source hadn’t seen in practice any of these policies institutionalised in an efficient way. Not able to speak on their current status.

The FFM team summarised – policies and laws exist to protect women, but these are not implemented? International diplomatic source agreed, absolutely. Asked if the laws and policies are sufficient or more are needed, international diplomatic source didn’t consider these were sufficient but only because their implementation hasn't been effective. It is hard to give credit to policies that are not actualized in in an efficient way. International diplomatic source did not mean policies were not working but instead putting in place more policies perhaps work needs to be done in improving their efficiency.

Asked about police enforcement of the law, international diplomatic source thought they are active in implementing the law but there is a gap in terms of their capacity and their ability to intervene, a lot to be learned. International diplomatic source considered it was police structures that perhaps are not equipped enough to handle sensitive matters in a proper way. If the police do not handle these cases sensitively this might disincentivise victims from approaching law enforcement.

Asked if the police are willing to assist, international diplomatic source agreed. However, regarding willingness, international diplomatic source felt there's still a lot of unlearning to be done so that the police don't have bias in situations like that. They tend to personalise it, thinking ‘if I was in this situation and I found that my partner was cheating and the child raised wasn't mine, I don't blame the guy for doing that’. So, because that's already a mentality that exists it is problematic in terms of whether or not they can sufficiently help a victim if they come reporting and access these services.

The FFT are aware that a GBV unit has been established in the police. Asked if international diplomatic source was aware of the unit and if had changed the way victims are treated, international diplomatic source wouldn't speak to whether it had brought a change – didn’t think it had. International diplomatic source gave an example in Molepolole from a year and a half ago when a woman was murdered in front of the police [full circumstances not provided]. International diplomatic source thought that officers need proper training to join this unit. They need psychological or psychiatric training to handle a victim of such a gruesome crime. International diplomatic source didn’t believe sufficient training had been done to provide them with the skills to deal with these sensitive cases.

Asked about what happens where cases are reported to the police, what is the conviction rate, do victims have a positive outcome. International diplomatic source said that conviction rates are not great. Describing these crimes as ‘acts of passion’ indicates an inherent sense of sympathy for the perpetrator. To say they had no intention of harming, they just acted out of passion because of the amount of emotion caused by the victim. So, because of this while a lot of perpetrators may not get away with the crime, they don't get the sentence we would expect them to get for the crime they have committed. Using the term ‘crimes of passion’ normalises crime to the effect that perpetrators can get away with a slap on the wrist for something that they should not.

Asked for data on the number of convictions and an explanation of the difference between reporting GBV cases and convictions, international diplomatic source did not have the data.

Asked if GBV victims get legal aid, international diplomatic source thought some do [get legal assistance], but didn’t know how accessible it was to all. Botswana has a very small population of 2.4million but people are very scattered. You cannot assume that specific amenities are accessible to all. In specific areas legal service assistance do not exist. But where it does, it may come at a cost. There is not a lot of community knowledge of how to access legal assistance. There is an NGO, BONELA, which provides legal assistance or finds lawyers who can provide legal advice. But an NGO of their size and resources cannot sufficiently serve all people.

The FFM team summarised – there is legal aid/assistance provided by the government, but a lack of accessibility is an issue. International diplomatic source agreed. There are 2 parts to accessibility: 1) there is a lack of education or knowledge that the provision exists to some communities. They don't know they have a right to legal aid (assistance); 2) proximity to those amenities is also an issue. Need to rethink how to make legal aid (assistance) more accessible to all. Language can also be a barrier – people assume that everyone speaks 2 languages, English and Tswana, but that is not the case if you move towards the northern part of the country. Some people there do not speak either. This makes it difficult for them to articulate when harm has been done and is even more of a barrier for someone to provide them with the legal assistance.

Asked if the government is taking any steps to provide support, international diplomatic source did not think so, not enough steps. Last week the country had a week of prayer organised by the government against GBV. International diplomatic source is Christian, believes in prayer, but more is needed than just holding hands and praying. International diplomatic source didn’t see any tangible change, does not see that the government intends to change things.

Asked that apart from the police and the government legal assistance, what other support is there for the women, international diplomatic source noted that there are shelters where they can enrol and seek refuge. One of the lessons from COVID is that a lot of women have been systemically unsafe even in the home. Didn’t think there's enough capacity nor funding going from the state to support women and children.

Asked if there are other safe houses in other parts of the country (than Gaborone), international diplomatic source said no. The international diplomatic source noted that there have been cases previously where government Officials / ministers have been accused of defiling children. There was evidence that they did, but nothing really happened. The socio-economic situation of some parts is an issue, Botswana is unequal country. So, there is an example, based on a true story, where a minister defiled a young girl but because the family were paid off, they dropped the case. We've seen this happen many times. If there were not extenuating circumstances, where the family felt like we can get a payout out of it and improve their home, a lot of women end up not reporting or dropping their cases.

Asked about the financial aspect of abuse and if there is pressure to withdraw cases, international diplomatic source considered families pressure women to do this. International diplomatic source advised meeting a non-profit organisation, Change Africa, a section of which deals with young mothers. The NGO gives support to different stores and ministries to get care packages to young mothers. International diplomatic source had attended 2 or 3 sessions run by the NGO where women have testified to being pressured to drop a case because it was with a family member - a cousin, an uncle - or with a neighbour. Worth having a discussion with the NGO about these case studies.
