Asked if the shelters and accommodations were government supported or run by NGOs, international diplomatic source thought these were government funded but started by individuals who get donations.

Asked if the NGOs provide legal aid and financial support, international diplomatic source did not know if they provide financial support, but they can provide a bed and food. The NGO BONELA would be the best group to talk to about this.

Asked whether a woman who has experienced GBV is able to relocate within Botswana, international diplomatic source noted that people have moved to the UK and sought asylum on the basis that they have faced abuse, but we cannot verify those stories. It may be that some people are just taking advantage of the situation that there's such an enormous amount of violence towards women in the country and in the hemisphere in general. International diplomatic source did not think that a lot of victims have been able to relocate outside of the country.

The FFM team clarified that they meant relocation within Botswana not to another country. International diplomatic source observed 100% they can, they can move to a family member. The FFM team asked if a victim of domestic or GBV in Maun, for example, could relocate to Gaborone. International diplomatic source thought it hard, although they had not been a victim of domestic violence. In a previous job, international diplomatic source had spoken to women and heard a lot of these stories [women not moving] and most of them due to having children or wanting to be close to their parents. Or they just don't have the financial means to move. They have nowhere to go and they tend not to go.

Asked if a person had the intention and the financial ability to move, for example a single woman or a single mother, international diplomatic source observed that the psychology of being abused is quite complex. Even in circumstances where they do have the financial means we have to think about their mental health. Are they in a state where they have the mental capacity to believe they can move and find a different life? International diplomatic source did not know but most of the time they get to a point where they're just too mentally exhausted and battered to think it’s a possibility for them.

Asked how society accepts a woman – single woman or single mother – who moved, for example, renting a house or treated by a neighbour, international diplomatic source did not think one would face discrimination [from other people]. But if one was married and was being harmed within the marriage and relocated with kids there will be some backlash from her in-laws because there is a traditional belief you should work things out. That's what most women in abusive marriages explained to international diplomatic source. The stigma [for moving away] might come from there. But international diplomatic source didn’t think people would generally discriminate against a woman or judge her or [not] accept them in society for being a lone woman.

Asked if the source had anything to add on GBV, international diplomatic source noted that it was regrettable that a country that is seen to be so democratic and peaceful has not had more pressure from external actors to it to account for ‘complicity’ in GBV. Yes, perhaps [a woman] won’t be shot in the street but equally it's bad for women living here. It's traumatic that women cannot live peacefully in their own country, but nobody does anything about it because BWA has such a brilliant reputation.

LGBT+

Asked if international diplomatic source had an idea about the size of the LGBT+ population, international diplomatic source did not know but thought it was a lot. Asked to clarify what was ‘a lot’, international diplomatic source considered as a ballpark about 200 or 300 who are out, openly gay or lesbian. Last month [June 2025] there was a Pride march to the UN offices [in Gaborone], and there were about that many people [in attendance].

Asked if LGBT+ people openly identify themselves, international diplomatic source thought some do, but did not believe all of them do. Asked why people are not open about their sexuality, international diplomatic source thought that BWA is still quite conservative and LGBT+ people would face a lot of discrimination from family and society. Even in the workplace people are very closed minded, people might look at them differently. They fear they would not be expected to be loved.

Asked if society accepted LGBT+ following the decriminalisation of same-sex sex, in general society accepts LGBT+ people to the extent that it does not affect them. International diplomatic source had conversations with neighbours who’ve said it’s [being LGBT+] ok as long as it is not their daughter or son. It's not like in South Africa where somebody would get murdered because of their sexual orientation. But international diplomatic source did not have lived experienced, heard in very rural areas it might be potentially very dangerous. People might become suicidal because of the verbal and emotional abuse they get.

Asked about other parts of the country [than Gaborone], if LGBT+ people live openly, international diplomatic source thought they might not be out of closet. People in specific areas in BWA are very closed minded - this is international diplomatic source ’s assumption. People think LGBT+ people are doing this out of fashion, influenced by Western ideology, it's not normal. We have quite a large Christian population, so there is a perception that God wouldn’t want us to do this [be LGBT+], it’s a sin. This doesn’t provide the right environment for people to feel able to come out in a safe and inclusive space, so people remain closeted.

Asked if there was discrimination in the workplace, international diplomatic source thought so. Definitely in schools. The school system doesn't necessarily speak about this, kids just react the way kids react.

Asked if someone faced discrimination, would they be protected by the law, international diplomatic source considered the law would protect the LGBT+ person but the question is what would the [police] officer do. Didn’t consider there was enough training for police officers to handle these cases [of abuse / discrimination against LGBT+ people]. International diplomatic source considered that a women who identified herself a lesbian after being sexually assaulted by a man and reported this to the police, international diplomatic source didn’t know if they would get the same treatment as a [straight] woman who said they were raped by a man. The FFT asked if it was correct to say the law provided protection, international diplomatic source thought yes, the law protects anyone.

Asked if international diplomatic source had any examples of people being harassed for their sexual orientation, international diplomatic source did not but had attended a LEGABIBO [Botswanan LGBT+ NGO] meeting where people were giving testimony about the impact of the withdrawal of USAID funding. From those accounts international diplomatic source got the sense that LGBT+ did not get the same help.

Asked if treatment was the same for a lesbian woman and a gay man, international diplomatic source thought [sex] might make a difference. When you have conversations people may say really disturbing things towards lesbians and gay men, particularly said by men. There is a false dichotomy that lesbian women are more likely go back to being ‘just’ women but once a man becomes gay they are apart. International diplomatic source thought it misinformation, lack of understanding and a lack of an appreciation of humanity. People definitely romanticise about lesbian women but think [being] the other [gay men] is just wrong. Lesbians are going through a phase whereas for men once they have done that [become gay it’s final].

Asked if lesbian or bi-women able to live together as a couple, international diplomatic source thought yes, seen that happen. Hadn’t seen situations where they would be discriminated, to international diplomatic source ’s knowledge. Asked if the situation might vary by location, international diplomatic source thought it might be more difficult to do this in less urban areas, like a village.

Asked if LGBT+ groups get support, international diplomatic source said yes, LEGABIBO gets funding from Kaleidoscope International Trust, a UK-based organisation, and, before the overseas development aid cuts, some funding from USAID. Most of the funding was focused on giving the LGBT+ community access to healthcare. Asked if the support extended to legal aid or shelters, international diplomatic source did not know. Asked to clarify if NGOs provide direct support such as legal assistance, international diplomatic source believed they did through LEGABIBO. For example, a few years ago LEGABIBO assisted a trans woman in a case against the government to allow them to change her name and gender on her ID. So, they been providing legal support that specifically meets the needs and aspirations of LGBT+ community but not sure if this is accessible to the entire community in the country.

Annex D - Interview with United Nations Population Fund

Date 8 July 2025
LocationBritish High Commission, Gaborone
AttendeesProgramme Specialist for Youth and Gender, UN Population Fund (UNFPA) 3 HO officials

Women and gender-based violence (GBV)

UN OFFICIAL explained that she is a programme specialist on youth and gender and has been with the UNFPA since April 1, 2025. This is her second stint with the UNFPA, previously she spent 2 years with the organisation in 2006 until 2008. After this she had various roles in civil society, including as executive director of the Botswana Council of NGOs (BOCONGO), and in other UN agencies including the International Labour Organisation and International Migration Organisation.

The FFM team asked UN OFFICIAL to summarise the position of women in Botswana (BWA). UN OFFICIAL explained that we have a very serious problem with GBV in BWA. The statistics are saying one in every 3 women has experienced GBV. When we talk of the question of women’s safety and security, that’s what women in this country are currently contending with. Economically, it's been challenging, but UN OFFICIAL thought there were areas where progress has been made. We have a lot of women in the informal sector. That's a sector that they find it easier to operate in because there's a lot they initiate – starting an enterprise, running a project. The informal sector generally has less bureaucratic processes and requirements and often has the flexibility that allows women to run their businesses and still do family care work. There are also limited employment opportunities with the employment rate at around 28%, which further pushes women to the informal sector. That's where most of women are. We've seen some improvements over time with women getting access to positions of leadership in the private sector, namely management, leadership and being [chief executive officers] CEOs, and [serving] on some boards of directors and so forth. But in the political space, we're seeing regression right now. We only have 6 women in Parliament, which is a drop from 11 [in the last Parliament]. So in terms of the targets, we've set ourselves on gender equality as far as women's representation and leadership is concerned, [the situation is] not so great. And then, of course, women are still also doing a lot of the care work when it comes to raising children, and even in some of the roles that involve a lot of care work, like teaching, day care, nursing.

The FFM team noted that UN OFFICIAL mentioned there are 6 women in Parliament. What was the total number of members? UN OFFICIAL explained that there are around 61. The FFM team asked whether women are represented in the public sector itself, in government. UN OFFICIAL thought there weren’t many issues there. She explained that she didn’t have the exact numbers but that a number of women hold the position of permanent secretary, which is [an official who heads a government ministry]. But [representation] varies according to the sector. We still have some male-dominated sectors like mining, which is still very much male-dominated from lower positions all the way up. And mining is [the backbone of the economy], despite the fact that the sector is not doing so great right now. [As regards] agriculture, Botswana does a lot of agriculture but ownership, for instance of cattle, is mainly by men. Some women whose husbands do agriculture may not even know how many cattle the family has.

The FFM team asked how the law protects women in BWA. Are they given equal rights? UN OFFICIAL noted that [there] are [equal rights] on paper, but there is a dual legal system: customary law and modern [statutory or common] law. The customary law is where the chiefs preside over matters, and things like that. [The dual system] has its own challenges. When there's an issue, let's say in the family, it would usually start at the customary setting, where it goes to the chiefs. It may end there, and [when] cases [do] end there – maybe it's a case of GBV – the family or the husband and wife would in most cases be told to reconcile. That’s the customary side. They tend to prioritise [reconciliation]. A lot of women tend to withdraw cases of GBV due to their economic dependence on the male perpetrators.

The FFM team asked if women have equal rights under customary law, UN OFFICIAL confirmed that they have had recently, for example, in inheritance. Now, modern [statutory] law recognises that women have equal rights to property, [including in matters of] inheritance. UN OFFICIAL thought that customary law is in most cases trying to conform to that as well, in terms of recognising that women have equal rights. But in practice, you still find cases where, for example, there’s a fight over inheritance or [over who should become] the next chief if a chief [dies leaving only daughters]. It's not always a very smooth transition to say the eldest daughter automatically becomes the chief [even though] it’s recognised on paper now that daughters of chiefs can be chiefs. In practice, it’s not always that easy; it’s always contentious.

The FFM team asked what types of GBV there are in BWA, UN OFFICIAL observed that there are all sorts. The most prevalent are sexual assault – UN OFFICIAL noted that rape statistics for BWA are the second highest in the world, so [the number of] sexual assaults is quite high – physical [violence], like beating, which is quite high; and economic [violence]. Economic is particularly in cases where the man is working but the woman isn’t, [so] she’s dependent on the partner. Sometimes they [withhold funds] because the women are dependent on them. That also leads to the pattern that has been observed [where] a lot of reported cases of GBV are withdrawn because the woman says that this person is the breadwinner and the caretaker, and if you take him to prison then the family has no means of sustenance.

The FFM team asked whether UN OFFICIAL had any numbers on sexual and physical assaults. UN OFFICIAL noted that there was a report she could share [of] a 2018 study. The UNFPA had been trying to support the government to update that. The 2018 study even broke down the different forms and the prevalence of [each form of GBV], which she observed was helpful. The FFM team asked who conducted the study, UN OFFICIAL noted the [then Ministry of Nationality, Immigration and] gender affairs department [in the government] with the support of partners – the [UN]FPA, Gender Links and others. The FFM team asked whether that was the most recent data, UN OFFICIAL confirmed that it was, adding that the UNFPA had been trying to support them to update it because it’s quite dated, but it’s the latest national study. She noted that there may be smaller ones – Botswana Gender-Based Violence Prevention and Support Centre also recently did something but on a smaller scale.

The FFM team asked who the main perpetrators of GBV are, UN OFFICIAL observed that it is men, all ages, but when you look at the numbers, mainly the youthful population, people between their 20s and 45. The FFM team asked whether they are mostly family or strangers, UN OFFICIAL noted that most of it is intimate partner violence, but when you look at the data, there's a lot perpetrated by family members – a brother having raped his sister or an uncle having raped a niece. It’s intimate partners, then family members, then others – just general strangers.

The FFM team asked what laws and policies there are to tackle the issue of GBV, UN OFFICIAL explained that currently, in terms of trying to deal with intimate partner violence, the courts rely on the Domestic Violence Act (DVA) [2008] because there is no GBV law right now, but there's a push towards that. So a lot of reliance is made on the DVA. When it’s a case of beating [a partner], what people are usually charged with is grievous bodily harm or common assault. That’s what the police reports would say. The FFM team asked under what law a husband would be prosecuted if he was violent towards his wife. UN OFFICIAL noted the DVA in the case of intimate partners or family relations. The FFM team asked under what circumstances a perpetrator would be charged with grievous bodily harm or common [assault]. UN OFFICIAL explained that sometimes a case would go through customary law [courts], like in the case of people in a village. [Their] first point of contact with the legal system would be to go to the chief, the kgosi, who is the leader of the village and relies on customary law. But sometimes cases are removed from the customary [law system] to the magistrate[s’] [courts], and then it depends but maybe from the magistrate to the higher courts. Not all cases that are heard in the customary court will ultimately make it to the magistrates’ court. The FFM team asked whether modern (statutory / common) law recognises customary law. UN OFFICIAL noted that it does. They are both legally recognised in the country, even with their contradictions. The dikgosi, the traditional leadership, set up that recognised [customary law] system.

The FFM team asked whether the customary law and the [non-customary] legal system are sufficient to tackle GBV, UN OFFICIAL thought that they are obviously not. She explained that in fact the contradictions cause big problems, particularly with GBV cases. The customary law leads more to [a victim being told] that it’s a family matter and they should go and talk to their uncles and so forth. Even where somebody has gone to the courts, like the magistrates’ court, imagine being issued with a restraining order and then going back to the community. The customary law has no power to enforce a restraining order. If anything, a victim might face [comments from] people in the community about her having taken her own husband to court and obtaining a restraining order against him. So, the 2 [legal systems] are in a lot of conflict in terms of GBV cases.

The FFM team asked whether there are any laws in addition to the DVA that protect women. For example, does rape, which is not in the DVA, come under a different law? UN OFFICIAL explained that a lot of [provisions to protect women] that are not in the DVA are in the Penal Code. The Penal Code and the DVA are the main ones [for protecting women].

The FFM team asked whether there are any loopholes in the protection that UN OFFICIAL sees. UN OFFICIAL noted that there are a lot of them. Just recently, about 2 to 3 weeks ago, we had a woman murdered at the University of Botswana [UB] in broad daylight at work. She had a restraining order against [the perpetrator]. Half the time, when a woman has a restraining order, no one knows about it. There are no first responders or anything to [step in to protect] her if the person who is subject to the restraining order violates it by approaching her. So there are loopholes in the protection system.

The FFM team asked whether the University of Botswana case was just one example or whether this kind of situation was common. UN OFFICIAL noted that it is very common, particularly with repeat offenders. People on bail, people with restraining orders are very common. That's why currently there's a bit of an uproar around bail. People feel like people perpetrate violence, they go to court, they are given bail, they come back and they commit the same crime – or even worse, to the point of killing – because they're out on bail. We have repeat offenders who've been out on bail multiple times.

The FFM team asked whether this was the law being weak, or was it its implementation? UN OFFICIAL thought both. The first weakness is the investigation part because judges rely on the evidence presented before them. [The decision whether] to grant or refuse bail is dependent on what evidence they are dealing with. The second [weakness] is the protection mechanism, for instance, [implementation in the case of bail and restraining orders]. While the law can guarantee somebody whose life is under threat protection by means of a restraining order, the implementation of that is a problem because it seems like it's just a piece of paper that somebody's carrying around and enforcement is a big problem in terms of protection.

The FFM team summarised that there are laws to provide protection but that implementation is an issue. The FFM team asked whether UN OFFICIAL thought the police had enough power to protect anyone who’s suffered GBV. If a woman made a complaint to the police, would they be able to protect her from GBV? UN OFFICIAL observed that they may have power in theory, on paper. When people see the police, when I’m walking around at midnight and I see the police, I might get a sense that the police are here for protection. We have the police arresting somebody who is perpetrating violence. They do investigations and so forth. The whole process will go to a point where there’s a woman being given a restraining order. One then wonders where the police come in to make sure that that restraining order is enforced. Can a woman just call and say that the person I have a restraining order against is violating it, they’re following me or they’re in my vicinity? Half the time, the police are challenged – ‘We don’t have a car, we don’t have resources.’ So, they may have the power, but are also limitations, particularly in terms of resources and other things.

The FFM team asked if it would be correct to summarise that the police have the willingness to protect, but they do not have the ability because of the resources. UN OFFICIAL observed that she couldn’t confidently say they have the willingness. If you call to report, you get multiple interrogations [questions by the police] and things like that. One’s life is under threat [from the perpetrator]. UN OFFICIAL noted that she was therefore not sure about the willingness. Maybe some [police officers are willing], but not all. She thought they weren’t all on the same page.

The FFM team asked about the GBV unit [Gender and Child Protection Branch] that was recently established by the Botswana Police Service. How efficient and effective is it? UN OFFICIAL noted that it’s perhaps still a bit too early [to say]. It's a relatively new unit, which is a step in the right direction towards recognising that we have a problem that needs a specific response, but it's still too new. It's not even countrywide. It's some police stations that have specific GBV units, with resources , with training, police officers and cars and everything to respond to cases like that. So it's still too new to see the impact, but we see the effort, one of them being that at least nowadays where such units are in these police stations when a woman comes to report, we've seen a difference in the way the case is handled. Initially, we'd come in and somebody would be shouting, ‘How can we help you?’ But this thing has had a positive change even just in the way the reporting is being handled. The big question is beyond the reporting because you have the report and then you do an investigation and then the person goes to court. That's where I think then some of the problems start. We now have the police saying they’ve done their job, they’ve investigated and handed [over] the evidence [to the Directorate of Public Prosecutions and the courts]. But then the magistrate is saying to grant bail or not – the loopholes – or if there’s insufficient evidence, they’ll still have to investigate better. Those are some of the challenges.

The FFM team asked how easy the reporting process was. Could someone quite easily report GBV to the police? UN OFFICIAL thought it would be relatively easy. You can pick up the phone and call. But the question would be whether they’d be there when you needed them, because sometimes you call in the middle of the night – a woman has been beaten, or sometimes you even call as a neighbour when a woman has been beaten next door, or your colleague – but the police tell you to come back [later], right now they don’t have a car. So the reporting part is easy; you just call 999 or you can physically go to the police station. The response is a different matter.

The FFM team noted that they had heard the GBV unit was set up a few years ago. They asked whether the unit provides officers, provides training and guidance, or whether it does something else. The GBV [unit] in the police station is under the police. They are in charge of GBV cases reported at the Police station. They are provided with specific training to handle GBV cases. The training is done as part of their police training, but then we also have specialised training where different organisations come and train them and so forth. Just a few weeks ago we had a session with the traditional leaders we are collaborating with, the [Directorate] of Public Prosecutions and the police. So, they'll have that as part of their pre-service training and then have specialised training specifically [provided by] that unit, but not necessarily [given] by the unit. I think the unit mainly does service provision within police stations.

The FFM team asked what ‘service provision’ meant. Was it handling cases? UN OFFICIAL confirmed yes. The FFM team asked for confirmation as to whether the GBV unit handles cases. UN OFFICIAL confirmed that it does. The FFM team noted that UN OFFICIAL had mentioned that the police might not investigate properly. Had UN OFFICIAL observed that? Did she have evidence of that process not working properly? UN OFFICIAL noted yes and added that, as she had said, there's a public outcry around the bail system. We have a lot of these repeat offenders out there. Bail is part of the legal system. You can't necessarily deny people bail simply because the public is saying these are repeat offenders. [Courts] say to grant or not grant bail, they consider the evidence that is presented before them, and the facts and merits of the case. In some cases, you hear that the investigators will be saying they’re still investigating, and in that case then the magistrate will say they can't keep somebody incarcerated while [the investigations are ongoing]. UN OFFICIAL thought the fact that there are a lot of perpetrators of GBV, particularly repeat offenders, who are out on bail because the investigations are still ongoing, says a lot. These are some of the things we're observing, but we don’t have data from the police or the courts. But if you speak to the police and ask them how many perpetrators of GBV are repeat offenders, how many of them have been granted bail and committed similar or even worse offences while out on bail, [it would be] quite a lot. Even the perpetrator of the UB murder was out on bail. So, a lot of them are repeat offenders and they commit most of these while they're out on bail.

The FFM team asked whether it’s more of an efficiency issue than a willingness or ability issue. UN OFFICIAL thought more of an efficiency issue.

The FFM team asked whether UN OFFICIAL had any data on the number of arrests, prosecutions and convictions. UN OFFICIAL noted she did not have those exact numbers. The UNFPA had also asked for them, but she could still try and get them. Currently, she did not have the official statistics.

The FFM team asked whether UN OFFICIAL had data on numbers of domestic violence cases or other GBV cases reported to the police. UN OFFICIAL noted they did not have the latest data. She explained that there's usually a reluctance [to share data]. You ask for that from the police. They'll refer you to the courts. There's usually a reluctance to share some of that. Generally in the country, getting a lot of access to administrative data, whether it's from Ministry of Health – the rates of teenage pregnancy, something as simple as that – [or elsewhere], is quite a challenge. Where it involves law enforcement, it's even it's harder. So we've asked for those statistics but we currently don't have them. Should we get them, we will share them.

The FFM team asked whether victims of GBV are able to get legal aid. UN OFFICIAL noted there is Legal Aid Botswana, which provides legal aid to people who may not necessarily have the means, and there’s also Botswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS, BONELA, an NGO, which provides legal aid support. And those who can would just get a lawyer, legal representation. And then there’s even the UB legal clinic, at the University of Botswana. In terms of legal representation, even the law provides that where somebody is not able to afford [a lawyer], one will be provided for them by the state.

The FFM team asked whether there are divisions of Legal Aid [Botswana] throughout the country or only in the main towns, UN OFFICIAL explained throughout the country where one asks, but that the question is whether everybody knows there's that provision. The FFM team asked how easy it is for someone in a rural area to access legal aid and legal support, UN OFFICIAL thought that was where the challenge lay. She thought Legal Aid Botswana had offices in Gaborone and also in Maun up north, so probably only 2 countrywide [the Legal Aid Botswana website indicates there are centres in 6 cities/towns: Gaborone, Francistown, Tsabong, Kasane, Maun and Palapye]. We may have legal aid, but to access it could be a challenge. And then BONELA, the NGO, the headquarters are here [Gaborone] and then they have project sites but they do a whole range of projects: HIV/AIDS, TB and stuff like that. But at least where you have a BONELA office, they may be able to facilitate with their headquarters, but where they are not, then that would be a challenge in hard-to-reach areas where [these organisations] would not have their offices. But you could try to phone. Asked whether this meant phoning BONELA or the government, UN OFFICIAL noted BONELA and Legal Aid [Botswana], to report and seek help by phone. Mobile network coverage is countrywide, but [approaching them by phone] would also have its own challenges. UN OFFICIAL thought if [someone] reported [a case], they’d probably be told to come to one [of the organisations’] offices, and that is where the challenges would probably start. She thought Legal Aid was only in Gaborone and Maun. BONELA’s headquarters are in Gaborone and then they have some project sites for different projects, not necessarily for GBV, and not countrywide either. Their projects are in Ghanzi and other areas, but because these are project sites, they’re not necessarily for providing legal aid to GBV victims.

The FFM team asked how many civil society groups there are in Botswana. UN OFFICIAL explained that when she was working for BOCONGO [Botswana Council of Non-Governmental Organisations] [where UN OFFICIAL served as executive director up between November 2023 and April 2025] they had around 300 individual members across the country, but these were working in a wide array of areas. Less than 20 worked specifically with GBV. Members are divided into 6 thematic groups: gender, human rights ; economic justice; arts and creative industry; Sustainable environment and natural resource management; democratic governance and inclusive social policy– UN OFFICIAL . The gender NGOs were part of the gender and human rights thematic working groups. [They included] Emang Basadi [Women’s Association], Gender Links and BONELA. Because BONELA do law and a lot of human rights issues, they will take on GBV. So, GBV [civil society groups]: about 20 to 30.

FFM team asked whether the NGOs provide support with employment, health and economic empowerment, UN OFFICIAL explained that there are some NGOs providing economic empowerment support to women, for women to start, sustain or even scale up enterprises. But when NGOs have a service like that, they are usually donor-funded, as with Women Against Rape in Maun or Cynthia Childcare Trust. UN OFFICIAL noted that Cynthia Childcare Trust was supported by the French Embassy specifically to run women’s economic empowerment programmes. So a lot of these are donor-funded, but the government of BWA’s gender affairs department also has a women’s economic empowerment programme where there's usually a grant set aside so individual women can apply, those that are starting enterprises, those that are scaling up. It’s about 500,000 pula [circa £26,870[footnote 486]] when it's a group of women or 100,000 pula [circa £5,360[footnote 487]] for an individual.

UN OFFICIAL added that there are other NGOs [supporting women with economic empowerment], for example, Ratong Centre and Botswana Gender-Based Violence Prevention and Support Centre (BGBVC). BGBVC offers support for women who are victims of GBV, and the second part [of its work] are economic empowerment programmes for victims of GBV. Women Against Rape in Maun also provide shelter[s] and while the women are there [they provide] economic empowerment programmes to try and help them self-sustain, so that they don't go back to the perpetrators. The Ratong Centre was actually set up by a woman who was a victim of GBV, so from her own experience now she helps other women by providing economic empowerment programmes. They also do therapy through the projects they do, like beadwork and things like that.

The FFM team asked how easy it is for a victim of GBV to access this support. UN OFFICIAL noted that it is easy. You can just walk in and they don’t charge you anything. The challenge is that GBV is spread across the country, but BGBVC is only here in Gaborone with satellite offices and shelters. Women Against Rape is in Maun. In other places, particularly the remotest places, there are no shelters so the shelters are limited. But if a woman is able to get herself to a shelter, it’s quite easy. These are open centres, but most have very limited capacity.

The FFM team asked about the number of women who can stay at the shelters. UN OFFICIAL was not sure but noted they are not big. She thought the capacity would not be more than 30 people because most shelters are just converted houses.

The FFM team asked whether a victim of GBV would be able to move from one city or area to another. How easy would this be for a lone woman or single mother? UN OFFICIAL noted that those who have the economic means can, but it's tough because a lot of victims are economically dependent on their partners. The houses they live in were bought by their partners. If you need shelter, where are you going to go? [What is your] means of sustenance? That's why a lot of the cases are withdrawn, because they say these men are the ones who provide support, but those that have the economic means can [continue with a court case].

UN OFFICIAL also observed that BWA is only small. There are cases in which perpetrators of GBV have travelled hundreds of kilometres [to find their victims]. There was a famous case of a former national team basketball player whose [partner] travelled more than 400 kilometres from Francistown [to Gaborone] to shoot her 8 times. UN OFFICIAL noted that these cases are common.

The FFM team asked whether this meant that it is common for a perpetrator to move around the country, UN OFFICIAL noted that even if a woman moves to a different village or town, it’s very easy for [the perpetrator] to find them if they're determined to do so. It may be easy for a woman to get on a bus and decide she’s moving from Gaborone to Francistown, but it's just as easy for the perpetrator to move and find her.

The FFM team asked how easy it would be for a woman to find accommodation, UN OFFICIAL noted that a woman who had the economic means [would be able to find accommodation]. But there had been a case in which a woman had moved to the BGBVC shelter [in Gaborone] and [her husband] had followed her and killed her in front of others in broad daylight. Imagine if a woman moved to a different village and, instead of being in a shelter, she just lived on her own. Many women are financially dependent on their partners, but if a woman who [is financially independent] moves away, there are cases where the perpetrator follows her and ultimately either rapes her again or kills her.

The FFM team asked how society views single women or single mothers. Is there any discrimination from society? UN OFFICIAL thought it would depend where the woman moved to. A city like Gaborone is multicultural and there are different people who are here for different business. But society is very traditional in people’s home villages because of the kgotla [customary court/community council] system, which means everybody knows everybody, everybody is tied to a kgotla and they have a traditional chief and they know each other by their family names. By moving from your home village to, say, another village, you're settling into an already established community, so obviously you're going to draw public attention. It depends on how traditional the place is that you're moving to, but ultimately people always get to know why you are there. In urban centres, it may not be so obvious.

The FFM team asked whether a woman moving to, for example, Gaborone or Francistown would face a societal backlash. UN OFFICIAL thought no, not really in urban centres. She noted that probably a woman moving would have the means to sustain herself because otherwise she would struggle and become stranded, and people might then ask where she had come from and make the connection to her history if she had been missing. If she has the means to move to an urban centre and self-sustain, it should be easy. But again, the fact that it’s easy for a woman to move means it’s very easy for the perpetrator to follow her.

The FFM team asked whether there were any numbers or data on how many women migrate from smaller villages and rural areas to towns such as Gaborone to avoid family issues, and numbers of cases of them being pursued? UN OFFICIAL noted that [UNFPA] did not have such data. [Lack of data] was why they had been talking to government about trying to update the 2018 study. The reason they get to hear about cases is because they end up with the police again. A woman was moving from Kasane because her boyfriend was abusing her and we only [got] to know about it from the police report that ended up in the mainstream media. It’s not even all the reports that end up in the media. The police are not so generous with their data.

The FFM team asked whether people generally migrate from the countryside to the towns and Gaborone. Is that a general pattern? UN OFFICIAL asked whether this meant specifically fleeing a perpetrator. The FFM team clarified that they meant in general. UN OFFICIAL noted that a lot of people come to towns seeking employment opportunities or economic empowerment opportunities and that there is a lot of internal migration. If you don't find them [economic opportunities], that's when the challenges begin.

The FFM team asked whether someone moving, for example, from Maun to Gaborone would be able to access healthcare and other public services. UN OFFICIAL observed that you can access healthcare anywhere; you don't have to be a resident of that locality. Women’s economic empowerment programmes are usually tied to a district. There'll be a budget under the Ministry of You and Gender Affairs and then it will be allocated to the different gender offices across the district because they'll have a sense of roughly how many people qualify and anything like that. But they’re generally accessible, so you can apply and try your luck anywhere, because in Botswana you can live anywhere.

UN OFFICIAL noted that to add one last thing, there had been a national outcry to declare GBV a national emergency. People had been demanding to see the president [speak about] the situation of GBV in this country. Unfortunately for the political leadership, in the general sense, the public is getting a bit frustrated. The president also made some unfortunate remarks [about GBV] recently. We were coming out of the festive season [Christmas 2024] and the number of reported rape cases and murders and everything was quite alarming just for that short period of the festive season. There was a public outcry to say that this is not on and that we need to declare this thing a national emergency. Unfortunately, there was a lot of silence from the government side, and people were frustrated that even the minister of gender was quiet, too. So ultimately the president spoke, and when he spoke, he said he didn’t even understand why people were talking about GBV, that it was very evident that we're generally a very violent society – men, women and children are violent. That also attracted a lot of public outcry to say this is the reason why it's classified. There was a meeting of CSOs [civil society organisations] about 2 weeks ago where they were strategizing about approaching the presidency in trying to push for GBV to be declared a national emergency, and that reasoning is that when we declare a national emergency, then you'll allocate the necessary resources. We had an initial strategy to end GBV. That strategy was not funded. The FFM team asked whether this meant a government strategy. UN OFFICIAL confirmed that it was a government strategy but explained that it had no resources, no budget. That's why people were now saying that we need to push for GBV to be declared a national emergency and make sure that the response is adequately resourced.

Lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+) people

The FFM team asked about the size of the LGBT+ population in the country. Was there any data on this? UN OFFICIAL noted that she did not have numbers but that organisations like LEGABIBO, Success Capital or Sisonke might know. Asked whether there was no census data or systematic collection, UN OFFICIAL confirmed that there was not and observed that there is a big problem with data [in BWA generally]. When data is available, people are guarded about it.

The FFM team asked how the LGBT+ population are treated. Are they discriminated against in law or in any other way? UN OFFICIAL noted that in terms of the written law, they're not. But in terms of practice – like how risky it is for them to get services from mainstream health facilities – there's still discrimination there, a lot of it from the service providers, though, because of [individual practitioners’] own personal beliefs. So despite the [court] judgment, the decriminalisation [of same sex acts in 2019], there's still a lot of discrimination. We saw it in the way it recently played out during the attempted Constitution[al] review of 2024. [The government proposed a constitutional amendment bill in March 2024 which, amongst other things, introduced protections for intersex people and people with disabilities. Some people interpreted ‘intersex’ to mean sexual orientation (including gay and lesbians) and opposed the inclusion of this group in the amendment.] We had different parts of society pushing back on what the government tried to do then. It was the whole process of the constitution review of 2024. But even in Parliament, one of the narratives that politicians [spun was] to say CSOs oppose[d] the constitution[al] review because they don't want [the government] to recognise transgender [people]. They were just playing out that narrative and pitting [different parts of] society against each other. So, there are still cases of discrimination. I'm sure LEGABIBO will have more concrete examples to share of the everyday lived realities of LGBT+ people’s lives.

The FFM team asked how lesbian and bisexual women are treated and whether this differs from the treatment of gay men. UN OFFICIAL thought BWA had not accepted gay men and lesbian women and that was why some rape cases were so-called corrective rape. A lot of them do not even come out. UN OFFICIAL thought this was because they do not feel safe to come out as a lesbian woman or a lesbian couple. You hardly see [them]. But we see gay men, but even they still get a bit of public backlash, people looking at them in a funny way and things like that. But lesbian women are not easy to see publicly, just freely walking around or freely relating.

The FFM team asked whether customary law protects lesbian and bi women. UN OFFICIAL observed that it does recognise they are there. It doesn't in writing spell out any discrimination. But UN OFFICIAL noted she did not have any experience of lesbian women who had gone to report something to the chief. Maybe LEGABIBO had such experience and would know how they are usually received. Society still frowns on gay and lesbian relations, and in the churches, in particular, you walk in when you are a gay man or a lesbian or you come out publicly and you get the looks and everything. UN OFFICIAL thought that as a result, not many do come out.

The FFM team asked if it would be right to summarise that there are lesbian women and an LGBT+ population in general, that they are not discriminated against by law but that there is discrimination or harassment that exists [in society]. UN OFFICIAL agreed. She noted that because of the court judgment, the law does not discriminate against LGBT+ people, but there are general public and service provider [negative] attitudes [against LGBT+ people].

The FFM team asked how easy it is for LGBT+ people to access services. Even if individual service providers [held negative attitudes], in general would it be easy for them to access services such as healthcare and education? UN OFFICIAL observed that healthcare and education are for everybody to access, regardless of orientation. [The issue] was mainly the attitudes of [individuals working in] service providers. The system itself is set up such that everybody should be able to access the service, but the practice becomes a different thing, if a gay man walks into a health facility and there’s a healthcare provider who has their own thoughts and ideas.

The FFM team asked if the government has a position on LGBT+ people or has just gone silent. UN OFFICIAL noted that the law has decriminalised same-sex relations. They won't get arrested for that. But in terms of marriages, there's no law [to allow them to] get married. Asked whether there is an absence of positive law, or law to protect LGBT+ people, UN OFFICIAL explained that there is no special protection granted in law; it’s just decriminalisation. Asked whether the government has a policy position on LGBT+, UN OFFICIAL noted that they do not.

The FFM team asked whether, in terms of education, healthcare and other public services, there is no systematic discrimination against LGBT+ people, and whether the issue is the attitudes of individuals within organisations who bring their own perspectives to how they deal with LGBT+ people. UN OFFICIAL confirmed this. She noted that, unfortunately, in cases like that, there's no specific law that [offers protection] in case you are discriminated against because of your sexual orientation. It's just the Penal Code and the Constitution.

The FFM team asked if the LGBT+ population are socially accepted in a more positive way in urban areas than rural areas. UN OFFICIAL thought this would also depend on the locality within urban areas and noted that she doubted that a gay man or lesbian woman would be able to walk around low-income shanty areas. She suggested asking LEGABIBO about Old Naledi or Extension 27, which are poorer areas of Gaborone. She noted that in the centre [of Gaborone], everybody minds their own business and an LGBT+ person wouldn't be bothered there. But in lower-income parts of town, people spend time being preoccupied with other people's lives. UN OFFICIAL thought there would be discrimination or name calling. If a woman goes to a taxi rank wearing a mini skirt, they start shouting at her, even though it’s in Gaborone. UN OFFICIAL thought a gay or lesbian couple would face the same thing there: name calling, harassment, or having obscenities shouted at them.

The FFM team asked if there were any examples of more severe violence against the LGBT+ population. UN OFFICIAL thought it would be a challenge [to provide examples], but that there definitely examples of sexual violence. [There’s] corrective rape, but [rape of] men, too. In prison, about a month ago, there was a reported case of corrective rape of a male prisoner who was raped by 2 male inmates. You get cases like that, like on one night before that, there was a man who was not even in prison who was raped by 2 men. It’s cases where [the man] claim[ed] to be [or identify as] a woman (trans men and trans women as well as bisexual men and women).

The FFM team asked whether, beside the above examples, there were any other documented cases? UN OFFICIAL noted that she knew of a number of cases but she was trying to remember whether they were gay men. There was another case in which men were raped by 2 men but she could not confirm whether the victims were gay. LEGABIBO would have more information.

The FFM team asked if a same-sex couple could move to a city like Gaborone, Maun or Francistown and live together. UN OFFICIAL confirmed that they could. She noted that urban areas would be a bit easier, and that it would still depend on the peculiarities of [their] whereabouts in the urban centre. She also thought it would depend on how open a couple were about their relationship because sometimes you live together and you're not open.

The FFM team asked if a same-sex couple could live openly. UN OFFICIAL observed that they would still be a bit shunned, particularly in rural areas. But if people didn’t know, they would just think it was 2 people living together. But if you're quite open and public about your relationship, Batswana still haven't really got used to that generally.

The FFM team asked if lesbians can be open about their sexual orientation. UN OFFICIAL thought the reason there are still not many living openly is safety. She recalled the case of a man in the military in BWA who moved to South Africa and married another man. There was a whole lot of hullabaloo here [even though] he had moved. He kept quiet, and then the one time he spoke, he said, ‘At least I'm open. I'm honest about my orientation and a lot of you who are talking about me are married to women but are gay.’ And then all the hullabaloo died down. UN OFFICIAL doubted he would have been so open in BWA. He was in the military. Also, a lot of people don’t come out because they fear a backlash from their families, because families haven’t really got used to the idea.

The FFM team asked who the perpetrators of corrective rape usually are. Would they be within the family or outsiders? UN OFFICIAL explained that in the cases she had come across,( cases I referred to are mainly those reported in the news of local radio stations), the perpetrators were not family members but community members outside the family, sometimes people the victim had grown up with but hardly ever total strangers.

Annex E - Interview with Interview with Feminist Alliance Botswana

Date 9 July 2025
LocationBritish High Commission, Gaborone
Attendees Co-founding member, Feminist Alliance Botswana; Chair, Feminist Alliance Botswana; 3 HO officials

Women and gender-based violence (GBV)

CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that she is an attorney in private practice and is one of the founding members of Feminist Alliance Botswana (FAB), which is a gender-centred organisation that was started in 2022. It is currently unregistered; it's just a movement, a coalition of gender activists and organisations that work in the gender space we want. Since its inception, it has worked with the British High Commission in areas of mutual interest, especially on gender equality and gender justice.

CHAIR explained that she is a supply chain management professional but is attending in her capacity as current chair of the FAB and working along the same lines that CO-FOUNDING MEMBER mentioned. They have been participating in giving a response to government action with regards to the involvement of women, the participation of the underprivileged and barriers to access to justice. CHAIR noted that she is there to give a voice to women in Botswana (BWA), less so LGBT+. But she recently had the privilege of listening at the CEDAW [Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women] Convention. They were [among] a group of civil society organisations that shared some of the challenges that they are all experiencing in Botswana and what they’re looking to see changed.

The FFM team asked FAB to summarise the position women face currently in BWA. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that the constitution recognises the equality of genders, and that discrimination on the basis of gender is considered illegal and unsupported in our democratic society. However, there will always be a conflict between what civil law provides and cultural norms that exist in the country. In terms of our tradition, like North African countries, our culture is based on a patriarchal system where men are more elevated. That permeates how we treat and ascribe rights, whether it's socioeconomic rights - not in terms of the civil law - but culturally. For example, if you're born to a local chief and your father passes away, it’s more likely that instead of a female first-born child succeeding, the [chieftainship] will probably be given to a male child, and in the absence of a male child the father's brother will then take over.

However, CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained, with time, more and more women, especially in that space [tribal chiefs], have been enforcing their rights, their rights to inherit and succeed their fathers’ thrones. [By way of example] She did not know if the FFM team would have the opportunity to meet the first female chief of the so-called 8 major [Tswana] tribes in BWA [Bangwato, Bakwena, Bangwaketse, Bakgatla, Barolong, Batlokwa, Balete and Batawana]. [In the past] all the chiefs have been male. [But] more and more women have been enforcing [their right to succeed as chief]. We've had this small tribes where women have gone to court to try and enforce their rights, their right to succeed their fathers has been recognised, but outright in terms of culture that would not be recognised. If you don't have, for example, the privilege or finances – resources - and the ability to enforce your cause, then you'll be disinherited and disenfranchised because of the patriarchal system. In recent times we have seen an increase in number of female chieftaincy heirs instituting legal proceedings to enforce their rights to succeed the throne upon the death of their fathers.

CO-FOUNDING MEMBER added that – although this is not a situation that’s peculiar to BWA – patriarchy continues to place a greater burden on women in terms of care work which burdens women over and above their everyday work lives. They're burdened with caring for elderly parents, children, children of deceased siblings, relatives, etc. We don’t see men being expected to do this. It’s culturally expected that because you're the woman, then you should bear the greater burden of nurturing and raising and caring for the family. We've seen it also within terms of inheritance rights, where in traditional practice there are certain assets of the family that cannot be inherited by a woman, especially if you're married. For example, the parents’ homestead would most likely go to the son not the daughter. And if a women’s brother has passed on, it will pass to the brother's first male child. But we've seen cases where some women have taken that to court to have it overturned. It also has to do with farmlands and cattle - women become impoverished because whereas the son inherits the father’s farm and cattle, the daughter is left to fend for herself and start afresh.

CHAIR noted that she recently had the privilege of listening to a conversation that was given by Priscilla [source unclear, not clarified], and in it she mentioned how even if a woman does succeed her father, her children cannot because they're likely to be born of a man who's not of that tribe. So in that regard, though a woman may become a chief her children cannot continue that lineage, it would revert to her brother. So, for example, if a female chief dies, none of her sons can inherit the throne. It would have to go back to her brothers or her brother's children. But for a man, who marries a woman of a different tribe, his children will inherit his title and wealth, culture teaches that a child inherits from their father’s lineage. CHAIR thought this has to do with the belief that the son carries the name of the family.

CHAIR explained that, also with regards to inheritance, parents born before the 1970s are still not in the practice of writing wills and there's a belief that your son inherits land. However, because of the legislation, women are able to [inherit]. But it takes knowing that you can question it for [a woman] to actually do it, and also to be able to afford to do so. That's where the mindset comes from, of men just defending what favours them. They are not defending their position of taking care of the whole family financially; they want the women to help them in that regard. They’re only defending the ownership aspect. But if we're going to go to work, let's both go to work and bring home the bread.

CHAIR added that, increasingly, more girls are doing better than boys in school and are finishing school in larger numbers. In [small and medium enterprises] SMEs or small businesses, there are a lot of women, yet in more established businesses, there are a lot of men [in leadership roles]. So where there’s structure, it's men, and when there's less structure, it's mostly women-led businesses. Recent studies have also shown that even in corporates [large companies], there are more women in management positions. If you were to look currently at the banks’ structure, Absa [Bank Botswana], the CEO is a woman and then there was a woman at Barclays [Botswana], and the other 3 are men. More women are advancing to senior management positions. However, it is important to note that only 6 members of Parliament are women [out of 69], of the 6 female MPs, 3 were elected by the electorates, whilst 3 are specially nominated by the President, which means they weren't elected by the people. In fact, we’ve regressed in terms of numbers as regards representation of women in political office.

The FFM team summarised that although women have equality in law and customary law, tradition favours men. Women are making progress in business and elsewhere, but it’s still [dominated by] men. Women are doing well in education, but it's not translating yet fully into equality and economic and social rights. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that it's important to highlight that because of the way BWA society is structured, more of the population only have access to traditional courts than civil courts, so unless tradition and traditional law change, women will continue to be disenfranchised in terms of enforcing their rights. This is because whereas civil law prohibits discrimination, in traditional courts judgments are made with clear gender biases.

The FFM team asked whether it would be possible for those people to go through the civil courts. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that it costs money, and it's multi-layered because you start off with a small mediation court, which is the traditional setting, before you go to a major customary court, and then after the customary court, they need to take it to the customary court of appeal. And if you're still not happy with it, that's when you take it to the High Court, which is governed by civil law. But all of that involves money, time and frustration.

The FFM team asked, what are the main types of gender-based violence (GBV) and which are the most common. Do FAB have verifiable data (the FFM team noted that they were finding data hard to obtain)? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that the FFM team are not the only ones [finding it hard to obtain data]. GBV is on the rise in BWA – [it includes] femicide by intimate partners, whether current or previous intimate partners, sexual assaults ranging from homosexual assaults to defilement, rape, physical abuse, financial abuse, emotional abuse and verbal abuse. But there’s a lack of awareness of what constitutes verbal abuse, so you find that it's under-reported.

CHAIR explained that [women] might only talk about it once they've left their relationship and reflected in conversation, ‘Oh, actually this person verbally abused me and that made me feel a certain way,’ but they never take it to the authorities.

The FFM team asked whether the main perpetrators of abuse are intimate partners. CHAIR noted that it is intimate partners and close family.

The FFM team asked, if other men in the community or strangers were perpetrators? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that with defilement, it is mostly known family members, neighbours. The FFM team asked what defilement is. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that it is the rape of a child under the age of 18. So, [defilement is perpetrated by] neighbours, family members and, sometimes, depending on the set-up of the family. You find that in one yard you have multiple homesteads and especially where the mother is forever away on work, some tenants tend to molest and defile the children.

The FFM team asked whether there are particular profiles of women or girls who are vulnerable or who are most prone to GBV. Are there any markers or patterns? CHAIR noted that with financial abuse, you'll find the most vulnerable women are those who are unable to find employment and/or earn less than their partner in the relationship. Because they end up needing to come to the man to say, ‘We are short of this’, then they experience financial abuse in that way.

CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that even with financial abuse, they’re seeing a rise in abuse of women aged 50 to 60 years old – older women who are single, whether widows, divorced or never married – who are preyed on by younger men.

The FFM team asked whether CO-FOUNDING MEMBER most victims are younger women, but that they’re seeing older women as well. CHAIR explained that mostly it’s younger women, but increasingly older women who are not married or in stable relationships are facing a situation where younger men are coming into their lives and pretending to be in love with them.

The FFM team noted that they had also heard of ritualised abuse through the traditional belief systems. Is that something that FAB is aware of? CHAIR noted that there haven’t been a lot of [these cases] recently. She thought the culture had been dynamic in terms of trying to eliminate abusive practices such as genital mutilation. They haven't [seen any cases]. They’re just seeing an increase in more modern types of abuse that you would get anywhere else. Also, there is online abuse. The FFM team asked whether that is harassment or similar. CHAIR confirmed that it is [harassment].

The FFM team asked what the information base is for the different types of abuse. How do FAB know that there is more abuse happening? Will people be reporting instances more if they're becoming more aware of these incidents? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that there has been an increase in terms of cases being reported. The FFM team asked whether this meant reported to FAB or to the police. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted to the police. And sometimes, there are some victims who feel uncomfortable reporting to the police, so they report to shelters or organisations that specifically work with GBV. They are the link between [the victims] and the law enforcement agencies.

The FFM team asked whether FAB is aware of any reliable data sets about reporting to the police on rape, femicide, sexual harassment. CHAIR explained that the information is disaggregated, but that the government admitted at the [UN Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women] CEDAW [review of Botswana, concluding comments in May 2025] that there is no central place you can find any such information holistically. She remembered a man from the Ministry of Justice mentioning how a few cases that were reported were successfully prosecuted in terms of abuse, and the number was just appalling. She recalled him saying 3 were successful, but there was no context of 3 out of how many. In terms of civil society organisations (CSOs) that help, they tend to also keep that information very private. She noted that if the FFM team are going to meet [CSOs], they will get a clearer picture of how many women the organisations are getting, how many are returning and how many are completely new cases.

CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that the data she had been able to get is from the Botswana Police Service, but it only goes up to 2021. It's 2020 up to 2023, and even under the cases, for example, on murder, the [data] doesn't disaggregate by intimate partner or stranger. She noted that overall there is an increase in terms of the reporting year on year. The FFM team asked whether this was from the police statistics. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER confirmed that it was. The FFM team asked whether it is a large increase observing that the BWA population is increasing and more women are reporting because they're more aware of their rights so were these factors too? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER thought it was also because there is knowledge now, knowledge of the interventions where people feel like they’ll get justice, which is a very important step.

CHAIR thought that, also, people are now leveraging the power of social media. A lot of cases, just like the MeToo movement, are talked about and people are bravely posting their stories online. That is how other people get the courage to come forward with their stories. And sometimes those are not reported. It's just somebody coming out and saying, ‘This is also my story.’ It’s a form of healing just to speak about it.

The FFM team summarised: the scale of GBV is quite hard to quantify, but that CO-FOUNDING MEMBER and CHAIR believe it’s growing. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER and CHAIR agreed.

The FFM team asked if the government has strong laws and policies to protect women? CHAIR explained that recently a woman at the University of Botswana was killed , https://www.mmegi.bw/news/brutal-murder-shocks-ub-staff/news by a former intimate partner and one of the facts that emerged the day after [her murder] was that he had actually been given a restraining order, which the police neglected to mention when he was applying for bail. That tells you that although the Minister of Youth [and Gender Affairs had stated] how [the government had been] doing gender training and GBV training for police officers, for officials, the questions that kept emerging were, ‘How do you monitor that the training is actually effective? Do you know if the police represented the facts more accurately after the training?’ Because this shows us that somebody didn't think that a restraining order was important to mention where a person’s life was threatened and they ended up eventually being killed. That’s just one of the things that shows you [although] training may be done no one is monitoring to see if it's effectual, if it's addressing the problems that it's supposed to address.

The FFM team noted that it was a horrific case, but queried how CO-FOUNDING MEMBER and CHAIR knew that it’s representative [of the GBV and the criminal justice process]? Is it just a one-off bad example? How do you know there’s a pattern? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that the case brought to the fore the weaknesses in both the judicial system and the police investigating system. If I commit a crime in Gaborone and I leave Gaborone with the case being opened against me and I've been charged in the magistrates’ court here [in Gaborone] and then I go to Francistown and I commit a similar offence or a different offence, the police and the magistrates’ courts in Francistown will not be able to pick that up because our systems operate in siloes. There is a lack of connectivity or systems that support magistrates courts, the DPP [Directorate of Public Prosecutions] which is the prosecuting arm [of the state criminal justice system], and the investigating unit of the Botswana Police Service. So in this instance, the restraining order, CO-FOUNDING MEMBER thought, was obtained in Mochudi, which is outside of Gaborone, but not far. When systems don't speak to each other, there's no way of knowing that this person has a restraining order against them or has been accused of a similar offence. It is something that the Administration of Justice [the judiciary] has spoken about and the police service has thought about, but they need to meet to develop a system that would then allow them to interlink with each police department.

The FFM team asked whether this was a technology issue. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER confirmed that it was [a lack of a national database]. She noted that it's also a resource issue, because their resources are limited. She explained that although CHAIR had rightly mentioned that the police are being trained, when you speak to individual station commanders of various police stations, they will tell you that it's very difficult to manage the resources. Transfers of police officers are not done by them, so you'll find that, [for example], in 2023, you have 10 police officers who were trained in GBV and gender mainstreaming, etc, and then in 2025, 10 of them are transferred to different units and your staff complement is not replaced with people who've undergone the training, so there's a lack of continuity in education of police officers and judicial officers.

The FFM team asked whether it was correct that the GBV unit was set up several years ago. CHAIR noted that it was set up last year [2024]. She explained that another issue is that sometimes things are talked about, like the one-stop desk for GBV. There's been a conversation around that for at least 2 years now but it's actually not there. We talk about it a lot, but there's no police station you can go to where they will say, ‘So this is the stop. This is where women can come and get all they need,’ because the key concern was disaggregation of the services, when you're raped you have to go from pillar to post. The FFM team asked whether this would be a one-stop shop approach that included healthcare. CHAIR confirmed yes, all in one spot. She explained that it's been talked about, but it's not been implemented. She thought that while some might say it's [an issue of] resources, we do have the people, it’s just that we're not intentional about assigning them to that cause.

CHAIR noted that recently, there was a call from civil society to the president and our rulers to say, why are we not declaring GBV a national crisis? It's been defended in the most absurd ways by the president on public platforms. He compared GBV to violence in general, and then recently, he said kids are violent because they are being beaten or corporal punishment is being administered at home. Yet the numbers [of GBV] are higher now than when actually parents used to use corporal punishment as a form of discipline in the old days.

The FFM team recapped that the government announces policies, but they don't seem to be well implemented. The FFM team asked for clarification as to whether the police GBV unit’s purpose is to set standards and provide training of police officers in a gender-sensitive way to deal with cases. Is that its role theoretically? CHAIR confirmed that it is.

The FFM team asked whether it would be correct to say that CHAIR and CO-FOUNDING MEMBER didn’t know what was actually done [by the police] in practice [regarding GBV cases]. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that she was trying to look for some statistics [on GBV incidents] that resulted in the outcry, the situation they were speaking about, because she thought there was a newspaper report on the number of people killed during the festive season in just 16 days. The FFM team asked whether this was last Christmas [2024]. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER confirmed that it was. The FFM team asked whether this was reported in the press. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER confirmed that it was. The FFM team asked whether the press were reacting to those data. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that they were, and that the data amounted to one woman every day having been killed. In some instances, it was a woman who was killed with her children. The government had just gone quiet about it. That’s what led to the outcry about it. Asked whether this was the outcry for [declaration of] a national emergency, CO-FOUNDING MEMBER confirmed it was.

The FFM team asked whether FAB had information about the number of people who were killed. CHAIR noted that they could get this. The FFM team noted that they would like to know the number of people killed, and out of them, how many were women. CHAIR explained that it was only women and that in Botswana, most of those killed in gender-based violence cases are women. Very rarely do women kill their male partners.

CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that she had found the statement that the Botswana Police issued: there were 60 women and girls who were raped, 19 murdered, 13 defiled from the period of 19 December 2024 to 2 January 2025.

The FFM team asked whether CO-FOUNDING MEMBER and CHAIR thought the police are generally well resourced and trained - are they capable – observing that the police can’t reasonably guarantee protection to everyone. CHAIR thought that there is an underreaction to the approach to abuse that often leads to either rape and/or murder by a partner. For example, if you say to the police, ‘I fought with my man or somebody on the street and they said they would kill me,’ they tend to underreact to that, or if you fought and it was almost physical, they'll tell you, ‘Go and talk it out.’ People don't just wake up and kill somebody; there’s usually a lead-up to it, especially where intimate partners are concerned. But because the police tend to underreact to the lead-up, it begs the question again of just how effective is the training that they are getting? If I left my house to come and tell you somebody said to me, ‘I will kill you,’ you must take that seriously. There's a reason why I thought I’d report it.

The FFM team asked whether that was a weakness in their training, in their investigatory processes. CHAIR noted yes and that it’s personal, cultural. Even cat-calling is normalised, when you're walking down the street. [Men] don't usually go as far as to grab you, which apparently happens in some countries, but just somebody saying unsavoury words as you walk by as an indicator that they could gain access to you without your permission, in the form of rape.

The FFM team asked whether there are also cases where a woman has reported a sexual incident that isn’t a rape to the police and they have investigated, leading to [arrest, prosecution and conviction]. The FFM team noted that the University of Botswana case had been mentioned, where there was a restraining order in place, so the police had done something, even though they hadn't done it as well as they perhaps should have. So does that happen too? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that conviction rates in Botswana are quite low. The FFM team asked whether this was GBV or crime generally. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that she would stick specifically to GBV. Convictions are generally low. She thought the last research that was done – she thought it was a 2018 study – indicated a conviction rate in terms of these specific crimes of less than 0.5%. It is predominantly because of the manner in which cases are investigated, the manner in which evidence is obtained and handled, and kept and preserved. Also, in most instances, cases take about 5 years [to proceed from arrest through the courts], from time of reporting to verdict / sentencing (if found guilty). So you will report in 2025 and your case will most likely be heard or finalised – you’ll get a conviction or an outcome – in 2030.

The FFM team asked whether CO-FOUNDING MEMBER and CHAIR thought there had been any change since the data set in 2018 because policy changes introduced by the government. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER thought not. She thought GBV is not taken seriously. For example, she explained that there was once a rise in livestock theft, and within the same year, [the government] came up with a policy and funded what they call a mobile livestock court that moves around the country prosecuting people for theft. This intervention [a mobile court, for example] is not being brought for GBV. There's a mobile court for traffic offences. [This is] saying something important [about the government’s attitudes towards] GBV.

The FFM team noted that during the Covid period [2020 to 2022], there GBV specialised courts. Were CO-FOUNDING MEMBER and CHAIR aware of this, and have the courts been more gender sensitive in their decision-making and provided training to magistrates and judges? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that there had been training. She thought training had been provided by several entities: UNICEF, UNDP [United Nations Development Programme] and even with other organisations like LEGABIBO and BONELA, local [non-government organisations] NGOs that work in the gender space. However, in terms of it translating into sensitivity and seriousness and the speed with which justice for GBV is meted out, there hadn’t been any change.

The FFM team asked whether the 2018 study looked at the courts and the police. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER confirmed that it did; it investigated the entire [GBV] ecosystem.

The FFM team asked why there is a discrepancy between number of GBV cases reported and the number of convictions. CHAIR thought CO-FOUNDING MEMBER had touched on this when she talked about the follow-through. If the evidence is barely collected, then what are you going to take to the court? That’s often why cases are stalled. And often dockets go missing – missing, how? Who stores them and where? The management of that process is quite poor, and while you [the FFM team] spoke to there being legislation being passed, what's missing is the follow-through in actually ensuring implementation and then looking at how many cases went missing before and how many we have reduced the rate of missing by. How many were being reported before and how many were carried through, and how many are being reported now that have been carried through?
