The absence of those numbers tells you that they've no intention to follow through and that is why it's quite easy to pass a law and quite another thing to follow that through for people.

The FFM team noted that rates of prosecution for sexual crimes and rape in the UK are quite low, too. Handling such crimes is a difficult process generally, so there may be legitimate police procedural and judicial process reasons for the low conviction rate other than the ineffectiveness of the state. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that there is also a lack of understanding of the nuances that are involved in such an intimately violating crime. It's absolutely there. There's bias in judicial offices. There was a study that was done in Tanzania or Kenya, in eastern Africa, about judicial biases when it comes to these cases, and they found that most of the time, it's lack of understanding of those nuances to say a person behaving like that is not ordinarily consenting or giving permission, but we lack objectivity when it comes to assessing and deciding on these things.

The FFM team recapped: it sounded like there was some progress at least in the state’s handling of GBV cases, and acceptance of some training. Would CO-FOUNDING MEMBER and CHAIR agree there is some progress in the police or the courts? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER thought there was always training for judicial officers, (such as both judges and magistrates.) although she explained that she was unsure about the content and the depth of it. She noted that every year they have a judicial officers’ conference and that one of the trainings that they receive continuously is on GBV and children's rights.

The FFM team asked whether women who experience GBV in all its forms are able to get support from Legal Aid Botswana. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that what Legal Aid provides is normally enforcement of civil rights [not criminal rights]. So if I'm violated, it's treated as a criminal case and I need to put it through the criminal system. Legal Aid won't prosecute the matter on my behalf. It has been mentioned that because of the length that it takes from the start to finalise a criminal matter, countries sue under civil law against the perpetrator, but that hasn't yet been tested. The FFM team asked whether civil cases would be supported by Legal Aid. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER confirmed that they would, but noted that the Legal Aid [means test] threshold leaves a lot of people out. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER thought the maximum someone could be earning was about 2,500 pula a month [approximately £130[footnote 488]]. But for a person who earns from zero to even 10,000 pula [approximately £520], it would be very expensive to afford the services of a lawyer [FFM team noted: Statistics Botswana estimated that average annual nominal gross domestic product (GDP) per person in 2024 was just over 104,000 pula (around £5,700)[footnote 489], about 8,600 pula (£470) a month. However, GDP per person is not necessarily the same as actual income per person].

The FFM team asked whether there is any state support for women other than legal a. For example financial, accommodation, or social service support. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that there are various NGOs in that space, for example Women Against Rape, an NGO in Maun. There is also the Ratong Centre, which is based in Gaborone, and Botswana Gender-Based Violence Prevention Support Centre, [also based in Gaborone]. They provide counselling and legal services, but not the full range [of services. The services that one receives from the shelters is limited due to constrained resources. For example, though they can provide counselling services, this is not long-term counselling. If they provide you with legal services, it would be for immediate protection such as obtaining a restraining order, but unlikely that they will provide legal services to get a maintenance order or institute divorce proceedings, depending on the circumstances of the case. They'll probably start off with obtaining a restraining order and seeking a protection order (Protection Order is an all-encompassing phrase used to mean any of the orders listed under section 7 of the Domestic Violence Act, particularly restraining order, tenancy or occupancy order. It generally refers to orders given to protect the survivor and children if any and their interests against the perpetrator), enforcing maintenance orders, etc. They also provide a temporary shelter. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER thought the maximum stay [at a shelter] would be 3 months. However, [the NGOs] also [state] that they are not able to provide victims of GBV with start-up capital. More often than not, [victims] have to leave their homes and start life afresh, and for a lot of them, it's very difficult to do that.

CHAIR agreed and added that there is no intervention by the government. The FFM team asked for confirmation that other than legal aid, the state provides no support, no shelters. CHAIR confirmed that it does not. Asked whether there are 3 shelters, CHAIR confirmed yes, 3.

The FFM team asked whether the shelters are all in Gaborone or elsewhere. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that there is one in Gaborone, one in Francistown and one in Ghanzi, but she was unsure if the Ghanzi one was closed down after COVID, because there was the need to open one in Francistown during COVID. There had been a spike in GBV cases.

CHAIR added that the one thing they may have neglected to mention is that as a GBV survivor, probably taking your issue through the courts, you’re often not protected from intimidation by the perpetrator and his family, which is a situation that one of their colleagues had faced. Even she, as the lawyer, was being harassed by the perpetrator and his family, and there was no protection. The FFM team asked whether there is no witness protection or any other support from the police. CHAIR confirmed that there is not.

The FFM team noted that the authorities do issue restraining orders. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER confirmed that they do. She added that there is an act called the Deserted Wives and Children Protection Act. Under that you can get speedy maintenance orders. That's what they try to enforce in most situations. The FFM team asked what a maintenance order is exactly. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that it is support for the spouse, financial support for the spouse and children.

The FFM team asked whether, if the restraining order is breached, the police can arrest the perpetrator. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER confirmed that they can. The FFM team asked whether CO-FOUNDING MEMBER and CHAIR knew if that does happen. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that it does happen and that there have been cases where restraining orders were breached and people were arrested, but that after about 7 days they were released.

The FFM team asked whether it is possible for a woman to choose to move away from her home area where she faces abuse or discrimination and move to another town. Would she be able to do so safely, and when she got there, could she make a life for herself away from the perpetrator, financially and in terms of the availability of accommodation, education or healthcare? In society, how would she be received? CHAIR explained that choosing to move away from a spouse means you're relying on your financial [means] to protect yourself. Often support will be from family members and/or friends, not from the state, in terms of setting you up. There is an unemployment rate of approximately 37% (for youth up to 35 years of age)[footnote 490], so if you're leaving a city, for example Gaborone, your probability of getting a job there [in the new location] as opposed to [Gaborone] is very low. So if you're moving, it means you're leaving your work, to what? If you're entrepreneurial, then you can start doing some entrepreneurial undertakings. But it's mostly for survival because you have to recognise there's no strategic thought behind it and/or market analysis to it. So unfortunately, when you leave such a setting, you are sacrificing your financial stability for your physical safety.

The FFM team asked whether moving to Gaborone would mean there were more prospects of survival. CHAIR noted that there would perhaps be more prospects for work and finding work than in most places in the country because most development has been centred here. Most companies are here, you find the headquarters of most companies here.

The FFM team asked, socially, how other people in, say, Gaborone or smaller towns would perceive a lone woman, maybe with children. How would they treat such a person? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER thought there would be no shame because – she had forgotten the statistics – there is a high percentage of single female-headed households in BWA so [it would not be unusual]. She thought that despite everything, Batswana are accommodating and understanding. They still have a communal sense of responsibility to each other, especially when it comes to sensitive issues like this. So you'd be able to start a life. You'd be able to find support where you are. A majority of women tend to rely on churches and social clubs for communal support.

CHAIR noted that most people go to back to their maternal homes. The FFM team asked whether that would be different from the area where they were abused. CHAIR confirmed that it would.

The FFM team noted that the other issue is the possibility of the perpetrator finding them. Botswana is a big country but with a small population. Can you disappear? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted no, you can’t disappear. [You see that] when you read up on intimate partner murders, like the one that happened just outside of Palapye in the village where a soldier followed the family who stayed there and he was based here in Gaborone. He went there and burnt the entire house down, killing, CO-FOUNDING MEMBER thought, the grandmother and her grandchildren. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER asked CHAIR whether she remembered that case. CHAIR noted that she did. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER: Given our small population it is difficult to disappear and start life afresh in another part of Botswana. The example given was of a solider who traced his former partner’s roots. Went to her home village in the Goodhope region, found his former partner’s family home, burnt it down killing four (4) people in the incident.

CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that [perpetrators] will always find ways. If a person is intent [on] killing you, they'll track you down and kill you. Because there is such a small population, it's very easy for a perpetrator to find where their partner is.

CHAIR added that often kids are involved, too, because when a woman gets pregnant, the boy’s family will come and say that they own [the unborn child]. So the male partner knows the family and where they stay. They know where the woman stays and where her mother and uncle are. It ends up that [the] male partner already knows where the woman is likely to run to because they’ve lived together. So if she tries to run away, he’ll know where to look, and if she has the resources to move from Francistown to Lobatse, for example, it won't be such an arduous task to pursue her and find her.

The FFM team asked whether this would be harder in Gaborone as a bigger place. CHAIR noted no, it’s a petri dish. It’s still quite small. Everybody knows everybody's business.

The FFM team noted that some of the cases discussed are from the newspapers but it is difficult to know significant – representative – they are of people’s daily experiences? How many cases did CO-FOUNDING MEMBER and CHAIR know where partners has pursued their estranged spouse who’s been abusing them? How often does that happen, too? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that it's actually more frequent than you would think. The FFM team asked what this observation was based on. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that especially where the male partner feels aggrieved – say, he feels like you’ve used him financially – he will pursue you and try to kill you. If your family tries to hide you, he kills the family. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER thought that in the current Court of Appeal session, there had been more than 5 cases where the accused murderer had murdered not his ex-lover, but family members. The FFM team asked whether CO-FOUNDING MEMBER was suggesting that there have been more cases but there have been 5 at the Court of Appeal. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted yes, definitely.

CHAIR added that the biggest challenge for Botswana is improving data and being specific about what it is that’s being recorded, because GBV is quite wide. If it's a murder then it becomes a murder case with other murder cases. Also, unless it's at the Court of Appeal (CoA) - and CO-FOUNDING MEMBER has access to [the CoA] because she's there [as a lawyer] and can discuss it with colleagues - we don't track to the level of ‘This is where the story of these people starts. There was a restraining order against him. She left him.’ Nobody actually documents that and puts it in national archives [to] follow-up and develop interventions that will help curb abuse at every level. When it gets to murder, we've failed [in] so many other steps. When it gets to rape, it means we've failed [in] so many other steps of making sure our streets are safe.

LGBT+ people

The FFM team asked whether CO-FOUNDING MEMBER and CHAIR were aware of the position of lesbian and bisexual women. The FFM team noted that recent court judgments had decriminalised same-sex sex for men and women, but there was no positive law to protect their status as an LGBT+ person. This meant there was an absence of negative law, but no positive law. What is the status of LGBT+ people in the eyes of the government and of people generally? How are they treated? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER thought the starting point would be the constitution, which prohibits discrimination on grounds such as race, gender and sexuality. But the CEDAW report [Concluding observations on the fifth periodic report of Botswana] contains a recommendation that the provisions criminalising same-sex relations should be specifically repealed, and that's one thing that the government still wants to do. It hasn’t yet been done. The win was the decriminalisation case. However, to date, it's still not been struck off the Penal Code. The previous government brought a bill to have it removed from the Penal Code and then there was protesting by religious organisations, and they withdrew the bill.

The FFM team asked whether that meant the provisions could become active again. Were they dead? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that the highest court had struck them down, so they are of no force in effect. But that doesn’t stop an overzealous police officer from charging you and harassing you under them. And then, like everything else, you would need to go through [the whole process of] going to court to enforce your rights. The FFM team asked whether it would be unlawful [for the police] to do that. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted yes, but that's where it stops. She thought that even with gender laws in BWA, we are in the habit of neutralising, not consciously trying to empower. We've made sure that our laws are gender-neutral, giving an impression that we are all equal before [in] the eyes [of] the law. However, there's nothing that has been done to consciously empower women in recognition of the disempowerments that have happened over the past decades, or however long. The same thing happens with the [LGBT+] community. It's as if by decriminalising, we are done, but there are other areas of the law that need to be looked at. Are we saying they'll have a right to get married, to have families, to adopt?

CHAIR added: to identify freely in cases of employment. The FFM team asked whether LGBT+ people have no protections in employment. CHAIR confirmed that they do not, adding that most [LGBT+] people hide [the sexual orientation or gender expression/identity].

CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that also, even in society, you're in a union with somebody. Is that union recognised? How are your inheritance rights protected? If my partner passes away today, do I have the right to enforce my inheritance against her family? For a heterosexual person, there's what we call a universal partnership, so after 5 to 10 years of living together, then you're recognised as being in a civil union and you have inheritance rights. The same is not afforded to same sex [relationships].

CHAIR added that because [LGBT+ couples] can't have kids themselves, there needs to be a law that allows them to engage, for example, a surrogate, and our laws on surrogacy are quite hazy. Even the structures in terms of where to go, which hospital, freezing eggs, are not established, and by virtue of that, they are discriminated against.

The FFM team summarised that the law is at best neutral and is not negative anymore. The FFM team asked whether, in terms of how they're treated, this government has a position on LGBT+ people. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that the new government had actually shied away from [publicly stating a position].

CHAIR added that if there's no issue in society that presses them to comment, [the government] will stay quiet on it.

The FFM team asked what LGBT+ people’s experience is in day-to-day life. Are they open? Do LGBT+ people women - face discrimination or violence because of who they are? Were CO-FOUNDING MEMBER and CHAIR aware of such cases? CO-FOUNDING MEMBER thought it was more passive-aggressive, so you would not be outwardly harassed, but yes, you would be made to feel uncomfortable and unsafe. That is why the majority of [LGBT+ people] have tried to create their own little communities and hang out in spots by themselves, outside of the larger society. It’s also because in cases where they've tried to go and report harassment at police stations, nothing much has really been done by the police. The most that people get charged with is nuisance, and that is a fine of 100 pula, something like that. The FFM team asked whether those communities are in and around Gaborone or outside Gaborone. CHAIR explained that they find themselves, they form themselves into groups, and they hang out together or with equally [accepting] people. But most hide [their sexual orientation] at work and then when they are outside, they won’t be able to tell a lot of people because of the fear of judgement and how it could negatively affect them in areas they are not intending because there's no recognition of their right to be LGBT+.

The FFM team asked what LGBT+ people’s situation would be in terms of, say, accommodation or getting access to healthcare or education. CHAIR noted that LEGABIBO would be able to clarify on this, but there was something about men, specifically, getting medical attention and nurses giving them attitude, such as, ‘Why do you have such a condition? What type of sexual intercourse are you having?’ That makes you [reluctant] to seek help because first of all, you have to accept your lifestyle in a judgemental way. For women, it's not as obvious, in terms of your sexual health, who you could be [sexually] engaging with, but for men, they [medical staff] have to ask you [about sexual partners and practices].

The FFM team asked what the situation would be if a woman was open about her sexual orientation [when accessing healthcare]. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that they don’t even ask that, our papers don't ask that. The problem in society is that a lot of people bring their personal beliefs to work. So even if company policy or government policy is pro recognition of alternative [sexual orientations or gender identities], [individuals] would bring their personal views to work and feel like it’s their obligation to then preach to you and seek to convert you and reorientate you and correct you [from being gay or lesbian to being heterosexual].

The FFM team asked whether, regarding the healthcare example, it wouldn't be the healthcare service providers’ policy or position that LGBT+ are not treated but individual healthcare workers expressing their personal opinions, their personal values. CHAIR confirmed this.

CO-FOUNDING MEMBER noted that it’s the same with sex workers. They face the same level of discrimination from healthcare service providers.

CHAIR added: and colleagues or others who often take advantage of them. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that accommodation is a bit tricky because there have been reports of instances where, because of their identity, [LGBT+ people] have been disowned by [their] family and therefore been made more vulnerable because they've been removed from the family household. But in terms of just an average landlord, where an LGBT+ person is trying to lease that property, there's no issue. In terms of access to education, there's absolutely no issue.

The FFM team asked what society’s attitude to LGBT+ people is generally. CO-FOUNDING MEMBER explained that especially in the traditional and religious sectors of society, they are even more vocal about [being anti-LGBT+]. When you speak to LEGABIBO, they will give you cases of correctional reorientation exercises – I won’t call it [conversion] therapy; it's not therapy. Some families go as far as to use physical violence, abuse, taking away the person’s dignity, shame, etc., trying to convert their child.

Annex F - Interview with Ministry of Justice and Correctional Services

Date 9 July 2025
LocationMinistry of Justice and Correctional Services (MOJCS), Gaborone
Attendees 3 MOJCS senior officials; 3 HO officials

The FFM team asked the officials for their assessment of the situation of women and occurrence of gender-based violence (GBV). OFFICIAL 1 noted that GBV is classified as violence under the Penal Code. So, any harm that a female may experience will be prosecuted once it's reported to the authorities. The police are mindful of GBV; government is mindful of GBV. Botswana (BWA) used to have customary law where a woman was treated as a child and the a man could chastise his wife. But the BWA courts ruled that this could not be countenanced in BWA – this was some years ago. But the government is now very much aware of the problem of GBV. The president, Duma Boko, has gone on record that BWA cannot countenance GBV and interventions are being put in place.

BWA has a well-functioning judicial system and when cases occur, they are reported to the police who prosecute the perpetrator (most are male) and action is taken.

The FFM asked if there were other laws/measures in addition to the Penal Code being put in place to protect women. OFFICIAL 1 noted that there are homes [shelters] where women, including married women, can be moved to and kept away from the perpetrator [of GBV]. But there is an ongoing discussion with the Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs (MYGA) to develop policies and processes to toughen laws relating to women.

OFFICIAL 2 noted that the constitution promotes equality and non-discrimination. However, [comments] from the [UN] human rights treaty body reviews with regard to women [have noted that] we have a discriminatory element in section 15 of the BWA Constitution. The President has said that his government will be human-rights-centric. He has explained that human rights should be placed at the centre of development. One of the ways this will be realised is through a constitutional review which commenced in 2022 but this government is going to ensure is finalised. Therefore, we are sure that section 15(4) [of the Constitution] will be looked into. We have created the Ministry of Youth and Gender (MofYG) which shows that the government takes gender issues seriously. The MofYG has a dedicated budget, minister and staff. We have a gender strategy and are currently circulating a GBV bill because when BWA was at the UN UPR [Universal Periodic Review, May 2023] many of the recommendations were on GBV - we do have escalating rates of GBV – and the bill is intended to address such issues.

OFFICIAL 2 continued that BWA also has existing law [to protect women from GBV] and institutions, such as MYGA and specialised GBV courts established during COVID, and the police have a toll-free line [which GBV victims can use]. There is a public awareness programme run by the MYGA and Sivil society. There are also shelters for GBV survivors operated by Non-Government Organisations (NGOs) supported by the government. These are some of the judicial, administrative and legal measures that government has put in place to address issues of gender equality and GBV.

OFFICIAL 3 added that the Ministry of Labour and Home Affairs (MLHA) has an office that seeks funds from the government to support NGOs, amongst which some support women.

The FFM team asked about the GBV bill and at what stage it had reached in the parliamentary process. OFFICIAL 2 noted that there is government memorandum, a draft bill is circulating amongst ministris. The BWA parliamentary process begins in July, if it does not make this session there is another starting in November.

The FFM team asked what the GBV bill was seeking to achieve. OFFICIAL 2 observed that the MoJCS could not comment on the full scope of the bill as it is the purview of the MYGA. The general objective of the Billt is to make concrete the various measures discussed: shelters, education [public campaigning against GBV], the roles of stakeholders – government and civil society – to domesticate international human rights instruments BWA is party to – including the UN Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol), and the Southern African Development Community’s (SADC) Protocol on Gender and Development - to ensure that there is adequate protection [for women].

The FFM team ask about the scale and nature of GBV and whether there was data or research on this topic. OFFICIAL 1 thought the MofYG would be better able to provide statistics on the scale and nature of GBV.

The FFM asked in the context of the criminal justice system, how many cases are reported to the police. OFFICIAL 1 noted that the police would have statistics on this. X noted that MoJCS has responsibility for prosecution of cases through the courts. Cases would only come to the MoJCS after completion of investigations by the police.

The FFM team asked if the MoJCS had data on prosecutions, convictions and disposal of cases. OFFICIAL 1 noted that the police are very effective at receiving cases and preparing these for trial but the challenge they face is that sometimes the couple reconciles. There is also the issue of economic livelihoods, especially for women. Sometimes the man is the caregiver and the provider, so a woman has to consider the economic costs/benefits [of pursuing a case]. That’s when cases are closed – unfortunately the police cannot force a victim to give evidence.

OFFICIAL 1 added there is still customary law. Parents are guardians of a marriage and often by virtue of customary law the expectation is for the couple to fight for the marriage even in tough situations. Sometimes the man can be the monster, but in spite of that, the couple cannot just walk away. There is also the practice of bogadi - dowry - where a man provides a ‘gift’ [of cattle, for example, to the wife’s family]. So, if there is a marriage breakdown the wife's family has to return the cattle [the gift]. So [there] sometimes [is the expectation] to hold on to the marriage and walk the course even if it's uncomfortable.

OFFICIAL 1 also noted that BWA has the Marriage Act [part of secular law] as well as customary marriage - it's a dual legal system. A person can marry under customary law or the Marriage Act. Both forms of marriages are valid, but for a marriage made under customary law a dowry is expected. OFFICIAL 1 did not know the statistics [of marriage breakdowns], but the caregiver sometimes has an upper hand.

The FFM team asked if most domestic GBV incidents go through the customary courts initially. OFFICIAL 1 said no. The police have a GBV unit and they are mindful of it. There is no longer mediation [by the police] because people used to reconcile at the Police stations after which the other party will kill the other, and the Police were blamed for not doing their mandate. Whenever a case is brought to the police, it is investigated and submitted to the Directirate of Public Prosecutions for consideration to prosecute.

The FFM team asked if customary law was a barrier to prosecution [of GBV cases]. OFFICIAL 1 commented he was referring to exceptions. With customary law, the person is not marrying an individual, they are marring the whole family. So, whenever there's a conflict, the family considers it is in the best interests of the parties to mediate. But of course, the couple can make whatever decisions they feel are necessary in the circumstances.

The FFM team asked if the customary marriage process is regulated. OFFICIAL 1 noted that yes it is regulated, there is the Customary Court Act.

The FFM asked if a case in customary court could switch to the civil courts. OFFICIAL 1 affirmed they can, ultimately the customary court of appeal and then the High Court (civil court).

The FFM team asked how does the MoJCS know that the police are effective, how is this measured? OFFICIAL 1 that will be based on statistics, which we do not have. Maybe in the past the handling of GBV cases may not have been effective but nowadays these cases are prepared for trial. Where a person alleges [a GBV offence] their case is facilitated because they have to prove that case before a court of law. But there are instances where a person who has registered a case chooses to withdraw their case.

The FFM team noted that police effectiveness may also be an issue of police training, resourcing and standards across the service? OFFICIAL 2 noted that the GBV unit was set up in the last 5 years, there is a toll-free line for reporting crime generally that people can ring, the police also have standard operating procedures for GBV cases.

OFFICIAL 2 added that with regard to effectiveness, the country realised that cases were being reported to the police, then due to a variety of situations victims would withdraw their cases, saying they had reconciled their situation, or the family advised them to step down. But following reconciliation the GBV would escalate, sometimes leading to the death of the victim. So, it was decided that the police will no longer accept the withdrawal of cases. It can only be done at court. So, all cases received go to the Director of Public Prosecutions and end up in court. But in court, prosecution depends on evidence submitted by witnesses for the state. There are situations where the victims refuse to give evidence, or they don’t attend court, which affects the outcome of the case.

The FFM team asked why victims do not give evidence. OFFICIAL 2 noted there are socio-economic issues, when the breadwinner is the accused and if imprisoned the family will suffer. There are also cultural issues as previously mentioned. People may feel regret after reporting an incident or the abusers reconcile themselves with the victim by offering an apology, maybe giving flowers or chocolates. Official X added that a victim becomes the state witness as required by the regulation of standards for GBV cases. So, when the case is in the court, it is the state vs the perpetrator [not the victim vs the perpetrator]. Victims whose request to withdraw the case at the Police Station, usually refuse to testify in Court, leading to low conviction rates.

The FFM team asked if there are other measures in place to protect victims of GBV, such as restraining orders or a witness protection programme. OFFICIAL 1 noted that there are restraining orders, and if these are violated a perpetrator can be imprisoned. OFFICIAL 2 added that the Domestic Violence Act (DVA) provides for safety measures for incidents in the home. The court can be approached to issue a restraining order. Although there was a recent case of woman who had a restraining order placed on her partner but who was killed at work in the University of Botswana (UB) [by him]. So there continues to be [public] discourse on whether these laws - the GBV bill, the penal code, the DVA and others – are effective. OFFICIAL 2 gave another example of a woman who was killed in a GBV shelter by her partner. The partner said that he wanted to reconcile with his wife, so the shelter allowed him in but he then killed her. There was a recent article by the president questioning whether stringent laws reduce GBV (as well as suicides, murder), arguing that BWA needs to find the root cause of the violence. Growing up, people know that if someone does something wrong, violence sorts it out, so BWA needs public discussion about the effectiveness of laws which provide penalties for violence. OFFICIAL 2 gave another example of a man who stabbed his 3 children to death, people will see this and want the death penalty [for such punishments] retained. [It is an example] that despite existence [of laws] violence continues. OFFICIAL 1 noted that the Department of Correctional Services and the police are looking to use tracking devices [to monitor offenders]. If someone is accused, then they will have the bracelet [tag] which monitors the person’s movements. So, if there's a restraining order the person would have a tag and if they breach the order then they would be arrested. The FFM team asked if this was being considered or had been trialled. OFFICIAL 1 said that the last meeting on this was 3 months ago when ministers had agreed it was the approach to take but did not know if the tagging had been trialled.

The FFM team asked about the murder of the woman at the UB which has been well documented in the media and whether it was representative of GBV crimes. OFFICIAL 2 thought it was subjective, also gave an example of a case of a female police officer who was stabbed by her partner outside of the police station. These cases are shocking and there has public discussion on how to make sure these don’t happen again. But although not the first of its kind [this type of violence] is not prevalent. So, [this will be achieved] through the GBV bill, continuing with the death penalty [to act as deterrence] but there is a need to find the root cause. Even if tags were used for restraining orders, if the woman is out at the mall or at work it will not be possible for the police to monitor these situations. As the president noted, it is not possible to monitor people in their home. Laws need to be made to work but there is also a need to change peoples’ mindsets.

The FFM team asked for confirmation that gender sensitive courts had been established and which courts – magistrate and/or high courts. OFFICIAL 1 the greatest impact has been at the magistrates’ courts because that's where cases originate and that's where the bulk of the cases are. The courts are GBV-friendly and the government has also piloted child-friendly justice system - children are also affected by GBV and sometimes they have to give evidence as they are molested. There are now child friendly police stations and evidence can even be given in camera if a child has to come before the court.

The FFM team asked what GBV-friendly meant in practice. OFFICIAL 2 this means the effective mainstreaming of gender across sectors, in this case the courts. Progress has been made, the MYGA has undertaken public awareness campaigns.

Last year, for example, there were workshops, through focus group discussions, through commemoration, and the media is also engaged, especially on gender sensitive reporting. We have a dual legal system [customary and secular courts], the nearest place of safety will [often] be the dikgosi (tribal chiefs). There are customary courts in every village, so there have been workshops for traditional / community leaders as well as for faith-based organisations and women themselves. Faith and religion have had an impact - in some religions people have been told that women should be submissive which can sometimes be misconstrued to mean women can be treated anyhow.

OFFICIAL 2 continued that child friendly justice, which is a MoJCS policy, is in place to help child victims and those who are in conflict with the law approach the courts. This is an interagency operation involving police officers, social workers, prison officers and magistrates. We've conducted capacity building with all those stakeholders under one roof so that we can identify gaps and find a common understanding in handling cases.

The FFM team asked if all these stakeholders had been brought together in one-stop centres. OFFICIAL 2 clarified that currently there have just been discussions of interagency cooperation. But the Police Commissioner is the chairperson of the inter-ministerial anti-GBV committee, formed in 2020 comprising of accounting officers of [relevant] ministries and stakeholders. The committee has been talking about establishing one-stop centres but these are not yet in place. The government had a pilot referral system a few years ago but it didn't materialise into a working system. The idea was that if someone reported to the police then was referred to a social worker or healthcare providers so that they did not have to relive their ordeal in the handovers. The committee is now working on establishing one-stop centres [for victims for GBV].

OFFICIAL 2 added that the child friendly justice system is giving the government an opportunity to bring service providers under one roof and to talk about how they can effectively work together. This will help when piloting or establishing the [GBV] one-stop centres. The FFM team summarised: the experience of setting up the child friendly centres would be useful in establishing similar centres for women/GBV cases. OFFICIAL 2 agreed.

The FFM team asked why there is an attrition of GBV cases from being reported to the police to these cases resulting in convictions and prison terms – besides reconciliation were there reasons why cases were dropped. OFFICIAL 1 considered that the courts would be best placed to answer the question [not within MoJCS remit].

The FFM asked about the prison services – was this under the MoJCS’s remit. OFFICIAL 1 noted they were a separate department.

The FFM asked how accessible is protection / justice. X noted that there are customary courts in every village, but not every village has a police station. The customary courts have first contact with people. The police are usually stationed at customary courts.

The FFM team asked what support is provided by the government in addition to protection, including whether there are government shelters for victims of GBV. OFFICIAL 2 noted there are no government shelters, but the government subvents civil society to provide shelters and support. There are also psychosocial organisations which are not necessarily in the shelters, some of which are supported by the government, but there is need for improvement in this area. Most people would go to their church or their parents rather than go to [publicly available] psychosocial services. There is a need to encourage people to trust the services and let them know where they are.

The FFM asked about campaigns to raise awareness of GBV and women’s rights. OFFICIAL 2 noted that the educational campaign is led by the MYGA. Each ministry, the business community and civil society also have a role in raising awareness, but the majority of awareness raising is by government.

The FFM team asked about the treatment of LGBT+ and government’s position on their rights and providing them protection. OFFICIAL 2 the constitution forbids discrimination and promotes equality. [LGBT+] are protected by the constitution – the fundamental law is clear, it is an issue of implementation. Society (and law) are evolving. BWA is gradually making progress, there have been landmark cases, starting with the registration of LGBT+ groups [in 2016]. Community tolerance is also improving with human rights education. OFFICIAL 2 continued that the [decriminalisation of same-sex sex] case [with the initial High Court ruling in 2019 followed by a Court of Appeal judgement in 2021] has not been implemented / repealed but this went to Parliament and was deferred as the government wanted to consult further. A lot has changed politically and in terms of policy - the president has said he wants the government to be human-rights centric. We will need time to see how this government can deal with this matter.

The FFM team summarised that there is no specific government position on LGBT+ people or the decision to defer the repealing of the same-sex criminalisation law in Parliament. OFFICIAL 2 affirmed that there's no position taken beyond that was previously stated: government needs to consult, adding there may have been constitutional issues around the separation of powers of parliament, as the law-making body, and the courts, which interpret the law. But it is something that can be resolved, BWA has the opportunity to do so.

The FFM team asked what would happen in practice, if a LGBT+ person faced a problem how would the police react. OFFICIAL 2 noted that the law [sections 164 and 167 of the Penal Code] are as good as non-existent. The case is about privacy, not about legalising same-sex marriage. So, one of the things the court was saying that it is not possible to police bedrooms and there were no cases of the police catching same sex people having consensual sex in their own homes. The law was discriminatory and didn’t work in practice. OFFICIAL 3 noted that there was a recent meeting at the Ministry of Labour discussing gender markers and how people can change their gender marker on official identification. OFFICIAL 2 added that there is already a law that recognises intersex babies on their birth certificates.

The FFM team if a LGBT+ person was harassed, could they go to the police for assistance. OFFICIAL 2 noted even before the high court case, the former president had said that LGBT+ people are like anyone else and they are entitled to protection, which is in the Constitution. It provides against discrimination, so everyone is entitled to report to the police if they experience violence.

OFFICIAL 2 also noted that society has progressed. BWA used to have issues where, for example, trans women would get attacked at bus stations, but this does not happen now. The law is there to protect people if they experience violence. The FFM team asked if the change in attitudes has come with the change of law. OFFICIAL 2 noted that people’s mindset has been changing [over time].

Annex G - Interview with Legal Aid Botswana

Date 9 July 2025
LocationLegal Aid Botswana offices, Gaborone
Attendees Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Legal Aid Botswana; 3 HO Officials

The FFM team explained that they are gathering information about gender-based violence (GBV) in Botswana (BWA), and the experiences of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people). CEO noted that Legal Aid Botswana (LAB) don’t focus on [LGBT+] people as a vulnerable group. Their mandate is to focus on indigents (poor or needy), to provide legal advice and representation to indigents. They serve the public as long as they are indigent. So [LGBT+] people don't get special treatment from Legal Aid Botswana by virtue of being in that demographic. For this reason, when we built our case management system, it was not one of the fields or elements that were included in the system to facilitate data collection, monitoring, and reporting to see how many of our clients come from this demographic and what the issues are. But we have not had a case where a [LGBT+ person] came to us for assistance having been discriminated against by virtue of being [LGBT+]. We haven't had those cases; we have had just ‘normal’ cases – litigation, criminal law, family law and so on without knowing whether or not any party is an LGBT+ person.

The CEO continued that with regards to GBV, LAB does assist. We assist in getting restraining orders and protection orders and we work closely with NGOs, particularly WAR [Women Against Rape] in Maun. We're actually in the same compound as WAR, leasing one of the offices there, so we get a lot of referrals from them and are singing from the same hymn book in terms of the Maun area.

CEO continued that in Gaborone, informally we also work with BONELA, but they deal with the demographic [victims of GBV] within their mandate whether there's indigence or not. But they will talk about it further on their side and if [an indigent] is coming to them and has an issue that doesn't fall within their focus area – for instance, you are gay, but the issue that you're coming for help for, from BONELA is inheritance which they do not deal with – they will refer such person to us because our focus includes succession and inheritance laws or property issues. That's how we're working. They have their objectives and demographics that they're focused on, so we complement each other.

Women and gender-based violence (GBV)

The FFM team asked CEO to explain who can get legal aid. What are the circumstances? CEO explained that in terms of criminal legal aid, for adults – an adult is 18 plus – we don’t represent them at the lower courts, which are the magistrates’ courts. If they are an adult, such a person will not have representation [as an] accused person or offender from LAB at such lower courts. If it's a child, which is a person who's 17 years and below, we will represent such a child who’s in conflict with the law, even in matters of GBV at both lower and higher courts. The FFM team asked for clarification that if a child is accused of GBV, LAB would represent them. CEO confirmed this, noting that everybody deserves to be represented and you are only guilty when a tribunal pronounces that you are guilty. Before then, you're just an accused person and if you are a child, you must be provided with legal representation in terms of the Children’s Act.

The FFM team asked whether being a child is the only requirement, the only criterion. CEO confirmed yes, as long as [the person] is a child, we don't apply the means test. If [the person is] an adult, we apply the means test and we do represent adults at the higher courts, meaning the High Court and the Court of Appeal. Most of these criminal matters are tried at the magistracy, which means that we rarely get involved at trial stage and only get involved at the appeal phase, from the convictions and/or sentencings or the judgments of the magistrate. For GBV in the form of murder/manslaughter, we would only be involved with such a person at Magistrates Court during the committal proceedings which is the formal process of the Magistrate referring such cases to the High Court for trial. We would also assist such persons at Magistrate level for bail applications. [That applies to] everybody, adults and minors, in terms of murder/manslaughter. For clarity, LAB provides representation at High Court and/or Court of Appeal where the Administration of Justice has failed to provide pro deo counsel for such persons. According to the High Court precepts, it is the Administration of Justice that has the duty to ensure that all persons who are charged with an offence whose sentence could be capital punishment are provided with counsel at the expense of the State (ie pro deo counsel). Where for some reason they fail to provide such pro deo counsel, then LAB would provide such representation. So if the outcome of the GBV was death, and the perpetrator charged with either manslaughter or murder, the entity responsible for providing counsel for such an accused in the first instance would be the Administration of Justice. If that fails, we come in and provide counsel, but we would apply the means test for adults as a condition precedent.

The FFM team asked what the means test is currently. CEO explained that the means test is an assessment that tests whether you are the intended recipient of their services, being a poor person who can't afford counsel, a lawyer, for themselves. The FFM team asked what the threshold is, CEO noted that she wished it was that easy. It’s a very complex and complicated calculation. The FFM team asked whether it is therefore not solely based on income, CEO explained that it's tangible assets as well, so you consider a person's moveable and immovable property as well as revenue and revenue-generating activities.

The FFM team summarised that legal aid is provided to children from the magistrates’ courts and higher courts, regardless of their circumstances. CEO agreed: both magistracy and the High Court [in the case of] children. The FFM team summarised that for adults, legal aid is provided for people in the High Court and parallel courts but it's means-tested and only if the High Court does not provide a free counsel themselves. CEO agreed.

The FFM team asked whether the High Court would also provide free counsel for children? CEO explained that they would provide free counsel. The primary provider of counsel in matters where somebody has died is with the High Court. But it may be that the matter that we're dealing with, the GBV, is a rape and not a death, and therefore that’s where LAB would come in.

The FFM team summarised that when there’s a case of death, the High Court would provide counsel, but in other cases, which may be serious, counsel would not be provided by the High Court. LAB may assist and then it's means-tested for adults and but not means tested for children. CEO agreed.

The FFM team asked how many cases of legal aid are provided by LAB each year, for example, for adults generally? CEO noted that probably 99% of legal aid is provided to adults. Explaining why: in our infancy, when we were established, we were directed to provide civil legal aid. Adding that LAB ran a criminal legal aid services pilot project from November 2023, ending 31st March [2025] – focused on children in conflict with the law to prepare the institution to wholly provide criminal legal aid having determined and solved associated challenges and obstacles. [In civil cases] people are generally [not] at risk of being incarcerated or executed. Generally, worldwide jurisdictions would focus their legal aid on criminal legal aid as life and liberty of persons are at risk under criminal law, but we started the other way round [providing legal aid for civil not criminal cases], it was therefore imperative to review our operations to also offer criminal legal aid. We are at that stage where as a country and as an institution are ready [to provide criminal legal aid]. Obviously there [has been] a lot of nudging from the international community, but we were ready, even without the nudging, to provide [criminal legal aid]. Happily, the government has embraced the idea, and we have been given a healthy budget for this financial year 2025/2026 to roll out criminal legal aid.

CEO added that when LAB started their operations, they generally focused on adults as opposed to children. The idea was that when you educate the adults, they’ll know which entity to approach if a child needs civil legal aid and can assist them, as opposed to us directly going to the child to educate them. Legal speaking for LAV to provide representation/advice the child must come with a legal guardian, which can be the parent but also includes a social worker. One fault with this system is perhaps that we therefore interact solely with the adult who comes with the child as the client and not keep the child in loop. But we have changed focus and from 2024 we are also focused on [educating] children [about] their rights.

The FFM team asked which children. CEO noted [simply] children, in terms of capacitating [educating] them [about] their rights and the obligations and the services of the various service providers who can render assistance should they be in need. And even if the child were to reach out on their own, we would know which adult institution to refer them to so that they can come with them to access our services. Whenever you [provide a] service, there has to be an adult to execute those legal acts that are necessary which require one to have the requisite authority, such as signing a power of attorney appointing LAB as their legal representative]. If it’s a child without parents, we get social workers to help.

CEO added that [LAB] provide a lot of public education in schools. We've made a documentary drama series for children talking about their rights – all of them, including issues that cover GBV. What are they to do? Who can help? What is GBV? What does it look like? It was broadcast on national television for quite a bit last year. We are also working with the Ministry of Basic Education and Child Welfare specifically to deal with these issues – (1) GBV, (2) children in conflict with the law. And it's very difficult because we're very stretched and therefore we can’t do everything in terms of advocacy for the victim as well as represent the accused at this point in time. We're just 32 lawyers practising law. The FFM team asked whether this is the entire LAB operation for the BWA population, CEO confirmed that it is the entire Legal Aid Botswana [for] the entire country.

The FFM team asked whether LAB is based in Gaborone only, CEO confirmed [that LAB is headquartered in] Gaborone [but has service centres in] Gaborone, Palapye, Francistown, Maun, Kasane and Tsabong. We are very few and so we can't do both representation of the offenders and representation of victims, which is why you see us working very closely with the NGOs as they are better positioned to champion victim rights. The FFM team asked whether working with NGOs was to extend their impact, CEO confirmed this and noted that it also [enabled them to have] a referral system. If a person is rejected under the means test, LAB can turn to an NGO which has a mandate that can receive [a person and provide legal advice].

The FFM team asked why LAB is involved in advocacy against GBV, if their role is to provide support to those who are accused. Why is that within their remit? CEO explained that legal aid has a pyramid structure. At the bottom is public education, and public education goes hand in hand with advocacy against the negative impact of how you utilise your human rights as against others, as well as how to enforce your rights. The next tier is legal advice, and the last tier is litigation, the courts and court representation. The idea is that the more the populace is informed, the less likely they are – in the case of criminal law – to breach the laws, and therefore they would approach us for advice, being informed that we are there to give guidance. And then the least effort would be on litigation, which is the most expensive part of providing legal aid services. So this is why we have to do advocacy.

The FFM team asked whether advocacy is therefore a preventive measure. CEO confirmed that it is, 100%. However, we are not set up like that. [Our structure is that] we [provide] legal representation [at the bottom], [then] legal advice, and public education and information at the top. And it's something that we are looking forward to changing, in a phased manner, because we are limited in terms of funds and public education, talks to people, community mobilisation and continued presence in all necessary areas, as opposed to visiting and then disappearing for a whole year or 2. We have to have [a] continued presence, whether through stakeholders or through having an actual footprint, no matter how small, maybe a small office. And when the resource is in a paralegal as opposed to a lawyer, that would be sufficient in terms of mobilisation and continued messaging.

The CEO continued that this is very important because some people commit offences without knowing that they are committing offences, and some customs still facilitate this because [the phenomenon in question] is an accepted tradition. The newspapers have recently been reporting child marriages. CEO noted that she did not know how true this is; they haven't gotten into that space. But the other [issue] is child labour. It's still there, particularly in rural BWA, and it may be that even the people who are practising it are not aware that they're practising it, particularly where the parents were brought up in that same environment.

Noting that CEO mentioned Legal Aid Botswana is now looking at criminal as well as civil cases, the FFM team asked what their budget was for last year. CEO noted it was 55 million pula [around £3million[footnote 491]], rounding it off. The FFM team asked whether that was the year 2023 to 2024, CEO explained it was for 2024 to 2025. The [breakdown of expenditure] was 70% [on] human capital (lawyers and support staff); 20% for fixed costs (operational costs, rent, ICT licensing, etc); and 10% for variable costs (fuel, toners, staff welfare, training, maintain buildings, vehicles and so on). It is a service that can only be given through people, and LAB is run and operated with corporate governance principles embedded. There is a compliance function, a risk management function and an internal audit, a strategy, a project management, facilities management, HR [human resources], finance, etc. That means professionals who can do those things properly and they need to be assisted by other people. So it’s not just the core in terms of legal professions; it's the other related professionals.

The FFM team asked how many cases LAB assisted in 2024 to 2025. CEO explained that she didn’t have the figures off the top of her head, but as a trend for the past 5 years, they register about 2,500 cases a year. The FFM team asked whether these are cases LAB supports through the courts, CEO noted they were cases supported through to disposal because disposal can be settlement, through the courts, through mediation or [by] withdrawal of the case. The FFM team asked whether these were cases supported from start to finish, wherever the finish may be, CEO confirmed that they were. She explained that not all cases are [completed] in one year. Some are brought forward from previous years – a similar number – about 1,800, 1,500, 2,000 - and a lot of them would be matters that are already before the courts and are waiting to be progressed at the courts. By and large, LAB dispose almost the same number of cases [as the number] that are registered a year. The FFM team asked whether cases may start several years before [disposal], CEO confirmed they may.

The FFM team asked whether the budget for 2025 to 2026 had increased because of criminal legal aid, CEO noted yes; this year’s budget is 65 million pula [around £3.5million[footnote 492]], with [the additional] 10 million [around £540,000[footnote 493]] intended for the criminal legal aid roll out ie resourcing the new unit (ie more office space, furniture, tools of trade, vehicles, hiring more lawyers with criminal law experience, training of new and existing counsels on criminal legal aid, as well as increasing the number of registered criminal cases.

The FFM team noted that CEO mentioned legal advice (in addition to supporting cases through the court process). Is that for anyone? Is it to help the defendant? CEO explained that it is for the intended demographic, which is the indigent. But there are 2 levels of qualification: the means test and prospects of success. Because funding is finite, they cannot take every case including frivolous cases and those with no prospects of success. So at means test, you are conditionally qualified for legal aid, and that step is done by a paralegal. And then the matter is put into the system and allocated to a lawyer and the lawyer assesses the prospects of success by looking at it and applying the law to it. Even if the matter is assessed as having no prospects of success, the person is given advice including written advice as to why there are no prospects of success. There will be cases where there are legal prospects and we have accepted them as matters, but to conclude them, there's no need to go to court; it is just advisory. For example, a land matter and the client requires advice only, we give the required written advice and the matter is settled. The FFM team asked whether providing legal advice only in case that has prospect of success would count as a disposal, CEO explained it would be a disposal of a case where the service required is advice. The FFM team asked whether legal advice described above was separate from the 2,500 cases in the courts. CEO answered in the affirmative, it was in addition to those cases. LAB hadn’t been capturing advice in their monitoring and evaluation, but they are doing so now. For 2024 to 2025, CEO thought there were about 300 cases of advice, but formal capturing only began when the year had already started, so [the figure] should look better this year [2025 to 2026].

The FFM team asked if, when deciding whether to defend a case, LAB uses a percentage estimate of the prospects of success in the same way as the Crown Prosecution Service does in the UK. CEO agreed that the LAB prospects of success test is something like it. However, LAB doesn’t use a percentage per se.

Looking at the case law, looking at the legislation, and the facts of the matter, if there is a chance of success, if the case is arguable, then they’ll take it on.

The FFM team asked of the 2,500 cases, and maybe the advice Legal Aid Botswana provides too, did CEO have any sense of how often GBV is a feature? The CEO noted that she wouldn't have the figures outright, and even then the figures would be inaccurate as such a field was not built into the case management system. The FFM team asked whether these would be civil cases, she confirmed that they would and observed that they would come through LAB’s family law unit environment and cases were generically captured as such. She noted that there are not many GBV cases because a self-service environment has been created by the Domestic Violence Act. The forms for restraining orders are built into the [Domestic Violence] Act . The police will assist the victim to go to the magistrate’s court and be assisted by the office of the Registrar to complete the necessary forms and get [the relevant order] without the need for counsel.

The FFM team asked whether GBV cases would be civil cases, they would be dealt with in the criminal courts. CEO agreed but noted that the police are involved, because the moment somebody's threatening [a woman], the first place [they] run to is the police. The FFM team sked whether she had any sense of how often restraining orders are [issued], CEO noted that she did not. The FFM team asked whether the police complete the application for the restraining order, CEO explained that it would be the person who actually submits it. The police just facilitate, or the registrar of the court facilitates. The FFM team asked for clarification as to whether the police and the registrar of the court help with restraining orders. CEO confirmed that they do, but explained that you are all sitting there with them and the form is busily being filled in, or the police escort (protect) the person to the court so that they can fill in the form at the registrar's office and get it all signed.

The FFM team confirmed with CEO that she did not have any sense of the number of restraining orders issues, CEO noted that she [didn’t] have, but that the Administration of Justice should have that information. She observed that for LAB there are very, very few because it's self-acting – the person [applies for the order themselves] themselves. The FFM team asked whether LAB would not come across them anyway because it's not really their work. CEO noted that they don’t come across a lot, but they do have one or 2, several.

The FFM team asked whether CEO has any sense of the police's willingness to be involved in restraining orders or help victims, CEO noted that she’d got the sense that there had been great improvement in th[is] space over time. Times past, the police used to encourage the parties to resolve the matters between themselves but with the increase of advocacy for women rights and against GBV, with the incidence of GBV increasing over time, particularly during the COVID era, the police responsiveness and treatment/interaction with victims vastly improved and the government also saw fit to even have courts that were designated for GBV cases so that they were dealt with quickly. The FFM team asked whether these GBV courts continue to exist, CEO noted that she believes they are continuing, but that the Administration of Justice should have that information.

The FFM team asked how easy is it for someone to access LAB. Can a person just turn up at LAB offices? CEO explained that people do just turn up, but there is a Facebook page and a website, [on] both of which [you can] interact with [LAB] and mak[e] an appointment so that there's somebody to receive you when you arrive [at one of the offices]. A person can [also] phone in and be processed, means-tested and so on and then an appointment can be set up for them with counsel. The same thing would happen with those that reach out either via Facebook or the website – they would be processed by the same office, it's called Client Services Office They are the bridge between those who reach out electronically, including [by telephone], and the actual centres throughout the country.

The FFM team asked whether people who seek LAB’s assistance would be defendants, whereas victims of GBV, to obtain the advice they need, would go somewhere else. CEO noted that they can come to us. The FFM team asked what would happen if they did so. Would LAB redirect them to other organisations who could provide legal advice? CEO explained that if they came to us, we would assist. It is the nature of the assistance provided under the DVA even if as discussed above, the DVA to a certain extent facilitates a victim to obtain remedies without the assistance of counsel. There are however various protective orders under the [Domestic Violence] Act, but if you are just a member of the public, you may not know. [GBV victims] do come, and LAB ascertains the facts and determines the correct order to apply for. If a woman has been cohabiting with an aggressor, the aggressor can be evicted from their home temporarily and the woman or partner is allowed to go on residing in that home. The orders include restraining order, tenancy order, occupancy order, eviction orders. The FFM team asked clarified that a victim of GBV can go LAB who would facilitate a restraining order or a maintenance order, CEO explained that [LAB] would facilitate whichever order needs to be made, but mostly people know only about restraining orders, which is regrettable because then you run away and the aggressor is stays in your house. There was a situation where a young lady was actually the owner of the property and the aggressor was in her house and wouldn't leave. This state of affairs carried on and on and she didn't know we could evict the person.

The FFM team asked whether, once a person obtains a (protective) order, that has to go to a magistrates’ court to be signed off and will then have legal force. CEO confirmed this and explained that the police out of mere practice would then help the person enforce it, although it is not their duty to do so.

The FFM team noted that CEO mentioned a lot of people did not know that they can obtain various protective orders or that LAB provides these services. What does LAB do to advertise their services. CEO explained that is the function of the public education she was talking about, and that they absolutely have to do that better. The FFM team noted that CEO mentioned having made a documentary. CEO explained that there was one that [LAB] put on national TV and there was one that we made for radio as well, both of them in Setswana. And it wasn’t just a documentary, it was a drama (educational docu-drama), something to hold your attention and entertain you. CEO thought each had 13 episodes, [each] about 24 minutes. We were funded by UNDP [United Nations Development Programme] for both the tv and radio programs. There was also a generic public legal education program funded by the Ministry alone, not necessarily on GBV. The FFM team asked whether this was the Ministry of Justice and Correctional Services, CEO confirmed that it was. She noted that there was a third one for children, which they co-produced with the one of the local film producers.

The FFM team asked what the response to the documentaries was. Did they get a good response? CEO confirmed that they had a [good] response. Regrettably, the broadcasting institution does not yet have the facility of actually measuring viewership of BTV [Botswana Television] or Radio Botswana, but what they did do for us was broadcast our programmes during what they knew was prime time. They [had] a lot of call-ins and there were some episodes which the public actually asked to be replayed. CEO recalled that one day one of her colleagues was in church and overheard a group of little children chatting about the radio [programme], the GBV one, because we'd used popular actors in the country and they were quite familiar with them. They were mimicking one of the episodes. So there was a good response to it, but we can't measure it. We placed the clips on our Facebook page as well, so that they're permanently there, and we also [use] YouTube. In terms of our other material, there are brochures on various [topics], and we're in the process of turning them into audiovisual [content]. We[‘ve] animated them and we’re putting them on our [online] platforms as well, so that if you can't read or reading is boring, you can at least look at th[ese] clip[s]. So that's what we are currently doing, but we could do with much more funding to do more.

CEO added that they are working very well with other stakeholders in the environment - civil society, Botswana Prison Service, Administration of Justice, DPP, Ombudsman, Tribal authorities etc. She thought their service provision could significantly improve if there was a closer working relationship with Botswana police and the social workers, but that it is ‘not all gloom and doom’. The FFM team asked whether it was a matter of promoting and educating, and increasing LAB’s profile, CEO noted that it’s about increasing their profile, knocking on doors, pinning down natural stakeholders to sign an MoU [memorandum of understanding] with them. Then they would more likely than not push [LAB’s] mandate with you as you would have explained that role, the purpose and why you need them, why they need you, because normally in terms of the mandate there would be a commonality. Justice is served when cases are disposed quickly and they move quicker if there's counsel on the other side. And because we're talking about human rights, it is best that an accused person has representation as soon as possible e.g. at the time of arrest or as soon thereafter as possible to guard against self-incrimination or wrongfully obtained confessions. So it's always best that LAB [are involved] sooner rather than later.

CEO added that because [LAB] are a human rights institution, they wish they could be doing advocacy [promoting human (people’s legal) rights] rather than defending [people], especially when you look at a GBV case and what has happened to the victim. But the balance is that everybody deserves to be represented and get a fair [trial]. That is the [essence] of what we call having a fair trial, that both parties must be equal before the law in terms of representation, with the offender having the same quality counsel as the prosecutor or state counsel. That is what a proper, thriving democracy should look like.

The FFM team asked whether CEO consider there to be a fair judicial process in BWA, CEO thought so. Having been a practising attorney and a prosecutor, she also knows as well that the fair judicial process would be better achieved if the offender was afforded counsel soon than later in the process.

On the point about the investigatory process, the FFM team noted a few sources they had spoken with had expressed the view that the police approach to investigating GBV cases, and the standard of evidence they obtained, could be stronger. CEO agreed. This observation was also made by one police officer at a certain conference, that not only in matters of GBV but in a lot of cases where the investigation is prosecutor led, the police are more likely to know what evidence to collect and how to collect it properly to ensure that the prosecution is successful. The FFM team asked whether, if there’s a lawyer or counsel representing the state, the case would be better run. CEO agreed that it should. She also observed that the police prosecute in the name of the DPP [Director of Public Prosecutions] or on behalf of the state or the DPP – a legacy situation. There was a project previously for the DPP to take over all prosecution to provide quality prosecution and ensure things were done in the best interests of the judicial system and the justice system. However, there were obstacles. The police have a footprint in every corner of the country, and in most areas there’s a magistrate. But there will not be a DPP [office in all areas] because the DPP was predominantly in the big cities and towns. Expanding in order to take over the function of prosecuting means you need a presence there. When you’ve been detaining someone and 48 hours elapses, a DPP representative ought to be there to go to court about the person’s detention, and there were just not enough lawyers to do that. There was not enough budget to hire that many lawyers. They had to amend the scope of the project of taking over prosecution from the police, so the police are still prosecuting and the DPP is prosecuting in areas where it has a footprint and resources. The FFM team asked whether that footprint where the DPP prosecutes is the main towns and cities – Gaborone, Maun, Francistown – not for all of the rural areas. CEO confirmed this, adding that they really tried to expand but the resourcing was an issue.

The FFM team asked whether, if a victim of GBV goes to the police in Gaborone and their report is accepted, they would then be given a lawyer by the DPP. CEO explained that they would not: a GBV case will have aspects of civil law and aspects of criminal law, so where the matter is under the DVA the DPP would not be involved and an entity such as LAB or certain NGOs, if approached by the victim, might represent them to access remedies under the DVA. But if somebody has been physically harmed criminal law would come to play and the DPP would be involved to represent the Sate in prosecuting the accused and where allowed by its precepts, LAB might represent such an accused person. Cases must be disposed quickly otherwise there is a negative impact on the victim, having to relive their experience over a protracted period of time and their healing process disrupted. The FFM team summarised that restraining orders are civil law, and that’s why LAB are able to handle them. But in future might they be able to do criminal law cases? CEO explained that they do not prosecute criminal law cases; they are defending the accused or the convicted. The FFM team asked whether this means that LAB mostly won’t be dealing with GBV unless they’re dealing with the perpetrator, CEO confirmed that this is the case where the perpetrator is charged criminally and prosecuted but where the matter is under the DVA, LAB appears for the victim seeking remedies for the victim.

The FFM team asked whether the NGOs who are involved in supporting women refer cases to LAB, CEO noted that some of them do. BONELA is typically one that they work with as well as Stepping Stones [International], although Stepping Stones is more focused on children. CEO noted that they do have to work a lot more closely with civil society, because civil society is an extension of – is part of – the legal aid system of the country. The FFM team asked whether this is because civil society provide legal advice on various topics, CEO noted that they also provide advocacy and representation by instructing attorneys in private practice to take on their identified cases. The FFM team confirmed that’s why LAB should work with them – same area of work, CEO confirmed this and observed that there is a growing requirement for government to also fund [the NGOs]. They are not necessarily competition for LAB because they are focussed on areas of vulnerability that LAB is not focused on, which are important – the LGBT demographic, or women, or the disabled for example. LAB helps indigents, not helping women [per se] or providing special treatment for women. A poor woman will get the same [access to legal aid services] as a poor man in terms of their focus, but somebody else is focussing on women somewhere out there, whether they're poor or not.

CEO noted that LAB think there is a lot of scope for doing more, but they are also wary of biting off more than they can chew. If you're going to provide a service, it has to be a quality service. It has to be the right service at the right time. LAB didn’t do criminal law, but now they’re embarking on criminal legal aid. The next will be a focus on medical negligence cases. But they can’t do everything because they only have 32 lawyers and finite resources.

The FFM team noted that there is some awareness that criminal law needs to be recognised, so there is some progression. CEO agreed. She noted that LAB received some funding from UNDP to do [awareness] campaign towards the end of last year, and that they sometimes get donations/grants from third parties for special projects/programs.

Ritual killings

The FFM team asked of CEO was aware of ritual killings. CEO observed that cases where body parts are used for traditional medicine are really not rife in the country – they are in fact few [such cases]. The FFM team asked whether she meant ritual killings, CEO confirmed that she did. She thought that in the year before the general elections [2023] and the year of the general elections [2024], it appeared from the newspapers – although CEO emphasised that she personally had no specific knowledge of this – that there were a number of people who disappeared, and when they were found, they had body parts missing. But it was ‘not such a number as to raise a hue and cry’. It wasn't like in some African countries, where albinos are actively being hunted down and things like that. CEO noted that it would therefore be irrational for people to leave Botswana seeking asylum because of ritual killings.

CEO added that there used to be a lot [of these cases] when she was a child but that she is now [in her 50s], so it’s a long time ago. When she was a child, they were more of normal parlance, but not so now. [In the past], they were typically the cases that would attract capital punishment.

LGBT+ people

CEO noted that even at a social level – outside work areas, etc – there’s a lot of acceptance of LGBT+ people, unlike in [other countries in the region] where you hear of molestation, corrective rape and that kind of thing. In Botswana people are not assaulted or killed for being [LGBT+].
