The FFM team asked whether it is more harassment than persecution, CEO observed that in her personal view, BW is at the stage the UK was at in the beginning, where [the UK] started with, ‘It's none of our business’. It’s illegal, and then it moves to, ‘Whatever adults do behind closed doors is their business and we have no business as a state peering inside somebody's bedroom or behind the wall.’ In past there were one or 2 cases of persons being prosecuted for homosexual acts, ie having carnal knowledge against the order of nature in terms of the Botswana Penal Code, but the cases went nowhere and fizzled out, the state generally took the position of looking the other way. Even though it has remained as an offence in the Penal Code, nobody's being prosecuted for it. The FFM team asked whether provisions in the penal code that criminalised same-sexual relations are not enforced, CEO confirmed that they are not. She noted that in the workplace, for instance, she has not seen [LGBT+ people] being persecuted, even years ago, at least where she has worked, and she has worked in about 5 or 6 places. The FFM team asked whether she knew they were gay or lesbian, CEO explained that she did because it's a small country, so you know each other. And nobody was persecuted for it.

CEO added that [there’s] quiet diplomacy, and the courts have said, through their judgements, that it was unconstitutional for [same-sex sex] to still appear as an offence [in the Penal Code]. She thought that something was now happening behind the scenes. She noted that she could not say [for sure that] it is, but no member of the LGBT+ demographic has been prosecuted in recent years or, to her knowledge, persecuted. Socially, you do know a lot of gay people, and they're holding all levels of positions in various organisations, including the government. The FFM team asked whether they are open about their sexual orientation, CEO explained that they are open in practising it but nobody’s going up to people and saying they’re gay. But they are open about their sexual orientation by openly consorting, although she explained that the level of intimacy that a heterosexual couple would – display in public would differ significantly from the level of intimacy an LGBT+ couple would display. LGBT+ people would generally have places they go to or things that they do together as a community, which heterosexual people attend as well, so they are not hidden from the public. The FFM team suggested things are ‘moving in the right direction’ for LGBT+ people, CEO agreed. The FFM team asked whether discrimination and violence are not things she would hear reports of, CEO confirmed that if they were happening she would hear of such reports but confirmed not having heard of same, adding that nobody should be running away from BW saying they're being persecuted for being a homosexual. The FFM team asked whether this was also the case for lesbians, CEO confirmed that it did.

Female genital mutilation and incest

The FFM team asked whether female genital mutilation (FGM) happens in BW, not a traditional practice in BW anyway? CEO thought not. It is not a BW tradition. The FFM team suggested it was not a Tswana tradition but might be practised by other tribes such as the Kalanga. CEO does not know.

CEO added that she was not sure about the issue of incest. Again, it would be notorious in certain areas more than other areas, and that's where it is one of the customs of a particular tribe. People practise these things without necessarily knowing they are wrong in terms of the law, and that's where public education has to come through and is very important in making sure that people move away from some of these practices. The FFM team asked whether it is the case that some of these practices may exist in rural, distant areas, but that in the main towns, in Gaborone, these things are not happening. CEO confirmed this.

The FFM team sked whether, if somebody needed to be protected from these practices, they would receive protection, CEO noted that they would because incest is an offence under the Penal Code. The FFM team asked whether FGM is criminalised, CEO noted that it would fall within the offence of grievous bodily harm and would therefore be covered by the Penal Code. The FFM team summarised that there is not a law that explicitly criminalises FGM per se but then again, it’s not practised, generally speaking. CEO confirmed: generally speaking.

Annex H - Interview with BGBVC

Date 10 July 2025
LocationBotswana Gender-Based Violence Prevention and Support Centre (BGBVC), Head Office, Gaborone
Attendees 6 BGBVC managers, including the Chief Executive; 3 HO Officials

Women and gender-based violence (GBV)

The FFM team asked BGBVC to give an overview of their organisation. CEO explained that they are an organisation that works on the prevention and response to GBV, their name sets out what they do: prevention and support. They work in 3 districts [across Botswana (BWA)] on 3 sites: the one they’re running here [in Gaborone], which is their head office, as well as Ghanzi and Francistown. BGBVC have existed for 27 years, working towards the prevention of GBV as well as response and protection, particularly of those that have experienced GBV. In the past, they have had conversations with UK organisations and even people leaving to go to the UK, to the US and other countries due to what they were experiencing.

The CEO explained that she would allow the team to speak about the problems [they see] and what they are doing in order to ensure prevention, response and protection for victims and survivors of GBV. The organisation is run by a board of trustees that oversees everything they do. BGBVC is known by government and society [generally] because they mostly work in communities.

TECHNICAL OFFICER explained that they have a support programme that is responsible for their response in providing care and support to survivors of GBV together with their families. They have drop-in centres in Gaborone, Francistown and Ghanzi where clients can just walk in and seek their services. They also have mobile outreach, where BGBVC go where the people are because some people are not comfortable coming to their centres and being seen as survivors of GBV. The main reason for the mobile outreach is mainly to take the services to the people; to make accessibility easier for those who cannot reach our centres or even are not aware of the available service.

TECHNICAL OFFICER noted that BGBVC works with the police, government bodies and other entities. Under their support programme, there are different types of services that are provided, the first being counselling to deal with the trauma that comes with GBV and its effects. They have recently introduced [the option of] telephone counselling. Within the support programme, BGBVC provides legal support, some of it through legal volunteers. BGBVC is also able to provide clients with drafting of different [protective] orders, including restraining orders and protection orders, (‘(a) an interim order; (b) a restraining order; (Technical Officer) a tenancy order; or (Social Care Officer) an occupancy order.’) or applications for divorce because of GBV. They introduce clients to the range of orders available and provide legal advice about other options open to them within the justice system.

TECHNICAL OFFICER explained that they also have the emergency shelters for those in imminent danger. A counsellor does a risk assessment and screens the client for eligibility for admission [to the shelters]. The [shelters] are primarily for those whose lives are in danger because of physical violence, threats to kill or sexual violence, especially for women and children who [need to be] removed from their homes. While [police] investigations are going on, a child can be removed from their home environment if necessary. While in the shelter they also receive other services. The shelters are in undisclosed locations for security – for the protection of clients and the BGBVC staff. Clients are admitted for a maximum of 3 months while BGBVC work around a discharge plan for ensuring their security once they leave the shelter. Shelter clients are mostly referred by the police and social workers, and BGBVC works with [these agencies] on a sustainable plan for ensuring each client’s security beyond the shelter. If the intervention hasn’t been completed after 3 months, this work continues, and depending on the security issues in the case, a client can stay for a year or more. BGBVC’s shelters are only in Gaborone and Francistown, 2 in Gaborone and currently one in Francistown.

TECHNICAL OFFICER noted that they also have a clinic on this site [their head office], so only in Gaborone, and it's specifically for survivors of GBV. They provide it with the purpose of clinical care because some clients come in having sustained injuries, so they treat injuries here. Some of them are survivors of rape, so they provide post-rape care – HIV prevention, preventing unwanted pregnancy, through emergency contraceptive. They also provide STI [sexually transmitted infection] screening and treatment, as well as mixed method contraceptives.

SOCIAL CARE OFFICER explained that he would speak about communications. He noted that BGBVC deploys different strategies to achieve the goal of making sure that people are aware of GBV, its prevalence and its context. They use the media space and the social media space – all the networks that are available, including Facebook and LinkedIn – to talk about the organisation. They use the mainstream media – TV, radio and newspapers – to disseminate information about GBV and for social marketing of services that are available at the organisation, the ones

TECHNICAL OFFICER spoke about in addition to others that are available.

TECHNICAL OFFICER explained that they also do what they call mobile outreaches, where their community mobilisers accompany a nurse or clinical staff and counsellors to go to communities]. [Those in the community] will be screened for GBV, and if they're eligible, they get referred to the counsellors to access the service. Currently, BGBVC has a school-based programme called ‘Connect with Respect’ to address respect in schools, especially issues of bullying and GBV. Through this programme, they are trying to identify students who are somehow susceptible to, or who have been through, GBV situations, especially at home or at school. The idea is to take the students through different GBV topics, but before that, they are pre-assessed for GBV – that is, they’re given a set of questions to share what they understand about GBV and their experiences. This is done in Ghanzi and Francistown only, for 7 schools in total.

TECHNICAL OFFICER noted that BGBVC also do capacity-building exercises for frontline workers or those who are at the forefront of responding to and addressing GBV: nurses, police officers, social workers, teachers and the like. They also capacitate tribal leaders and take them through GBV education to enable them to identify GBV and how to better handle cases. These are the people who actually deal with very sensitive cases, and much as BGBVC is aware of traditional norms and perceptions, they need these people to align that to the current situation. They promote the organisation [BGBVC], its services and, by extension, other services that are available out there.

The FFM team asked whether BGBVC’s funding is mainly from the government and other donors. CEO noted the government. The FFM team asked this meant only the Botswana (BWA) government. CEO explained that they’ve had [funding from] the US government, the Finnish Government and the European Union, but currently it's mainly [the BWA government]. [They own one property, but] for the 2 shelters that they are renting, [funding comes from] a private company, a private sector partner.

The FFM team asked BGBVC to summarise the general position of women in BWA and how they are treated. CEO observed that BWA has a dual legal system [customary law and statutory (common) law. Customary law is at loggerheads with the legal provisions [of statutory law]. BWA has a relatively good legal framework to address the rights of women. However, there is still a need for a mindset change to appreciate these from the traditional and cultural perspectives. Culturally, women lack power compared to men so they are usually on the lower receiving end of anything that protects them. There have been efforts [to address this] for quite some time now. TECHNICAL OFFICER spoke just now about working with the chiefs, and the government is also making those efforts because they are the custodians of the culture. They are the custodians of what happens in the society, in the communities, to try and help them to change their mind[set] so that they can actually help to protect women. But where we sit, we have a problem in that women are still treated as a minority, or they are subservient to men generally because of cultural beliefs and practices. We can have beautiful rules like we have but when you get home, you don’t pull out a [legislative] act and say, ‘This is how you're supposed to treat women according to the law.’ At home, people mostly live according to the customary practices.

BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT MANAGER noted that there’s a culture of silence in BWA because all of these things happen, but some are not reported. That's one of the risks.

CEO observed that there's also the stigma that’s attached to GBV because it's always, ‘Why did he do this to you?’ If it goes there, it means it’s [the woman’s] fault. So there's a stigma that comes with intimate partner violence, with [being expected to] stay in a marriage that is dysfunctional. Leaving is associated with a number of things, including ‘being a failure’.

The FM team asked what types of GBV there are in Botswana. A listed sexual violence, physical violence, emotional violence and economic violence.

CEO added that this mostly happens within the domestic arena, so it's mostly domestic violence. There’s a high [prevalence] of domestic violence and intimate partner violence.

The FFM team asked how prevalent it is. A noted that according to a study conducted in 2018 [Botswana National Relationship Study], one in 3 women experience GBV and one in 5 men [experience GBV].

The FFM team asked whether the situation is still the same, or whether it is getting worse or better. BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT MANAGER noted that it’s a disadvantage that we don't have data. Usually, we rely on police data but GBV is mostly underreported. The situation might be higher. We’ve been getting a lot of reports of GBV, including femicide. There are frequent reports of GBV/femicide cases in media.

SOCIAL CARE OFFICER added that it’s mostly not reported [by victims] because of the fear of being exposed.

CEO explained that 2 studies were done, one in 2012 [The Gender Based Violence Indicators Study] and the other in 2018 [Botswana National Relationship Study]. They both indicated that reporting was very low. For instance, the 2018 study said that GBV reported [to the researchers] in the study was 7 times more than what was reported to the police. Now that the police have a special unit that deals with GBV (Gender and Child Protection Branch we want to believe that reporting has increased a lot. Police statistics show that the total number of reported cases to the police in 2024 only was 32,172. This is the total number of all cases of all types [of crime] reported to the police. Out of that, the total number of what the police say was recorded as GBV is 11,287. What is important is that this is just what is reported, and we know as we've been in communities that there are lots and lots of cases that don't get reported.

The FFM team asked whether that number showed how many cases were taken to court and prosecuted and convicted. CEO noted no, this was reports to the police. They categorised them by offence: murder, defilement, assault, common assault occasioning actual bodily harm, unlawful wounding, threat to kill, neglect of children. The FFM team asked whether that number was provided specifically to BGBVC, CEO explained that it is a national figure for 2023 to 2024, published by the police. BGBVC asked for it and the police shared it.

The FFM team asked whether the number of reported cases has changed over time. CEO observed that it’s difficult to know, but when you look at the trends, it shows that it’s increasing. CEO thought that what has increased is mostly the reporting. More people, as they become aware [of GBV], are starting to talk more than they used to. But what we can confidently say is that GBV is [at its] highest now.

The FFM team noted that CEO mentioned reporting had increased because of the police GBV unit that was set up. CEO observed that [reporting of GBV had] especially increased with that [unit’s creation], but also BGBVC are going out and explaining what GBV is [to communities]. When [BGBVC] started some years ago, people didn’t know, but even now there are still people that think that it's only GBV if it's physical. So [BGBVC] are trying to create awareness as to what GBV looks like, because a lot of times it can present itself in different ways. If my boyfriend or my husband keeps calling me every 30 minutes, I might interpret it as love, when it's actually control. So, they’re trying to get people to understand things like that.

The FFM team asked whether technology, maybe social media, is playing a role, too. SOCIAL CARE OFFICER noted that it is playing a role, especially in intimate relationships, especially ex-partners where one is trying to move away from the other and they don’t want to explicit details to be shared, whatever they shared during the relationship, either videos or pictures. [Their ex-partner says,] ‘It's either we get back together, or I share this material in public.’ It has happened a lot so that people end up living in this situation. SOCIAL CARE OFFICER explained that he had read that, and that some people actually end up committing suicide or contemplating it because of the shame.

The FFM team asked whether social media helps with reporting, because there’s more information available to people. Do people report more because they see more examples of the experiences of other people? SOCIAL CARE OFFICER confirmed that this was the case. CEO added that culturally, people stay [in relationships where there is GBV]. It's normal; some things have been normalised. As we create awareness through social media, through media, through workplace presentations, people begin to say, ‘Oh, so this is actually not normal.

Actually, there are people who are talking about it. So that means that I can also talk.’

The FFM team asked whether those who come to BGBVC for support are usually from rural or urban areas. TECHNICAL OFFICER observed that it’s a mixture of both, but mostly urban. B noted that BGBVC has centres in urban areas, and that this may also go to the fact that in urban areas, there’s more sensitisation and awareness of GBV.

SOCIAL CARE OFFICER thought that in urban areas, accessibility of resources also plays a part. In rural areas, they have no place to go [except for] the police. Some places don’t have social workers.

The FFM team summarised that we don't know if the numbers of cases are changing. We know that more cases are being reported. The FFM team then asked whether, in the cases that BGBVC sees as an organisation, the numbers for each year had changed. If they had, was that because promotion is better and people know you? How many people does BGBVC support, and is that only women, or men as well? CEO explained that they do support men.

B noted that BGBVC cannot confidently say cases are increasing. They know there is a clear suspicion that cases are increasing, but what they mostly see is that people are [bringing cases to light] because of greater awareness. They keep on seeing an increase in the number of cases they deal with every year, but they cannot confidently conclude that this is because there’s an increase in prevalence.

The FFM team asked whether there is a particular profile for the women they see – age, background or other particular factors they notice? B noted that there are certain patterns. [By age group], 15 to 19, 20 to 24, all the way up to around 34 – those are the ones most [commonly] abused based on who comes to BGBVC, and then a few in older age groups. B observed that it seemed the older a woman gets, the less likely it is she will be in a GBV [situation]. They are mostly young girls dating older men. The studies identified 2 types of perpetrator: young men, first of all, are the perpetrators when it comes to young girls, and then there’s the older men they date for money.

The FFM team asked whether Botswana has sufficient laws and policies to protect women from GBV. B noted that he would not use the word ‘adequate’, but whether they are sufficient or not, there are both policies and laws. How they are implemented is a different story. He noted that, to a certain extent, he appreciated that there is this law, policy, but then we don't see much of those being implemented.

SOCIAL CARE OFFICER added that in the Domestic Violence Act 2008, there are protection orders. There has been a debate in regard to that because [a woman was killed by her ex-partner at the University of Botswana recently even though] there was a restraining order [against him]. The question is, how effective are they at this point? That is where the problem lies. Some of these policies are there, the regulations are there, but the issue is [implementation].

B noted that another factor is public knowledge. There are laws, but ordinary people are pretty much unaware of what the law is. The study from 2018 showed that less than 53% of all men and women were aware of the Domestic Violence Act and the Penal Code. People don’t really know what laws there are.

The FFM team asked whether BGBVC as an organisation gets a lot of support from the state, from the police. A noted that they do get support from the police, and some cases are referred to BGBVC by the police themselves. We’re one of the 2 organisations in the country that have emergency shelters, so whenever they have a victim that needs protection from the perpetrator, they bring them to us.

TECHNICAL OFFICER noted that they also have referrals from government social workers.

The FFM team asked whether referrals can only be made in the cities where BGBVC has shelters. What happens when you’re outside of those locations?

TECHNICAL OFFICER noted that no, [the shelters] are available to women nationwide so they can get a referral from anywhere. WAR [Women Against Rape] in Maun has another shelter.

B observed that the police also refer them [people] for other services. We also refer [people] to the police, so the relationship is bidirectional, because there are women who come to us first before reporting to the police.

The FFM team summarised that it works both ways. The asked what the capacity is at the shelters. How many women can BGBVC accommodate? TECHNICAL OFFICER explained that they have 2 shelters in Gaborone. They can accommodate 16 to 18 people in one, and the other is for 8 people. The one in Francistown can also accommodate 16 to 18 people. There are many rooms inside that can accommodate families or individuals.

The FFM team asked whether that capacity is sufficient or is it difficult to cope with demand for shelters. B noted that they can never say they don’t need any more. The reality is, at this time, they need more shelters. However, the rationale behind it is the number [of people] coming to the shelter, and that is mostly dependent on sensitisation. There are still a lot of women out there who don’t know that there [are] shelters despite the awareness [-raising efforts]. There’s still more that needs to be done because there are women who still would rather stay in an abusive environment and risk their lives. However, we still need more shelters. The FFM team asked whether the shelters are usually at full capacity, B noted yes, because you can stay in a shelter for a maximum of 3 months, or more based on circumstances. In terms of new applications, there may not be too many at a time, but there will be those who are already in the shelter, so they are usually fully occupied.

The FFM team asked how easy is it to access BGBVC’s services, how easy for someone to walk in. BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT MANAGER thought that in terms of accessibility, one thing is that it’s free, which means everyone can just come and access their services. In terms of location, maybe that's where we need to [raise] a lot of awareness. We also wanted to commit to the demand for services offsite, without the clients coming to us. We utilise social media to market [our] services, and we work with other NGOs [non-governmental organisations], CSOs [civil society organisations] who link clients to our centres. But in terms of coverage, we're only in Gaborone, Ghanzi and Francistown. If we were doing really well, we would cover all areas in Botswana, but because of limited resources, we can’t.

The FFM team asked what would happen next if a victim of GBV knocked on the gate outside. BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT MANAGER asked whether this meant in terms of the process. The FFM team confirmed that it did. TECHNICAL OFFICER noted that the FFM team had seen their security [The FFM team were met by a security guard who checked and scanned their bags, and required them to sign-in, providing name and contact details] and explained that they had intensified their security because of [previous] cases [where problems occurred]. When [new clients] come here, the security officer checks them, and then they’re ushered to the clinic. Our approach is that we don’t know how critical it is for each of them to receive medical attention. So before they sit down with the counsellor, their [medical] vitals are taken, such as blood pressure. If they’re injured, they’re provided with medical attention. Then, with a counsellor, they do a screening to see whether they need the shelter or will be able to go home. If they need the shelter, they are transported to the shelter. It also depends on the counsellor because they will find out what’s important for the client. For example, if they want to report to the police, we ensure that they reach the police safely. If they want to see a legal adviser to work out their options, legal advisers can come and see them here.

The FFM team asked whether these legal advisers are from outside, not [in-house], and do they work pro bono? TECHNICAL OFFICER confirmed that the lawyers don’t work for them; they are volunteers who are called in when needed. Also, we have a Memorandum of Understanding [MoU] with Legal Aid Botswana, and they can provide legal support. The FFM team asked how easy it is for the victim to access that support. TECHNICAL OFFICER explained that now they have the MoU, they have a contact person. The FFM team asked whether the MoU is recent. TECHNICAL OFFICER noted that it was since the beginning of the year [2025].

The FFM team asked whether a woman always has to go to a shelter, or whether they can just come and get advice or medical care. And can they get advice over the phone? Does that happen too? TECHNICAL OFFICER confirmed yes. The FFM team asked if it’s correct that it’s only women in a really difficult situation or at risk (of harm) who go to the shelters. TECHNICAL OFFICER confirmed that yes, we have the shelters particularly for those [women], and then there are those who come here for [other] services. They can come here for trauma counselling, come every week and then go home.

The FFM team asked how many CSOs there are that provide the same kind of support as BGBVC. CEO explained that there are only 2 providing these services [shelter and other services]: BGBVC and another one in Maun. They do everything BGBVC does except they don’t have a medical clinic. The FFM team asked whether CEO was referring to WAR. CEO confirmed yes, and noted that there are organisations such as Men and Boys for Gender Equality and others where their mandate isn’t really around GBV, but they are doing their best to also try and create awareness in communities on ethics, law and HIV/AIDS. There’s BONELA, there's the Human Rights Centre, there’s also LEGABIBO. There are also Tebelopele wellness centres, (Source confirms Tebelopele wellness centres is still operating (as of 25 Sept 2025) however other sources suggests it stopped operating in February 2025, see: Gov't confirms Tebelopele nationwide shutdown:: Mmegi Online) their main mandate is HIV, but they've also integrated GBV. Even the Botswana Christian Health & AIDS Intervention Programme have integrated some community work on GBV. BGBVC and WAR are providing both prevention and response services, while the other organisations were mostly doing prevention (awareness creation) and referring to us for response.

The FFM team asked whether BGBVC works with these other NGOs. Do some of them refer cases to BGBVC? CEO explained that they work together but that their collaboration in activities has reduced a little bit over the years. But they are all members of the Botswana Council of NGOs, BOCONGO, and under BOCONGO they are together within what is called the ‘gender and human rights thematic group’. So they have conversations once in a while where they talk about what to do about what is happening. But, CEO thought, it hasn't been really as it used to be. There's also another organisation called Molao Matters. Their main mandate is legal support. They’re also a member of the gender and human rights thematic group. The FFM team asked where they were based. CEO noted that they are in Francistown, but they have people in Gaborone. They mostly work with lawyers who volunteer their services, so wherever there’s a lawyer who is willing, anywhere in the country, they become part of it.

The FFM team asked whether BGBVC gets a lot of referrals from NGOs. BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT MANAGER noted they would share the data. The FFM team asked whether the data breaks down the number of police referrals they receive. BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT MANAGER explained that when they do their data, they look at it a bit differently. The way they categorise them, the police stand alone as one of the stakeholders and then they have the other partners that they’re working with as another category. So yes, [the number of police referrals] is there.

The FFM team asked when the police GBV unit was created. CEO noted in 2021, the Gender and Child Protection Branch [was established]. The FFM team asked what this branch actually does. They had been told the branch provides guidance and training, but is there anything more than that? What’s their role and function? CEO explained that across the country, they have about 8 child-friendly police stations, or child-friendly centres, which are trying to facilitate children to go [to the police]. Whether that’s working is another story, but they have developed those, they have created those in 8 districts so far, in collaboration with UNICEF. In Gaborone, at least, we do refer to them if we have cases of children, and they also refer cases to us.

TECHNICAL OFFICER added that BGBVC has a good relationship with the child friendly centre and the police in general in Gaborone. They are usually responsive when we call for them.

The FFM team asked what the Gender and Child Protection Branch does, particularly regarding women in the GBV space. Had it made any difference? TECHNICAL OFFICER explained that the branch is responsible for GBV cases plus children. In the past, the reporting system was stigmatising. There were issues of confidentiality in receiving cases, which deterred people from taking action. Now they’ve allowed for confidentiality, and that’s one of the reasons GBV cases are now not reported in the normal setting of the police station. The 8 branches have a separate space for GBV cases. They mostly hire psychologists, social workers and those who are trained to provide counselling as well. So, they’re not just dealing with cases; they can also provide counselling.

CEO added that there are social workers and psychologists.

The FFM team summarised that there is a separate space for handling gender and child cases, and there are social workers as well as police officers, so it’s a safe space to make your case. TECHNICAL OFFICER noted that special skills are needed to get information from a child. The reason why it’s child-friendly is that they’re cultivating that comfort for the child, so the police officers managing those branches don’t even wear uniforms. The FFM team asked whether the focus is mainly on children and less on women who have no children. Could a woman without a child go alone? TECHNICAL OFFICER confirmed that they could; it doesn’t matter.

The FFM team asked where the 8 districts are. CEO explained that she wasn’t sure about all of them but that she knew there’s Kasane, Ghanzi, Francistown and Gaborone.

The FFM team asked whether, besides these spaces to deal with GBV and childcare cases, the police had received training generally on gender sensitivity, for example. Had other things changed since 2021? Were things getting better with the police? What was BGBVC’s view on the processing of cases? CEO observed that the feedback they got from people is that, particularly generally on the police around GBV, there’s still a lot to be done. What the police have now done is that at the police college itself they have a module where they are trying to teach the police about GBV and sensitive reporting and such things. But BGBVC still gets people that come and say they went to the police, but they weren’t assisted or that this and that happened. [The police] should actually be sensitive and have a clear understanding of GBV. Recently, the police also attended online training on working with perpetrators [of GBV]. They attended in large numbers.

CEO added that BGBVC keeps on trying to go back to saying that we really need to do something. We need to record cases of people who say they went to the police and document that so that when we go to approach [the police], we go with evidence that this person came, this is what happened. The whole idea is to support them to be able to support victims and survivors. CEO noted that BGBVC is not looking for problems so that they can point a finger. It’s mostly about, how can we support you to support survivors when they come to you [the police]?

The FFM team noted that BGBVC had mentioned restraining orders and protection orders, which the FFM team thought the police get involved in. They asked whether the police arrest the perpetrators of GBV crimes. Are perpetrators prosecuted? Do BGBVC get involved in helping clients through this process? CEO noted that what they know is that the whole criminal justice system needs to do better. It’s not just the police, because it starts with the police but it goes to the Directorate of Public Prosecutions (DPP), it goes to the courts and then the prisons, because prisons have a different role. For them, it's when somebody has already been convicted, or when someone is waiting to go for trial.

CEO noted that she had heard a High Court judge speak at a crime prevention conference in March [2025], and that he said, ‘There is a need to do better as [a] criminal justice system,’ and, ‘We are not doing OK.’ At the end, he made recommendations and one was that we need to speed up cases.

CEO observed that following an upsurge of cases during Covid, the Chief Justice had announced that special GBV courts would be set up. CEO thought these had been set up, but that it hadn’t been possible to continue with them because they weren’t necessarily planned; they were just a response to what was happening [at that time]. CEO had received new information the week before the FFM interview [July 2025] confirming that these courts were no longer in existence, that they were tried but it was not happening again. CEO continued that the High Court judge [at the conference referred to above], when he spoke, had said cases of murder, for instance, if they reach his court, have been on the table somewhere between the police and the DPP for a minimum of 5 or 6 years. She noted that this means justice is delayed, and because of bail, the person could actually be out, not only walking the streets but threatening the survivor and her family. There are restraining orders, but they [perpetrators] don't care about restraining [orders].

The FFM asked for confirmation as to whether someone accused of murder might not be on remand but on bail. CEO confirmed yes, on bail. There are lots of people on bail for murder, and then they commit crimes again. Even when there are restraining orders, they break them. BGBVC knew ‘a whole lot of cases’ where a person hadn’t been arrested again for [violating] a restraining order. It’s a serious problem and it means that the victims, the survivors, their families are suffering and are not safe at all.

The FFM team asked whether, when GBV cases get to court, the courts are looking at them fairly. In the disposal of cases, are perpetrators found guilty? CEO noted that the [number] of disposal of cases is very low, so there’s a backlog. The FFM team asked whether that was because there are lots of cases so it’s taking a long time, or because the number of cases actually getting to court is low, meaning [cases] fall away [before trial] for various reasons. What’s going on from when a case is reported to the police to a decision by the courts? CEO noted that in the case where the woman was murdered at the University of Botswana [in June 2025], one of the things the magistrate said was that the police failed in their duty because the man was subject to a restraining order. He had defiled the woman’s daughter years ago. They had withdrawn the case but the woman had a restraining order against him. They had been to court that day, the same day that he murdered her. He followed her afterwards because he was given bail even though there was a restraining order. So [cases go through the criminal justice system], but another thing the High Court judge said – and this magistrate also – is that it's very important that when you bring a case [before the court], you bring the history. Where a person has repeatedly committed crimes, it cannot be [just] a single incident. CEO thought this showed that there is negligence – either negligence or a certain level of ignorance, but she suspected more likely negligence.

The FFM team asked whether this was negligence on the part of the police in gathering the evidence. CEO confirmed this, noting that the magistrate had been very frustrated – how had the restraining order been missed, and how could we find ourselves granting bail when we shouldn’t have, to someone who was already in our system? And then he leaves and goes and commits murder the same day.

The FFM team noted that all the sources they had spoken to had mentioned this case. It’s a sensational case but did BGBVC think it is representative of GBV cases and the criminal justice system? Does it express something about the criminal justice system that rings true, is that why everyone talks about it? CEO noted that it’s very recent, and very sensational because it's not like it's the only one. The week before, another woman had just been murdered, and that same week, a man had driven a truck into a house and killed a child of his ex-girlfriend. So maybe it's because of the sensitisation around the case, but there are other cases. The Kgomokasitwa case – the man was on bail and was supposed to go to court for defilement. He gave his own reasons, but basically he wanted to wipe out the whole family so there wouldn’t be a witness to the defilement. When it was about to go to court, he went and even looked for the police officer who was handling the case. He murdered 3 people, he threatened 2 and he set the house on fire, so now there are 6 counts against him for murder, attempted murder and arson. That says a lot about the justice system, particularly the police. When they go [into court], what do they present?

CEO added that BGBVC have their own case of a woman who was murdered here [at BGBVC in Gaborone]. It has not even made its way to court. It happened in May 2023. She was murdered by her husband in our office, our counselling room. The FFM team asked whether the man is on bail, CEO noted that he wasn’t given bail. He's still in prison. But just a few weeks later, a man murdered his wife and girlfriend and he was given bail. Security and safety of survivors is a big problem. BGBVC have bars on their windows and there are people where they need to say to their security guard, ‘Here's a picture. When this person comes, it's not safe.’

The FFM team asked what the responsibility of the police is and what is the responsibility of the DPP is in preparing cases for court. CEO explained that they both have a role, but the role of the police is to arrest and then do investigations and then they have to hand over to the DPP for the DPP to say with these investigations, ‘What evidence do we have and what can we take before the court?’ and so to cut off the investigation [if there is no evidence].

CEO added that as regards safety, there is an issue they are trying to address: it’s confrontation, which is traumatic to survivors. What they do – and CEO asked the police and they said this is part of their investigation – is that if [the victim has] reported the perpetrator and they are talking to him, they will call [her] even if he is there. [The victim has to] confront them – ‘Yes, you did it.’ There's ‘No, I didn't,’ ‘Yes [you did]’, that kind of thing, which is very traumatic. They're trying to improve it for the children to not have it face to face, maybe to do it but while the child is in a different room. But for adult survivors and victims, there’s still confrontation in front of the police. It's complicated because the police say if they don’t do that, they won’t have heard the other side of the story in the presence of the other person. But the other person who is being asked to come and confront [the alleged perpetrator] is obviously already traumatised. How are they going find courage in the presence of [the perpetrator]? It’s an issue mostly of processes, and we can only say what we see.

The FFM team noted that when the police created the GBV unit, the idea was to introduce changes to process – standard operating procedures and training programmes for the police - to be more gender-sensitive. Is that not something BGBVC has observed? CEO noted that the police have the gender units for children, and then in the police stations, they have what they call gender desk officers or gender-focal persons. If that gender-focal person is not there, that means any other police [officer will deal with the matter]. In the Domestic Violence Act there are provisions [to the effect that] when someone comes into report [a GBV case], they cannot be assisted in the community service centre [of the police station]. But a lot of people just come in and [report in front of everyone], and no effort is made.

CEO added that there's a lot that compromises the safety and the security of people who are experiencing GBV, coupled with the attitude of the community. When [GBV] cases are being discussed on social media, the moment a man says, ‘I killed her because I bought her a car,’ even if it's a lie, society starts supporting him [in comments on the post]. So how safe am I if I have experienced GBV and then I'm out there in the community and somebody says that they hit me or they attempted to murder me because I did something and everybody supports that? How safe am I if I have to be in the streets of Gaborone? That person has already presented [their version of events] and I probably don’t have the opportunity to present mine. Their story has already flown, so even if I give my side of the story, everybody has already believed theirs.

SOCIAL CARE OFFICER added that there’s a lot of support for perpetrators on social media. No one is going to speak for the victim.

CEO noted that ‘What’s the price tag of a relationship?’ is the question that no one’s going to answer.

The FFM team noted that the new government says it has a human rights focus, and the president is a former human rights lawyer. The FFM team noted that they had been told the previous day that the president was involved in litigation repealing the LGBT+ law. Are there signs the government is taking GBV violence (more) seriously and is looking to make improvements on GBV and justice generally? CEO thought that we are still to see but that the young Minister of Youth and Gender is making efforts with her team. The FFM team asked whether that is Ms [Lesego] Chombo. CEO confirmed yes, Miss Chombo, who is also a lawyer. What we need to see is the commitment at the higher level. We've had the speeches. Now we want to see the action and we are looking forward to the action. CEO thought that was all they could say.

LGBT+ people

The FFM team explained that they would like to ask about lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people). Would BGBVC be able to comment on this group? Was it within their knowledge? BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT MANAGER observed that they were not really informed, but that there are cases where LGBT+ survivors come [to BGBVC] and they provide services. B noted that he did not remember [any LGBT+ person coming to BGBVC]. CEO recalled a time when LGBT+ people needed clinical services because where they used to go was closed and they were affected by that situation. CEO noted that since last year, BGBVC’s clinic, their team had been going for drop-in -centres of some of the LGBTQI+ organisations to provide clinical services.

The FFM team asked whether, therefore, a member of the LGBT+ community who wants to access BGBVC’s services can do so. A confirmed that they can, and BGBVC can provide those services. SOCIAL CARE OFFICER noted that they wouldn’t know with some people whether they were LGBT+ or not. He thought they had probably assisted them a lot without knowing they are [LGBT+]. Nothing is specified on their national ID (SOGIE characteristics). A observed that they don’t disclose that.

BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT MANAGER noted that they have partnerships with organisations that specifically help [LGBT+ people] and are invited to go into their space, but their approach when they go there is just to provide services. [BGBVC] don’t get involved in advocacy.

The FFM team asked whether they had a general sense that things are changing for LGBT+ people. They noted that 4 or 5 years ago, the law banning same-sex sexual activity was struck down by the courts, although it’s still on the statute books. Had there been any changes socially since then? BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT MANAGER thought socially, there's still a lot of pushback. There’s a lot that needs to be done around education, because even if the laws are changed, the community needs education to understand. That’s where they need advocacy and education by organisations, to understand the dynamics around sexuality. [LGBT+ people] are far from being recognised as a community and really having their needs met. For example, some have had issues with changing [the gender marker on their] ID [cards]. Even if the law is maybe trying to progress, they are still challenges in terms of implementation. SOCIAL CARE OFFICER agreed that the LGBT+ community [encounter] pushback, but noted that there haven’t really been a lot of violent cases or such in comparison to other countries.

The FFM team asked whether, generally, then they don’t hear of beatings or killings. B confirmed that they don’t. There’s pushback on same sex [relationships], but people are not violent towards them. The other challenge now is that organisations supporting them have always been funded by USAID [United States Agency for International Development]. When [US President Donald] Trump came in, he stopped that, so that means a lot of things. A lot of [LGBT+ people] now don’t get services they used to get. In the future, there might be funding again. That might change. But it’s not where we are right now.

BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT MANAGER thought that’s where the danger is. They’re saying government facilities should be in a position to provide the same services as the NGOs that used to receive funding. Those NGOs cannot provide services without resources. Those communities [such as LGBT+ people] actually feel like they're left out. So in terms of [LGBT+ people] getting health services, especially those related to HIV and other things, they might have to opt to move out of the country, to go to a base where they feel like their rights are respected and they will be able to access all the things they need.

Ritual killings and other traditional practices

The FFM team asked whether ritual killing is something you hear about in BWA, or any other harmful traditional practices. B confirmed that you hear about it, there is that practice, but he noted that he couldn’t say how many cases there are. The FFM team asked whether they tend to be in rural areas, not in Gaborone or other urban centres. B confirmed that it’s not urban [centres]. SOCIAL CARE OFFICER thought it might not be that important. They’re actually [just] suspicions, so a person will disappear or not be found, and suspicion is generally directed towards someone, but it’s never substantiated.

The FFM team asked whether they come across female genital mutilation (FGM). CEO noted that it’s not a tradition that’s documented. It’s not a traditional practice in BWA. Maybe up north, maybe some communities, but even if it was there, she thought it had been lost, or that maybe we don't know. The FFM team noted that a source had mentioned the Kalanga [tribe] as (maybe) practising FGM near the border with Zimbabwe. CEO noted yes, maybe.

Annex I - Interview with Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs

Date 11 July 2025
LocationMinistry of Youth and Gender Affairs (MYGA), Gaborone
Attendees 6 MYGA senior officials; 3 officials from HO

Women and gender-based violence

Officials explained that they would provide the FFM team with a general overview of gender-based violence (GBV):

First of all, we've got data in terms of studies on GBV in Botswana (BWA), the type that is prevalent and even the gravity that obtains in the country. The 2012 study [The gender based violence indicators study – Botswana] that we did indicated that 67% of women have suffered some form of violence [at least] once in their lifetime, and then 44% of the men admitted to having perpetrated gender based violence at some point in their [life]time. That was just the initial/preliminary study to determine if there is indeed gender-based violence in the country.

The second study that we did, which is the [2018] national relationship study, [looked] at both men and women as perpetrators and survivors of GBV. That study indicated that 37% of women have suffered some form of violence in their lifetime, and 21% of men also indicated that they have suffered some form of violence. The study further revealed that the most prevalent form of [gender-based] violence is between intimate partners. The type of violence that women suffer varies from economic to sexual to physical. The [type] that prevails amongst men is emotional abuse, and it's mostly from unpalatable language that's used on men.

We didn't just end there. We also went into finding perceptions, perceptions in terms of how women and men should relate [at a] household level. There were varying positions. For example, there were questions around who should make final decisions on utilisation [of] or expending household income. There were some females who'd say it should be the men. There were men who were saying it should be joint or it should be the female.

After the 2012 study, we then decided [to come up with] a strategy to address GBV. Those documents we can readily share. We then adopted a GBV strategy, which was a 5-year strategy. That strategy was looking at prevention, protection, and care and support, trying to holistically address GBV. Also after the 2012 study, we wanted to address perceptions, which are mostly culturally based. In 2012, we started engaging our traditional leaders, the dikgosi, because we believe they are fundamental to addressing issues of GBV, particularly as they also play a mediation role. So 2012, we engaged them; 2015, they developed their action plan in terms of how they are going to deal with gender-based violence. That's the one part.

The second layer of that is that we developed a training manual for the same leaders because they are very close to the people, and also some tools that they can use to track gender-based violence cases within their communities. There has also been engagement with civil society organisations, who are critical [in addressing] gender-based violence, in [recognition] of the fact that they reside in communities.

The third layer again was also to train the faith-based sector. Every religion has its own sacred text and we had also realised that sometimes they are gender-biased. So we trained the faith leaders, and I would say all religions in Botswana have been reached. That exercise continues, of course, with the civil society organisations [CSOs]. Beyond that, we also acknowledge the CSOs who are capacitated regularly on GBV, and we also track the emerging complications around gender-based violence and we have dialogues around those and how we can actually adjust our programmes to address those specific cases.

I should also mention that from the study, GBV manifestations differ per locality. What would obtain in the North would not obtain in the South because of the diversity of the groups. So our programming is community-specific because it targets a particular community based on the issues that prevail in their communities.

Beyond that came the issue of speeding up the hearing of GBV cases in terms of prosecution. [During] Covid, specialised courts that dealt with GBV were established to speed up the GBV cases, and also to get them moving there has been some training for magistrates to actually equip them with the skills to be able to address gender-based violence cases. Let me also quickly point out that [in] 2019, the government also undertook a Violence Against Children Survey (VACS) that specifically focused on violence against children. Under the Botswana Police Service, there’s a Gender and Child Protection Branch it was set up in April 2021 after the two Studies to facilitate friendly GBV service in the Police facilities. which has developed facilities that are child-friendly where children can report their cases and where they can actually sit during a court hearing – that is, they can sit in the comfort of a facility that is tailor-made for children.

Beyond that, the government has also established oversight institutions. We have the National Children's Council, which provides oversight over children's matters. Then we have the National Gender Commission, which looks broadly at gender issues in the country, including GBV. Above that, we also have a high-level structure, the Inter-Ministerial Committee on GBV, which is now, I would loosely say, a sub-cabinet committee because it comprises of 8 ministers, and that body is chaired by the minister responsible for youth and gender affairs. Then we have civil society. That provides shelters where there's a need to house victims. And broadly, that is our response to gender-based violence.

Officials added that there are also District Gender Committees, which are responsible for coordinating the gender response at district level. There has been keen interest [in this]: [some] districts have cascaded it to village gender committees. Also, with the Children’s Council, there are District Child Protection Committees. These work hand in hand, but they also report to the district's Development Committee, which is the highest coordinating structure at district level.

Officials noted the 2018 National Relationship Study indicated that 37% women and 21% men had suffered some form of violence and that 0ver 90% of children who grew up in a violent environment are more likely to be victims or perpetrators of GBV.

Officials observed that, to expand on that, there has been engagement with the wives of chiefs, the Bahumagadi, who are also leaders, so that they also participate in the GBV response. The Former First Lady also had a programme around addressing GBV where she has engaged with different community leaders. The targeting of the programme considered the results of the surveys mentioned [above] plus statistics from the police, so that the interventions were specific to communities that presented a high prevalence of rape.

Officials noted that this was the background to how GBV is being dealt with. With the number of cases rising, the ministry, and the government, are intentional on stepping up prevention as well as a response to GBV. They are currently working on [introducing] one-stop service centres, which will have all of the service providers in one place. [This means that] any victim or survivor can just make one report and then everybody will do what needs to be done to ensure convenience and really make sure that they are protected.

Officials added that users of the Domestic Violence Act [2008] have pointed to a number of gaps in the act. We are currently [working on] a GBV to keep closing the gaps to ensure that people are safe and that perpetrators are adequately dealt with. The other gap we have identified is that when restraining orders are issued, enforcement can be problematic because [the woman] who has applied for the restraining order is the one who has to sound the alarm when the perpetrator is within her radius. If he [, the perpetrator, approaches] unnoticed, that is dangerous. So we see the need to start using technology and modernising our services for effectiveness.

Officials continued that, generally, government doesn't tolerate [ineffectiveness]. In the past 2 or 3 years, a number of laws were passed aimed at protecting [people from GBV] and dealing with perpetrators. The Bail Act was amended to ensure that if a perpetrator applies for bail, the survivor should have a say before the decision is taken as to whether or not bail is granted. The FFM team asked whether the Bail Act was enacted last year [2024], A confirmed that it was. She noted that as well as amendments to the Penal Code, there is the Sexual Offences Registry Act [2021]. The government has really been proactive in trying to address this problem and we continue to find ways of dealing effectively with it.

Officials explained that they work together with civil society, and that right now civil society is advocating for GBV to be declared a national crisis so that it is dealt with as an emergency. Consultations are still ongoing. BWA once had a disaster in relation to HIV/AIDS. That's the kind of approach that is being advocated for. So we can say GBV is a concern in this country, but measures are in place to tackle it.

The FFM team noted that A mentioned amendments to the Penal Code. D explained that the Penal Code has been revised. The age of consent [was raised from 16 to 18]. At the Police Stations, GBV cases are heard by trained personnel at secluded offices designated for such to ensure protection and privacy of the victim. During Court sessions, rape cases are heard in camera. A lot of [legislative] changes have been made [in relation to] GBV. D thought that although changes such as [the enactment of] the Sexual Offenders Registry Act and even the Abolition of Marital Power Act [2004] [which granted equal legal capacity to both spouses] had contributed [to improvements], it was [if] the more laws were put in place, the more GBV cases had been increasing. Also, as GBV increases, the financial situation is going down. This is what we’re facing.

Officials added that whereas [the offence of] rape initially focused on women as victims, [the law had been changed to recognise that] men, too, could be victims of rape.

Another aspect [of the legislative changes] was the one Officials was talking about in terms of [the] age [of consent] now being aligned to other instruments such as the Children's Act [2009]. We [now] say a child is anybody up to the age of 18 years [old], which harmonises those [laws]. To sum up, this continuous review of laws also tries to harmonise them and also looks at international instruments that we are party to and those that we continue to become party to. The FFM team asked whether harmonising meant making gender equal or consistent across men and women. Officials explained that harmonisation means, for example, if one act contravenes what you want to put forth as a measure to address a certain issue, then you have to make sure that they are aligned such that they are not in conflict.

The FFM team noted that A mentioned a GBV bill. Had that actually got as far as Parliament or was it just an idea? Officials explained that they had sent a memo to seek Cabinet authorisation to start drafting the law, so that there can be just one law that people can refer to when they deal with [GBV] cases. When they use the Domestic Violence Act, they're all over the place.

The FFM team asked whether the sex offenders list was still a bill rather than an act. Officials explained that there is an act [Sexual Offenders Registry Act, 2021] which is yet to be operationalised, but it has been assented into law. A thought the debate had been that the police are the ones to implement it, and the police say they would rely on judgments from the courts [in order to flag a sex offender’s conviction for a particular offence]. Officials thought they were still trying to work out an end-to-end system that could facilitate that. The FFM team asked whether that meant [a system to] link up all the data in the cases. A confirmed that it did. The FFM team asked to confirm that this is now the law, A confirmed this.

The FFM team noted that A had mentioned a series of strategies and programmes going back to 2011 and 2012 onwards. Had these been recently updated? With the new government, had there been new strategies and new programmes? Had the 5-year strategy been rolled over, and was there any update to that? Officials explained that they were currently reviewing the gender policy and that they had recently appointed a consultant. There is the gender strategy and the World Bank is helping with that. We are very alert to ensure that we keep up with the unfolding situation. Another thing we are looking into is coming up with a gender equality bill because some of these things are really emanating from stereotypes. So there’s a need to intensify education and change norms that may be harmful so that increasingly everybody, starting from a young age – formation – should just understand that women have all equal opportunities in life. That way, we feel respect and recognition that no one is entitled to end anyone's life or harm anyone. The FFM team asked whether that was essence the bill under consultation. A noted yes, adding that there’s been a lot of consultation in this country. There’s mounting pressure to say even the constitution needs to be reviewed to entrench gender equality as a fundamental human right. It’s a growing thing, it will not happen overnight, but we hope to change the mindset, change the norms and stereotypes, working together with [traditional and religious leaders], with everybody, so that we can all be in sync. Officials noted that she understood GBV is not peculiar to Botswana; even in Europe they are experiencing a rise in cases.

The FFM team noted that Botswana had recently made submissions and had discussions with the UN Committee on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women. Were there recommendations and suggestions they were accepting and taking forward? Officials noted that Following Botswana’s appearance before the Committee, the Government has been issued with a list of recommendations by the Committee. Expectation is that these should be implemented to improve the status of women. Since these were recently received, we are yet to internalise them and plan for their implementation.

The FFM team noted that on data, the Ministry had referred to the 2012 Gender Links study and the 2018 relationship study. Had there been any updated research, or was any updated research on GBV planned? Officials noted that they hadn’t done any new study, but that there were systems [for checking] occurrence. We have data coming from civil society organisations. We have data coming from shelters and then we also have crime statistics from Statistics Botswana. So in the interim, those are our reference. The FFM team asked what data civil society was providing, Officials explained that it was the cases they had dealt with. For example, people don't always report to the authorities, but they report to different organisations. The Ministry receives a few walk- in GBV clients who are often referred to Service Providers based on their needs. These include District Commissioners, Counsellors, the Police, Legal AID and Shelters. So you will have, for example, the Ministry of Local Government and Traditional Affairs because that's where social workers are and those mostly deal with children's matters, plus other civil society organisations that deal with children's matters, so they will have statistics of the cases they handle. It could be per week, it could be per month, per quarter. The Shelters also receive walk-in clients who report their cases. The Social Workers at the Shelters assess them to determine whether they can be referred to appropriate service providers or whether they need to be housed for their protection. The Shelters can also assist clients to apply for a Restraining Order where their life is at risk. And then we also have the CSOs. Those are the people that would share data in terms of the cases they have dealt with and [documented].

The FFM team asked how many CSOs were working in the gender field. Officials thought several and that they're doing different work, focusing on different areas. Most CSOs will be providing counselling. They will also be raising awareness [about] GBV. Then there are those that are actually providing shelter, and there are 2 of those, one in Maun called Women Against Rape, and Botswana Gender-Based Violence Prevention and Support Centre [BGBVC], which has shelters in Francistown and Gaborone. [BGBVC] also has other offices like Ghanzi where they are just providing services like other NGOs, raising awareness on GBV and [providing] counselling. There also faith-based organisations that are also providing the same, raising awareness and counselling, and may refer cases to the police.There are a lot of referrals, and people even go to the health sector, the Ministry of Health, those that need counselling, but those also who need care, medical care if they have sustained injuries. There's a lot of referrals between social workers, the police and the civil society organisations. You find that most of the work that is done is on raising awareness and then counselling, but there is really a need for more shelters. That's why [A] was talking about a one-stop centre, because we’ve found that this is a critical need to make sure that people who need shelters can be provided within their own district, not far. Right now, we have 3 [shelters] and it's really limited.

Officials noted that they had had entities such as USAID [United States Agency for International Development] supporting civil society, but now that kind of financial support was drying up. If any [support] was available in the UK, they would be very grateful, civil society is doing sterling work.

Officials explained that, also, when it comes to financing for CSOs for gender equality, many times when [international] development partners send out calls for proposals, a country like BWA is excluded because it's a middle income country. Now, with the high cases of GBV and the financial situation the country is experiencing, we are saying, ‘Look at Botswana differently.’ Officials added that Botswana Police Service is aware of GBV that affects persons with disabilities and they have trained officers that deal with such cases. However, we note that there are still gaps in terms of specifics looking at the particular disability of an individual, but it’s an issue that they are very much alive to.

The FFM team noted that the Ministry officials had mentioned programmes at the district and village level. Were all of these programmes educational? D explained that mostly there are CSOs in different districts, but we also have gender offices and the Ministry of Local Government and Traditional Affairs, where we have social workers, and also the Ministry of Health. They also raise awareness on GBV. So really we have stakeholders in collaboration with the faith-based organisations, with the traditional leaders, the dikgosi, that have been trained on GBV. They're also doing something because they have an extra plan that they’re implementing. At the village level, you’ll find it’s more about awareness raising.

The FFM team summarised that there's a wide range of law and of programmes to support women and prevent violence against women and children, including various CSOs. The FFM team continued, what would happen in practice with protection? Can a woman get protection from the authorities when there are lots of reported cases? In the criminal justice process, would a woman who had experienced GBV get protection from the police and disposal of her case in the courts? Did the Ministry officials have any comments on that and on the efficacy or efficiency of that process, too? Officials noted that since Covid [2020 to 2022] there had been a directive from the Chief Justice to all magistrates to prioritise GBV cases, so that is the attitude. In Botswana, all cases start at Magistrate level and are elevated to the High Court based on their gravity such as murder or where an individual appeals the decision of the Magistrate Court, hence the Directive was to the Magistrates, who are more spread in the country than the High Court. Maybe here and there, there could be slippages, but they know that such cases need to be prioritised. The FFM team noted that one source they had spoken to had suggested that that was true during Covid, but that this focus on GBV case with specialised courts did not continue. Officials observed that it is continuing. The FFM team asked whether there are specialised courts or whether it’s just a prioritisation amongst the judges. Officials explained that special courts doesn’t mean the facility, it doesn’t mean a building where GBV cases are heard because there are mobile courts that move to where the cases are. They are specialised courts in terms of prioritising. But by travelling, they [ensure] that hearings are done where they are closer to the people. Furthermore, many times, GBV cases are heard after [usual work] hours or at weekends.

Officials added that there's always room for improvement and that she didn’t want to say everything is perfect, but a lot is being done. Officials observed that, [on the subject of] protection, what they have noticed is that because GBV happens mostly between intimate partners, [a woman] could report [her partner] and be given a protection order [restraining order], but because of their intimacy and the dynamics of their relationship, they could still violate the protection order. For example, if I'm given a restraining order [against the male partner], then because of the manner in which we relate, I can choose to still have contact with him despite that order. In reported cases, we have noticed that [women who have reported a male partner] can choose to drop the charges and the prosecution cannot continue in their absence. It’s just one of the gaps we have realised, and it's mostly women who choose to drop the cases for various reasons. Some women drop cases at the police [station] thereby preventing them to continue with prosecution. This has been a major concern and efforts to educate and support women to stand for their rights continue.

Officials explained that the police attitude is that they don’t allow any dropping of cases [brought by women against male partners/perpetrators], but even though the police refuse to drop the case, when it goes forward to the magistrates’ court, [the victim] can just choose [to drop the case]. I was the witness so I can just choose not to participate. The FFM team asked whether, in saying it’s the police attitude, Officials meant it’s their process, their protocol, not to drop cases. Officials confirmed this. She added that it’s a complex situation [between the couple]. If the man is bringing the bread home and he [beats] me to a pulp, my kids still need to eat and I go kneeling [before him] and say, ‘Give them bread.’ That’s part of that thing [relationship]. So they mistreat women.

The FFM team observed that the issue is therefore not only how to protect women but also how to support them. Officials thought it was a vicious circle and a complex issue because there's also societal pressure [in that] when you have reported your partner or husband, you have pressures from both [the woman’s and man’s] families. So sometimes we are dealing with that, but also economic pressures, as [Officials] say. Even if you have got a court order that says the man should be paying for the house and [you] can stay there, the man will stop paying rent and the landlord will chase you out because of the economic dependency of women, who are sometimes not working. Officials thought that it’s sometimes easy to put the legal systems [in place] to address this, but when it comes to [the] social [situation], that’s another issue.

The FFM team asked whether, if women are forced back into a situation where they are at risk, there is scope to provide the support they need in some fashion, such as shelters. If shelters are temporary, as the FFM team understood them to be, how could somebody who may be vulnerable be supported? Officials thought there were several aspects to it, [the first being] that shelters themselves have training in terms of trying to equip [women] with skills to undertake income-generating activities – culinary, sewing, knitting, etc. And then there’s a social inquiry report which goes to the ministers responsible for social services, who say this person needs to at least to be enrolled [with social services] because of their inability to be employed at a point in time. So that is now at a bigger level. There are those measures. The FFM team asked whether this meant an assessment undertaken by social workers in shelters as to the direction in which the issue should go. Officials confirmed this.

Following discussions about LGBT+ people (see below), the FFM team asked further questions on GBV. The FFM team noted that every source they had spoken with had mentioned a particular case 2 weeks ago [June 2025], in which a woman was murdered at the University of Botswana by her ex-partner, who had a restraining order against him. The FFM wondered about the significance of this case. Is it simply because it was recent and sensational? Is it the circumstances and is there anything representative about it, anything beyond being horrible and tragic? Are people reading into it that there’s a failing system generally? Officials noted that a colleague of hers made a comment that when you’re intimate, things get complicated. One of the Officials recalled that the day that incident happened, she happened to have a meeting with the Deputy Commissioner of Police, and he said that there was a lot more to it, that it’s not just something that happened that day. There would have been a lot of history. The FFM team asked whether that history indicated a failure on the part of the police. Officials thought not exactly the police. The FFM team asked if it was somebody else, Officials noted that the intimate relationship often influences the action to be taken by the victim and that this is why awareness building is very important. The woman should know that you have to take care of yourself. I shouldn't allow him to keep coming [back] when I want him.

The FFM team noted that there was also mention of a restraining order in the University of Botswana case and that, according to a newspaper article (Weekend Post, June 2025) the FFM team had read, the magistrate in that case was critical of the police. Officials observed that the magistrate was not happy, and what was especially mentioned was that she was not aware that previously the individual had a restraining order against him when he was asking for bail, because that could have been one of the determining factors. That showed a lapse.

Officials added that the reason why the Bail Act was adopted last year [2024] was because there was an outcry from the public that people who are released on bail tend to re-offend, particularly for GBV where they have threatened to kill. Then they are arraigned, and they will eventually be released on bail and go on to commit the offence. [The University of Botswana case] was a test case where the Bail Act was applied to the individual.

Officials noted that what we also see in that case is that [the murder was committed] in a workplace and some people witnessed it first hand. That now says there's a need for protection while in the workplace and even to capacitate individuals on how to deal with that. We have very small efforts in terms of self-defence skills. It's still at the initial stage, but those are things that we can actually build onto. There was also the religious aspect of the same case, which says you can have somebody being ordained, maybe to the highest office within a religious organisation, but they are still amenable to [committing this kind of crime]. The FFM team asked whether it was correct that the perpetrator in the University of Botswana case was a priest/pastor. Officials confirmed this. It now goes to the University of Botswana to say they need to introspect as well. Also, the write-ups [of the case indicate] that there are still some societal pressures and traditional expectations in terms of economic relationships between [couples]. There’s a lot that we are learning from that incident.

The FFM team asked whether this kind of case is very common. Officials noted that when you come to BWA, you'll find that at any one point in time, there's a particular case that society is obsessed with, and it's still fresh in their mind. Officials had realized this over time. There was a case where a woman was actually killed at the BGBVC shelter Office in Gaborone in 2023, so if you were to come at that point in time, the case that [everyone] would have told you about was that case. There was another incident that happened in Kopong, but Officials thought this and [the Gaborone case mentioned above] were too close [for the Kopong case to generate much attention]. There was the Ramotswa case where somebody was killed and then there's this one [the University of Botswana case].
