Officials thought that if you come and interview people, there's something that is still fresh in their minds and it's really disturbing. D thought that [each time], within a few months, another case will come and [become] the one people will talk about.

Officials noted that people were saying about [the University of Botswana case] that the lady was 10 years younger than the man. She was an executive assistant and they said he was a security guard. People had said they were not operating at the same level.

The FFM team summarised regarding the Bail Act that the act was introduced, it tightens the criteria on which you release somebody but there's no case law to determine how it's going to be applied. Is that right? Is there a test case? Officials confirmed this and noted that. The Bail Act was adopted as a response to issues of concern from citizens. It was enacted last year. Ordinarily, we would want to see implementation like [Officials] highlighted earlier on about the Sexual Offenders Registry, but we still want to have it implemented. So, we would be following and as we say, there was one test case where the individual [applied] for bail and they were denied bail on the basis of the provisions within the Bail Act. So that person remains in custody, probably because they are seen as a danger to the individual. When you adopt a law, you need to have a case to test [the] effectiveness of the law. It has been tested and proven to work. But not every lawyer is happy with that because they say the principle is that a person is deemed innocent until proven guilty. We are however hopeful that we will witness more cases where the Act is applied in favour of victims/survivors.

LGBT+ people

Officials provided an overview of the position of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people). I think we became alive to the [LGBT+] community around 2011, 2012 during the HIV/AIDS era. There was a study that was done in terms of men having sex with men [MSM]. That was the basis of engaging in this dialogue and I think that's when we generally became alive to the issue; that was the initial phase. From that time, the advocacy has been that they should be given services [without discrimination]. A lot of work had to be done especially with the health workers to [educate them] such that their responsibilities are to treat and nothing else, and not consider other issues beyond just treatment. And then as time progressed, other populations also enrolled into the [programmes for] MSM. (MSM refers only to male having sex with males. However, services are provided to the LGBTQI+ without discrimination, under the universal treatment programme. Botswana provides universal treatment through the public healthcare system, which aims to give all citizens access to necessary healthcare services without financial hardship. This includes Anti-Retroviral Therapy (ART).) The programmes are designed for key populations such as male having sex with males (MSM) and these include treatment. Health practitioners in this case are expected to treat the patient as they present and not discriminate them or ask them questions not related to the case they are presenting.

So we had lesbians and [trans people] and other populations enrolling. As it is now, we have an institution [CSO] called BONELA, which advocates for human rights, and currently there are advocacies around non-discrimination of the [LGBT+] community and their inclusion in programming. Beyond that, there was an issue in terms of [the] registration [of LGBT+ organisations] some time back – I think 4 years [ago] or so – but that government acceded [to the case to allow LGBT+ organisations to be registered CSOs]. [LEGABIBO] They are an organisation that is currently registered.

We also note that there's some level of abuse that happens within that community. It’s within, which is ‘intra’, and then it's also a bit outside, in terms of where they believe they are sometimes discriminated [against], so we are [aware of those issues]. But we cannot say it's something that is as extensive as the general GBV that happens in the wider community, because even with the police statistics we don't have so much reported cases of discrimination and violence against LGBT+ people]. We are cognisant of the fact that they might not be comfortable to report, but the police are fully aware of that community. That’s how far I can go in terms of the [LGBT+] community.

Officials added that the constitution of Botswana prohibits any form of discrimination based on sex so the [LGBT+] community have access to services. Just like him, just like me, there is no law discriminating against them. Officials thought that a few years ago, there was a case lost in which the [LGBT+] community challenged a section of the Penal Code which they found offensive [the sections 164, 165 and 167 which criminalised same-sex sex]. The matter went as far as the Court of Appeal and the judgment handed down aligned with the Constitution to say that the section of the Penal Code was unconstitutional and it was struck off. So [although] people keep saying that we still have this [sections of the Penal Code], no, the judgment dealt with that. So, if they receive any mistreatment, like a man can mistreat a woman, they can go press charges.

The FFM team summarised: the government position is neutral with regard to LGBT+ people - they're just people; they're entitled to services. The FFM team noted that they had heard that maybe where there is discrimination, it may be on an individual basis. For example, if an LGBT+ person seeks healthcare, sometimes a healthcare worker brings their own views and values to that interaction. The healthcare service, as an organisation, is not saying you should not provide medical care to LGBT+ people. If they face a problem from other Batswana, [LGBT+ people] can go to the police. Officials confirmed this. The FFM asked whether the MYGA were aware, as a government, of reporting of this happening. Officials observed that it's just like a young person who complains that when they go to the clinic, [a healthcare worker there] is elderly and they start asking the young person why they need sex at this early age, and [the young person] is aggrieved. But it's not like they're being discriminated against; it’s just that that person has a horrible attitude. The data from the police is not disaggregated by sexual orientation but by male and female only. There might be need to consider other variable such as the LGBTQI+ community and others.

The Constitution of Botswana prohibits discrimination including on the basis of sex. The LGBTQI+ community is therefore at liberty to report their grievance to the police. This is derived from the fact that they pursued their recognition and registration of their Organisation through the High Court which ruled in their favour.

The FFM team asked whether the ministry officials knew the [size] of the LGBT+ population in the country. Noting that it was a very interesting question, Officials observed that [only] if everybody was out of the closet could they reliably [provide figures]. The FFM team asked whether there are openly gay people [in BWA]. MYGA Officials confirmed that there are. She added that they express themselves and demand rights. They are free to advocate for their rights if they think they are not represented in any way. Officials noted that they were aware that in some countries there will be mob attacks on [LGBT+ people]. We don't have that. We mingle with [LGBT+ people], we mix with them. Officials observed that we have [LGBT+] relatives. Officials explained that they have also started dialogues because [some people feel uneasy about LGBT+ people]. [These dialogues take place] even in rural communities to talk about [LGBT+ people] and that we need to embrace them because it could be somebody's child. Of course, it’s something that we are not used to, so we [prepare people] by saying that it could even be [someone] in your household. So when you look at another person, think about what if it was your own child or your own nephew or niece. We have those conversations.

The FFM team asked whether having those discussions is part of the gender and youth programming. Officials confirmed this. The FFM team asked whether, as a ministry, they have any other policies or programmes in place to raise awareness of LGBT+ people. C noted that they do because there are different aspects of gender. One of them, for example, will be programming for men. We also programme for emerging issues, which [LGBT+] is a part of, so we have that public engagement. The FFM team asked whether this meant there was no separate programme for LGBT+, and that LGBT+ was part of other programmes for wider society. Officials confirmed this. Officials added that she thought it was one of the areas where civil society really needs financial assistance because the Americans had been big in supporting that [but now USAID funding has been withdrawn]. Officials observed that [LGBT+ people] have also benefitted [from international or BW government funding], like LEGABIBO, which is the registered [LGBT+ NGO] and has been supported by the National AIDS & Health Promotion Agency (NAHPA) which provides helps through the HIV programmes. There are some programmes targeting LGBTQI+ community, some of which are implemented by Government (NAHPA)and others by the CSOs. Most of the financial support to CSOs was from Donors/Partners such as USAID.

Officials noted the other part we need to highlight is that when we do our national consultations on any matter, whether it's policy, whether it's programming, they always touch other constituents that we reach out to. Officials noted that the FFM team talked earlier about CEDAW, [LGBT+ organisations] were part of the initial drafting of the country reports. They were also able to submit a shadow report, so they are free to express themselves.

Officials noted that there are still people who are grappling with the concept of ‘I look at you, I see a male but you tell me you're a female inside of you.’ This is not aligned to the culture or tradition, so we do have pockets of strongly held belief. The government is expected to be reviewing the situation. Officials thought such robust discussions would be intended to help everybody appreciate that we may not be the same, but it's just one society.

The FFM team asked whether the constitutional review is ongoing. Officials explained that it had yet to start. We are waiting with anticipation because the new administration emphasises that it is human rights based.

Annex J - Interview with Love Botswana

Date 14 July 2025
LocationLove Botswana, Life Centre, Maun
AttendeesCommunity Outreach and Development Social Worker and member of the District Gender Committee of Ngamiland Communications, media and public relations officer Village Church Coordinator and member of the District Gender Committee of Ngamiland (joined interview 40 minutes after start) 3 HO officials

Women and gender-based violence (GBV)

The FFM team asked Love Botswana (LB) to briefly summarise their work. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER explained that LB is one of the largest faith-based organisations in Botswana. It houses many programmes. They have Metro World Child, which teaches life skills to primary school children, and Reach for Life which cater to the youth, accompanied with a Bible teaching topics for youth.

Based on an American partnership, they offer various other things for youth. COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker explained that Operation Blessing is a programme where they help the elderly, the disadvantaged, the vulnerable. They do assessments for them.

The FFM team asked whether that includes women. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that it does – the disabled, the vulnerable, the dejected and women from the villages with different needs. They provide them with clothing, food and weekly check-ins. They go to these people every Friday and do an assessment with a social worker, and there are follow-up weekly visits. As another effort to take them from being dependent to [self-sufficient], they help them make small-scale businesses or other ways of generating revenue for themselves.

The FFM team asked whether, if LB sees any problems, they also refer people to government agencies or the police. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER and COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker confirmed that they do. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker added that this is to other services outside.

The FFM team asked whether they provide legal advice, COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker explained that most of the time, for legal advice, they do referrals [to other organisations].

The FFM team explained that their question revolves mostly around women. Can LB summarise their experiences – primarily in the work they do around Maun – of women’s position in Botswana (BWA), and GBV? The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER first noted an additional programme called Babelegi Mmogo [formerly run by Love Botswana] from 2013. In BWA there is a community culture, so everything is done in the community. Like the saying ‘It takes a village’, normally the community helps people take care of each other, and that’s the meaning of Babelegi Mmogo. It was a programme that helped vulnerable teens, girls and women, often where there were cases of rape, abuse, GBV as well. That was one of the ways Love Botswana responded to the GBV that was prevalent in their surroundings.

The FFM team asked when the programme ran from and to. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker explained it had already stopped running when he joined Love Botswana more than 2 years ago, so it had been a few years.

The FFM team asked for confirmation that neither COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker nor the COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER had been involved in Babelegi Mmogo. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that they had not.

The FFM asked what the position of women is in BWA and the frequency of GBV. COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL officer noted that with GBV, the people most affected are women. The violence they currently face is mostly domestic violence, physical violence and sexual violence.

COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER added: emotional violence.

COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL officer agreed that there is emotional violence but thought that was most relevant on the male side. Mostly, women are affected by sexual and physical violence. The FFM team asked whether the emotional violence which affects men is perpetrated by women. COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL officer confirmed that it is. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that most women are affected by sexual and physical violence, so that is many women. We think it’s a pandemic at this point, something that’s being talked about nationwide, and to the point where we have brought it forward to the Minister of Youth and Gender Affairs. It’s been sparking a lot of conversation. It’s women that are primarily affected or are victims of GBV, but there’s a small section of men, too. For men, it’s not as physical against them; it’s more emotional abuse.

The FFM team asked whether the law generally, and government measures, are effective at stopping GBV. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought no, adding that laws are relaxed in a way, for GBV. COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL officer thought some of the rules are able to mostly protect women and children, but that the effectiveness of the law is poor. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER commented that the law is very ‘cool’, very lacklustre. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that even if the culprit gets apprehended, they are released back to the community again and they repeat the same thing.

The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that there had been a problem recently – or in fact as an ongoing culture – where the victim would go and report the case, then the police would oversee a meeting between the victim and the perpetrator and say that it was a family matter. Instead of filing a report, they [the police] mostly try to resolve it, so it tends to die out before it becomes a case. The rare times when the victim insists that they want to take it further, the perpetrator does get apprehended and there’s a trial, and then after a few months they get released on bail or get early release and they go out and perpetrate the same thing. In most cases, this leads to the death of victims. The FFM team asked whether Love Botswana had numbers of cases or any sense of scale. Did they know how many cases of GBV against women get resolved locally and how many are dealt with by the police and result in arrests? COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that they did not have those statistics. WAR [Women Against Rape] might have better statistics because they focus on that. LB has statistics for what they manage, the number of clients they deal with. The FFM team asked whether Love Botswana could share those statistics. COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker confirmed that they could and noted that in the last quarter, they had 13 women coming for counselling sessions. The FFM team asked whether they had numbers over time, maybe for the last 2 or 3 years, to show if there had been any change. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker thought the problem with the numbers is that most of them [GBV victims] come and then they don't go to the police station, so it's hard for us to track them. But the previous quarter, we had 18, so it’s dropped.

The FFM team asked whether these figures represented women in the country who had been abused. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that they deal with different [types of] cases and that there were 213 cases overall. They explained that 213 was the total number of cases for the quarter, not just GBV – for example, neglect.

The FFM team summarised that LB handled 213 cases generally [in the previous quarter] [of which] 13 are GBV only or where the GBV is clear. [Inaudible]. The FFM team asked how LB came across these cases. COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker explained that it is through self-referrals; [people] come to [LB’s] offices. LB hasn’t had agency referrals. Most of them are just members of the community or self-referrals. The FFM team asked whether LB had ever referred individuals to the police. COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that they had referred them to WAR, but then once they end up in WAR, most of the women go to the police.

The FFM team noted that COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker mentioned it is typically women who experience problems with GBV. The FFM team asked who the main perpetrators usually are. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted lovers, partners, husbands, also parents. The FFM team asked if women face GBV from strangers also? COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that they do have those cases, that they exist but they are rare. The FFM team asked whether perpetrators were mostly community or family. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker thought community, stranger, or sexually assaulted and abandoned at the side of the road or killed. There are such cases, but they’re not referred to LB. It’s not safe for women after 7pm. It’s a very common thing to happen in BWA. The FFM team asked whether anyone had collected any numbers on this. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought no, or maybe WAR. The FFM team asked whether that would be numbers for the whole of Botswana. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that it would.

The FFM team noted that COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER described a process whereby a woman who faces problems may approach the police and they encourage mediation. Might that also happen via the process of the customary courts? COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that they [the police have] tried to mediate because they've been very prepared in mediation. But with the recent outcomes they’ve seen with GBV, the danger that women are facing, they’ve come from mediation to questioning whether what they typically do in this situation is working, and they’ve tried to move more towards action. The FFM team asked whether the COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER was talking about the police and the GBV desks. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that she was. She thought [the desks] started about 3 or 4 months ago.

The FFM team asked whether it was in Maun that they started then. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought no, in Botswana.

The FFM team explained that they had been told that the GBV unit was created in April 2021, so 4 years earlier. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that it was created in 2021 but thought it was not operational then. The FFM team explained that the police had mentioned 2021. Asked whether in practice, in Maun, it had only been in the last 3 months, COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed yes, it was only the last 3 months.

The FFM team asked whether they thought the change in approach was making a difference. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought it was making a difference but very slowly because the culture has already been instilled around GBV. [The change] is not immediate even once the laws are in place.

The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL officer noted that when most of these cases get to the courts, the victims withdraw the cases and there’s no way you can stop them. The FFM team asked why women withdraw the cases. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought it might be because of coercion at home or because of mediation, or they get scared about leaving people [ or because the majority of perpetrators are breadwinners]. It’s a number of factors. Asked whether this was [based on] her impression, COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that it was.

The FFM team summarised that women face problems, mediation happens often, the police encourage mediation, but maybe their approach is changing with the GBV unit and the police saying, ‘We'll move to take this forward.’ The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER agreed.

The FFM team noted that when women do pursue a case, the perpetrator is arrested and goes to trial. Had LB heard of any cases going to trial? The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that there’s a department in Botswana that has to reassess the cases for the police, to see if they can go forward to court for a trial.

The FFM team asked whether this is the Director of Public Prosecutions, the DPP. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker confirmed it is. The FFM team asked whether this is done by the DPP, not by the police. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker explained that the police handle the case and gather the evidence and then they refer the case to the DPP. The DPP has to fact-check before referring it to court. Sometimes cases don’t have enough evidence.

The FFM team asked what happens – are these cases sometimes not taken forward? The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker confirmed that they are sometimes not, noting that sometimes with a case, they [the victims?] don't care to wait, they don’t care enough.

The FFM team asked whether it is just part of the investigatory / judicial process, that sometimes there isn't enough evidence. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker agreed [that this happens].

The FFM team asked whether they were suggesting that this represents a problem, that the system isn’t working. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought they didn’t have much more to say on that. It was just something they’d noted.

The FFM team asked whether, if the evidence is not strong, that says something about how the police conduct the investigation. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker thought yes, noting that they write up the investigation, [and sometimes the people involved in the investigation processes do not provide the police with enough information] but when it goes to the DPP, the cases carry little or no weight to proceed to the courts and end up taking a long time to be resolved.

The FFM team asked whether this was COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker’s impression or whether he knew actual places where this has happened or that he had learned about when talking to people or reading newspapers. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker explained that it’s something he hears from the DPP in the District Gender Committee. The FFM team asked whether they mentioned the quality of the evidence and what they had told members in these committee meetings.

The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that they talk about the processes and procedures and all of the challenges they’re facing taking cases to trial. It's because they don't have enough evidence from the police.

The FFM team noted that LB mentioned in cases where people are arrested and detained, they are released again. The FFM team asked what their experience was of that. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that if the police haven’t gathered enough evidence, the person can be released.

The FFM team noted that LB mentioned people then reoffend. Had they seen evidence or examples of that? The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that there’s a high number [of such cases] but that the FFM team would need to check that with Statistics Botswana. It’s a high number, like a pandemic of re-perpetrating. The FFM team explained that they asked a lot about data, but no one had been able to provide data even though they had mentioned this to a lot of people. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that in Botswana, it’s hard to get data. It’s not posted.

The FFM asked what Love Botswana’s experience had been locally, noting that without data, it might be their perception, but was it their impression that there’s a high perpetration [of GBV] rate in Maun and Ngamiland? The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought yes. Two women were killed in [Maun]. Last month, there were 2 women that were killed by GBV, one with a gun and one with a knife. There was one in Thito. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought she died. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought in Maun in the last 6 months, there had therefore been about 5 cases that she was aware of.

The FFM team asked how the COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER knew these cases were GBV. Do the police document that, or is it because it said in the newspaper that the partner or somebody killed a woman because she’s a woman? The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER explained that it was because the police said it was a crime referred to as passion killing here in Botswana.

The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER recalled that a man had killed his ex-girlfriend’s kids. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL officer noted that he did not remember that, but that there was someone in the military. The FFM team asked whether this was a case in the south of BWA in which a soldier had killed a family [which another source had mentioned]. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL officer explained that it was not; it was in the Northwest district, in Maun. A male had killed his girlfriend. The FFM team asked whether COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL officer knew if the perpetrators in these cases had been arrested. COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker explained that the majority of them, once they commit the crime, also take their own lives.

The FFM team asked whether this meant the perpetrators kill themselves before they’ve been arrested. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed this, explaining that they kill their partner or their wife and then they kill themselves.

The FFM team noted that these sounded like bad cases but how representative are they of GBV generally. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that in most cases where women experience GBV beyond sexual harassment, the men tend to kill themselves. Only a few are arrested. The FFM team asked whether that was country-wide or just in the Maun area. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought country-wide but suggested asking the police for statistics.

The FFM team asked what GBV means to the interviewees. What types are there? The FFM team noted that the interviewees had talked about a wide range: psychological, sexual, fiscal, and ranging in seriousness from name-calling through to murder. Did they think all of this was taking place? Were there any other forms besides this going on? The FFM team noted that some sources they had spoken with had suggested that there are traditional ritual killings. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER agreed that there are ritual practices that go on in the country as well. There is another type of GBV: financial, where the husband withholds the main source of income they depend on. As for ritualistic killings, that would be more a matter of perception. There are not many of those.

The FFM team asked whether LB does not come across those. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that they do not. COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that, according to the news, it happened a lot before the new government. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER added that this was around 2021. The FFM team asked whether there had been any cases in this area that they had been aware of. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER and the COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL officer noted there had not. The FFM team noted that when they had asked this question in this and other interviews with sources, there seemed to be no well-founded specific example. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought it was more hearsay and that the FFM team would be getting more speculation and rumours than fact-based examples.

The FFM team noted that if you travel out of Maun, you see some very small villages and hamlets. They asked whether there is a variation in the experience of women in the smaller villages and settlements compared to Maun itself. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that there’s the perception that it varies. A lot of cases are from the rural settlements. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL officer also thought cases were from rural areas. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that [women in rural areas] don’t have access to where they could report, for instance, WAR. The first responders aren’t close to them. There’s also a community mindset, so if someone’s abused by their uncle or their parents, they don’t disclose it.

The FFM team asked whether there would be a government representative there. Are there police posts in these small settlements? The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that there are police and social workers.

The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that while there are some areas where it’s possible to find police posts, some areas are very remote with nothing. So the way organisations work is to go there to make them aware of GBV.

The FFM team asked whether it would be an accurate description to say that there is more information and services in Maun and maybe the bigger settlements, but as you get to smaller places, it's basically harder for women to access support. COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker and COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that this was accurate.

The FFM team asked what the age range is of the women or children most affected by gender-based violence. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that she did not have any statistics on that so it would mostly be her perception.

The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that it is mostly youth that is affected. Sixty percent of the population is youth. The FFM team asked what age youth is exactly. The COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that youth is 18 to 35. The FFM team asked whether this meant most people in BWA are young and therefore most people affected by GBV are young. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed this. The FFM team asked if there were any other reasons. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that most cases are ‘passion killings’, adding that they couldn’t really speak for the ones where it’s a family member. The FFM team asked whether it could be the parents. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that it could.

[VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR entered.]

The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR gave his name and explained that he is part of LB. He [lives] in Maun and works for the Village Church, doing village outreach, which he co-ordinates. He also helps with Love Botswana projects and is working with a project called [name missing] and overseeing the Village Church. The FFM team asked what the Village Church is and what it does. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR explained that it’s a mission and its mandate is to reach out with the gospel in the community. There was a church in Maun for 20 years but – VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR thought in 2023 – that church closed. Now they have 7 branches in BWA and 3 in Namibia, so a total of 10.

The FFM team asked whether it’s simply a church bringing Christianity to the people. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed this.

The FFM team explained that they are looking at GBV in BWA, what happens, what perceptions, what support there is for the women who’ve experienced it. They asked if that is something the VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR could speak about. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR (VCC) thought yes, it’s a subject he knows.

The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER explained that the [VCC] also serves on the [District] Gender Committee, and because of his outreach work, he comes into contact with GBV in the villages. He’s also a pastor.

The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that his background means he has been coming into contact with GBV for more than 20 years.

The FFM team explained that they had been asking about how common GBV is, whether women can get support and protection from the police and NGOs, whether that protection is effective, and the perpetrator is arrested and goes on to trial. These are issues the team wanted to understand better. Did the VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR have any observations on that? The VCC noted that the [church] mission had been seeing this issue for more than 20 years. The government is trying with systems, but GBV is embedded within the culture, so it is normal. It's not an easy thing to deal with even when the systems are there. The VCC explained that his interpretation is that the government has tried a lot of interventions on gender whereby women are sent to the Police Department. There is a unit that deals with GBV, and then also within our district, there are the government officers that are dealing with GBV. Within the communities, there are also NGOs that are dealing with GBV. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR thought that [in Maun] there is only one house [shelter] where survivors can go for support. So, systems are there, but the response from the community is very slow. The FFM team asked whether the house referred to was the WAR shelter. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed this.

The FFM team asked what NGOs there are that support women around GBV in Maun. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that there are several organisations dealing with the issue of GBV, and their approach to GBV is one of prevention, which means you get messaging around GBV. There is an organisation called BOCAIP [Botswana Christian AIDS Intervention Programme, also known as Botswana Christian Health & AIDS Intervention Programme (BOCHAIP)] dealing with issues around GBV, giving out messages. We also have BONELA. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR thought BONELA also deals with issues around GBV, and they’re dealing with it from a legal perspective, sending out legal organisations, dealing with barriers in the areas where people have no access to services. There’s also an organisation called Silence Kills, dealing with GBV for the lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people) community. They also come into contact with GBV cases. [LB] also provides support there. LB also helps as an organisation, Just Hope [Foundation] too. They’re dealing with counselling for people experiencing issues around GBV. The FFM team asked whether BOCAIP operates nationwide or just in the Maun area. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that BOCAIP is a national organisation, an NGO, and it has an office in Maun. BONELA also has an office here. Just Hope is a national organisation that has an office in Maun.

The FFM team noted that the government is trying to put systems in place including the district GBV committee. Did the VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR get the impression that these systems are making a difference, that it’s an issue but that things are improving in terms of support and protection? The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR thought things were improving in terms of legislation, but that the impact is not there. Even cases that are reported, that are legitimate, will stay [in the criminal justice system] for a very long time without being judged. There are a lot of loopholes within the system itself. If there are 10 cases of rape, only one case will have been tried in 3 months and the other cases will still be under investigation or information will still be missing. The system is there, but because this system is not utilised fully. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted he did not know whether this is because of the people that are dealing with the system or the community that utilise the system – there are a lot of gaps within the system itself. Even when legitimate cases are admitted to the system, the system is just not dealing with them to bring out the result. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR thought the system was not working fairly.

The FFM team asked the VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR what he meant by ‘fair’ - fair in terms of getting justice, or just that it takes a long time? The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted ‘fairly’ because of the system itself. There are a lot of human justifications as to whether this case passes or is still staying here, so on the basis of that, it's not fair, like giving out an exam, because it is based on whether the people dealing with it pass these cases. The FFM team asked whether it requires people in the system to take the case forward. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed that it does. The FFM team asked whether that doesn’t always happen, and whether it takes a long time sometimes. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed both points. The FFM team asked VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR about the basis for the assessment he’d provided – was it based on him seeing cases go through the system or based on reading newspapers? Where did he get this information from? The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that he gets this information from referring cases to the system and that the system takes a long time. Also, he needs information because he sits on the District Gender Committee, where they see all the cases that are in the district. That is when they see all the cases within the district that are being brought forward within the system, but that only one case has been dealt with, so it's gone through.

The FFM team asked whether they see previous cases from all the departments [at the district gender committee]. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed yes, from all different departments, government departments, NGOs. They are part of [the district gender] committee where all the cases within the district are there. They also have to provide intervention if they see that there are a lot of instances in a particular area. They can say they are part of the driver for the system in the district. The FFM team checked that the district is Ngamiland. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed this.

The FFM team asked how many cases they see at the committee. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR explained that the general committee deals with different cases. From memory, he thought there were 5 cases brought into the system in the last quarter, from January to March [2025], but only one was being tried [in court]. The other cases lacked information and were still being investigated [by the police]. The FFM team asked if the individuals who committed the rapes had been arrested and detained. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted they had not. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER explained that they were out on bail. The FFM team asked whether they had been arrested but then released. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed that they had and noted that they were released on bail because that was within the law. He thought this was if they had been detained for over 14 days, and then after that, when the investigation had been done, [inaudible].

The FFM team asked whether one person was still under arrest and was going to trial. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed this.

The FFM team noted that they had heard the bail system was allowing people to be released quite easily, but that sources also had told them there was a new Bail Act in 2024, which has made the bail system stronger. Did LB know anything about that? The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that they had heard that, but that they hadn’t seen it at the community level. They hadn’t seen the strengthening of the system because the cases are there, the incidents are there. People don’t get it at the community level and survivors might not understand why this person isn’t being held in jail, but that is the law. The person can’t be kept in jail because they haven’t been found guilty. As service providers, they are still saying that even though the bail system has been strengthened, it is not actually serving the process.

The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR added that especially when you are a service provider, sometimes you get frustrated that we are making it very hard to bring out cases from the community with the evidence that the system requires – when this happens. There are so many pieces to it and you come all this way and all these people have been bailed and after maybe 6 months, only one is still detained. The FFM team asked, to give an idea of scale, how many people live in Ngamiland. The VCC thought that at the last census [in 2022], there were about 80,000. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that Maun is quite small.

The FFM team asked whether, other than rape, there are serious GBV cases that get reported to the committee, for example, physical violence or sexual violence that isn’t always rape, attacks, beating up. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR explained that the beating or sexual violence cases come through the police, within the police system. The only such cases that come to the committee are if there’s a sexual component where younger people are impregnated, so their first contact would be the hospital, but the hospital will treat them as a patient, not as a case. The committee says those are cases, but they are hard to follow up. The law doesn’t allow the hospital to report them. Also, for example, with emotional abuse, not all cases are reported. Some of the individuals who have been wronged will say that they have forgiven the person, and they are no longer interested in pursuing the case, so cases might be dropped.

The FFM team asked whether 5 rape cases is a typical number. Is it like that every quarter or does it vary? The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR explained that it varies, but they never go down, they always increase. He noted that the numbers they are seeing every quarter made him doubt [the effectiveness of] their interventions – either they are not programming well, or they are mischannelling their efforts. The FFM team asked if the population is growing. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed that it is – people want to come to Maun.

The FFM team asked whether the increase in case numbers might reflect the fact that there are more people. Are the numbers going up faster than the population is growing? VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR thought it was not that the population is growing that much, but the numbers of cases the committee are receiving every quarter are growing. The FFM team asked whether that could also be because of campaigning, so people have information about their rights or where to go to report. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR thought it might be because they realise now that this is GBV. [Previously,] they were expected to be quiet, but our message is for people to be free. He also thought that especially with the police, numbers had been missing within the police system. It had not been easy to access. The FFM team asked whether he meant in the past. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed that he did. Now they were seeing a lot of cases coming through the system.

The FFM team asked whether there is now more reporting to the police. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed that there is. The FFM team asked whether this means the police have improved how they handle these cases. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed this and noted that the improvement had resulted from the creation of the GBV unit, so that the people dealing with these cases are trained and know how to improve them. They are not yet at a place where they are sufficient, but they are at a place where they can handle cases and make referrals. The FFM team asked whether these referrals are to healthcare or social services, for example. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed that they are. The FFM team asked whether the police are better now at handling and gathering information about those cases. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed this.

The FFM team asked whether, in Maun, the police have a room where, if a woman comes in and says she has been assaulted, they can speak to her in private. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that it is still a challenge in that regard because, he thought, the unit is outside the police station, some distance away. It’s not always that you will find an appropriate person from the GBV unit in the main police station, only in their satellite office. When you go to the main police, what you will find are just general police and they may still investigate in front of everyone. The FFM team asked whether it is not possible for a victim to ask to be taken to the unit. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that it is not possible. [inaudible, source did not clarify]. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER explained that people come [to the main police station] without knowing about the [GBV] unit.

The FFM team asked whether the police do not make it clear what to do. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that when you go to the police, you find nice GBV billboards [outside the police station]. But the system itself within [the station], when you go there with a GBV case, is not quite a scandal but is nowhere near the way it should be even at a district level. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR explained that he thought the police representative at the Gender Committee shared with them that the police wanted the committee itself to do something about that. The FFM asked the VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR to clarify whether the police had actually said that they want help. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed that they had.

The FFM team noted that they had spoken to the police, and that the police said that if an officer from the GBV unit is not present, other police are trained in handling GBV cases sympathetically. They also said that when you go to the station to report GBV, they will take you to a separate area. Did the VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR agree with that? The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that there are some survivors of violence who will testify to that. But the majority of them would say that is not how it is. The improvement is not the standard way. But the police are doing their best with GBV cases. The FFM team asked whether the police’s attitude is that they’re willing to help. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that it is.

The FFM team asked whether the courts have GBV specialism when they handle these cases. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that on the Gender Committee, the DPP is among the representatives. They [the DPP] have to be trained on GBV. They will only apply the law that has to be applied to cases of GBV. But even hospitals need a faster response. You’ll find people who’ve experienced rape queuing with other people. What they’re trying to do at the district level is to have a phone campaign whereby you can speak to a particular person wherever, whenever there are failing cases about gender so that you can be treated with sensitivity.

The FFM team asked whether a woman who experiences a problem in a remote village can move to Maun, Francistown or Gaborone to avoid the problem. Can she move and make a life there? The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER asked whether this would be to relocate after the case. The FFM team clarified that it would be to escape and avoid harm. Would there be any barriers to moving and making a life? COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought relocation would be fairly easy depending on income and whether she’s able to move jobs. There’s a high level of unemployment, but COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought that in most cases, it would be very possible.

The FFM team asked whether a woman escaping from GBV would be able to get healthcare and a flat, somewhere to live. And would people not be bothered if a single woman moved? COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that there’s no stigma, and healthcare is free. They also have a temporary rescue centre for children aged 0 to 5. Where there’s been neglect or sexual abuse, the children are removed from their home and are sent to the centre while the case is before the courts. Cases can take a long time, so they do extended court orders. The FFM team asked whether the children would be in Ngamiland or taken outside the district. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER explained that they are taken to a secure rescue centre in Maun.

The FFM team asked whether, in general, people are accepting of single women households. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that women are. She added that it’s a norm. The FFM team noted that there are more women than men and asked about the reason for this. Was it because men migrate for work? COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought that maybe the birth statistics are such that more females have been born than males, but she didn’t think that in most cases men were migrating outside BWA. The FFM team asked whether there were just more women. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought there were.

The FFM team noted that earlier in the interview there had been discussion of the effectiveness of the criminal justice system – reporting a crime to the police, it being resolved, going to the courts. Was the same true for all rights? Could the criminal justice system be better overall? And is it getting better or worse? Is it more difficult for GBV, say, than any other criminal action – burglary, for example? COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that, based on her observation, less time and effort goes into GBV. Compared to common murder cases or theft, she thought GBV had less priority, although more of a spotlight had been shone on it now. The FFM team asked whether COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought, therefore, that the situation could change. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought it could.

The FFM team asked whether VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR and COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker shared this view. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that he did. He explained that with cases of GBV, the justice system is not responding as it should. In Maun, there is only the High Court, and it’s not handling most of the cases. There is a massive crisis, and the justice system is just not that responsive. For some time, they [the government] have wanted to improve the justice system. There were mobile courts, but they weren’t really the answer. The FFM team asked the VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR to confirm whether there are mobile courts. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed that there are but explained that he had never experienced one. He noted that mobile courts being implemented and showcasing the results that actually come from a mobile court, or from any initiative that they [the government] are trying, are not really coming out. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that as COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER mentioned, if there is a case where there is a theft of an animal, you will hear about it, or if there is just the suspicion of a stolen diamond, there will be a quick response. He recalled that some years back, there was an intervention where there were a lot of cases of livestock theft. When those kind of things happen, the justice system only transfers all its resources to that, but not to GBV, even though there is a GBV crisis.

The FFM team summarised that the police respond reasonably well and people get prosecuted, but GBV crimes are not treated with the same urgency. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR agreed, adding that women are neglected and GBV crimes are not treated the same [as other crimes]. The FFM team further summarised that this may be changing because of what Love Botswana had described earlier as a pandemic. Did they think this new, human rights focused government is going to change things or has started to change things? COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that it did position itself as a human rights forward government, with the president as a lawyer who strongly believes in human rights. One of the things he did when he came into government, to the presidency, was to restore the rights of some indigenous people. So it positioned itself as a human rights nation, but with the high GBV numbers, they separated GBV from the Ministry of Sports and Culture and made the Ministry of Sports and Culture and the Ministry of [Youth and Gender Affairs], so then it could tackle gender affairs. But the minister that is in place right now hasn’t put any policies in place yet to help with GBV. The FFM team asked whether this was Miss [Lesego] Chombo. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed this. In the beginning, the government wanted to position itself as [focused on] human rights, but the way it’s looking now, it's not mentioning which policy direction it will take. COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL worker noted that the Domestic Violence Act 2008 is outdated. A lot of policies in BWA are outdated, but we don’t know if they’re being reviewed.

The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought this was the problem and did not think the government had even talked about a review. The FFM team noted that they had talked to a lot of people and the suggestion was that there are discussions about a GBV bill. The COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that yes, 2 months ago they said that.

The FFM team noted that when they spoke to sources in Gaborone, they all talked about the case of the murder of a woman at the University of Botswana. Had LB heard about this case, and did they have any views on it? The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that the case had shattered him. As an activist, there seemed to be so little voice for issues around GBV. A woman getting a restraining order and something like that happens, that says a lot about our system and about how the government is assisting with that system. The court system and judges – are they sensitive to some of these cases? They are judging and issuing restraining orders, but they need to be able to read the room, be able to read the case. What is this case? What might this be about? We haven't brought in the element of psychology within our system when we are dealing with these issues. We bring in the law in these cases, but with GBV we’re dealing with deeper emotions, intense emotions, and that has to be brought out. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR added that there was also an incident here in Maun a long time ago. He thought the First Lady back then was assisting. She was in Maun talking about issues of GBV and a woman was murdered in a shelter. The FFM team asked whether that was a case some years ago, under a previous government. The VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed that it was. The FFM team asked whether she was a symbol of perhaps the state protection system not working so well, the VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that we are saying we’re protecting these people by giving them a restraining order, a shelter, but how do we now bring protection around all these interventions? A shelter cannot protect that person – when are we going to have security around all shelters? The government is not even looking at the profile of security systems. Not just with a piece of paper, not just with an order – we need to provide safety to these people. It’s about actually putting in some attention. The FFM team summarised that the law is quite strong, but it needs to be implemented by actually providing security. Was that what EW thought when he saw these cases? VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed that it was.

LGBT+ people

The FFM team asked what the experience was of the LGBT+ community – lesbian, gay, bisexual and trans people – in Maun and Botswana. Were LB aware of people who had been open about that in their conversation? COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER noted that it would be more their perception because they don’t deal with that, they don’t have programmes for that community. But under the previous government [which was in power from November 2019 to October 2024], in Gaborone and Maun they were more open, more public about it. The FFM asked whether the period she was referring to was since the last government. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER clarified that it was during the last years of the previous government. It was not so much a focus on their rights, but more just on them being there. It used to be a taboo, a secret, but now they have been more open.

The FFM team asked whether there have been Pride marches in Maun. COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER thought not.

The FFM team asked whether there have been in Gaborone, COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER confirmed that there have.

COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND DEVELOPMENT SOCIAL noted that these were organised by LEGABIBO.

VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR explained that for a very long time, LB has been around the [LGBT+] community, giving them services. ESS noted that since 2016, he personally had been working and interacting with organisations providing this community with services. He thought that in Maun there are 2 organisations providing services focusing on the LGBT community. These organisations also sit on the Gender Committee. There is also a Technical Advice Committee for HIV/AIDS, which is for organisations that are providing services around HIV/AIDS. These organisations also provide LGBT+ people with GBV intervention and health interventions. They go out in a bus at night and bring them access to the services. At some point they were providing them with specific condoms. So there has been a movement in Maun.

VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR recalled having attended meetings where the chief was effectively saying, ‘You don’t want to have anything to do with this topic.’ But over the years, from 2016 to now, VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR thought things had changed slowly and the chiefs were now more open. The FFM team asked whether this meant they were more receptive to discussion. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR confirmed this.

The FFM team summarised that there are NGOs helping specifically on LGBT+, and that is part of the wider gender NGO community. They help run support and access services. Had LB observed problems with arrest or LGBT+ people being harmed in some way? COMMUNICATIONS, MEDIA AND PUBLIC RELATIONS OFFICER asked whether this meant hate crimes. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR explained that he did not have access to the HIV/AIDS committee, but that those who sit on that committee hear of LGBT+ people not being treated fairly by the community and within households, so there are still those incidents. As organisations were dealing specifically with those people, he wondered if the message was really getting through. The FFM team asked whether ‘not treated fairly’ meant VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR had heard of cases of violence or abuse. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted that it’s sufficient. It’s soft violence. It’s gender-based and also HIV/AIDS.

The FFM team asked whether LGBT+ people were directly impacted by GBV or other violence. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR noted yes, there had been reports within the HIV/AIDS committee. The FFM team asked whether the HIV/AIDS committee is [different from] the Gender Committee. VILLAGE CHURCH COORDINATOR explained that they are 2 separate committees.

Annex K - Interview with Women Against Rape

Date 14 July 2025
LocationWomen Against Rape (WAR) office, Maun
Attendees Executive Director, WAR; 3 HO Officials

The FFM team asked EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR to summarise the work of WAR. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that WAR was founded in 1993 and registered as a trust in 1995. It was primarily to deal with rape cases as at the time, rape wasn't taken so seriously [under] Botswana law [at the time], and victims of rape were not getting support.

WAR started as a support group for victims of rape, then also started going into schools and teaching about violence and rape, and that if there were children in school who had experienced rape at home or elsewhere, they should report it so that they could be assisted. The organisation grew from just dealing with rape to now dealing with GBV in general. [WAR] started at this office [in Maun], and in 2005 built a shelter [ a prefabricated house was donated] donated by Debswana Orapa [diamond] Mine.

WAR’s vision is to have no violence in Ngamiland and Botswana as a whole. They are doing this by providing psychosocial support, which is counselling, and public education. They do a lot of public education on prevention [of GBV], including prevention of re-victimisation for those who have experienced violence. As for response, they provide services to those who have been affected, such as offering a shelter and offering support. Their first approach is to visit legal practitioners. They used to have their own legal practitioner but then because of funding they piloted [using] government [funded] legal aid. The pilot was successful and there is now a proper Legal Aid Act (2013). The government is renting space from WAR to run Legal Aid [through the Legal Aid Botswana (LAB)] from their office, which is useful because WAR’s clients just refer straight to the office.

In addition to psychosocial support, education and provision of the shelter, WAR does research. They have published a number of research papers on GBV and alcohol, and on children's understanding of sexual and reproductive health. This they did with Amplify Change, a British non-governmental organisation (NGO), and they have worked with the University of Rutgers in New Jersey on the publication of findings from their work in schools. They also work with the University of Botswana. Their partners in the work they do are mostly government. They work with the [Ministry of Youth and] Gender Affairs, social services, the dikgosi [traditional chiefs] and the police. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that the police should have been [the first group mentioned]. WAR is also in a network of NGOs as a member of NCONGO [Ngamiland Council of Non-Governmental Organisations] in Ngamiland and BOCONGO [Botswana Council of Non-Governmental Organisations] in Gaborone.

Currently, WAR’s main funding comes from government, [the Ministry of Youth and] Gender Affairs, but they have had funding from a variety of funders including Oak Foundation, Raising Voices in Uganda, Amplify Change, Canada Fund for Local Initiatives, Stephen Lewis Foundation and embassies like the British [High Commission]. They worked with the British [High Commission] during Covid, just a short project with Men and Boys for Gender Equality. They have an ongoing relationship with the French embassy, which puts up calls for proposals and WAR responds. Currently, they are running a project with the French embassy, the [US] embassy and the [US] Peace Corps Volunteers. So WAR has a variety of donors and partners.

The FFM team asked how many staff WAR has. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that they currently have 25 staff members as well as 3 volunteers – 2 German volunteers and one American – who they also work with. Just now, the government has stopped its volunteers, but the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought they would open this up again when they have volunteers, like an internship programme under which WAR applies to the government and is given interns. Of the last 3 interns WAR had, they ended up hiring one, who is now the shelter manager. Another one has finished his counselling internship training but because of a lack of funding they can't absorb him.

The FFM team asked whether WAR’s staff include medically trained staff and trained counsellors. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that all of their counsellors have done a Bachelors [degree in] Counselling or have done social work. The FFM team asked how many counsellors WAR has. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that there are 6 counsellors and the shelter manager also has a degree in social work. They don't have a clinical psychologist, so for clinical psychology they refer to Letsholathebe II Memorial Hospital, a referral hospital.

The FFM team asked whether WAR has only one shelter. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed this. She explained that the shelter could accommodate up to 20 people, but they limit it to 16. They went up to 16 during Covid, but the facility is not big enough to take 20 people because of the need for showers and [for] cooking – the kitchen is not so big. It's just a house. There is food and a bed and psychosocial support and everything that you get in a house. As well as the manager, there are 3 members of staff there who work on a rotational basis, so it's covered 24 hours. There's always a member of staff there and sheltered abused women and children, boys up to the age of 14years. WAR doesn’t know if that age limit will go down, but it's 14 for puberty, and before this age WAR considers that boys are not sexually active. Up until then, they can keep the boys with the girls, but once the boys are over 14, they can't take them in the shelter. Then either the boys are sent to SOS villages or social workers will find alternative housing for them.

The FFM team asked whether SOS is also an NGO. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it is an NGO, called SOS Villages. They are in Gaborone, Serowe, Francistown and somewhere else [according to the SOS website the organisation works in Francistown, Serowe and Tlokweng]. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought there were 4 such homes in Botswana. The FFM team asked whether SOS Villages is an international NGO, the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it is.

The FFM asked how long women can remain at the shelter. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that when WAR started the shelter, they said 3 months, but 3 months is just on paper. The women can stay up to maybe 6 months and then they leave. But the children can stay up to 2 years or even more. It depends on when the case gets concluded. Sometimes the adults will leave the shelter before the case is concluded because they have a life outside of the shelter and they feel this has been put on hold; it's been like they're now in prison when the men are out. The adults’ way of thinking is different from children’s and you can't hold an adult in a shelter. So adults can choose to say that they would prefer to be outside the shelter while they wait for the case to be concluded, whereas with children, because they are admitted with a court order and a social worker report, it's only the court that can remove the child from the shelter. If, for example, a child was placed in the shelter for a 6-month period initially but the case was still not concluded after 6 months, the social workers would go back to court and get another court order for WAR to do an extension, and then the social workers have to support WAR in looking after the child until then. If children in the shelter are of school age, WAR makes sure that they go to school and takes them to school and picks them up again.

The FFM team asked whether all the women and children in the shelter are involved in legal cases, in police investigations and court cases. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that the adults are. The adult cases can be where a woman runs away and goes to the police and says, ‘My husband, my partner, is beating me. I’m scared of going home. There's nobody to talk to. Please help me.’ And then the police, assessing the situation, feel maybe they don't have a car to find this person, or they have looked around but they can't find him. Then they will say, ‘Women Against Rape, can you hold on to this woman until we find the perpetrator? And once we’ve found that perpetrator and understood the situation, then we can take her out [of the shelter], or she will stay in if there is a case to be investigated.’ So women can come in while the police are doing an investigation. They can also come in when there is a court case going on where they need protection, sometimes because of a threat to kill. If someone threatens to kill you in Botswana, you can be taken into protection. And then the perpetrator will be in a cell or they look for him and then they go to the magistrates’ court to get a restraining order or something.

The FFM team asked whether, if a woman is threatened, the WAR shelter is the only one available for her to go to. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that in Maun, yes, the WAR shelter is the only one. There are only 3 shelters in Botswana: one in Gaborone, one in Francistown and the WAR shelter in Maun. The FFM team asked who operates the shelter in Francistown. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that it’s the Botswana Gender-Based Violence Prevention and Support Centre [BGBVC], and that they also operate the one in Gaborone.

The FFM team asked whether the WAR shelter caters for women only in the Maun area or whether they take women from further afield. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that they take women from all over the country. They had a case of a couple where the woman was abused so much that she needed to be taken out of Maun. They felt that the husband knew where the shelter was and was capable of coming to threaten WAR or threaten WAR and the shelter, which he did. But they negotiated with the women's shelter in Gaborone to send the woman to Gaborone. She was assisted in Gabs [Gaborone] and the man was here. Sometimes, [the women’s shelter in Gaborone] have cases where they feel the woman will be safer far away from the perpetrator. So they work together, they co-operate. The FFM team asked whether it's the stakeholders, the NGOs, who work together. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it is. Organisations that operate the shelters in Botswana, WAR and BGBVC.

The FFM team asked whether the location of the shelter in Maun is undisclosed and whether, as far as they can, WAR keeps it secret. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that they try but Botswana is so small that people end up knowing. Even clients, when they get out, say, ‘Oh, I was at a shelter,’ [and someone asks,] ‘Where is this?’ So what they do is try to keep it safe and secure. There’s a high boundary wall with barbed wire that [is electrified], and a motorised gate. The gates are always closed. In order for someone to go to the shelter, the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR has to tell the shelter in advance who is coming, so you can’t just knock and go in – they won't let you in. Even if the police need to collect a client, they have to get permission [to enter]. A member of staff from WAR has to inform the shelter that police officers will be driving such and such a car, so please bring the client. The FFM team asked for confirmation that WAR has no guard. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed this, explaining that it’s something they are looking at, but because of funding, they don't have a guard. They intend to have one, in addition to the other measures they have in place. Their offices have panic buttons in case somebody comes in and threatens them. But the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that if somebody was sitting here [pointing to one side of the desk] and she was sitting there [on opposite sides of her desk], it's a long way to go to that panic button. So security is always an issue.

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR recounted how an incident happened at the counselling centre in Gaborone (at BGBVC in around 2023) where the perpetrator agreed to come for a counselling session but ended up stabbing [his wife]. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that there was a security guard, there were panic buttons, there was everything, so sometimes you don't know what you could have done to prevent that. Security is always at the forefront of what WAR does.

The FFM team asked whether women can walk in to WAR’s office, and whether they contact the organisation by phone and other means. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that they have a toll-free number and the WAR number, which is an emergency number that women can send a message or a WhatsApp message to. Women can ask for a ‘call me back’ and the call is always with a counsellor or with EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR herself. They have to respond if a woman sends them an SMS [text message]. So women can contact WAR directly and at this centre [the WAR office], and that number is 24 hours. Toll free number is 0800 600 387 and the 24hr emergency number is +267 71 311 244. The toll-free number diverts to the emergency number if not answered immediately. The Executive Director and the Head of Counselling alternate in taking the emergency phone after hours and at weekends.

The FFM team asked whether WAR works closely with the police, social services and other NGOs in this space. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that they work with the mohumagadi [wives of traditional leaders], counsellors, S&CD government social workers and other NGOs’ social workers. They are all in a network. The police can call the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR after hours or call the WAR number after hours, and they are always available. The FFM team asked for clarification of S & DC (S&CD = Social and community development officers). The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that it is the government social workers – social and community development, or the department of social protection. The FFM team asked for confirmation that this is government. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it is.

The FFM team asked EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR what her sense is of the position of women, the prevalence of GBV and the ability of women to get protection in Botswana at this point in time. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that the past few months had been ‘really, really dire’. For example, that morning there had been another announcement that a woman around Francistown – EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought in Masunga – was hacked [to death] by her husband, who then hanged himself. The past few weeks there had been no week that passed by without a woman being killed at the hands of her lover. Gender-based violence against women in Botswana, it’s there, it’s quite rife today. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR did not think it was getting better because the numbers in Botswana are not going down. It has reached the point where she wakes up thinking, ‘What am I going to hear today?’ It's quite an issue, a serious issue.

The FFM team noted that they had spoken to sources in government and civil society and that it was quite hard to get data on numbers. Is that the case, that data is a big issue in Botswana? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that if she gave the FFM team her numbers, they would be much, much lower than what they would get from the police, and the police numbers would be much lower than what they would get from the hospital. Each stakeholder has their customers, has their numbers. People will go to the hospital and they know that the hospital will not go to the police. Those who go to the police are the ones who feel threatened that this person might kill them. But if they feel it's something that you can put a bandage on or look after, then they'll go to the hospital. Those who come here [to WAR], they also want WAR to take them through the system. So everyone gets their people. If you go to, say, faith-based organisations, they will get people who believe in God and want to be prayed for or pray for the perpetrator. So each one of us gets their own kind of people.

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that also, as a country, Botswana doesn’t have a central point where all this data can be entered, so that if she sees a person, Love Botswana sees them and the police see them, they don't count the person three times. They see that this person went there and there and there. Now she needs to go to the hospital or somewhere, but there is no central record.

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that WAR piloted a referral system in 2018, working with MEASURE Evaluation, a research organisation from the US, and the [now Ministry of Youth and] Gender Affairs. WAR was representing Gender Affairs, piloting the programme of the project. It was a referral system using a phone, and one of the supporters was Orange Botswana. Orange Botswana gave data for the phones and WAR were coordinating the whole project, supported by MEASURE Evaluation. WAR piloted in Maun and Shorobe, a small place [just outside of Maun] and then Stepping Stones International in Mochudi piloted Mochudi and Artesia. It was a big village and a smaller village, to see how it all worked.
