The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that through the application, when a client came to WAR, they would log them into the system and then say, ‘Go to the police.’ Then they would press ‘Referral to the police’ and their contact person, the focal person at the police, would receive the message. WAR would say to the client, ‘Go to the police and see so-and-so,’ and read the name. When the client arrived, they could say which officer they were looking for and be directed to their office. The officer would already know their story and could explain the next steps. If the officer said they needed to go to hospital, they could send a referral – plus what WAR did, what the police did – to the hospital where they could then see a social worker or a doctor or a nurse. On arrival, the clinic would already know their story, so it cut down on the client having to repeat themselves, and WAR could make sure that they went because their job as the co-ordinators of that project was to follow the client. They could see if the police had received the client so they could follow up if necessary, and they could see when the client had been to all the services they needed so they knew when the referral was complete. As part of the project, WAR used to have monthly meetings with all the stakeholders to review the cases and see, ‘Why did this case stop here? Why did this one go there?’

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that the project was for a year, and then they wrote a report, but the government didn't have funding to continue with it. MEASURE Evaluation wrote a report and WAR reported to the government, which knew that it was working, but the project has been shelved. Hopefully, it will be resuscitated.

The FFM team summarised that there isn't a comprehensive data set about numbers of gender-based violence cases. It's piecemeal. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR agreed, adding that there's no central database for government to be able to say, ‘This is the extent [of the problem].’ The only figures are the 2018 relationship study and the 2012 [Gender Based Violence Indicators Study - Botswana] survey. The 2012 survey said 67% of women had been abused, and then they said, ‘Let's redo this.’ Then the numbers were released, and then it came to 37%, which is like almost what the global picture looks like. But those figures are only for the survey that was done. There is no daily administrative collection from different service providers, and no central point where the data is collected.

The FFM team asked if WAR has data on how many people have come to them, say, in the last 4 years. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that they have. The FFM team asked if this data includes the types of GBV experienced. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted yes, all the types of GBV and all presentations, whether somebody comes here and they’re depressed, they’re unemployed, because WAR counsels everyone. They don't just say they take GBV; anybody who needs counselling comes. The FFM team asked whether EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR could share the numbers for GBV, and for the last several years. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that she could. The FFM team asked whether EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR could say there has been a pattern over 4 or 5 years. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that they had looked but there is no pattern. Some years it goes up, then it comes down, then it goes up, then it comes down.

The FFM team noted that they had spoken to many sources and that they had said there is more awareness now about GBV. Did EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR think the numbers are high because a lot of people are reporting it? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought the numbers are high because people are now aware that GBV is wrong. It's like talking about child marriages. In Botswana, if you search anywhere, you'll find that Botswana doesn't have child marriages because we're not reporting child marriages, we are not even defining them as child marriages. It's just that this child is living with this man. But there's no certificate that says they're married, so technically they're not married because the chief didn't marry them. The magistrate didn't marry them. Nobody married them, even though they're in a marriage set-up. So, we can easily hide child marriages because the chiefs will tell you, ‘I never marry anyone below the age of 18,’ which is true. You go to the records, you won't find anything, but the children will be there.

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that similarly with GBV, people choose when to report and when not to report, so you can't really say the numbers are low or they're increasing. If people are resorting to violence, others in similar situations will also resort to violence because they hear it. [Another reason is that] Batswana are [now] more aware of their human rights. They are more aware of the laws that are there to protect them, like the Domestic Violence Act, the Penal Code, the sexual assault register. There's more publicity when the laws come out. There are a lot of NGOs coming up. There are a lot of lawyers, MolaoMatters organisation in Francistown, coming up to say, ‘We want to help.’ When we publicise the law, when an act comes up, it will be discussed on the radio, discussed in the ?? So there's more access to information now. People are now recognising, ‘This is wrong. There's something I can do about this.’ So it's quite hard to tell if it's changed since the 2018 study. We don't know if it's gone up or down. We can't know until we do a survey.

The FFM team noted that it sounded like reporting is better and people are talking about it more since then. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought ‘maybe, yes’, and agreed that they are talking about it. She noted that personally, she hadn’t seen a change that would tell her that something is happening; it’s just that people know about it. But are they doing something about it?

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that, also, there are a number of issues why people don't report, because there’s poverty and this person is the only one who's looking after me. I live in his house. He's looking after my children. If he goes to prison, what am I going to do? So it's also mixed with bread-and-butter issues.

The FFM team asked whether overall the government has a willingness to tackle GBV. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought the government is willing to tackle GBV considering the conventions they have signed. They've acceded to CEDAW [UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women]. They've also acceded to the AU [African Union] protocol, the Maputo Protocol. They have signed the SADC [Southern African Development Community] Protocol on Gender and Development 2018. The past president, [Ian] Khama, signed it. They've changed the laws that [treated] women [as] minors. In 1999, there was a comprehensive review of Botswana laws to make men and women equal, including the abolition of marital rights [abolition of a husband’s marital power over the person and property of his wife under common law]. [But] you know the Children's Act recognises that men have a right on their child regardless of marriage? The Domestic Violence Act of 2008 which [includes] protection orders. Just recently – 2020, 2021, 2022 – there was the sexual assault registry bill, which became an act 2 years ago. The FFM team asked for clarification as to whether this was the Sexual Offenders Register Act [2021]. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted yes, and if you are convicted of a sexual crime, you will go [onto the register]. So there are many laws. The problem is implementation.

The FFM team summarised that the law is comprehensive. As for policies and other measures the government is taking, did EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR think they were robust? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that she didn’t know whether to say they're robust because the magistrates and the police are part of the government. If investigation officers are not doing what they're supposed to do, or they're short of capacity somewhere, meaning knowledge as well as numbers and resources, if I go and report and the police say they don't have a car, what's going to happen to the evidence?

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that recently, there was a case where the woman ended up in the UK on asylum. The woman had been abused by a man in Francistown. The woman went to the women's shelter in Francistown and was then transferred to Gaborone. He thought the woman and their children were in EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR’s room. He came to WAR’s office. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR was sitting there, and he banged on [the desk] and said, “I want my wife.” He was threatening WAR, so they reported him to the police. The police didn’t even check. The man was detained and ended up in court in Francistown, but [was acquitted] of all these things he had done. The magistrate asked where the witness [his wife] was, but the witness was in the UK and there was no defendant. The magistrate said, “Who’s bringing the case here?” The man was let off, not because he hadn’t done anything, but because of that technicality. So if the courts are still not cooperating to end GBV there will be technicalities and perpetrators will be let off the crimes they committed it's a problem.

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that, also, it takes time for a GBV case to be heard. WAR have had cases that have taken up to 2 years before they appear in court. During Covid, the government piloted GBV courts. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought this was in Molepolole. In a 3-month pilot, they pushed so many cases, it showed that they really need a GBV court. All they have to do is designate one day in a week to attend to GBV cases, like they do one day in a week to do maintenance courts. Maintenance courts are held on Wednesdays. So if they say, ‘In the morning, we do maintenance. In the afternoon, we do GBV,’ or, ‘The following day, we do GBV,’ this can work. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that there are mobile courts for drinking and driving. The FFM team asked whether for all sorts of other crimes there are mobile courts, but not for GBV. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that there are such courts for drinking and driving but not for GBV.

The FFM team asked whether the specialised GBV courts that existed during Covid still exist. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained no, they are not there anymore. It was just a pilot because GBV went up during Covid, so they piloted [in particular] spots (areas of the country – Molepolole) and they moved a lot of cases. It showed that there's a need. The FFM team asked whether the courts closed and they stopped the pilot. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted yes, just like the referral system WAR piloted, they stopped the pilot. The FFM team asked whether the GBV court pilot was not taken forward. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it was not.

The FFM team noted that, going back to the police and implementation of the law, they had heard that a GBV unit was set up by the police in 2021 and was designed to improve the police performance on managing GBV cases. What was EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR’s view? The FFM team added that they understood there is now a section in Maun itself, but that was more recent.

What was EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR’s perspective on that? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that it's a very good initiative, something that, if they had resources, would work. But what we see now is, like the one in Maun specifically, they only deal with children. It’s their children's unit, it's not gender-based violence. We still go to the main police office. There's a child-friendly unit. Only that is separate from the main place, separate from the main police station. So from that [perspective] of looking after children, it's fine. There’s GBV-specific at the police station, you still have to queue. I take people, then I have to sit and wait while they are attending other issues.

The FFM team asked whether this meant that they hadn’t created a different, separate space for these cases, but that they have specially trained officers. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that they say [they have specially trained officers], yes. Specially trained officers are probably there. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought GBV is now part of their curriculum. The FFM team noted that they understood GBV is generally part of the curriculum but that the police had told them that there is also a special unit, and that about 250 officers have been part of this unit, specialising in gender-based violence cases. The FFM team asked whether, when EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR takes someone to the police and they wait and then speak to a police officer, are they taken in a separate space? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted yes, they do have private rooms because GBV is attended by CID, the Criminal Investigation Department. Those CID officers are the ones who work on GBV. The FFM team asked whether this is always the case. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that when you go to the police anytime, you'll be handled by the police or any police officer. The CID work during the day, but after hours, any police officer would be there to help. Officers in the special unit are there, they are trained, but they do other things as well. They’re in the CID, criminal investigation. So they're part of that system, and they only work during the day. If I go to the police after hours, I will be assisted by the person who's there, not – or not necessarily – a GBV person. The FFM team asked whether they would still be separate from other people. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed yes, they take you into a separate room.

The FFM team asked whether the police's performance had improved or changed in the last few years. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted yes. She thought there had been more training, more interaction with WAR and more interaction from government as well. Setting up the Gender and Child Protection Unit had helped, even though they're still working on children, not everyone. But at least it's something that's there. There’s intent.

The FFM team asked whether the police are better at managing cases, collecting evidence and investigating? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that she didn’t know about collecting evidence because WAR had lost a number of cases due to lack of evidence, especially working with children. Working with children, it's very traumatic. You can have 10 children and win only one case, of 10 different children that you know. So there seems to be a disconnect in terms of the technicality between collection of evidence by the police and what the magistrate wants.

The FFM team asked whether EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR sees cases are progressed by the police to the courts and end up in a disposal. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that she did. She noted that the conviction rate is quite low in GBV but she thought that was a worldwide phenomenon. The FFM team noted that they also understood that conviction rates were generally low, at least for rape. But GBV includes lots of types of crime. Could EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR define it? What are we talking about when we say GBV? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that you're talking about sexual violence, physical violence, emotional and economic. It can happen to people of all genders, all ages. The FFM team summarised that it’s quite a broad range of acts and that some are more severe or grave than others. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR agreed with both points. She noted that the most critical types that WAR deals with are sexual violence and physical violence. The FFM team asked whether this included rape and possibly femicide, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it did. The FFM team asked whether cases result in convictions. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that conviction rates are very low. The FFM team asked whether this was true for other crimes, too, or just for gender-based violence. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that she was not sure because she specialises in gender-based violence. GBV crimes are the ones she keeps an eye on; the others, she was not so sure.

The FFM team asked whether WAR see cases within the shelters that end up in disposal. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that they had had cases at the shelter that were thrown out of court. The perpetrator was set free. The FFM team asked whether there had been cases that had resulted in convictions as well. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted yes, they had some success, not all doom and gloom, and 10% success. The FFM team asked whether that was changing. Were they beginning to be more successful? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted no, there had been no difference since she had been with WAR [2009]. WAR wanted to do a survey. The survey was done in Chobe, Gantsi and Ngami districts. They consulted someone to come and do it for them between 2007 and 2009 and the conviction rate then was below 10%. It's still below 10% now. The FFM team asked whether that was for the serious crimes, for rape and sexual violence? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that was correct – rape and sexual violence. The FFM team asked why she thought that was, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that she had no idea. It’s a lot of issues. There’s the evidence – the crime will happen here and then you collect evidence, maybe 3 days [later] if it's sexual violence or physical violence. Then they go to the hospital, then it goes to the DPP, who will then say, ‘Oh, we need to look for this, we need to look for this,’ before they can register it at court. After registering it at court, they will be told to come after 6 months, and then, ‘Oh, we’ll give you a date next year this time.’ Then we postpone because the perpetrator is not feeling well and then we postpone again because the perpetrator’s parent has died so they can't testify. And that's 2 years. So during that time, what's happening to this person [the victim]?

The FFM team asked whether there are sometimes restraining orders. And is there bail? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted yes, there are restraining orders and there will be bail. There’ll be people from my family and there can be family discussions. The FFM team asked if this was a mediation discussion. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that mediation is going on, and by the time the court says, ‘Now we've got a date. Let's go to court,’ this person might say, ‘I'm not going to,’ or, ‘I have forgiven him.’ The FFM team asked whether there were, therefore, multiple reasons for the low conviction rate. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that there were. She noted that there are a lot of broken systems. There's the family which is broken. There's the police, there's the DPP, there’s the magistrates’ court, there’s us, there's social services. There are so many players. There's the church. You also get faith-based [organisations]. The FFM team asked whether the church was helping women or playing a role in mediation. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that they play a role in mediation.

The FFM team asked how easy it is to access legal aid. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that [Lega Aid Botswana] are here [within WAR’s premises]. There’s a means test, so they come in and check: How much do you earn? Who are you looking after? What are your expenses? And they come to a certain level. The FFM team asked whether legal aid is for the defendant. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it is. The FFM team asked whether it is not for the victim. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted this was not correct; it is for the victim, too. The FFM team asked whether that is in civil cases. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it is. The FFM team noted that these were not criminal cases, but they understood LAB might be looking at criminal cases in the future. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought they had started and explained that they are looking for a bigger place, then they will open.

The FFM team asked for confirmation that GBV cases are in the criminal courts. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that GBV is criminal, but currently it's civil because they apply for restraining orders. The FFM team asked whether restraining orders are civil cases, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that both restraining orders and tenancy orders are civil matters. The FFM team asked whether, at that point, a victim could get advice from LAB. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that then they can do the [means] test. Yes, they can get advice, or if they want a divorce, then they can fight for property and come for legal aid.

The FFM team asked whether restraining orders are effective. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that the perpetrators actually say, ‘So what do you expect this piece of paper to do to me?’ The FFM team asked whether that meant a person would have to get the court to enforce them. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that they are actually enforced by the police. But where are the police? Remember, they met the woman who was killed in Gabs [Gaborone], the university one.

The FFM team noted that they had been told that because restraining orders are issued by the court, the police don’t know about it unless the victim tells them. A lot of times, the women (victim) doesn't go to the police. Could that be a reason why such orders are not enforced? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that this was not how she understood it. The way she understood it is that you go to court to be given a restraining order, then the police have to enforce it. The police take the restraining order, too. The FFM team asked whether this meant the court issues it and gives it to the police and says, ‘You now have to make sure this happens.’ EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that the order is actually given to the complainant, the victim. The FFM team asked whether they then have to go to the police? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that they then have to go to the police.

The FFM team summarised that the court issues the restraining order to the complainant. She takes it to the police. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed yes, to the police. The FFM team asked whether, if she didn’t go, the police would not be aware of it. Did that ever happen at all? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that [the courts] do give [the restraining orders to the police]. The restraining orders are served to the perpetrators by the police. The FFM team asked whether the police actually enforce some of them, but not all. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that the police will give you a restraining order, but they’re not going to be guarding you to make sure there’s 200 metres to that person [the victim]. There will be a paper and then they [the police] go back to their office. That's why the perpetrators are thinking, ‘A restraining order is just a paper, it's not a person guarding me not to go.’ So it's out of the willingness of the person to say, ‘I must respect this.’ Noting that restraining orders are not the same as a witness protection regime, the FFM team asked whether, if the victim says, ‘The other person’s breached the restraining order, they got close to me,’ they can ring the police and the police should arrest that person. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed yes, they should. The FFM team asked if they actually do. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR repeated that they should. The FFM team asked whether EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR knew of any cases where the police have enforced a restraining order. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that she knew they always give it, but whether they enforce it, she didn’t know.

The FFM team noted that bail had come up as an issue because some sources had said bail is easy to obtain for people who've committed various crimes, including gender-based violence. But last year, a new act was introduced to make the criteria for release tighter. Did EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR have any experience of the bail system and whether it's changed since then? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that the change was saying that the victim should have a say, should come to court and convince the court why they shouldn't give this person bail. So if the person is my husband or my partner and has threatened to kill me, and now they are going to apply for bail, then I have to go to court and convince the court why they shouldn't be. That’s the change. So it's not that they can't get it, but the victim has to come and plead. The FFM team asked whether this had increased the burden for victims. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that it had. She added that the burden is to want the victim to come and say, ‘Keep protecting me, please.’ The FFM team noted that previously they didn't have that opportunity. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR agreed that no, they didn’t. The FFM team noted that it would be a new opportunity to build the evidence. Could they now add their own evidence to the evidence covered by the police? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that they could. The FFM team asked whether that should, in theory, make it better, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that they hoped so. They had yet to see it tested. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought no one had tested it yet and noted that she hadn’t yet heard of a case.

The FFM team noted that they had heard of a case the police told them about. The woman’s case is being used as a test case. But it’s quite new so maybe some guidelines will be coming through. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that they would keep their ear to the ground.

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR raised the issue of protection for WAR. The FFM team noted that they had visited BGBVC in Gaborone (who have a guard) and during that meeting BGBVC mentioned the murder EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR referred to, about the husband and his wife a few years ago at the BGBVC offices. The FFM team noted that WAR’s work can be dangerous. The FFM team summarised that EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR had talked about the support WAR provides and that they interact with the police and deal with referrals and refer cases to the police and to other NGOs. Was that right? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it was.

The FFM team also summarised that there seemed to be an ecosystem of service providers working together, trying to make things better. Was that correct? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it was.

The FFM team further summarised that the police had shown some willingness and there was a general government willingness to make things better. But the issues around implementation could be better. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that yes, it could be better.

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that an issue the FFM team had not touched on was tradition. She explained that in Botswana, traditionally, women – like women in the Old Testament in the Bible – are considered minors to men, and it’s considered that they should listen to men. The FFM team asked whether ‘minors’ meant they’re supposed to be like a child. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that it meant ‘less than a man’. It's only nowadays that the young generation, the current generation, is talking about equality and doing things in a manner that whether you are a woman, whether you are a man, whether you are LGBT+, you are a person, full stop.

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that her generation and those older than her who are still in the workplace are from that crop of traditionalists. So even when you go to the police and you find an elder person who reports that [her] husband is beating [her], they will ask you, ‘Have you talked to your uncles? Have you talked to your aunts?’ But you're coming to the police to help you. The police will ask, ‘Have you talked to them?’ because that's the culture, that's the tradition. And the victim has been abused so many times before they go to the police because they've been going around the village to their uncle, to their aunt, who have been saying, ‘No, we'll talk to him. It will be fine.’ By the time they go to the police, they’ve been to all these people, so that also delays and escalates the violence. So the community as well needs to get that education, needs to understand that they need to be protecting this woman.

The FFM team asked whether that is something that happens more in rural areas, but whether in towns and cities there’s been a change. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that it happens to everyone. But yes, when you're in the rural areas, you are more vulnerable because of the vulnerabilities that you are living under. The FFM team noted that these might include that it's a small police station, people around us know, but in the cities maybe there are younger police who are better trained and you’re not so part of the community. Maybe in the cities there’s more accessibility – access to justice. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed all these points. She added that greater accessibility in the cities even included access to information – just knowing where you can go, who can help you. The FFM team noted that in the cities there would be NGOs, like WAR. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR observed that she sometimes shuddered to think what would happen in Maun if there was no WAR, if there was no shelter here. It would be a total disaster.

The FFM team asked whether there are other NGOs that help in the GBV space in Maun besides WAR. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that WAR is the only one who have a shelter, and they specialise in GBV, when others are attempting it on other levels, like on the church point or looking after children only. Love Botswana have their own needs they’re looking after, like their shelter for children, some with multiple disabilities. The FFM team noted that they had spoken to Love Botswana and there is an overlapping response because gender-based violence comes up. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR agreed.

The FFM team, turning to relocation, noted that Botswana is a big place with a small population. They asked whether there are barriers for a woman from, say, a small settlement to move to Maun or from Maun to, say, Gaborone or Francistown to avoid the perpetrator. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that movement is not restricted, in the simple way of can you get on a bus. The FFM team asked whether living and surviving in a new place is possible, too.

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that it’s very, very difficult. You have to move from your place. To move from, say, Maun and go to Francistown, you must know somebody in Francistown or you must have a job that you are going to that will sustain you. You first of all think, ‘Where am I going to stay? How am I going to sustain myself?’ so that you must have found a job. There must be someone who says, ‘I will take you in.’ That ‘I will take you in’ must happen before you can move and just go, because you can’t just go into a shelter, you have to go through the police. They don't just come straight through the police, and you don't house them forever. The other option is going through social services. Social services have destitute programmes, and for you to qualify as a destitute we have to evaluate 1,2,3,4, and if you are found to be able to work, then you don't get that funding.

The FFM team summarised that a lot of the difficulty is economic – if you haven’t got access to an income, you can't find somewhere to stay. But once there, you could get access to healthcare because it’s public and free, and access to government services. It's just whether you can support yourself. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that [it also depends on] whether you are going to qualify for those government services, because it's not everyone who can. Even for poor people, it’s not everyone who receives support.

The FFM team asked whether you can move if you have your own financial means. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed yes. The FFM team asked whether there are barriers. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that there are none. The FFM team asked whether you can live as a single woman or lone woman, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed yes, you can move and live in a rental. People have built houses. And if you've got children, the children will easily be admitted in a school because of the law that children must go to school. There's no school that can refuse your children going into a public school. So if I have children, I don't say, ‘Where will my children go to school?’ Wherever I land, they'll go to school. Like the children who come to our shelter – when they come in, we insist that the social workers bring their school forms, they transfer them, then they come here, we find them a school as well, and there's no school that can refuse. So the issue is finding a place to stay and something to take care of yourself, and a job can do that. The FFM team asked whether that depends on their backgrounds and who they know and what qualifications they have. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted yes.

The FFM team asked whether there is stigma around being a lone woman or a lone woman with children. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought that there is not anymore – there are so many such women. She thought that in Botswana, the marriage statistics are going down. Single families are now everywhere, so there's no stigma around them. She didn’t think so anyway. The FFM team noted that others had said the same and that the situation is quite different in some societies. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that in Botswana, it’s changed.

Lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people)

The FFM team noted that they didn’t know if LGBT+ is a space EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR knows about. The FFM team asked what EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR’s view is of the position of LGBT+ people, perhaps women particularly, and their experiences. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought that we are getting there slowly. There’s an organisation called LEGABIBO [who represent and advocate on behalf of LGBT+ people]. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought BONELA also works with them. WAR also works with them, but not as much as [other groups] in Gabs [Gaborone].

Gabs is where [LGBT+ people] are more concentrated, and the activist organisations are more in Gaborone. Here, there is a satellite [organisation], just a few people that WAR works with. [LGBT+] organisations are allowed to be registered, and even [for trans people] to change markers, that has been allowed. The FFM team clarified if that meant gender markers. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed yes. The only thing that is still outstanding, that is still appearing in the Penal Code, is sexual relations. You can't have sex with the same sex. But it’s an unenforced law.

The FFM team asked whether, in EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR’s experience, LGBT+ people experience discrimination, violence, stigma or anything else, in Maun particularly, or more widely. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought stigma was still there, in the general population. She noted that she didn’t know about healthcare service because most of [LGBT+ people] get their service [assistance] from the LGBT+ organisations. For instance, before the government provided lubes, they could only get them from BONELA, from Men and Boys for Gender Equality, or Men for Health. We have an organisation, Men for Health, that is [in Maun]. BONELA, we have an office [in Maun]. That's where they could get some of the commodities (such as lubes and condoms) that they needed, but they were not available in mainstream government health services. There was some concern that some individuals in [accessing] health [services] would say, ‘We treat, we don't ask any questions,’ but people would feel not accepted or not treated with respect when they went for healthcare. That was part of BONELA’s motion in the last [Country Co-ordinating Mechanism] CCM, when they were dealing with the Global Fund. There was the motion on health, access to health and removing barriers to access to health. WAR was part of that, but they were working on access to health for young people and BONELA was doing it for LGBT+ [people]. It’s a campaign that's been going on because people feel they are not being accepted, especially in health[care].

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that for her, [the issue] is the general community. There are still people who are labelling [LGBT+ people] and this is where the faith people come in. The Botswana Council of Churches (BCC) and [Evangelical Fellowship of Botswana] EFB, the Lutheran church, have a curriculum that they've been [sending] around to teach churches about how to address LGBT issues as a church. And it's not all the churches – the Botswana Council of Churches and others. There's still resistance. The FFM asked whether that meant the EFB and the BCC are anti-LGBT. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained no, they are pro. They’re teaching churches how to approach it. The FFM team asked whether this teaching was on acceptance of LGBT+ people. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed yes, they are teaching them to be inclusive. There's a whole curriculum. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that she did not have it with her, but if the FFM team visited BCC in Gabs, BCC would show them.

The FFM team asked whether they are big, these churches and the church association. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that they are. BCC is the Roman Catholic Church, the Methodist Church, UCCSA [United Congregational Church of Southern Africa]. It’s Lutheran, it’s Anglican and there are other churches. The FFM asked whether they are LGBT accepting. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that they are, but noted that it is slow.

The FFM team asked whether, in EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR’s experience, treatment of LGBT+ people varies from place to place, from Maun to Gaborone, elsewhere. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it does. The FFM team asked whether EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR was aware of anything more than stigma. Can people be open? If they are, do they face violence or other forms of discrimination? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that there's discrimination, and coming out is very slow. Not everyone who comes out comes out to everyone. So there’s still the stigma. The discrimination is still there. The FFM team asked what form the discrimination takes. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that it’s just, ‘How can you behave like that? What are you pretending to be?’ The FFM team asked whether there would be discrimination in getting a job or finding somewhere to live or going to a school? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted no. During Covid, WAR had cases where some lesbian girls were chased away from home and we went to find them a place to stay. They couldn't bring their girlfriends right into the home and they were chased away. So it's the same for that. You relocate. The FFM team asked whether WAR relocated them. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that they had, they had found them a place. WAR worked with Success Capital in Gabs. They went to Success Capital and booked them accommodation. The FFM team asked what happened after that. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that Covid finished, and they went back to their own homes. During Covid there was movement restrictions, so if you were with your parents, you were to stay there. After Covid, they went back to their own homes. The FFM team asked if they lived together. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that they did.

The FFM team summarised that there is slow change. Some of the church groups and some NGOs work to support LGBT+ people in various ways. They face stigma, it varies from place to place, but there is not more than stigma, not violence? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted she hadn’t heard of violence. It might be there, but –

The FFM team asked whether as far as she knew there was no violence. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed this. She explained that it’s like, my way rather than your way. It's just the talk, the emotional abuse and the isolation.

The FFM team asked whether LGBT+ people could relocate if they were having problems in one area. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted yes. The FFM team summarised that the problems faced were economic really.

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that there’s a woman here who has opened a little shelter for girls, lesbian women. The FFM team asked whether this is in Maun. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that it is and explained that GG represents Safe Places International. She was part of the church training, and she explained what it means to be a lesbian, to be gay.

Annex L - Interview with diplomatic staff at the French Embassy

Date 10 July 2025
LocationFrench Embassy, Gaborone
Attendees 2 French Embassy officials; 3 HO officials

FFM team asked OFFICIAL 1 and OFFICIAL 2 to provide background to their roles. OFFICIAL 1 is French Embassy’s (FE) economic and cooperation officer, leading on gender programmes. OFFICIAL 2 is the communication officer and assists on gender-related programmes.

OFFICIAL 1 noted that the FE is small, for example it only provides consular services once a month. It covers a few subjects, including feminist diplomacy which is a priority for the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The FE has a number of [gender-related] programmes including on socio-economic empowerment which are undertaken in collaboration with the Botswana Council of NGOs (BOCONGO). The FE supports 3 organisations on gender-based violence (GBV), women survivors and making sure they can reintegrate. These include:

  • the Botswana Gender Based Violence Prevention and Support Centre (BGBVC), supported in Ghanzi [western Botswana (BWA)] to spread FE support [across the country] and it is quite a socio-economically deprived area. It is a small project involving 25 to 50 beneficiaries, supporting them through horticulture – they are able to sell their produce, organise themselves in co-operatives and share their income. They can also link up with other survivors [of GBV] including a few men.
  • Women Against Rape (WAR) in Maun, Ngamiland. The project is to provide comprehensive sexual education (CSE). So far covered 6 schools involving around 600-700 students. Interesting to see how students perceive GBV and understand ‘consent’ [in a sexual relationship]. WAR have been approached by the police’s GBV and child protection unit to see how they can collaborate on GBV specific sessions in schools. WAR also provides counselling to teenage mothers (14 to 19 year olds), which is an issue in the area - there is quite a lot of stigma about [teenage pregnancy]. Additionally, there are parent/child counselling sessions with 100 parents so far working with the Kgotla (the traditional villages [community councils])
  • Research Excellence, a research institute, which is looking at the integration [back into society] of female ex-prisoners

OFFICIAL 1 continued that the FE also has an advocacy project called Sichaba, which means community, about gender equality featuring survivors of GBV.

OFFICIAL 1 noted that the FE also has a media parity programme which is at [a southern Africa] regional level including BWA about gender sensitive reporting in the media. They are working with 5 media houses in BWA. OFFICIAL 2 added that this includes BTV, which is the only public [broadcaster], YTV, a private [broadcaster], the Weekend Post, a privately [owned newspaper], Duma FM, [a privately owned radio station], and the Patriot on Sunday, a [privately owned newspaper].

The FFM team asked OFFICIAL 1 to summarise the situation for women facing GBV. OFFICIAL 1 noted that BWA is a middle-income economy so in terms of social challenges was quite surprised to see that GBV as such a big issue. OFFICIAL 1 noted the national relationship study of 2018 reported that 2 out of 3 women are subjected to GBV. That's 7 years ago and it's assumed that the numbers are much more concerning than this, but there's a real lack of data.

OFFICIAL 1 continued that recently there have been big cases in the news. For example, there was a woman killed inside of the University of Botswana which was quite shocking – that a person would go and kill inside a university, a sacred place. There were also reports that this woman had been subjected to threats which was concerning. Usually [for serious incidents] a minister would go [to the scene of the incident] but we have not seen this which speaks to how seriously this is being taken (though this is open to interpretation). The civil society organisations (CSOs) we spoke to were surprised by that. OFFICIAL 1 also noted that otherwise BGBVC also had been a case of a woman who was killed on their site in 2023. So, women die every day, we know it happens quite often [but do not have the numbers]. The FE is working with CSOs, for instance WAR which has a shelter in Maun. WAR keeps the address private because they want to avoid this kind of situation [the murder of the woman at the BGBVC shelter]. They have very strict protocols for security to make sure [similar incidents] do not happen - this shows the extent of fear around this.

OFFICIAL 1 further noted that in terms of legal system there is the Domestic Violence Act of 2008 (DVA 2008) - the BGBVC’s director was a big actor in this. The law has not been updated, it is the main law on GBV prevention.

The FFM team asked how many women have been supported by the FE’s programmes and partners. OFFICIAL 1 noted that the beneficiaries of our current programme which started in 2024 is expected to be 6,000. So far around 900 to 1,000 have been helped. Most of them are students who have been trained on CSE courses. So not all of them are women that were subjected to GBV, so maybe 100 are GBV related.

The FFM team asked about data on levels of violence, with the last comprehensive study dating to 2018. Does the FE have data or a sense of the current levels of GBV. OFFICIAL 1 no, not that we've seen - we're looking into it. What we have heard from the main CSOs working on this is that during COVID GBV got worse - everywhere in the world. The CSOs were really overwhelmed with the amount of help they were being asked for and were themselves mentally challenged because it was too much to carry. What we've learned from lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+) organisations is that with the rise of anti-rights movements sometimes the language [against LGBT+ people] can be more violent in the media – not something we can verify, but a general feeling.

OFFICIAL 2 noted that since the new current government [came to power] there has been more talk about GBV in the press as people are urging the government to pass an anti-GBV law and to declare a national state of emergency. So, there is more [reporting and commentary on GBV] in the press but no data on it. OFFICIAL 1 added that there is more about GBV in the press as the current government [has stated its focus] is about human rights, so expectations are higher.

The FFM team asked what types of GBV occur in BWA. OFFICIAL 1 what we see through our programmes is psychological and physical violence. There is also economic violence, as a woman is often dependent on a man. When they would try to leave, they experience violence or even worse.

The FFM team asked who are the main perpetrators of GBV. OFFICIAL 1 noted that what they see through their programmes, it's mostly domestic violence.

OFFICIAL 1 had read that – in World Population Review (WPR) [report on occurrence of rape in 2023; this data relates to incidents in 2010] – BWA had the highest incidence of rape in the world. The FFM team noted that they had come across this data and that the WPR aggregated the information from other sources, such as police statistics. The FFM team asked whether women’s increased awareness of their rights might be a reason for the high rates of reporting (compared to other countries). OFFICIAL 1 was not sure. Did not see in comparison with other countries that would be the case but had not seen the figures. But OFFICIAL 1’s impression was that was not necessarily the case - haven't seen huge [awareness] campaigns of reporting. Mostly see a lot of censorship, self-censorship. OFFICIAL 2 noted that women can report to the police, but they were not separated [from the perpetrator or other people in the police station] when disclosing information about what happened to them. This does not encourage them to report if they cannot ensure safety and privacy. The FFM team recapped that women are not able to report safely and confidentially at police stations. OFFICIAL 1 noted, yes, that as far as they are aware. The FFM team clarified what was mean by self-censorship. OFFICIAL 1 explained that this was the woman [not speaking out/reporting an incident]. We also hear that there is the tradition of fixing household problems in private, at the Kgotla, which is the local village. So, before things escalate they gather at the Kgotla and try and sort it out without it being everyone's business.

The FFM team asked what the profile of the victims is. OFFICIAL 1 could not say for sure, but young women. FFM team clarified age. OFFICIAL 1 thought from the age of 14 to late 20s. The FFM asked whether this was in rural or urban areas, OFFICIAL 1 noted all types of areas.

The FFM team asked if there were gaps in law and policy protecting women from GBV. OFFICIAL 1 noted that CSOs have been calling for a national state of emergency so everyone can be on the same page as to identifying GBV as a big issue. A good start would be bringing the DVA 2008 up to date. Some sources have also been calling for specialised courts with specialised judges that will be trained on [GBV]. The FE is talking with its partners about abortion. There is not much on this except in the Penal Code: it is an exception when abortion is authorised - in cases of rape, defilement, and death / danger to the mother. But when talking with partners/CSOs, the FE has found that [people’s] general understanding is that abortion is not authorised at all. So, women who would fall into those 3 specific cases would think it's illegal, so not get the help they need from health specialists. Amongst health specialists, personal beliefs have a role [in not authorising an abortion] as BWA is quite a religious country. OFFICIAL 1 continued that clarifying law/policy [on GBV] would be a first step. Also introducing a state of emergency would be a signal [of the government taking GBV seriously].

The FFM team asked if the government had indicated that it intended to address GBV. OFFICIAL 1 noted that the government is really big on human rights, would expect women's rights to be part of human rights. But since the election [of the government in October 2024] there have been executive/high level statements that have been perceived by CSOs as discouraging, a bad signal. The statements are usually made in conferences but then are plastered in the media. OFFICIAL 1 [noted the president] made a declaration about GBV that was perceived as putting the blame on women.

The FFM team asked if women who experience GBV are able to get protection. OFFICIAL 1 considered CSOs play a big role in [providing] protection in the social and health sectors. CSOs have been complementary to public service and definitely do a lot in [supporting] these women, for example WAR’s shelter, and making sure they have a police officer to talk to. They provide the link between state services, like the police, and women in need / survivors [of GBV]. If they weren't there the situation would be very dire.

The FFM team asked if the police are effective at investigating cases. OFFICIAL 1 could not judge but it varies. The FFM team noted that there is GBV unit in the police, is this unit able to provide protection. OFFICIAL 1 did not know. The FFM team asked what the purpose of GBV unit in the police. OFFICIAL 1 thought it was created as a need was specifically identified to help women and to make sure that GBV acts wouldn't go unpunished. The unit is for GBV and child protection. The FE do not work directly with them, the fact that they exist is a good thing, but did not know enough about their day-to-day work to say [how effective the GBV unit is or what it does exactly].

The FFM team asked if the FE were aware of data on the number of arrests, prosecutions and convictions. The FFM team noted that there was a general lack of data, all evidence is anecdotal, therefore it is difficult to assess what is happening generally. OFFICIAL 1 acknowledged it was difficult to get a clear picture of the situation [without data], did not have more specific figures. OFFICIAL 1 observed that general political atmosphere right now with these statements by the government [see above] and recent killings [see above], nothing really happened afterwards - there was a week of prayers that was organised rather than something concrete to address the issue. The woman who was murdered at the University of Botswana (UofB) was murdered during the week of prayer.

The FFM team noted that most of the sources they had spoken to had mentioned the UofB case. Was it representative of GBV / crimes against women generally, why had it gained such public interest? OFFICIAL 1 thought it [had gained public interest] because the woman had taken [several] measures to protect herself – she had gone to the police, had got a restraining order, (OFFICIAL 1 believed the woman) had talked about [her concerns] with colleagues, and that it happened inside the university where there's security at the entrance and people around (it's not just a domestic case) – but it still happened. It's a perfect case study of a [woman doing everything she could to protect herself but still being murdered].

The FFM team asked if similar cases had been reported. OFFICIAL 1 had not been in BWA for a long time but, yes, there [was the case of the woman murdered] inside BGBVC in 2023. A similar case [to the UofB incident] of a woman reaching out for help from specialists and it happened inside the [woman’s] shelter.

The FFM noted that they had spoken to the BGBVC, who had said that the perpetrator of the murder at the shelter had been arrested and remained in detention – so the police did do something. Is this sort of incident common? OFFICIAL 1 did not how common, BGBVC see it everyday would be better placed to comment.

The FFM team asked how many CSOs worked on GBV. OFFICIAL 1 was not sure, knew the big names, maybe 10 to 20. OFFICIAL 2 noted that some CSOs work on issues that are not directly linked to GBV The FFM team asked if the CSOs operated all around the country. OFFICIAL 1 not necessarily in the big cities, but where the most need is identified.

The FFM team asked how easy would it be for a woman to ask for help from one of the CSOs. OFFICIAL 1 probably hard, but did not know, for women in a rural area as there is less infrastructure to go to a police station but assume [this is the case]. The women on our projects, for instance, had difficulties in going to a place as there's no transport and it was hard for them to move around the city. This would be an obstacle when trying to reach out for help. Economic means are very dire - complicated. There is a lot of poverty in the villages. The FFM team clarified if it was hard to move around because of safety or a lack of transport. OFFICIAL 1 talking about rural areas, not seen a lot of public transport. OFFICIAL 1 recalled recent field mission to Ghanzi, women mentioned that they would like more cars driving them to the horticulture site because they have to walk to pick-up point as there only one or 2 buses. That is hard for them to do because of distances and some are very old. So might be obstacle if they had to go to a police station. So, thinking about women with limited financial means.

The FFM team asked if the CSOs provide legal aid / advice. OFFICIAL 1 thought they did, but not the CSOs’ main function. It's more health and social support.

The FFM asked whether a woman could relocate within BWA to avoid harm, are there any barriers. OFFICIAL 1 thought there are multiple issues. There's still this big weight of community even if you have the economic means. There's a system around you - it wouldn't be seen in the right way by the family or the community, especially for women with kids.

The FFM team asked if OFFICIAL 1 / OFFICIAL 2 had any examples. OFFICIAL 1 noted the FE did a symposium about GBV. There was a woman with a child who had been subjected to defilement but was told by the family not to talk about it. She removed herself from the family circle, but this was always seen as a barrier to the family. There’s social exclusion from the group, as there is [an issue] about the reputation and protection of the honour of the family. OFFICIAL 2 knows of a specific case where a woman talked about her experienced in a documentary that was recently released on TV in BWA – she testified about what happened. The woman was defiled as a child but left her home after she had become 18 (and was now around 30).

The FFM team confirmed that the FE did not have data on arrests, detentions and convictions. OFFICIAL 1 said they did not.

The FFM team asked if the FE knew of any examples where the police have done something correctly or have not worked well? No examples provided.

OFFICIAL 1 added that in relation to migration, a lot of women go to South Africa (SA) to get an abortion. Women need to find the money to get a bus or flight to SA, if they cannot they keep their child. That's why there are so many cases of teenage mothers.

The FFM team asked if the FE knew the size of the LGBT+ population. OFFICIAL 1/ Official 2 did not know.

The FFM team asked if the FE worked with LGBT+ groups. OFFICIAL 1, yes, good partners with [Lesbians, Gays and Bisexuals of Botswana] LEGABIBO. The FE organised the first open conference about safeguarding LGBT+ rights in 2024, which was attended by France’s LGBT+ ambassador. The conference was at the National Museum, was open with national TV there. It was a bit of an unknown, the FE were not sure if the [anti-LGBT+ rights] would show up and try to disturb the event. But it went well in spite of the coverage of the trans women on the panel by the national TV who was referred to as ‘Mr’, that shows that work has to be done.

The FFM team asked how accepting society is of LGBT+ people. OFFICIAL 1 would not describe BWA society as ‘accepting’ of LGBT+ people but that it is [seen as] a private matter and it is overall respected as a private matter. So, people wouldn't point [LGBT+ people] out and LGBT+ organisations can still hold their conferences / events. There will still be homophobic reactions as everywhere in the world. Trans women and lesbians are subjected to specific kinds of violence. The BWA ombudsman organised a conference [along with the Botswanan Trans Initiative and the Global Equality Caucus] at the beginning of 2025 specifically on trans rights. There were 2 organisations specialised in trans rights and individuals sharing their struggles. What came up was that for trans women and lesbians were often threatened with corrective rape. Trans people that are identifiable are subjected to more physical violence [than other groups] – there were witnesses of that. OFFICIAL 2 added that sometimes there was violence from the family.

The FFM team asked if LGBT+ people face danger to their lives, physical harm. OFFICIAL 1 noted that there’s a difference between sexuality [sexual orientation] and gender identity. The most at risk at are trans people as for most people it goes further than being just gay. So, trans people might find themselves in a situation where their life at risk.

The FFM team asked about if the state persecutes LGBT+ people. OFFICIAL 1 would not say so. More about [the lack of] services in place to cater to their needs. For instance, gender reassignment treatment [is not available]. Very hard to find, only a few doctors doing it. Wouldn’t say that [the state] is a problem.

The FFM team asked if a LGBT+ would be able to help from the police. OFFICIAL 1 noted, based on the experiences of the trans people attending the conference who went to the police to report violence, no they were not getting help.

The FFM team asked about how these cases were rejected. OFFICIAL 1 observed that, regarding the specific cases, they were made fun of at the police station.

The FFM team asked about the experiences of lesbian, gay and bisexual people, could they be open about their sexual orientation. OFFICIAL 1 would not say they are open, maybe passive – people would assume they are [LGB], but not talk about it, and the LGB people wouldn't speak about their sexuality. For example, if we take a TV presenter or some someone public. Not heard of anyone saying, ‘I'm openly [gay]’, coming out. But, of course, people within those organisations would say so, but never publicly. People keep quiet about their sexuality unless they are activists. They would not show up to a school as a gay couple. The FFM team asked if there were others LGBT+ people might be open – a bar or restaurant, or a same sex couple living together – OFFICIAL 1 noted as long as it's private, it's not an issue. But didn’t know, for instance, if [a same-sex couple] would tell their neighbours that they're gay, or just let them assume they're roommates.

The FFM team asked if the FE are aware of violence and discrimination of LGB people? Women are threatened with corrective rape. The FFM team asked of specific examples of LGB experiencing violence, of it actually happening. OFFICIAL 1 was aware of a case at the [ombudsman’s] conference of assault [of a lesbian or trans person]. Thought it happens.

The FFM team asked if the experience of gay men and lesbians / bisexual women was different. OFFICIAL 1 thought it might, because of gender dynamics lesbians and bisexual women might be taken less seriously [than men]. In general, OFFICIAL 1’s impression was that women in lesbian relationships are subjected to less harsh violence because women are already open with one another, emotionally. But gay men might be more shocking to see than lesbians [for the general public]. Lesbians face more specific violence, fetishized. While men, it might be more like violence. The FFM team confirmed that it was OFFICIAL 1’s perception, not aware of specific cases, OFFICIAL 1 yes [not aware of specific cases].

The FFM team asked if there had been a shift in attitudes towards LGBT+ people since the decriminalisation of same-sex sexual relations in 2019. OFFICIAL 1 had only been in BWA for 2 years [so could not comment on changes before then]. The FFM team observed that they had been told that the president was a human rights lawyer and had been involved in the court case that legalised the registration of LGBT+ groups. OFFICIAL 1 noted that the case was about the registration of LEGABIBO. The FE had been told the president had had more of a technical role rather than as an advocate in those cases. The ombudsman has been very progressive on this since the new government was elected. The ombudsman has been very vocal on LGBT+ rights, organising conferences - a good signal. Though the ombudsman collected a lot of [material] during this conference it was not made public.

Annex M - Interview with officials at the Ministry for State President

Date 9 July 2025
LocationMinistry for State President (MSP), Gaborone
Attendees Senior officials, MSP; 3 Home Office officials

The fact finding mission (FFM) team asked what the Ministry of the State President’s (MSP) role is in managing the police and the criminal justice system generally. OFFICIALS observed that FFM’s terms of reference (ToR) is something the police would be better placed to comment on than the MSP; the ToR are not really matters the MSP can comment on. OFFICIALS continued [that] the MSP is like a big corporate services office for the president. The Botswana Defence Force (BDF) and the police report directly to the president but the MSP’s minister [assists] the president on all issues relating to defence, security and safety - on policy matters and other issues - that have to be taken to cabinet and Parliament. OFFICIALS noted that in late [2024]/early [2025] the then Ministry of Defence and Security was dismantled and put together under the MSP. [The permanent secretary’s office and the MSP minister have responsibility to support the police and BDF on] logistical issues - getting all the resources they need and facilitation on legal issues. [These] usually have to pass through the MSP minister's desk because he will be the one responsible for tabling all the programmes, policies and strategies through to cabinet and to Parliament. [However,] [on] the core mandate of the police and [the BDF] [covering defence, security and safety], their accounting officers – the [armed forces’] commander and the [police] commissioner - report directly to the President.

The FFM team asked about the government's position on addressing of gender-based violence (GBV). OFFICIALS noted that while approaching gender issues is mainstreamed across government, the core mandate and co-ordination of gender-related matters lies with the Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs (MYGA). So, they will be in a better position to talk about [gender-related] processes, programmes and initiatives, and how these are working.

The FFM team asked about the scale and size of GBV, and how the justice system worked in practice, specifically how are the police resourced - how many police stations, for example – and number of police? OFFICIALS noted that the police, working with the MYGA, will be in a better position to say, and provide statistics [and detail on initiatives]. The police have introduced a lot of measures to proactively deal with GBV [and] have specialised teams to look into [GBV]. OFFICIALS added that in terms of how the rest of the government deal with [GBV/gender], in every ministry there will be a liaison person with the MYGA, with programmes that are trying to stop GBV mainstreamed through the ministries. [one of the officials] noted the police had set up child friendly centres as one way to deal with GBV, there are [non-government organisation (NGO)] referral centres and homes [to assist victims]. It is a very strong programme with training provided by the UK, [officers at the centres interview] young people and [child victims can give evidence using] video conferencing. If you want to visit [or discuss] the programme, the police [can assist]. The FFM team asked if women can use the child friendly centres. [Official A] noted that the [centres] cater for all victims but while that is the case they are customised to [create an] ambience and feel [amenable to] a young person.

The FFM team asked if tackling GBV is a priority for government, if so what steps has the government taken to address GBV. OFFICIALS noted that GBV is a priority for government, so it lies within MSP. GBV is an issue that needs to be dealt with very seriously and [is] now reflected in resourcing. [So], the police [are] resourced to ensure that child friendly centres are put up to protect [children] and that within the police, which is for the MSP as a whole, we are developing strategic partnerships with the other organisations - civil society organisations - that take care of the victims of GBV. Measures have been put in place by the police to ensure safety generally, which is an issue. OFFICIALS added that it's very interesting about GBV, we talk about children and women, but it has become very clear that there are some men who are very much abused. We are trying to, especially as we work with churches and civil society, to ensure that as a government [GBV] is a very high priority.

OFFICIALS noted that the MSP has a unit - I [previously mentioned] about the mainstreaming and placing of officers that are [in] contact with the MYGA - headed by our senior health and safety officer, where we ensure that issues of public awareness or sensitisation [are addressed], or counselling for [MSP staff] who are going through challenging times, who experience [GBV].

The FFM team asked examples of measures taken to tackle GBV? OFFICIALS noted that apart from public information available, we [the MSP] have people come in to do counselling. We call in experts to talk [to staff] about things that cause dispute at home, [for example] financial literacy issues, we also continuously have ministry staff educated by civil society – there is one we do almost on an annual basis where we pay the Health and Family Foundation (HFF) [which works] help[ing] men and women to try to live properly together and deal with [GBV] issues [which] are causing divisions. The HFF reaches out to us for our staff to attend [training sessions] - a very high number of soldiers and our police and [ministry staff have] attended.

The OFFICIALS continued there are so many causes of GBV and for some of them, if we deal with the root causes, we can deal with the issue. But when it goes to the point where people really feel like they're being abused at home - it's a very private thing that people don't usually deal with, or want to talk about it – we allow our [the MSP’s health and safety unit] to obtain professional counselling to try to help colleagues who are going through the difficult times. We have had [a] few [colleagues] who were brave enough to say, ‘I'm going through a difficult time … ‘ and we find resources to pay for professional counselling.

The FFM team asked if the inter-ministerial communities/structure still exist? OFFICIALS noted, yes it’s coordinated by the MYGA and deals with GBV, the MSP are members represented by the police.

OFFICIALS added the MSP is also responsible for the welfare of people with disabilities. GBV is one of those things that is prevalent within disability constituencies. We've been working very hard to [raise] general public awareness, talking to different stakeholders about it - the 2 main NGOs that deal with people with disability - the Botswana Council for Disabled and the Botswana Federation for Disabled. We deal with them to raise awareness, we empower them. One is the [lack of] economic [opportunity for disabled people]: we've been trying to talk to different sectors [in] the economy to create affirmative action [programmes] as some of [the disabled people] are really [cap]able people. But without a push from government to ensure that [disabled] people are [able to work] so that [they] can be independent and not be subjected to [a] lack [of opportunity / income], making them dependent economically on other people, which sometimes leads to GBV.

The FFM team asked if that is something the MSP does, or is that something the government does generally through different departments? It is coordinated from the MSP. For all disability [issues] we deal with 4 ministries: Health; Local Government; Education; and Labour and Employment. Those are the major ministries that we deal with in coordinating on issues of disability, but like gender and youth issues, every government department is expected to mainstream [disability issues] within their programmes and policies. So, we have structures in place that deal with all issues that affect people with disabilities. We talk on a quarterly basis to the other ministries [about disability].

The FFM team asked if there is a similar process for gender? OFFICIALS believed that the core gender-related budgeting, programmes, coordination lies with the MYGA. So, [for example], I know the campaign that I talked about - the Family Health Foundation - is supported by the MYGA. I believe there are other civil society organisations dealing with GBV that are supported by the MYGA. When we do our [ministerial] annual budgets to ask for money for disability, including the gender-based issues of disability, is coordinated [by] MSP.

Officials noted there are components and pockets [operated] by individual ministries. But the overall project [to combat GBV] is a primary concern for the government. We spoke about subvention funds [government grants] for most of the NGOs, the NGO Council. Some of the NGOs we have mentioned benefit from these subvention funds, so it might be that their contact ministry is the Ministry of Labour, where they get the subvention [grant] but the implementing ministry is MYGA. So, it's cross cutting through the ministries, so [you] keep getting different pieces of information from [different] sources.

The FFM team asked how the LGBT+ population are treated by government and society generally. Officials noted our courts affirmed that LGBT groups can exist / decriminalised. It may be of interest that the president [who is a lawyer] was involved in litigation [to register LGBT+ NGOs]. The official was not aware of any cases of discrimination of LGBT+ people. The FFM team queried if this was by government or society. The official noted by government and society generally.

Officials asked if the FFM team had meetings with the Ministry of Health? How they handled victims of GBV and LGBT+ people, the health sector response and how they manage [might be of interest], as they have special programmes [affecting these groups]. Officials recommended speaking to the National AIDS & Health Promotion Agency (NAHPA) which have programmes for LGBT+ people.

OFFICIALS added that the president has always been vocal about human rights issues. Last year [2024] around the election was the start of revision of the Constitution, which was not completed. It was a consultation around the country [during which] a lot of issues were raised [by] different parts of society and thought this process will continue. The country does not discriminate, but there are instances where people feel discriminated [against] and they have raised some articles within the Constitution that they felt should really be dealt with, and that is the core conversation that is ongoing. Parts of our Constitution demand a referendum and this may be one of them.

Annex N - Interview with Ministry of Labour and Internal Affairs

Date 10 July 2025
LocationMinistry of Labour and Internal Affairs (MLIA), Gaborone
Attendees 4 MLIA senior officials; 3 HO officials

Women and gender-based violence (GBV)

The FFM team asked about the position of women, their treatment and their ability to obtain protection. OFFICIALS explained that gender falls within the Ministry of Youth and Gender [Affairs] [MYGA] but that [the officials could comment] based on their own experiences, including OFFICIALS commenting from a woman’s perspective. One of the male OFFICIALs noted that his own understanding of the situation in Botswana (BWA) is that women are treated very well. There's no discrimination or belittling of women. Women are given the protection they need and there are laws in effect which are trying to address [GBV]. Even the police have taken a posture whereby when a woman comes in to report her boyfriend or husband, the husband is never asked any questions [there and then]. He's immediately taken by the police and is kept away [from her] and interrogated. So we are taking GBV issues very seriously to avoid any escalation in those issues.

A female OFFICIAL thought most of the FFM team’s areas of interest were [within the remit of the MYGA]. She explained that she wouldn’t want to share her own experiences while attending in an official capacity. But she observed that, in terms of discrimination, BWA has many laws [protecting women against it]. In the past, there was a provision within the Citizenship Act 1984 [that only men could] pass on their citizenship to their children. But that provision was declared null and void [in a court case] and the law was amended in 1995 so that now, women can pass on citizenship in the same way as men. XXX in the delta XXX create a balance between men and women [not clarified by source]. Leave [from work] used to be unpaid in the case of women, but not now. In terms of the Botswana Defence Force, a provision [banning women from enlisting] was done away with, so women can join the army.

OFFICIALS thought BWA had made significant progress over the years to try and do away with laws that discriminate [against women].

OFFICIALS added that there is also the Public Procurement Act and fulfilment laws which [promote] economic inclusion. Actually, we give more of an advantage to women and youth than we do to the elderly. We realised that for a long time as an African society, obviously we’d been a patriarchal society. But after [the citizenship ruling], we moved to try to change the situation. There's been a lot of movement. But [as regards] the issue of unpaid leave that OFFICIALS spoke about earlier, the bill is currently before Parliament. [Women] were getting [maternity pay] at a certain percentage [of their income], and it was only for 12 weeks. But the current law that is before Parliament would push that up. OFFICIALS thought the bill was at the Second Reading stage. They noted that if Parliament approves the bill, the period of maternity pay will increase. Women in [the civil service] take maternity leave on full pay. The private sector used to choose whether to pay a certain percentage [of a woman’s usual salary] but the bill would mandate that they pay 70%. We are also pushing for the remaining 30% [to be paid from] a Social Security Fund to which both the employee and the employer would contribute percentages, [which are still to be determined]. At the end of the day, we want women who go on maternity leave to receive 100% of their salary, and the employer will be cushioned by the fund.

OFFICIALS also noted that previously in BWA those holding positions of authority were men like [OFFICIAL], but right now we are moving from there. There are many women like [OFFICIAL] who hold positions of responsibility. Sometimes the conditions are not the same. When we go for interview for these positions, if the performance is equal, women are given preference. There are women specially elected to Parliament as well, sometimes a lot of them, because we want to increase the number. The OFFICIALS added that the head of the civil service and the deputy head [are women].

The FFM team noted that the ministry is responsible for labour and labour law. To summarise, were the officials making the point that the government is trying to address any residual inequalities in labour law? OFFICIALS noted yes, and explained that the bill that is before Parliament will ratify most of the ILO [International Labour Organisation] conventions and is in line with ILO [standards].

During discussion of freedom of movement (below), OFFICIALS noted that in this country, we have laws against GBV. GBV is enshrined in our Penal Code. The police have a unit on GBV specifically to deal with these issues so they are in a better position to speak [on this because] they would have experience in dealing with the issue. But there are remedies available to take action against [perpetrators of GBV]. There are countries that have a higher rate of killing, a high risk of violence. Crime is a social phenomenon. You may not eradicate crime, but you can manage crime to certain levels. So we cannot say completely there will not be GBV. The most important thing is that if it happens, there is a remedy and people are protected. If people go unprotected, then that is an issue.

[Following discussions on the subject of witchcraft (below)] OFFICIALS noted that according to reported cases, most GBV happens in major towns and cities. They thought this was very surprising. OFFICIALS added that culture has evolved and is not as it was before. In the past, only a man could take over as a king or chief, but now, if a woman is next in line, she takes over. [This applied to] chiefs as far as the Namibian border. The female chief next door to here [central Gaborone] is one of the most respected.

OFFICIALS noted that ‘crimes of passion’, as we used to call them, are mostly in urban areas. Usually in rural areas, people fight over things. In urban areas, they are more educated and they fight over people. A military captain killed a woman and child [in BWA] after they had lived together in South Africa and Australia. Cultural assimilation here has gone through a lot. Culture is used as an excuse not to address the real issue. OFFICIALS added that kgotlas [customary courts] are very progressive nowadays. It’s highly unlikely that someone would get away with GBV.

OFFICIALS explained that men sometimes feel what is happening is oppressing men. Women are in control of the home. If a man has done this and this, he’s immediately in trouble.
