If you’re a man and you go to the kgotla, you’ve broken a taboo and you’re in trouble. Now, you see young boys hitting girls, but these issues are never discussed. It’s a matter of how boys are being raised.

The FFM team asked whether customary law had provided a certain culture. OFFICIALS thought yes, but that people don’t respect that now.

OFFICIALS noted that the easiest remedy is to go to the customary court because it’s not expensive, but that he would rather go to the civil court. Most of the cases that come … [not clarified by source.]

Freedom of movement and identity documents

OFFICIALS noted that of the FFM team’s other areas of interest, only freedom of movement was [within the ministry’s remit].

OFFICIALS explained that the rights and freedoms of individuals are enshrined in the Constitution, which is a reference point. No person can be discriminated against on the basis of gender, on the basis of sex, on the basis of religious affiliation. They are all listed there, so there is law to protect people. If your rights are not observed, you can approach a court of law, you can approach the authorities such as the police, and then your rights can be protected. Every person in this country has the right of freedom of movement. If movement is restricted, there's something they can do. They can approach the authorities and report it. The basis of these provisions and the law is really to protect individuals.

The FFM team asked whether the MILA is responsible for passport issuance. OFFICIALS confirmed that it is.

The FFM team asked whether women can obtain passports in the same way as men. OFFICIALS confirmed this. The FFM team asked whether there are ID cards in Botswana. OFFICIALS confirmed that there are. The FFM team asked whether obtaining an ID card in BWA is straightforward. OFFICIALS explained that there is a law, the National Registration Act. When a person is born, they're supposed to be registered at the Registrar’s office for that area. After registration, when the person reaches a [16], they get the ID. Everyone has an ID because for them to go to school, to access education, they have to produce the ID.

OFFICIALS noted that when they are born, we start them off with the birth certificate. When they are 16, they acquire national registration ID. [They can apply for] a passport when they want it.

The FFM team asked whether this was a digitised system, on a digital database. OFFICIALS explained that we don’t have e-ID, but we are working towards that. It's one of the projects that we are currently embarking on.

The FFM team summarised that ID cards are important to access public services and to move around the country. They asked whether, if you lose

your card or relocate, for example, from Francistown to Gaborone, you can easily get a new card. Can you re-register? OFFICIALS and OFFICIALS confirmed yes. OFFICIALS explained that you just pay a nominal fee.

The FFM team asked whether a person just goes to a local office of the MLIA, to apply for their first ID card or get a new card. OFFICIALS noted yes. If you are applying for the first time … [unclear notes, source did not clarify]. If you renew it, you pay a fee [unclear notes, source did not clarify]. We issue birth certificates so we have the records already. The FFM team asked whether birth certificates are universal. OFFICIALS confirmed that they are. The FFM team asked whether a woman would be able to get a replacement ID card if she moved from one town to another. OFFICIALS confirmed this. OFFICIALS added that you need an ID card for everything. A passport is optional.

The FFM team asked whether there are lots of MLIA offices that issue ID cards. OFFICIALS noted that there are. We have people in remote areas and we have to go and register them. [This is done by] the Civil and National Registration. They do outreach to remote dwellers. They issue birth certificates, marriage certificates, death certificates and [proof of] change of surname.

The FFM team asked how long it takes for a passport to be issued. OFFICIALS noted 5 working days, but this would depend whether it was an emergency or not. Asked whether a premium issuance would be payable for an emergency issuance, OFFICIALS explained that there used to be 3 services: 5 working days, 2 working days and an express service of 24 hours. There were different prices for each, but now the 2-day service and express service have been stopped.

LGBT+ people

The FFM team asked whether it is possible for a person to change their gender marker on an ID document. OFFICIALS and OFFICIALS noted that they were unable to answer the question.

The OFFICIALS observed that there was a court case brought by someone he went to school with, who changed her gender marker to female. OFFICIALS added that there’s a difference between BWA and what is happening in the Western world. [In the West], if I wake up one morning and I feel like a woman, I would say that I’m a woman. [But] you have to have certain physical features [to be a woman in BWA].

OFFICIALS noted that it boils down to remedies and whether you can seek redress. She explained that there was a case, Kgositau [Kgositau v. Attorney General of Botswana], [in which the High Court ruled in favour of a trans woman who was seeking to change her gender marker]. OFFICIALS explained that the government has not yet come to a final policy decision [on changes to gender markers].

The FFM team asked whether a person would need to go to court in order to change their gender marker. OFFICIALS explained that we need to see the medical report that suggests this person has transitioned, then the authorities don’t have a problem with that. The FFM team asked whether this meant a person would need a court order, or a court order with medical documents. OFFICIALS explained that the court [in the Kgositau case] said it would be discriminatory and against the Constitution [to refuse a gender marker change]. We are free to rely on that court ruling because the Kgositau case is case law. The FFM team asked whether this was because BWE has a common law system like the UK. The OFFICIALS confirmed yes. Asked whether this meant individuals would not need to go to court [in order to change their gender marker], the OFFICIALS confirmed no [a court order would not be needed].

OFFICIALS added that under the Societies Act, we’ve been able to register [LGBT+] associations or societies because of [non-discrimination]. The court case challenge started in 2016 [the FFM team asked for clarification of the law, source did not provide this]. The FFM team asked whether the groups receive funding. OFFICIALS noted that the Ministry of Youth and Gender [Affairs] gives money to youth groups.

The OFFICIALS added that some of the [LGBT+] NGOs are members of BOCONGO [Botswana Council of Non-Governmental Organisations], so they receive funding that way. Member organisations are grouped by thematic focus, such as governance and corruption, or gender. [LGBT+ NGOs] are beneficiaries under the thematic group on gender.

Witchcraft

OFFICIALS explained that there are a lot of myths around witchcraft. The FFM team noted that it seemed to get mixed in with gender issues in rural areas. The OFFICIALS thought witchcraft was highly unlikely to be a reason for a person to flee to the UK, but added that Bowono was known as the centre of witchcraft [in Botswana]. [If a person needed to leave], it would be best to go to Gaborone or Francistown. They did not need to go to the UK, [joking] that [the power of] witchcraft had no geographical limits.

Annex O - Interview with Mosaditia Women in Tourism

Date 14 July 2025
LocationLove Botswana, Kingdom City, Maun
AttendeesTrustee – 1; Trustee – 2; Vice Chair; Member; Regional Member; Vice Secretary; Secretary; Official; Mosaditia Women in Tourism (MWT); 3 HO officials

The Mosaditia Women in Tourism Trust (MWTT) explained that they are an NGO started in 2019 and consisted of 9 women. Their purpose is to support gender equality in the tourist industry, operating in Maun, their sponsor is Alistair MacFarlane. Still relatively new, helped one woman to date.

The FFM team asked about the situation of women. OFFICIAL noted that Botswana is not that poor. Some women live nicely, some live with more difficulty [particularly] if we are talking about rural areas. The FFM team asked if they could expand. Less women in the Parliament. We agree men can do things better so that’s why women vote for men. Some women in parliament were elected, the rest were nominated. The FFM team asked if the situation had changed over time, is it getting better. OFFICIAL thought it is getting better as there are a lot of women in high positions – senior positions in the police and prisons. Women are in some high positions and maybe through education, teaching other woman, it is now time for women to have high office. In the past, our beliefs or our culture didn't allow women to thrive. We were just baby-making machines, someone who worked on the farm or was a housewife. So now it is getting better, women are getting out there, some have responsibility, some are single mothers but are doing fine.

The FFM team asked if it is the same in rural areas. OFFICIAL doubted it will be seen [women’s progress? – source did not clarify], the cost of living and lifestyle changes [impacted this], so maybe in towns people think women can do it. In rural areas, women are being oppressed as the culture they still believe in won’t allow women [to be equal to men / do the same work as men].

The FFM team asked about prevalence of gender-based violence (GBV). OFFICIAL noted that it is heartbreaking. Reading the news, every day there is a woman who has been killed, raped and [experienced] all sorts of things. The FFM team asked about how prevalent GBV is amongst women who MWTT have assisted. OFFICIAL could not say, the MWTT is still new.

The FFM team asked what types of GBV. OFFICIAL noted they are different. Some occurs at office, home and even in churches. GBV is everywhere. The FFM team clarified what types – for example, physical. OFFICIAL noted financial, physical and emotional. The FFM team asked if men are affected. OFFICIAL noted that a boy might be beaten [by his father]. The boy might grow up thinking that society should copy that. This is not correct, a man should be a protector or a provider.

The FFM team asked who are the perpetrators of GBV. OFFICIAL noted men, look at prison figures – many men.

The FFM team asked if laws and policies were sufficient to protect women. OFFICIAL, thought, yes [but] some laws and policies have left us behind. In Botswana (BWA), there is the death penalty [for certain crimes]. But when a man [kills a woman], the government decides the man has rights [so does not apply the death penalty], takes cares of the man.

The FFM team asked if the law provides enough protection. OFFICIAL doubted this.

The FFM team asked if the police can provide protection. OFFICIAL they do protect [women] but they do not have enough resources, to go to rural areas. If ask, they may come after 2 hours or say they do not have a car by which time the incident has happened.

The FFM team asked what would happen if a woman goes to the police station. OFFICIAL considered that [a woman] would be treated fairly although did not know that much [about this]. Had not come across any woman who said that [they had not been treated fairly] but it takes forever to solve [cases].

The FFM team summarised, laws and policies are there, the police are there, but sometimes protection is not effective. Is that correct? OFFICIAL, yes that is correct.

The FFM team asked what other support women get. OFFICIAL noted there is support from churches and civil society organisations. The FFM team asked if it is easy to obtain support. OFFICIAL, noted yes, it is, but sometimes the help can’t reach people.

The FFM team asked about assistance from the traditional justice system. OFFICIAL noted that the traditional system is not that effective. We have the dikgosi [traditional chiefs], we have their support. The FFM team asked if the traditional justice supports women who face GBV. OFFICIAL no. Normally these go to the High Court.

The FFM team asked if there are enough NGOs (non-government organisations) and church groups to provide support. OFFICIAL considered no, there are not enough. In rural areas where there are high numbers of GBV [cases], people don’t report. Some women suffer in silence, because they are being oppressed.

The FFM team asked why women do not report GBV – they do not know they can or because they cannot. OFFICIAL thought [women] cannot express [what happens]. For example, maybe my husband is violating my daughter, I’ll know. Because he is the provider, I'll decide to keep [quiet].

The FFM team asked if it was mainly because of the economic reasons that women did not report incidents of GBV. OFFICIAL, yes, because of the economic situation. The FFM team asked if there any other reasons. OFFICIAL thought maybe culture. Some cultures don’t allow women to have a say. Even some churches don’t allow women to have a say. Women should just keep quiet when a man talks. A woman should just follow what a man says.

The FFM team asked if women are aware of their rights (to be protected from GBV). OFFICIAL did not consider there is enough [awareness], because [awareness campaigns are?] mostly held in towns, in cities - how about those in rural areas [can’t make out comment]? It takes time, maybe people go to towns [only] once in a while.

The FFM team asked if women have access to legal aid. OFFICIAL, noted that yes, we do have legal aid in Maun. But some people don’t know it is there. It takes a long time to tell them it’s there. The FFM team asked how easy is it to access legal aid. OFFICIAL thought very easy, but there is just a lack information about [its availability], some people don’t know what they are missing. The FFM team asked who provides access to legal aid. OFFICIAL noted that the government provides this.

The FFM team asked if there are shelters (in Maun). OFFICIAL noted there is, but the location is not disclosed. The FFM team asked easy is it to access the shelter. OFFICIAL normally if a woman is sexually molested/harassed/beaten, they go to the police who take them to the shelter.

The FFM team asked about single women who face GBV, are they able to obtain protection. OFFICIAL yes [they face GBV]. As much as a married woman, every woman has the right woman to protection, to go for legal aid, as long as they feel it is safe and it is open for them.

The FFM team noted that the police now have a GBV unit. Has this changed how the police handle GBV cases. OFFICIAL noted definitely this makes [a difference]. [Women] are free to speak, [previously] when people coming and going [a woman] would not be able to express themselves. When indoors [in private] a woman is able to say anything. It's safe, definitely it's good.

The FFM team asked when the GBV unit was introduced in Maun. OFFICIAL noted not very long ago, maybe 3 months.

The FFM team asked if a woman could relocate to avoid GBV. OFFICIAL, yes, they are free as long as their finances allow, they can move. Some won't move because of their financial status, their beliefs and their culture. BWA is a free country, people can leave when they want and live where they want.

The FFM team asked how society would see a (single) woman who had moved to an area. OFFICIAL noted that maybe [in the past], society would not accept single women, but in this era they would just be accepted.

The FFM team asked if a woman who moved would be able to access public services. OFFICIAL noted that education, health, everything is free, so everyone can access this. It's only their [mistaken] beliefs that might prevent [them from relocating], for example a belief that their children can’t go to school. [But] everyone has the right to education. The FFM team asked if the state is doing enough about this, for example in rural areas. OFFICIAL noted that the government takes responsibility for providing healthcare and education, including boarding schools.

The FFM team asked if a woman makes a complaint about a perpetrator of GBV, are they dealt with properly. OFFICIAL noted that sometimes [the government does] fail us. Most women who are killed, they will have reported the case to the police, the perpetrator is arrested but later is released and kills the woman. The FFM team asked if this is common. OFFICIAL thought yes, there are many cases. The FFM team asked how OFFICIAL knew that it was common – from experience or newspapers. OFFICIAL explained that they knew the women. On that, the government has failed us. Some perpetrators are given bail then [kill a woman]. Some perpetrators kill one person then, after bail, will kill the witness.

The FFM team noted that the government had introduced the Bail Act (in 2024) to reduce releasing people on bail who go on to reoffend. Were MWTT aware of the act. OFFICIAL noted maybe it has been introduced on papers [only]. Perpetrators [of GBV] are roaming around, bail is not working as these people should be in prison; people would be alive now.

The FFM asked if MWWT were aware of cases of perpetrators [of GBV] who had been arrested, prosecuted and put in prison. OFFICIAL, yes, some are. But many are on bail.

The FFM team asked why women withdraw GBV cases. OFFICIAL noted beliefs and support. [A woman may] report [her] husband, then withdraw as he is the provider. Some family members will come after the woman.

The FFM team clarified which men were the perpetrators of GBV. OFFICIAL noted boyfriends and husbands. Some are strangers but mostly partners. Also other family members.

The FFM team has there been a change with the new government towards GBV. OFFICIAL are hopeful for change as the president is a lawyer, but too early [to say].

The FFM team asked about the number of LGBT+ people. OFFICIAL noted they are there, they open. Some have got their society, their interests. Thought they are free, not oppressed – everyone has a right to do what they want to do, live how they want to live it.

The FFM team asked if the MWTT have come across the LGBT+ population? OFFICIAL no. Maybe because the MWTT is still starting.

The FFM team asked if MWTT knew of the LGBT+ people in Maun. OFFICIAL knew of 2 people, a woman who was married but now lives with a woman. The FFM team asked if she was open, living with another woman. OFFICIAL – she lives with another women, don’t know if she is open – maybe with friends. The FFM team asked if the woman had problems from other members of society. OFFICIAL Yes. Society changes them. People believe it is a taboo. Yes, some LGBT+ people are attacked but not brutal. The FFM team asked if these attitudes vary from Maun to villages. OFFICIAL yes it changes. In Gaborone, a city, everyone expresses how they want to live. Here in Maun, it is a rural area, [people] still have [beliefs] and some may be afraid to come out because of the culture. Asked whether this observation was from having been to Gaborone [and seen the situation there], OFFICIAL noted that even if you only go for 2 or 3 days and then come back, you can see the difference.

The FFM team noted that OFFICIAL had mentioned knowing 2 LGBT+ people. Was the second one a gay man? OFFICIAL yes. Asked about his experiences, OFFICIAL noted that he has a partner but does not disclose this. People are sometimes distrustful of LGBT+ people because of [situations in which they do not initially realise a trans woman is trans].

The FFM team asked if there had been any cases of witchcraft, ritual killings. OFFICIAL – no, not in Botswana. Can’t say it doesn’t happen but not aware of cases. TRUSTEE - 1 noted that this may have happened in the past, maybe in 1960s and 1970s but now this doesn’t happen. We have stories of this happening, but we haven’t seen cases. Christianity was not as practised as much as today, ritual practices were there but most people are now Christian, so we don’t see this happen. The FFM team asked if that was mainly in rural areas, TRUSTEE - 1 noted yes.

TRUSTEE-1 commented on the experiences of women going to the police. It depends on the type of the police officer [they report their case to]. Some are willing to help but others might [blame the woman], saying she [spent the perpetrator’s money on alcohol]. Most of the cases where women are killed, they reported to the police once or twice. The police don’t follow up or question the perpetrator but let him go free. The FFM team asked if the police’s GBV unit is helping. TRUSTEE-1 [might be helping]. Children were expelled from school, the police were there [showing they take this seriously]. We are hoping for the best. As OFFICIAL was saying, if a woman is married and her husband is abusive [in front of male children], then the children will think this is normal. Now the police are taking an interest, we hope there will be change.

TRUSTEE-1 added that in the past, women only did the cooking and cleaning, but now women should be capable. Women are working for safari companies. TRUSTEE-1 noted that she is a manager but is paid less [than her male counterparts]. Some women [in other companies] have had to agree to become the girlfriend of [a male boss/colleague] because he threatened that otherwise he would get them fired. But women have a voice and the situation is getting better.

The FFM team asked whether the government is helping women to find employment. OFFICIAL noted yes. Asked whether other NGOs are also helping, OFFICIAL confirmed that they are. The FFM team asked whether help is available for [securing] employment opportunities for women. OFFICIAL noted yes, there are funds being kept specifically for women and women can apply for a grant [interview notes unclear, source did not clarify]. Asked whether a grant is easy to get, OFFICIAL noted that it is. Mainly [the issue is] that women feel they can’t do it. All in all, the government is trying to uplift women.

The FFM team summarised that help and support are there but women need to access them. OFFICIAL agreed and noted that every woman can access them. The FFM team asked whether there are special provisions for women in rural areas. OFFICIAL explained that in the case of some tenders [for government contracts], the government says they are specifically for women, or prioritise women. Asked if it is a women-friendly government, OFFICIAL confirmed that it is. She noted that the culture is dynamic, the culture is changing.

Annex P - Interview with Bana Ba Letsatsi

Date 14 July 2025
LocationLove Botswana Life Centre, Maun
AttendeesSocial Worker, Rehabilitation Centre, Psychosocial Department, Bana Ba Letsatsi; Community Officer, Psychosocial Department, Bana Ba Letsatsi; 3 HO officials

Women and gender-based violence (GBV)

The FFM team asked for an overview of Bana Ba Letsatsi’s (BBL) work. The social worker explained that BBL is a non-governmental organisation that runs a rehabilitation centre for school dropouts at primary level. BBL was established in 2002 in response to growing numbers of XXX [source did not clarify]. They keep children off the streets and away from negative influences. They empower them through education and psychosocial support, through one year of rehabilitation. They provide the conditions to enable all of the children to become confident and responsible adults. The main department is their Psychosocial Department, and they also have Education and Operations departments.

The services provided by BBL are counselling, sponsored recreation, daily meals, transport and education, with the most important service being psychosocial support. BBL has a Psychosocial Support Office through which children are recruited to a programme that supports them to return to mainstream schools. BBL does home visits around Maun and the outskirts of Maun to identify cases where children between 6 and 14 years old have dropped out of school. They do assessments to determine [school] entry points, they do school visits and they also run a school holiday programme to keep the children off the streets. During school holidays, they also invite stakeholders to come and educate and assist the children. They also undertake casework management.

The Education Department is headed by Mr. XXX. Under education, they teach life skills and provide activities to encourage the children to have more responsibility and to be the successful adults of tomorrow. They hold health and hygiene workshops for the kids and they provide education in partnership with the Ministry of Basic Education. There are about 158 children at BBL – 55 girls and 103 boys. They have 47 children who are attending mainstream schools, whom BBL have taken back to school this year [2025]. BBL have been to one XXX [source did not clarify], and there are 60 children who are attending classes out of school with BBL. BBL call it ‘OSEC’, which stands for ‘Out of School Education for Children’. That education is the reason the Ministry of Basic Education provides them with teachers. BBL has 5 teachers.

The Operations Department takes care of BBL’s daily programmes such as cleaning, cooking and finance.

The FFM team asked whether BBL’s money comes from the Ministry of Education and other donors. Social worker explained that the Ministry of Basic Education only provides them with 2 teachers. As regards finances, they are supported by volunteers from outside the country, volunteers from safari companies and individuals, especially providing or supporting them with food, clothes and toiletries.

The FFM asked whether BBL works in Maun and the Maun area, the social worker replied that they work in Maun and the surrounding areas. In some cases, when they rehabilitate children, they find that the children need to leave their challenges behind. If BBL find the kids’ homes are not suitable for children, they end up taking them to boarding schools outside Maun so that they can have a good environment which is conducive to their education. They have kids as far as Shakawe and as far as XXX [source did not clarify]. The FFM team asked how far away that is. Social worker noted that it is 5 hours away.

The FFM team explained that their main focus is on gender-based violence and asked whether – perhaps through the experiences of the children BBL supports – they would be able to comment on the position of women and their treatment in Botswana. The social worker noted that BBL focusses their policy on ‘hard families’ with socioeconomic challenges or issues relating to the shebeens. The FFM asked for clarification of the meaning of shebeens. Social worker explained that the shebeens are homes where they sell traditional alcohol. You’ll find children who live there being exposed to gender-based violence. Parents fight in front of them. There are issues of a lack of parental support, and some are child-headed families. There are parents of kids hiding their needs because the parents are driving them to have to reach things.

The FFM team asked whether BBL observe much gender-based violence in the population groups they go out and help, or in the entire community. The social worker noted that there is GBV but that government social workers deal with that. The FFM team asked whether there is a lot of GBV amongst the families of the 158 kids, including the 55 girls. Social worker noted there are a few cases and that the teachers see it when they go out, especially where the parents want to take the child from school while they go away and drink alcohol. One other thing is that they don’t have stable homes. They move from one place to another where they can’t be traced. The FFM team summarised that the children get neglected, sometimes perhaps assaulted, and then maybe the parents move, so BBL can’t keep track of them for their teams to give support. Social worker agreed, explaining that BBL have their phone numbers but they change their numbers and this can happen anytime so it’s difficult to keep track of them.

The social worker added that some children’s lives are at risk. Some of them are on the outskirts of Maun and travel 30 kilometres every day. They’re at danger from elephants. The FFM team asked if this meant 30km walking. SOCIAL WORKER confirmed this. The FFM team asked whether this was walking to school, and whether there was no bus or other transport. Social worker explained that there is a community bus but sometimes the bus is not there. Community members give them a lift sometimes but in most cases they walk. The FFM team commented that this must mean the children are walking for 4 or 5 hours. Social worker noted that sometimes they can go a week without attending school. They say, ‘Sorry we didn’t come to school. We saw footprints of elephants so we couldn’t risk it.’ BBL understand this. The FFM team asked whether it is all of the children, or only some, who have to walk like that. Social worker explained that out of the 158 children, about 10 do.

The FFM team asked whether BBL see gender-based violence cases amongst the girls they support. Social worker noted that the chances are very slim. The FFM team asked why that is. Social worker noted that the main cases they see are not gender-based violence. The FFM team noted that they were dealing with a different type of situation. When they do see GBV cases, do they refer them to the authorities, to social services and to the police? SOCIAL WORKER explained that they refer them to drug and alcohol abuse and shelters and other stakeholders. Most of their cases involve indigence. If there are issues of gender-based violence, they refer them to the government social workers, the police or shelters. The FFM team asked for confirmation that BBL do not have shelters. Social worker confirmed that they do not.

The FFM team asked whether these other stakeholders, particularly the police, are effective at providing support and investigating. SOCIAL WORKER noted that they are very effective. Stakeholders like the police come to talk about their services, what children can do if they’re being abused at home. The FFM team asked if any of these cases end up with the parents being arrested and punished. SOCIAL WORKER confirmed that they do. [Unclear, source did not clarify] BBL check if their kids’ attendance is OK and how their emotions are going. After that, they do home visits to assess the environment. They once had 2 cases in which parents abandoned their kids, and BBL referred the parents to the police. They were in detention for at least 5 days and then they went back home. The FFM asked whether sometimes, when the parents have disappeared or aren’t suitable for looking after children, children are relocated to other families, or whether there are any orphanages or care centres for children in Maun or elsewhere. SOCIAL WORKER explained not in Maun. [Unclear, source did not clarify] accommodating 0 to 5 years, but not a shelter. In the afternoon and evening, the rest of the day, they have to go home. The FFM team asked for confirmation as to whether children must always go back to their parents and BBL provide support [only] during the day. SOCIAL WORKER confirmed this, adding that this is their main challenge because they are trying to mould the children’s behaviour.

The FFM team asked whether there are many children BBL can’t reach who need support as well, or whether they think they are addressing the needs of the most vulnerable children in the district. SOCIAL WORKER noted that most of BBL’s cases involve the use of alcohol and drugs, and most of the kids are from that background. They don’t have a shelter. [unclear, did not clarify]

The FFM team asked whether most of the children they support are from quite poor families in rural areas, not in Maun itself but on the outskirts. SOCIAL WORKER agreed and noted that the parents use drugs or alcohol and the kids continue that. The FFM team summarised that in most of these households they use drugs and alcohol already, sometimes they sell it and the children are affected either by starting themselves or by being abused in some fashion by their parents. SOCIAL WORKER agreed, adding that the children can spread bad habits by introducing them to other kids.

The FFM team asked whether BBL were able to comment more widely on the position of women and gender-based violence in Maun. Was that something they were aware of, or did they have any comments based on their personal experience? SOCIAL WORKER noted that the number of GBV cases in Maun is high. Kids are being abused by their caregivers, the people who are supposed to protect them. Most of it is where the parents work on safaris in the deltas. Their uncles take care of them and there are some cases of rape, defilement, teenage pregnancy, usually because of the absence of the parents. The FFM team asked whether there is data recorded about how often this happens. SOCIAL WORKER did not have data.

The FFM team noted that the SOCIAL WORKER mentioned that the police are quite responsive and asked whether that is true for these GBV cases. Do the police respond and take action? Are they helpful? COMMUNITY OFFICER thought sometimes, noting that perpetrators can be found guilty. SOCIAL WORKER noted that perpetrators get [prison sentences of] 10 to 15 years. The FFM team asked whether that was specifically for harming a child. What was the crime committed? COMMUNITY OFFICER cited defilement. SOCIAL WORKER cited rape or defilement.

The FFM team asked whether this meant the police are very responsive for child cases, or whether this applied to adult women as well. SOCIAL WORKER noted that the police have youth-friendly, child-friendly policies. BBL don’t refer them to the main police; they take them to a special police station. COMMUNITY OFFICER added that the police there wear ordinary clothes, and there are TVs. The FFM team asked how big the child-friendly station is. How many police officers work there? COMMUNITY OFFICER thought about 4 [police officers]. The FFM team asked whether the child-friendly station is always accessible. Can you ring up or go to it? Is there a police officer there 24 hours a day? SOCIAL WORKER explained that it is not open 24 hours but that BBL work with WAR [Women Against Rape]. If there’s a case that requires urgent attention, they refer it to WAR, and WAR refers it to the police in the morning, or you can refer it to the main police. The FFM team noted that some of the children are in small communities and asked whether they can access the police, too. SOCIAL WORKER confirmed that they can, adding that they [BBL and the child] can just sit down to discuss it [with the police]. The FFM asked whether this meant in the child-friendly office. SOCIAL WORKER confirmed that it did. The FFM team asked whether the child-friendly office covers the whole area. SOCIAL WORKER confirmed this.

The FFM team asked whether there are any other NGOs that help children, and girls in particular, in this area [in and around Maun]. SOCIAL WORKER cited Bana Ba Letsatsi and Love Botswana. The FFM team asked for confirmation that the government provides support by the social services for children. SOCIAL WORKER agreed and explained that there are special programmes for children. The FFM team asked whether BBL knew how many social workers there are in the area. SOCIAL WORKER explained that there are social workers in their meetings, at all the schools in Maun and [working with?] all community leaders such as chiefs. The FFM team asked if this meant the dikgosi, SOCIAL WORKER confirmed this. The FFM team asked whether the police and the government social workers work together as a community. SOCIAL WORKER thought yes. The FFM team asked whether the NGOs, too, work with them, whether they all work together. SOCIAL WORKER thought yes.

The FFM team asked how many social workers work in Maun. SOCIAL WORKER thought more than 20. The FFM team noted that it is a big area. Did BBL consider this to be enough? SOCIAL WORKER explained that there is the District Council, and under the district they have the Department of Social Welfare and Development of Maun, where the social workers’ office is. In most cases, you’ll find that from there they reach 18 wards or extensions. They are based in their extensions, in their wards, or like BBL are in this area, there is the social worker and then there are smaller [unclear, source did not clarify]. The FFM team asked whether the district referred to was the Maun district or Ngamiland [the North West District, of which Maun is the capital]. SOCIAL WORKER noted Maun. The FFM team asked for clarification as to whether within Maun there are wards, smaller administrative units, and whether each one has a social worker. SOCIAL WORKER confirmed this. The FFM team asked whether there are about 20 or 25 wards in Maun. SOCIAL WORKER confirmed this.

Lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people)

The FFM team explained that the other topic they are investigating is the experiences of lesbian, gay, bisexual and trans people (LGBT+). Does BBL, in their work, have children who are somehow affected, or gay or lesbian children? SOCIAL WORKER explained that they do not currently have the most at-risk [LGBT+] children, that they have not identified one, but that in the community they see LGBT+ youth every day. The FFM asked whether ‘youth’ referred to those aged 14 to 30. SOCIAL WORKER explained that it meant from the age of 18. The FFM team asked whether it therefore meant young adults. SOCIAL WORKER confirmed this. The LGBT+ youth used to work for the organisation Botswana XXX Association [unclear, source did not clarify] on programmes that were provided in Maun. The FFM team asked whether that was connected with UNAIDS and HIV/AIDS. SOCIAL WORKER confirmed this.

The FFM summarised that generally now, SOCIAL WORKER and COMMUNITY OFFICER do not have any experience with LGBT+ people in their work, but that they do in the wider community. Did they have any other observations – how LGBT+ people are treated, and are they open (about sexual orientation / gender identity)? SOCIAL WORKER noted that back in the day, they used to face discrimination and stigma and they didn’t open up. The FFM team asked if this has changed. SOCIAL WORKER noted that they are coming out of the closet and introducing themselves to people. Back in the day, people would disown them, but nowadays in the community, there’s education and services and people have accepted them and accepted living with them. The FFM team asked who provides the services. Is it the NGOs and the government? SOCIAL WORKER confirmed that it is. Nowadays, we find that basically [unclear]. They provide HIV testing and counselling. XXX [source unclear] have introduced HIV testing at their facilities. Most people can access XXX [source unclear] but they are not able to XXX [unclear, source did not clarify].

The FFM team asked whether SOCIAL WORKER knows LGBT+ people who are open about their sexual orientation. SOCIAL WORKER explained that she did but they have lost touch, so not now.

The FFM team asked whether attitudes towards LGBT+ people differ in the small settlements or villages around Maun compared to Gaborone. SOCIAL WORKER thought it would be difficult for LGBT+ people in the villages around Maun to speak about [their sexual orientation or gender identity] but that in Gaborone they can come out. Those in towns can speak, they can come out. They know that. They don’t let anyone silence their rights.

The FFM team asked whether that is true for gender-based violence, too, that it’s more difficult to speak up about it in small settlements. SOCIAL WORKER thought yes, because in towns, they have access to all the services. The FFM team asked whether services referred to health, education and all the administration, the government, and getting a job. SOCIAL WORKER agreed and noted that it included other organisations, too, like BONELA. The FFM team noted that they also know of LEGABIBO. SOCIAL WORKER acknowledged LEGABIBO and noted that there is another LGBT+ NGO [in Maun], Pink Triangle.

During discussion on witchcraft and ritual killings [see below], SOCIAL WORKER noted that the most [socially?] at-risk population are gays and lesbians. The main challenge is that back in the day, people were not able to come out of the closet and lesbian and gay men got married. The FFM team asked whether these were marriages to heterosexual partners. SOCIAL WORKER confirmed that they were, noting that as time goes on, there will be challenges in those marriage because nowadays they want to come out. In fact, now their marriages are at risk. They want to belong to the [LGBT+] community so they will go through a divorce. The FFM summarised that people who are actually gay and married to women want to break up those marriages and that they were hiding their sexual orientation. SOCIAL WORKER agreed.

Witchcraft and ritual killings

The FFM team asked whether, in the communities where they work with children, BBL had ever come across ritual killings or witchcraft. COMMUNITY OFFICER thought these happened in the old days, but not nowadays, or if they do happen, there are only a few [cases]. The FFM team asked for confirmation that BBL had not heard of or witnessed any witchcraft or ritual killings in their experience in rural areas. COMMUNITY OFFICER confirmed they had not, but noted [unclear, source did not clarify]. The FFM team asked whether this was in Maun or somewhere else far away. COMMUNITY OFFICER [unclear, source did not clarify]

Female genital mutilation (FGM)

The FFM team explained that they are also interested in FGM and asked if BBL knew what that is. SOCIAL WORKER replied that she did not know. The FFM team explained that it is sometimes referred to as ‘cutting’. SOCIAL WORKER noted that it happened back in the day. The FFM team asked whether this was in Botswana or just in other countries in Africa. SOCIAL WORKER The FFM team noted that sometimes the word used is ‘circumcised’ and asked whether it used to happen that boys were circumcised and girls were circumcised. SOCIAL WORKER noted that it did, in the Kgatleng district near Gaborone. The FFM team asked whether, as far as SOCIAL WORKER was aware, it had now stopped. SOCIAL WORKER noted that it had [stopped] because of the rights in the Children's Act. The FFM team asked for clarification as to which act. SOCIAL WORKER clarified that she was referring to the 2009 Children's Act, which she noted recognises that the lives of children are precious.

COMMUNITY OFFICER explained that the introduction of education changed the situation around circumcision, too.

Annex Q - Interview with acting Deputy Commissioner, North-West District

Date 15 July 2025
LocationNorth-West District offices, Maun
Attendees Acting Deputy Commissioner (ADC), North-West District (Ngamiland); 3 HO officials

The FFM team asked about the NWD’s role in relation to gender-based violence (GBV) in the district. The ADC explained that she had not expected to meet the FFM team so did not have all relevant background information to hand. The ADC also stated that she will obtain information on statistics relating to GBV as well as the district’s policies and action plans. The district is also involved in the co-ordination of stakeholders on GBV, such as the Red Cross [the police, the Directorate of Public Prosecutions (DPP) and Women Against Rape (WAR)], [through] the Gender Committee. There are many organisations working on GBV.

The ADC continued, GBV is an issue now. In the past weeks the minister had declared we [must] do community mobilisation on GBV. So, we have [started] on reaching out to the community, going to the Kgotla and prayer (for the victims and to sensitise the public). Many people are victims, but they don’t come out, there are many unreported issues about GBV. Women who depend on a man, if they report they lose a source of income. What we are saying, come out and see how the district can help – to facilitate support for survivors. Unfortunately, we do not have many shelters in Botswana (BWA). We have psychosocial support and legal aid. Also, the courts prioritise GBV cases. The ADC further noted that unfortunately we do not have a mobilisation budget, need funds to reach areas. The Gender Committee are trying to monitor [GBV] and see how we are doing as a district.

  • The FFM team asked if the district collate numbers on GBV cases. The
  • ADC did not have these to hand but can provide these later. [The FFM team
  • agreed to write to the ADC after the meeting to ask for GBV statistics however
  • the source did not respond]. It was during COVID that the issue of GBV came
  • out.The FFM team asked if the ADC had the impression that GBV cases
  • had increased in the district. The ADC thought the number of cases was
  • going up. The police will be able to provide statistics [on reported GBV] cases.
  • The FFM team asked where the statistics the ADC referred to came from.
  • The ADC noted that [these were presented to] Gender Committee, with
  • [statistics provided by]: the police the Directorate of Public Prosecutions
  • (which say they have many cases [including many withdrawals])the [government / district] social and welfare office
  • Women Against Rape

The cases include assault, rape and so on. The statistics from different stakeholders give an idea about [the number of] cases. The FFM team asked how ADC defined GBV – rape, assault? ADC agreed these cases were included.

The FFM team asked if there were more cases of GBV or more reports of cases. The ADC could not say there are more cases, not all cases are reported. But nationally cases are increasing, and people don’t come forward [to report cases]. So, the statistics that are available are not a true reflection of what is actually happening.

The FFM team asked if the cases that are reported are processed by the police and prosecuted in the courts and how effective is that process. The ADC noted that the police file the cases and undertake investigations. The FFM team asked if cases were prosecuted / going to court in the district. The ADC could not say if these cases went to the court, the DPP would have this data. The FFM team confirmed that the ADC did not get feedback on the outcomes of cases in court, the ADC agreed. The ADC added that the reason the various organisations come together in the Gender Committee is to discuss cases going to court. There is a trend for women to withdraw cases [from being investigated / go to court]. Currently, the ADC understood that [the police] no longer allow [GBV] cases to be withdrawn [from investigation]. The FFM team asked if police procedure to always investigate GBV cases was a change. The ADC agreed, adding now there is a GBV unit in the police designated for handling cases, which is also part of the [Gender Committee]. The FFM team asked if the new GBV unit had improved how the police handle GBV cases. The ADC noted there is a national crisis at the moment, and didn’t know if the numbers will drop in a few months – repeated did not have statistics, the NWD does not record these [cases].

The FFM team asked if the government’s law, policies and campaigns against GBV are strong enough. The ADC noted that [there are protections]: the Children’s Act, the Penal Code and the Criminal Procedure Act which criminalises rape and sexual assault. There is an ongoing national review of the laws [on GBV] but the ADC was not involved in this, could not comment further. The FFM team asked if the ADC thought the policies in place are sufficient to provide protection. The ADC noted that the laws need review, but the government is trying by all means to combat [GBV]. The FFM team asked how effective these laws are. The ADC noted this comes back to the statistics. Adding that [for example], [a woman] can get a restraining order but that does not stop someone coming to [the woman’s home], there is no protection. So, we need to see how best to issue a protection [restraining] order, how to protect that individual. The FFM team asked if the woman has to ring the police to come [if the restraining order is breached]. The ADC agreed.

The FFM team asked what NGO support is there for women in Maun? The ADC noted there is WAR, Red Cross – they provide psychosocial support – there are many [organisations]: LEGABIBO, Tshidilo Stimulation Centre, Love Botswana, Queen Esther. Also prisons and DPP, the tribal administration, the district health team, and the Department of Youth and Gender. These [address] GBV but also mainstreaming of gender.

The FFM team asked if a woman faces GBV, is she able to move to avoid this. The ADC noted that family may offer support, but there are not shelters to accommodate a large number. So, this is the challenge, the lack of shelters. The FFM team asked if a woman could move by herself to avoid a persecutor, for example to Gaborone. The ADC noted people can move anywhere [but] they will need money and somewhere to stay. The FFM team asked if the persecutor would be able to follow the woman. The ADC did not know, did not follow up on GBV cases. Only hear about cases at the Gender Committee, do not have information about what happens to cases reported to the police.

The FFM team asked about LGBT+ cases. The ADC did not have any statistics on these cases or other information.

Annex R - Interview with Botswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS

Date 16 July 2025
LocationBotswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS (BONELA) office, Metsimotlhabe, Gaborone
AttendeesExecutive Director, BONELA; Community and Advocacy Assistant, BONELA; Programs Co-ordinator, BONELA; Form Manager, BONELA; 3 HO Officials

Women and gender-based violence (GBV)

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained that BONELA was formed in 2002 with the primary role of integrating ethics, law and human rights in national response to the HIV/AIDS crisis but works on health holistically. BONELA works with marginalised and vulnerable groups including women; children; migrants; sex workers; lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+) people; rural area dwellers; and prisoners – specifically in health and HIV/AIDs.

BONELA uses strategic impact mitigation as an approach to promote and fulfil human rights. They provide free legal services to those who have been violated and who fall within the scope of their work. BONELA also do advocacy, working with government to ensure that policies and laws protect marginalised communities. They also provide direct services including HIV testing, the provision of condoms and lubes, and all services relating to sexual and reproductive health.

BONELA does a lot of community organising, mobilisation and coordination to ensure that the public is aware of their responsibilities and the rights of marginalised groups. They also do research on marginalised groups primarily to inform policy. BONELA also ensure that the groups they work with are organised and part of their role is to mentor especially for LGBT+ organisations that are coming up and provide them with resources through grants. BONELA also get money from the government which they manage and disperse to the groups they work with.

One of the main issues that BONELA are currently working on is GBV, which is cross-cutting and affects all communities in equal measure but there are some groups that are more vulnerable. It's an area that currently is of great concern in the country second only to HIV because it affects the socio-economic status of people. BONELA are seeing a growing number of problems as a result of GBV. They are also seeing an increased number of femicides where women are killed by men, just yesterday there was a report of a police officer who was killed by a husband with an axe. It goes to show no woman is safe, including when with the police. So that's one area where BONELA are really focusing their attention on because it also has impact on the HIV response. If a woman is in an abusive relationship, she can't negotiate safe sex. She can't negotiate, for instance, the number of children she wants to have. She is not at liberty to explore economically how she can better herself, so she becomes really vulnerable. These are some of the issues that BONELA are working with.

The FFM team asked if BONELA had an in-house lawyer or is this outsourced? The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted we have in-house lawyers but also outsource because as an NGO we can't go to court, so we need a law firm. So, we identify cases, the internal lawyers do preparations for a case and then transfer it to the [external] lawyers who take it to court. We maintain the lawyers through a retainer. The FFM team asked how many in-house lawyers, the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR stated that currently BONELA has one (they have been affected by the USAID cuts). Usually BONELA has 2 lawyers, covering the whole country.

The FFM team asked if BONELA has research on GBV or LGBT+ issues. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that by research she meant community-based collection. So, we have a programme where we have community members identify issues within communities. Then we compile these data and share with policy makers so that the necessary policy shifts are made.

The FFM team asked about how BONELA is funded, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR stated that since 2016 BONELA’s biggest donor has been the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (Global Fund), but this has been affected by the current US administration’s withdrawal of funding. So, the Global Fund has since ‘packed’ [stopped] the funding that is supposed to come to countries, so we are currently operating without the Global Fund. We also have funding from the European Union (EU), we have 2 grants i) from the local office focussing on GBV and ii) from Brussels [directly] primarily focusing on strategic impact mitigation for LGBT+ communities – we are actually working on this in BWA, Madagascar and Mauritius. Additionally, we have funding from the Finnish Embassy focussing on GBV. We receive funding from the Botswanan (BWA) government focussing on key populations including LGBT+ communities. We play a coordination role where we receive money on behalf of other organisations and then disperse the money to the respective organisation.

The FFM team asked besides reducing the number of lawyers had there been other impacts from losing the Global Fund funding, the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR said yes. We had 86 officers in total, now we have 16 so a big cut. We also had to close our offices in districts outside of Gaborone. Previously we had about 11 offices, now we only have one office. The impact has been huge. The government is also struggling with cash flow so sometimes we have a contract with government, but then money does not come.

The FFM team asked how much of BONELA’s work relates to GBV, the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought all their work relates to GBV, in HIV programmes which include work on GBV as well as standalone GBV programmes. We have 2 donations specifically for GBV which accounts for about 30% of our funding.

The Programs Co-ordinator added that BONELA has GBV cascade programming where we meet communities at the grassroots level and if someone has experienced violence, we link them to the service providers, social workers/services, to a clinic, to the police to open a case and until they are done with the assistance. Sometimes we provide them with PEP [Post-Exposure Prophylaxis], sometimes contraceptives. Asked if BONELA receives referrals, Programs Co-ordinator confirmed BONELA does, for example from the Botswana GBV Prevention and Support Centre (BGBVPSC), to provide counselling. If their clients need legal assistance, they link them to us.

The FFM team asked BONELA to summarise the situation of women in BWA, the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought it very difficult to paint a picture. We have reached crisis levels looking at the numbers that are reported on a daily basis. But what is being reported is only the tip of the iceberg because many of these issues are not reported, some happen in rural areas which are not reported or do not reach mainstream media. It is a national crisis for us, a national problem. We are seeing skyrocketing cases of sexual violence.

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought BWA was top or in the top 5 countries in the world in terms of sexual violence, which is insane because while BWA is a big country it has a very small population. What is more concerning is that at a national level there doesn’t seem to be a strategy that we can be confident will take us out of the current situation. We are do not doing enough research to understand why GBV is happening so that we can begin to close the gaps. Now there is gender inequality. There are so many theories of why this is - how we raise boys and socialise boys into men, but these theories have not been tested. This renders our national response not as robust and precise as it should be. For any pandemic your prevention strategies should be done with precision, but this is not currently the case with GBV. We are shooting in the dark, not knowing if we are hitting the mark. Everybody wants to do something, but there isn't that level of coordination that directs resources in the right direction. It keeps happening, the more we talk about it, the more it happens.

It's disturbing family life because it affects all types of families, women-headed families who experience GBV from their boyfriends. Also shocking is that you find a married man killing a single woman who they are having an extra marital relationship with, despite the fact they are married. Even in married couples there is GBV. In religious, ‘in-cut’ [unclear, source did not clarify], poor, middle class and upper middle-class families, women experienced GBV. Makes you wonder how social cohesion can have broken so much. There is no respect for life and no consideration for future generations because they are going to be affected by this in the long term.

The FFM team asked about the levels of GBV and if it had reached ‘pandemic proportions’, what data is this based on, for example, police statistics? The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that we don't have the numbers – police statistics were released at the start of 2025. Currently we use police statistics, but not every case is documented by the police. But as BONELA works in communities – we have first-hand experience of what is happening. There isn't a day that goes by without a couple experiencing problems or one issue or another.

The FFM team asked to what extent is the increase a result of greater awareness and reporting, the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought that there is evidence of an increase in number [of GBV cases]. Wouldn't say the awareness raising doesn't have an impact in getting people to report. The sad reality is that the cases which are mostly documented are those which have reached a vital stage, where somebody has lost their life. It’s not like we are seeing more people in GBV relationships reporting more because we only see GBV cases at the end, when can be done.

The FFM team noted that EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR mentioned different types of GBV, for example, sexual violence is particularly prevalent. Did BONELA know of the relative prevalence of the different forms of GBV? The government’s relationship study of 2018 attempts to categorise the different types of GBV as experienced by participants. From that report, physical violence was reported as the most prevalent, economic / financial GBV, emotional and sexual violence were less so. There is a different report on sexual violence. However, data is our biggest challenge as currently when it comes to GBV we are reliant on data produced by the police, but most cases do not reach the police - they are not reported. So, there is quite a lot of data that is not included [in published datasets]. This is where community-led monitoring becomes important. For instance, as BONELA we can say of the 150 GBV clients we have met 30% or 50% reported physical GBV, 20% financial or economic GBV and so on. There is quite a lot of effort by civil society, government and development partners but coordination remains a problem. So, any figures you get need to be taken with a pinch of salt, they are not representative of the country situation. The FFM team asked if 150 cases referred above was a real dataset, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR said this was an illustration.

The FFM team asked if BONELA documented cases by year and type, and if these give a sense of what is going on. Yes, BONELA keeps a record, they screen every client for GBV. They also do referrals depending on the issue. The entry point is doing outreach in the community, having a discussion with someone and GBV comes into the discussion. We did a project in schools and lot of cases came out that young people were being ‘defiled’.

The FFM team asked what extent violence is committed by intimate partners (IP) or other perpetrators, for women in general its intimate partners, in marriages, and people who co-habiting and boyfriends and girlfriends. Intimate partner violence (IPV) is the most prevalent. Also see a lot of violence against children where the husband will kill the mother and children. Programs Co-ordinator noted that religious communities report that sometimes where a case is reported and the perpetrator is released on bail then they ‘pass’ [abuse] a child or rape another person. Bail is an issue, with perpetrators re-offending.

The form manager suggested that there needs to be a programme in prisons to rehabilitate offenders, so they don't come out with the same behaviour and nothing has changed as there has been no intervention. There is a need to do something in addition to restraining orders, for example there was a case of man who killed his partner at the University of Botswana in June 2025 who had a restraining order. Raises the question to what extent the police are able to enforce the law - there needs to be a systematic approach, identifying all the gaps and solutions on how to address these as well as recourse for the victims, otherwise the system is porous and you won't get results.

The FFM team asked what laws and policies are in place to protect women from GBV. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted there is

  • the Penal Code, which prevents assault and provides prison terms for offences
  • the Domestic Violence Act (DVA), which also provides protection including protection orders and places of safety.

The challenge has been implementation or enforcement of the law.

The FFM team asked if the law needed to be strengthened or is there anything missing to protect women, the EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought yes. We would like the DVA to have more punitive measures or provision to prosecute from a criminal perspective [the ACT defines domestic violence and provides for various Orders to help protect victims but does not set out penalties for acts of domestic violence]. We also think bail needs to be reconsidered for domestic violence cases - we do not consider bail should be given in domestic violence cases until the state has established there is no risk for victims. We are seeing perpetrators get bail and recommit offences. We also want to see better access to safe havens or safe spaces. Currently, we have very few across the country and removing victims from GBV [situations] is a challenge. We would like to see provision for women, children, men and vulnerable groups, for example, trans men and women. Most safe spaces we have at the moment are for women and children only, so more resources need to be made available in order to help protect all people.

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that the Children's Act, 2009 (CA) is a good piece of legislation for protecting children against violations but there is need for resources to implement it. Cases relating to children can take a long time to be handled. For example, where a child is raped, it takes 5 years for them to get justice and in some instances the child says they don’t want to deal with that, they just want to put the situation behind them.

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR added that the CA also provides for policing by different stakeholders, including ordinary members of society. If a person sees a child being abused and they don’t do anything about it the person is liable too [unclear, source did not confirm]. People see children being abused all the time but they do not do anything about it. This might be because they don't understand that they have a legal responsibility to report a case relating to child abuse. It might also be because of how a reported incident is handled by the authorities. For example, sometimes you report an incident to the police, but they don’t have a car to reach the place. So, we need to strengthen our laws, ensure the laws in place are being fully implemented and, most importantly, we need the resources to implement the law.

The form manager noted that the other issue, particularly with children, is engaging with the victim in an open court, and that although it has been suggested that there would be child friendly courts these have not been established. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that children’s courts are supposed to hear cases in camera but because of lack of resources, even in terms of having the physical building, it becomes a challenge to implement the act. Programs Co-ordinator added that law enforcement officers need to implement the law with a human lens because sometimes you have a client saying that they had a dispute with their partner, the police say they will mediate and tell them to go back [to the partner]. The next day they are assaulted or even killed. So, the police need a bit of training to approach these cases in a better manner. The form manager thought it is the police not assuming that [GBV] is a serious issue.

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that what the police have done, which is innovative, it just needs to be scaled up, is create gender desks in police stations. These help in terms of expediting access to justice for victims and in terms of dealing with cases from a gender lens, which is critical. Unfortunately, not every police station has these desks, but it's long overdue that each police station should have such a desk. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR added that when we know there is a gender desk [at a police station] we report cases directly to them and it makes life very easy. The officers don't take GBV issues lightly. They act on the cases fast, more so than other police officers.

The FFM team clarified if BONELA knew what proportion of police stations have GBV desks and are these still being rolled out, you will have to ask the police, they keep upscaling [further point but unclear, source did not clarify].

The form manager added that in a discussion with the police they had talked about how to strengthen the police further. They wanted to be able to capture data, disaggregated data, the different kinds of violations, to establish the profile of perpetrators so it is easier engage to say ok what is creating these sort of behaviour by the perpetrator before they get there commit GBV.

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that there was an attempt to create GBV courts, a pilot project in Molepolole, one of the epicentres of violence. We are yet to see whether that really improves access to justice. The FFM team queried whether the GBV courts were still in place, as they understood from other sources these had been introduced during COVID but it was unclear if they continued. BONELA thought the pilot in Molepolole was ongoing but were not sure.

The FFM team asked if BONELA were aware of the Bail Act 2024, if it was making a difference and how bail is dealt with. Form manager noted some people from BONELA engaged with the technical working group [created to discuss] the Act. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR said that BONELA specifically called for a focussed intervention for GBV cases. The FFM Team asked if that meant BONELA did not consider the Bail Act had made any difference for GBV cases. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR said not quite. There are loopholes. For instance, there was a recent case of a woman who was killed at the University of Botswana by her partner in front of people. The perpetrator had [previously] got bail, but the magistrate had been unaware of the protection order in place. There should be a comprehensive process that allows for proper screening of perpetrators and that should be the determinant whether they are eligible for bail.

The FFM team clarified if BONELA were able to participate in the Bail The Act’s consultation process and if their recommendations were accepted. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed that she was able provide input to the process and their recommendation was reflected in the Act. But she added we are realising that it [the recommendation] does not necessarily address the challenges we are experiencing in relation to GBV.

The FFM team asked if there are any specific laws that protect women from rape in marriage. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that the penal code addresses rape in general but not specifically marital rape. BONELA once had a case of a married woman whose husband was HIV positive and she was not, but the husband wanted to have unprotected sex. We wanted to showcase that rape does happen within marriage but at the time the response we got [from the government?] was that the current law addresses rape including in marriage. But don’t think this is a fair assessment, as a woman who is raped in a marriage faces a lot of challenges in reporting such an incident and dealing with the issue. There’s one’s own stigma and external stigma. Also, we have something called ‘bride price’ – ‘lobola’ – which a family pays [for a wife], say 8 cows, 12 cows, that instils the idea that when somebody has paid – that token - then they own you. When people count their properties, a woman is included.

The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought this was an issue behind GBV because men have a sense of entitlement for women. This is a challenge for a woman because the family has paid lobola so in her mind she has an obligation to provide conjugal rights regardless of what the context is. We cannot then say existing laws will help us deal with that [the traditional practice of bride price/lobola or how women are traditionally perceived]. It is the same issue when we say the Penal Code helps us deal with GBV, it can't because GBV is complicated. We are talking about a crime committed by somebody with whom you sleep in the same bed. A woman’s risk is greater [than a man], she can’t even fall asleep, she doesn’t know when her partner is going to strike. So, our laws ought to be aligned to the type of crime. The Programs Co-ordinator added that BONELA and other NGOs recommended during a consultation / workshop in 2017 that marital rape should be expressly penalised.

The Form manager noted that a key intervention should be sensitising traditional leadership because it has to change. As long as this mindset [of woman’s perceived role / position in society] remains the victim will not have agency to seek recourse or support. There isn't even the option to go and talk to somebody about it. The FFM team asked if there had been some efforts to sensitive traditional leaders, the Form manager noted that there had been some – a couple of years ago there were projects to raise awareness about child marriage and a lot of engagement with traditional leaders on which BONELA did some great work. Although discussions were primarily about child marriage, it included GBV. But not enough, more is needed and to cover the whole country.

The FFM team noted that they had heard there are a lot of reports of GBV to the police, but these do not necessarily lead to prosecution and conviction. Did BONELA know what the reasons were for this. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that the perpetrator is in most cases the breadwinner, so a woman will drop the charges because they say to themselves ‘What am I going to do?’, ‘What is the family going to say?’. We’ve also had women say that the perpetrator is the father of my child/children and she does not want to deprive them of their father. There are also issues relating to societal stigma. There's this phenomenon where people want to maintain a certain facade which is not necessarily true. This especially happens for families who have a link to religious or Christian backgrounds where there's concern about what people say. If [the perpetrator] is a pastor, even worse - what do people say about the men of God?

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR continued that there are also cultural issues. In BWA culture, when a woman gets married there is a tradition of older women providing counsel, asking the bride to put a blanket over her shoulders and telling her that everything that happens in your household must stay under this blanket. So, this is socialising a woman not to say anything if she has issues [problems within the marriage]. That's exactly what happens, people experience GBV and don't tell anyone.

But EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR added the main reason [women do not report issues] is the economic situation of women.

The FFM team asked if BONELA were aware of any examples of convictions and sentencing of perpetrators of GBV, BONELA were aware of cases of convictions but, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, noted that what is concerning is that GBV cases where a woman is killed are reduced from murder to manslaughter [for a killing of a woman] because the law recognises ‘a crime of passion’. There is a case we are using to raise this as an issue although we can do nothing about the case as it was decided by the Court of Appeal [BWA’s highest court]. A woman was killed by her boyfriend who was given a death sentence, but this was reduced to 25 years. The family came to us for help about this case and reduction in the sentence. So, we/our lawyer are looking at the case to see if there were loopholes that merited a reduction in sentencing. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that there are quite a lot of similar instances. For example, there is the case of the Botswana Defence Force soldier who killed his girlfriend and his wife. The perpetrator claimed that his girlfriend made him kill his wife and is claiming self-defence; he is out on bail.

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that we need better handling of GBV cases in the way the victims are prepared for evidence, the way that the prosecution handles evidence. Women feel that justice is not working for them. Even the language we use - ‘passion killing’ - it's almost as if we are unnoticed.

The FFM team asked what issues there are with preparing the prosecution case? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted, for example, a case where a question arose about whether the perpetrator was a good father. But if the man has killed his wife, why bring up the question – it is not a test about how good a father he is. It is a test about the man becoming something not human to the extent that they ended someone’s life. Now he is with the children, but he hired people to kill his wife. Can’t the children are [sic] subjected to an alternative situation, maybe living with relatives or taken into foster care [not clear what was said, source did not clarify].

The FFM team noted that it is difficult to assess the merits of a case without knowing all the facts. They asked if BONELA knew of cases of GBV other than femicide – rape, sexual or physical violence – committed by men against their partners which have gone through the courts and resulted in disposal – do men get convicted for rape, sexual assault, as well as murder? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted they do.

The FFM team asked about timeliness in the criminal justice system (CJS). EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that it is a general problem of disposing cases. As there are many GBV cases it becomes even more evident that cases are taking longer than they should through the CJS.

The FFM team asked if overall the CJS deals with GBV worse than other types of cases? Or is it the CJS generally? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR it is the CJS more broadly. There is not a peculiar system for GBV cases, they follow the same route for being disposed as other cases. Form manager added that timeliness is a challenge. If GBV cases are handled in the same way as other cases, you create a bottleneck and that is when people are more likely to withdraw their case and thought this needed to be looked into. There is a propensity for victims to withdraw case but the government should take these cases forward anyway, this would make a difference.

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR also noted that there was another issue, protection for service providers. We have had a number of cases where lawyers supporting victims have become victims, so that they end up moving houses because they are being threatened. Their families are threatened, so a programme around defending the defenders is needed. The FFM team clarified that the lawyers were being threatened by the perpetrators and their families, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR agreed. The FFM team asked if this depended on the perpetrator, and what did BONELA mean exactly. The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted we have a case right now of lawyer who is being harassed by a perpetrator who is using the government infrastructure and the police to harass the lawyer, claiming defamation. They are even using the police to facilitate them, to harass the lawyer who in this case is a victim because they are subjected to this just because they provided a service. The lawyer helped a woman leave BWA for the UK, running away from an abusive partner. The FFM team asked, is the partner politically connected? The EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR clarified that she was not sure if the man was politically connected but he is influential in the community. The FFM team asked if it is a live case [in BWA]? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted yes, it is. The man is out [of detention] now, it went to court not sure if the case has stopped now. This was a case BONELA were involved in. The FFM team asked if the wife got assistance from the government / police? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR explained, it is a female lawyer [who is facing harassment]. The perpetrator went to the police claiming that the lawyer has defamed him and brought instability in his family by facilitating the departure of his wife and children to the UK. The lawyer wrote to the authorities pleading to be protected. The victim is still assisting the BWA government in the case.

The FFM team asked whether apart from the police is there any state support for survivors of GBV? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR said no, there isn’t much. We know of a victim of GBV in South Africa who fled to BWA, left everything, came only with her children but could not get assistance in getting justice in South Africa or BWA. Her expectation was that the BWA government would help her and her children. But there was nothing in place to help her and her family.

The FFM team asked about support from NGOs, and if this is accessible nationwide. Form manager said there are only 2 shelters. The FFM team asked if these were BGBVPSC shelter in Gaborone and the War Against Rape shelter in Maun, BONELA confirmed this was the case. The Form manager added that there is a framework to expand these, the government is keen to expand them but resources are problem. The FFM team asked whether these additional shelters had been planned by the government or something the government would like to do.
