The Form manager noted that under Global Funding round 6 (GC6) during COVID, part of the bid for funding was to build 5 additional shelters for vulnerable populations and adolescents / women as there was a spike in young people being violated at that time. But not sure what happened. The ideal would be to have shelters in each of the main cities/towns.

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR added that BONELA had had an emergency fund to assist sex workers, who experience a lot of violence. When they experience violence they could notify us, we provide support and connect them to the police. If they needed immediate shelter, we would provide this. We also provided toiletries and medical supplies. This was a 3-year project that ended in 2024, funded by Dutch government. The same is needed for victims of GBV as most needs are not met at the time of reporting an incident. For instance, victims spend a lot of time at a police station before there can be any form of incarceration. There needs to be rapid response support from that point which would help facilitate access to the justice system in a more dignified way. Some might go to the police station not properly dressed or needing medication.

The FFM team asked how realistic or viable it is for somebody to move away from the area where their abusive partner is to escape the violence and set up a new life? The form manager said that sounds like a witness protection system, we don’t have mature system like that as in other countries. The FFM team asked if the barrier would be that the perpetrator would find the woman or is the financial difficulties in relocating. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought some women experience difficulties in taking their children to another area, as the law requires the woman to have an affidavit to take the children. The Form manager noted that the affidavit was needed to leave the country, it is easier to move within BWA. The FFM team clarified that the affidavit is only need for women who intend to take their children out of the country and there is no legal barrier for moving within the country. BONELA agreed. The FFM team asked if internal relocation is possible within the country? Form manager answered yes, the only barrier is financial resources.

LGBT+ people

During discussion on GBV Community and Advocacy Assistant noted that one of BONELA’s projects was to be in-service delivery training on human rights focussing on LGBT+ people for healthcare workers and law enforcement officers at the police college and rehabilitation and detention officers. This was to be part of the Global Fund’s grant cycle 7 (GC7) but there have been delays in receiving the money. BONELA has had high level consultation meetings with the Police Commissioner to bring them on board about the challenges in relation to the LGBT+ people as [these were mentioned in the legal environment assessment just mentioned?]. BONELA was going to do the training with the human rights office at the National AIDS and Health Promotion Agency [unclear if correct agency, source did not clarify]. BONELA has created modules for how service providers include human rights based on the Triple A Framework [?] and on the 7 principles of the right to health, such as non-discrimination and treating people with dignity regardless of their [sexual] orientation or how they express themselves.

The Form manager added that regardless of a person’s sexual orientation or how they identify the case should be taken forward. The challenge is that oftentimes needs a person needs to be accompanied when they are referred to a service provider. This is so that the person is safe in that process, when they get to a police station or go to a health facility. So, the person does not feel alone and stigmatised and someone to help the person get access to whatever service they need. As Community and Advocacy Assistant says sometimes the barrier is stigma, so there is need to train people on sensitisation and change attitudes as well as simultaneously providing services to people.

Community and Advocacy Assistant noted in the context of the law and access justice a lot of key populations - marginal groups - are unable to access because of the way the law disrespects these people. For example, if a LGBT+ person goes to the police it is difficult for them to get assistance because of the attitudes towards and stereotypes about LGBT+ people or sexual acts. The police might say ‘Why are you standing by the road?’ or Why are you dressed like a woman when you are a man? That’s why these guys are trying to rape you because you want to be a woman.’ These are some of the attitudes of law enforcement [officers] that are sometimes a problem.

The FFM team asked whether the unhelpful / discriminatory treatment of LGBT+ people seeking help from the police described previously is widespread and representative of the police in general or the views of individual officers. Community and Advocacy Assistant gave an example, which arose when BONELA were training the police. We asked what they do if a transwoman came into a station and had to be detained. Would they put her with men, women or by herself? One of the officers said they would look at the person’s ID and check the gender marker. If a man, they would put them with men who were detained. They may even charge the individual for impersonating someone else. Sometimes it is like this. There was also case of a transwoman being beaten up at a nightclub, this occurred while the court case to decriminalise same-sex sex was going on but before the judgement had been reached (which occurred in 2019).

The Community and Advocacy Assistant added that we cannot really say if 50% of the police are on board or not [with handling LGBT+ cases appropriately and sensitively], we haven’t done a dipstick [survey] of attitudes. The government’s relationship study of 2018 is old and did not specifically analyse the context for LGBT+ people. There is a gap in evidence which makes it a challenge in convincing government officials of the support needed for LGBT+ people - we have referred LGBT+ people to BGBVPSC for shelter. We only have anecdotal evidence, but government officials consider this anecdotal and want official data. So, this makes it difficult to respond to the challenges faced by LGBT+ people.

The FFM team asked if there are different ways or additional ways in which the LGBT+ experience GBV violence in Botswana, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that with regard to BONELA’s data that IPV is the most prevalent form of violence but also see also cases of extortion, blackmail, harassment and forced disclosure [from strangers?]. GBV against LGBT+ in our data is mostly from intimate partners more than GBV experienced in communities or within the family. The FFM team clarified that LGBT+ that it was from intimate partners not stranger violence, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR agreed. Form manager added that it was not like [the violence experienced] in South Africa. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that what is prevalent is stigma, quite a lot of online based. The FFM team checked if online stigma / abuse would be considered GBV and captured in statistics by BONELA, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR confirmed yes.

The FFM team asked what is society’s view of the LGBT+ community at the moment? Form manager said if you had asked this question 2 years ago the answer would have been different. There has been a good shift around acceptance by the government. There is more public engagement than there used to be. However, because of global anti-gender movements and the rise of religious extremism there seem to be pockets of religious leaders trying to push back, who see their counterparts in other African countries coming up with extreme laws and say, ‘Why aren't we doing the same?’ So, it's basically more a religious backlash. But in terms of the governments, service provision and at a community level, there seems to have been more progress.

The Form manager continued that now the new US administration’s rhetoric has almost given people permission to say, ‘This is an issue. This is wrong.’ Previously people had resigned themselves to LGBT+ issues not being a big deal, life goes on, you can provide services, you can do whatever you're doing. Now people/society feel they have agency to be a little bit more negative and anti [LGBT+].

The FFM team asked what the government’s views are. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that there was a case that challenged the constitutionality of the Penal Code law criminalising same-sex sexual conduct. The High Court ruled [in 2019] that the law was unconstitutional and recommended that it was struck down, making the issue final. But the issue was then how to take this a step further and ensure that there are protections for LGBT+ people, and most importantly that the law was actually struck down from the Penal Code. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR continued that the government of that time decided that a bill was needed to remove the law from the Penal Code, which was when we gained an appreciation of society’s views. Whilst LGBT+ have always existed in BWA and have experienced stigma but not to the extent that life became uncomfortable. But during the debate on the bill there was a lot of hostility and hate.

The FFM team asked how this hostility was manifested, in discrimination or violence? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that there were media statements and protests, to the extent that the bill was withdrawn from parliament and the law remains on the statute books [but not active] because it was causing so much instability with the 2 distinct camps at each other’s throats. In the process the LGBT+ community were bruised, they were described as worse than dogs because even a dog knows which hole to use! Those were some of the horrible statements articulated in the public domain. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR wondered how LGBT+ people who were directly affected felt, what it did to their self-esteem. She felt – as a non-LGBT+ person – they had been rendered a non-entity, as non-human beings.

EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR continued that BWA may not have the greatest numbers of violent [incidents] against the LGBT+ people, but it doesn't mean we have the most welcoming environment where people can thrive, feel accepted and feel included.

Programs Co-ordinator remembered that BONELA was contacted by the media for an article asking BONELA what they thought about LGBT+ people marrying. The article was published online and the response was appalling. There was stigma everywhere, people saying that this was unchristian, coming from the Devil. Programs Co-ordinator thought the article incited a lot of rage against LGBT+ people.

The FFM team noted the situation described above was before the last 2 years, so have things improved? Form manager noted that when the bill was withdrawn from Parliament the conversation ended, and life went back to how it was. The FFM team asked when the bill was withdrawn, BONELA were unsure – in the last one to 2 years [media reporting states parliament deferred the debate of the bill in August 2023]. The FFM team asked if the anti-LGBT+ statements were made by parliamentarians, religious groups and other members of the community? Form manager stated both [parliamentarians and others members of the community]. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that some parliamentarians represented the views of some religious groups who were organising in a co-ordinated way to have their voices heard. They even threatened parliamentarians by saying if you support the bill, forget about the Christian vote.

The FFM team clarified, since the bill was withdrawn [public discourse] has gone quiet about [LGBT+ issues]. BONELA agreed. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR added that we don’t know how the current government will approach the issue. It says it is a human-rights focussed government, but this is politics and we doubt if they will bring the bill back.

The FFM team asked if in the current environment can LGBT+ people be open about sexuality and/or gender identity. Form manager noted there was Pride in the same year [of the bill’s withdrawal from parliament in 2023 [date unclear, source did not clarify]. We have Pride in Gaborone and Francistown [International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia, Intersex-phobia and Transphobia, 17 May]. The FFM team asked if the people who attend Pride are NGOs and international groups, not ordinary people? Form manager noted it is activists. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR said you find ordinary youngsters from the community, those from who are open and out. But a lot of people are in the closet. But it doesn’t matter whether a person is out or not, there should be environment where everyone feels safe. Wouldn’t say that is the case.

The FFM team noted that BONELA suggested there were not high levels of violence. Did they have any idea of the numbers of cases? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that BONELA do not have any numbers. The FFM team asked if there are reports of anti-LGBT+ violence in the media. BONELA agreed there are. The FFM team asked who the perpetrators were? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted the case of 2 trans people in Maun. Programs Co-ordinator added there was a case of a trans woman who was beaten by a mob of boys because she dressed like a woman. The FFM team asked if the cases reported in the media are mostly about trans people? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR agreed they are mostly against trans people, not heard of cases against lesbian or gay [in the media]. We handled a case of a lesbian who faced violence from the family. The family consulted a pastor who advised that they needed to beat the girl – Form manager added to ‘beat the devil out of her’. We had to take her to a safe space. She has since relocated to Canada.

The FFM team asked if an openly LGBT+ who experienced violence could go to the police and get redress? Form manager thought alone it would be hard. As we mentioned earlier, one of BONELA’s community monitoring programmes is to accompany a victim through the [reporting] process, to make sure she gets assisted and that the service provider understands the person is not alone. Quite often a person starts the process but gets shunned at some point and then the case disappears. But if the service provider [such as the police] knows the victim has support from an organisation like BONELLA they are more inclined to assist. The FFM team asked if a LGBT+ person with the support could approach the police and get help. Form manager and Programs Co-ordinator said yes, with support. If they get abused, we find out on social media. Programs Co-ordinator noted that, for example, that a person might say I was abused by this mob of boys or by these people at Sunday soccer, I went to the police but they laughed at me saying that of course they are trans. We identify they need assistance. Alone it is very hard to get assistance.

The FFM team asked if there are examples of people having been convicted of violent attacks against LGBT+ people? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that there was one case. Even though there was evidence that the person was assaulted, nobody came forward to say they witnessed the incident. Most of these cases just die out.

The FFM team asked if LGBT+ people’s experiences vary, for example in Gaborone compared to a smaller settlement. The Form manager thought they would get more support in towns, rural areas they would not understand.

The FFM team asked in Gaborone there were safe places or areas of the city where the LGBT+ community can meet openly? BONELA said yes. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that there are safe spaces where LGBT+ people can come together. Most NGOs create safe spaces where people can be free, be themselves. They can address social security issues, those living with HIV are able to access help. Stigma free space.

The FFM team asked without NGO support, were there places LGBT+ people could go. BONELA thought no. Form manager thought perhaps a club but it may not be for LGBT+ people. But more LGBT+ people may hang out there, so it becomes known.

The FFM team asked if LGBT+ people would be accepted in the clubs. Form manager noted there have been some situations where people drink and claim they have been deceived [by a trans person] and results in violence. LGBT+ people hook up but may be drugged and robbed. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that there are dating platforms – tinder, grindr – there is ‘gay for pay’, where LGBT+ people – gay men - are targeted, they experience sexual violence, extortion, blackmail. The FFM team asked if this is growing, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR and Form manager thought it was. When LGBT+ people have groups and discussions, they talk/share about these issues.

The FFM team commented that the situation described by BONELA sounded negative but at the same time they considered things had improved for LGBT+ people. In what ways had the situation improved? EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR considered that it had moved positively on the side of government in terms of service provision and [funding for key populations with grants] providing vulnerable populations with grants, but there are still gaps in accessing health services, gender changing surgery, therapy, change of gender marker [on ID] is not available. The decriminalisation case was a historic moment, but it did not have such a big impact on the day-to-day struggles of the LGBT+ community.

The FFM team stated that they had heard that there was a court case which determined that it was possible to change a person’s gender marker on their ID, as long as the person had the correct medical documents. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR thought it not possible and added that not everyone who wants to change their marker will present from a hormonal point of view in the same way. For instance, if the person wants to present as a woman but has male [sexual] organs the government want evidence of more oestrogen than testosterone. In most cases, people do not have the correct hormone levels.

The FFM team commented that if a person has sex-change treatment it may be possible to change their gender marker. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that people self-medicate. The court case has set a precedent for those individuals with a particular medical history. Form manager noted that a person still needs resources. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR anyone who says they have been born the wrong sex, there should be a process: for counselling and surgery. Currently there is not that process. Programs Co-ordinator noted that most trans people do not have the resources to transition. Form manager said BONELA knew of only one person who had transitioned. They had transition surgery in BWA and Thailand. Not clear if the surgery in BWA was on done on the public or private healthcare.

The FFM team asked if it is possible for an (openly) gay or lesbian couple to live together. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR noted that most gay men are married (to a woman). The FFM team asked if 2 people of the same sex could live together. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR said it is possible, BONELA knew of cases. They referred to 2 women who had married in another country and come to BWA and lived together. Also, the case of a trans woman BONELA knew, but she had got married [to a woman] while her ID still stated she was a man. The FFM team confirmed that the law does not allow 2 people of the same sex to marry, BONELA agreed.

Annex S - Interview with Lesbians, Gays, and Bisexuals of Botswana

Date 16 July 2025
LocationLesbians, Gays, and Bisexuals of Botswana (LEGABIBO), LEGABIBO office, Gaborone
Attendees Chief Executive Officer (CEO), LEGABIBO; Health and Wellness Officer (second half of interview), LEGABIBO; 3 HO officials

Lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people)

CEO explained that LEGABIBO’s work is primarily the promotion and protection of the human rights of sexual minorities. She had [previously] heard people say ‘[LGBT+] rights’, but that wasn’t quite correct because there is no such thing. It’s just the human rights of people. It’s not that [LGBT+] people are in search of special rights. [For example], the same right to housing that a heterosexual person wants is the same right to housing that a lesbian wants. LEGABIBO has been operational since 2016 legally, by registration, but in terms of their work and their reach, they have been in existence since the late ’90s when they were housed under BONELA [Botswana Network on Ethics, Law and HIV/AIDS]. LEGABIBO is primarily focused on sexual minorities and the intersections of human rights, so issues of gender-based violence, intimate partner violence, are at the core of the work that they do.

The FFM team asked CEO to describe the position of LGBT+ people in Botswana in relation to the government and society at large. CEO explained that the legal status of LGBT+ persons in this country is that, [following] a [High] court decision in 2019 that was reaffirmed [by the Court of Appeal] in 2021, consensual same-sex acts are not illegal. Prior to that, it was a very contentious issue in this country, particularly because the government was of the view that Batswana as a population were not, quote unquote, ready for homosexuality. A lot of research had to be done primarily by LEGABIBO and other stakeholders to prove the case of, firstly, our visibility as [LGBT+] people and also to prove the case of it being a discriminatory clause to have in our statutes.

CEO added that in 2019, there was a case called [Attorney General v. Motshidiemang], in which sections 164, 165 and 167 of the Penal Code were contested. Everyone can appreciate where the language used in these – [such as] ‘carnal knowledge’ – comes from, because even though, strictly speaking, Botswana wasn’t colonised, the laws that inform the country to date are still very much [British] Victorian era-led. In 2019, it was decided at the High Court that, indeed, [LGBT+] people are entitled to non-discrimination just like everybody else; they're entitled to freedom of movement, dignity and so forth. The government then appealed that decision and went to the Court of Appeal, where it was decided in 2021, finally, that indeed non-discrimination has no place in the society of Botswana, particularly as it pertains to [LGBT+] persons. That’s the legal [position].

CEO explained that the societal part is quite different. In fact, LEGABIBO’s organisational strategy at the moment is called ‘Beyond the Rainbow’ because we're trying to see beyond the legal realm. CEO thought a lot of people revered the country as having made wonderful strides [in changing the law] and quite early on, at a point where people didn't think that would happen in Botswana, but it did. But what we then found was that there was still a disconnect with the average person about what the legal rulings mean. So we've had to do the tremendous work of translating legal wins into digestible sentiments for the average person, whether they're there [at a point of acceptance – unclear, source did not clarify] or not, because again, it is important to emphasise that those 2 judgments were important, not just for [LGBT+] persons, but for human rights in general.

CEO further explained that the legal status is that consensual same-sex sex is not criminalised. However, [the constitutionality of] section 167 of the Penal Code remains [untested at the Court of Appeal, although the High Court declared it unconstitutional – unclear, source did not clarify]. We are deeply concerned about that as an organisation because [section 167] speaks to gross indecency and that is yet to be defined by the courts. You can appreciate the danger of not defining it. [Gross indecency] tends to have a slightly more harmful impact on lesbians and queer women because the carnal knowledge aspect of [the Penal Code] was more centred around men who have sex with men. So nobody has quite confronted the movement of queerness as it pertains to women and lesbians and bisexual women, which I might argue is a very patriarchal thing, but that’s the status of things legally.

CEO noted that as an organisation, we maintain that there is still a lot to do in terms of sensitisation. Even just the country in and of itself, we’ve gone through 2 very different government changes since 2019. We have a new government now that wants to be human rights centred. We are hopeful and remain hopeful that they will carry the conversation forward in terms of making sure that human rights are not just an ideology but a lived reality for all, not just for certain people in society. In our instance, we still see instances of homophobia. People come in here all the time because a lot of our work also is documenting human rights violations. In a month, we have at least 3 cases of people coming in citing discrimination on the basis of their sexual orientation or perceived gender expression or identity, even though again, we have wonderful legislation. For example, section 23 of the Employment Act makes it clear that we cannot discriminate against somebody at their workplace on the basis of their sexual orientation. So you have this wonderful legal framework, but a huge disconnect. With the police, for example, people from our community have cited instances of either not reporting violations [to avoid being] further stigmatised or – particularly amongst the trans community – being misgendered [when they do report] because there's a disconnect between how they present themselves versus their legal gender recognition. [The latter happens] even though, again, in 2017, Botswana did wonderfully by having 2 cases that clearly outlined that to change a gender marker is a human right, so ideally a trans person should be able to just go to the relevant [government] office and have their ID changed. But we receive at least 6 of those [cases] per month where they're unable to access the service because there's a disconnect between what [documents] they presented and who they are. Legally, on paper, Botswana is doing great, but there's a long journey ahead of us in terms of contextualising what that legal status means for the average person.

The FFM team asked whether anyone has ever been prosecuted for gross indecency. The law is there, so has it ever been used? CEO noted that she feels very passionately about this because it speaks to issues of democracy and separation of powers. Under the current legal framework of Botswana, the highest court is the Court of Appeal. The understanding is that once the courts have decided on something, it becomes a thing for Parliament to table, whether it's scrapping a provision or fixing it. But it's not an issue for debating. However, what we witnessed the last year [mid-2024 to mid-2025] and the year before that [mid-2023 to mid-2024] was pushback from the faith-based organisations, particularly the Evangelical Fellowship of Botswana. [In July 2023], they staged a very intense protest across [Gaborone], essentially [forcing] the government to send the amendment bill [to remove the Penal Code provisions criminalising same-sex sex] back to Parliament for debate. It was meant to go for debate in the previous Parliament. My question and my concern is what does it mean for the Court of Appeal to decide something and then for a religious group to say, ‘No, think about it again.’ And then the judiciary thinking about it means there's no separation of powers. It also means that there's no recognition and value of a legal judgment, because what is the value of it if it can be debated? Even in [previous] judgments, the judges have unanimously said that somebody's sexuality is not a morality issue, that it’s not about whether you like it or not, or about giving it the green light; it’s an innate part of a human being. CEO thought that [the decline in] the funding space this year [from international donors], and just global politics, have emboldened certain stakeholders like the churches. With the mobilisation that we do, now we're witnessing a regression where they've said harmful things even to members that attend the church.

The FFM team summarised that provisions in the Penal Code were annulled by the courts and the matter went to Parliament for the provisions to be removed from the statute books. CEO agreed. The FFM team further summarised that this then ended up being debated in Parliament and publicly, about which the churches were quite animated about. So the provisions still remain on the law books but they’re not applied because the court annulled them. CEO noted that unfortunately it was due to be tabled by the previous government. Now we're waiting to see if this new government will pick it up again.

On the issue of a transgender person changing their gender marker, the FFM team noted that they understood there were cases where this had been allowed but that the individual who is transitioning is required to provide medical evidence. Was that correct? What was CEO’s understanding? CEO noted that the requirement to do that is a distinct disconnect from what the courts have decided. In 2017, there were two legal cases, the first one being [ND v. Attorney General of Botswana and others]. ND is a trans man and chose to remain anonymous. Then there was also the Kgositau case [involving] a trans woman. [Both litigants] had decided to be quite vocal about it. Both of those cases were decided maybe 2 months apart. Their legal arguments are basically the same and the takeaway from both of the cases is that to change your gender marker is a human right because it resonates with your identity and it's an iCEOate part of who you are. It's like your sexuality, just like any other part. They even handed down specific instructions to say, ‘I should be able to go to a certain office to say I would like to change my gender.’ Even we as LEGABIBO had drafted guidelines for them to say, ‘OK, given what the judgment has said, these are the step-by-step ways in which people should be assisted when they're seeking to change their gender markers.’ But in our experience, people are now being sent to court to get a court order and to then come back to the [government] office to say ‘OK, the court has said I can do this’, which is not what's meant to be happening. There have been other instances where people have had to seek psychological counselling almost to [confirm] it's not some sort of gender dysphoria, which is quite dehumanising.

The FFM team summarised that the court ruling was in effect that you could just go to an immigration office (which issues ID documents). CEO noted absolutely, yes. The FFM team further summarised that the court ruling was that you could just tell the office and they would change your marker, but now there are barriers. You have to provide evidence. CEO agreed, adding that these are barriers that were not prescribed by the court at all.

The FFM team asked whether it was individual officers creating barriers or a government position. CEO explained that the ND case was versus the government, but the way it is, for example, if someone wants to sue a police person, they end up suing the Commissioner, and the Commissioner is the body of the government. [In the gender marker cases] it was particularly the ministry that deals with immigration and so on. The FFM team asked whether it was that department that had introduced the barriers. Was it a government policy to make people provide evidence? CEO explained that her sense was that they hadn’t taken it seriously enough in terms of translating what this means to the requisite people. So, for example, if a health bill comes, she understood that there would be training for nurses and doctors to induct them on [how to implement it]. But that's yet to happen [for gender markers] because government has not spelled out exactly what it is that is expected. We, in collaboration with other CSOs [civil society organisations], have put together a toolkit of sorts to [show] this is how we should go about it, using the judgment itself, and they remain unwilling to engage. The FFM team asked whether some people are able to change their sex markers on their ID cards or whether they are all facing barriers, CEO noted that, honestly, she was not sure she knew of anyone outside of the two litigants in the court cases [who had been able to change their marker].

The FFM asked whether the government has a position towards LGBT+ people since these various rulings. CEO explained that the previous government had made a very sharp [unclear, source did not clarify] in agreement with the community to say, ‘We stand with them, we stand with human rights.’ CEO thought that even towards the end of the previous [government’s] tenure, there was a constitutional review that was actively engaging on these matters to [address the question] of whether sexual orientation should be added as a basis of non-discrimination in the Constitution. As things stand, it just has your typical sex, race, colour, but the argument from a lot of CSOs was that we need to include sexual orientation as a basis. The pushback was that we've already decriminalised same-sex sex, so why do we now need to include sex again?

The CEO added that you get the sense that there's a hesitancy pertaining to queerness as an umbrella term. But the government has been willing to engage quite positively when it comes to matters of intersex. CEO thought that was because it's a pathologized identity. It's a lot easier to [think], ‘[What a] shame,’ [about intersex characteristics as opposed to] trans identities, which are seen more as an active choice to be contrarian. She thought the government had a lot of sympathy towards [intersex people]. Even intersex-based and [intersex-]led CSOs have had a lot more success with engaging with the government, perhaps because they're seeing it through a health lens.

CEO added that she was not sure but she thought that because of the country’s history with HIV, gays and transgender men had always been the focal point through a health lens because of HIV. For example, the health programming that we used to have even prior to the stop work order was very much male-centric. She thought that had a lot to do with the origins of how people understood HIV. But very rarely do you see there being an intersection between HIV and lesbian women, for example, or intersections between HIV and bisexual women. [As for] the health responses you see if you walk into a government health facility, you're more than guaranteed to come away with condoms; [lubricants], not so much.

The FFM team asked if CEO had any sense of numbers in terms of the LGBT+ community broadly and of those who are open about their sexual orientation or gender identity. CEO noted that she did not have numbers, but LEGABIBO was in the process of doing such a study because they are trying to evaluate public perceptions pre- and post-[unclear, source did not clarify] to see if there's really been empirical changes in people's demands and hearts. But research is deeply underfunded in Botswana, so they would need to beg and beg. CEO noted that she did have numbers for the people that were affected during the funding freeze. LEGABIBO did a very rapid study on the number of people that were able to access services, for example, versus before the funding freeze. CEO offered to share that report. They got the stop work order on 28th January [2025] and only resumed activities under [a] waiver a month ago [mid-June]. The FFM team asked whether they had done a quick survey of the population groups affected, CEO confirmed yes. The FFM team asked whether she was referring to the USAID [United States Agency for International Development] funding freeze, CEO confirmed that she was.

The FFM team noted that they had heard there had been a Pride event in Gaborone attended by about 200 to 300 people in June 2025. CEO confirmed this. Asked how often this takes place and whether there are Pride events in cities other than Gaborone, CEO noted that it was important to say that, from a long time ago, whenever the global North coughs, so to speak, it’s the [African] continent that gets the flu. We really underestimated the wonderful work that USAID and PEPFAR [the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief] were able to do, not just on a development level, but also with health and gender equality. CEO thought that the current US administration capitalises a lot on misinformation, so a lot of what was being churned out from the States at the time emboldened [anti-LGBT+ people] and discouraged [LGBT+] people on the [African] continent who already knew what their rights were. Now people were hearing, ‘Oh, I can't be a lesbian anymore because Trump said 1,2,3,4,’ ‘I can't be trans anymore because Trump said there's only 2 genders,’ which again is just an extension of colonialism.

CEO added that [comparing] this year’s Pride activities with the previous year's, there's a real, palpable difference in terms of there being almost the resistance of the community itself. Partners are more than willing, but the community itself in a lot of ways feels ostracised. We as an organisation have had to do a lot of reassurance work and also just restorative justice as well to assure people because the impact of [the funding freeze] was quite dire for us at multiple levels. For example, we have our offices here in Gaborone, but we also have drop-in centres [DICs], one in Francistown, one in Kasane. We used to have one in Maun and we have one in Letlhakane. As a result of the funding freeze, because those were predominantly funded by Epic and PEPFAR, we had to close them down. They were not just offices; they were also safe spaces where you could come in and just play a game of snooker, play cards, utilise the Internet. We were intentional about creating those spaces because we understand that members of our community aren’t necessarily people that are going to feel comfortable walking into a health facility to say, ‘Can I please have ARVs [antiretrovirals]?’ The closures were hard-hitting. CEO noted that having to send that e-mail [about the closures] was one of the toughest things she had had to do this year because [it meant that] they couldn't afford it, and also from the viewpoint of staff retention. They went from having close to 30 staff to a skeleton staff of about 8, so the layers are far-reaching.

The FFM team asked if that was during the freeze. And had they now been able to reopen the clinics and re-recruit? CEO explained that, fortunately, we have been able to open our DICs across the region. But the [USAID] waiver has very specific parameters under which we can operate, which limits the scope of the work that we were doing before. For example, gender-based violence [GBV], particularly [intimate partner violence], was a huge component of the work that we were doing to the extent that we were having outreach activities, knowledge dissemination, just community building around getting to understand what GBV looks like. Under the waiver, we can’t actively discuss GBV. We can't discuss abortion or contraceptives. What we're now being tasked with is having to either find alternative funding or to get creative about the ways in which we mobilise around such thematic areas. But the scary thing is – and this is also evident in the Health and wellness officer et I’ll share based on research we conducted during the funding freeze – that a lot of members of our community indicated witnessing a spike in violence in their lived experience. For one lesbian woman in Maun, [the problems] were at multiple levels. Firstly, it was having to lose her job because she was working for a CSO that [had its funding frozen], and in the absence of a job that meant she didn’t have her own space where she could stay. So she’s been compelled to move back home with her parents, where she hasn't lived for many, many years, and they are deeply homophobic towards her. Now the homophobia has escalated at home because even the family members are [saying], ‘Well, you see, the world was right about you guys.’ So it has very far-reaching consequences.

CEO added that, at this moment in time, even going to the police is a very difficult thing to do because [the police] themselves are also a structural barrier, a reason why people often don't report, particularly if they’re the same gender [as the police officer]. For men, CEO had noticed, [if you say that the man who hit you is also your boyfriend, the police will ridicule you]. For women who want to report violence, then for starters, in this country, same-sex activity between women is deeply sexualised. It's not seen for what it is; it’s more like erotica. Nobody takes women's sexual attraction to each other seriously. It's more like, ‘OK, that's cute. You’ll grow out of it,’ or, ‘Everybody gets curious, but at the end of the day, we all know you're going to marry a man and have 6 kids.’ So even for them, when they get there, there's also the intersecting identities of being a woman and [therefore] inherently unsafe because the country itself is unsafe. Then there's an added layer of your sexuality, so those things combined make it very discouraging for survivors of violence.

The FFM team summarised that men in a patriarchal society have the expectation of being ridiculed for being gay and women are expected to be mothers and have children and not have relationships with women. CEO agreed.

The FFM team asked whether, despite there being discrimination, the government itself doesn't go out its way to harm LGBT+ people. CEO noted that the question was a tricky one to answer. She would argue that just because they're not actively doing anything to protect [the LGBT+ community] doesn't necessarily mean that they're doing enough to prevent it either. They’re being passive.

The CEO noted that as at the festive season last year [Christmas 2024], the GBV [statistics] were incredibly high], and that she was a little discouraged because the government's response to GBV had been to pray about it. She thought the FFM team would have heard about the National Week of Prayer [in June 2025]. LEGABIBO had written back to the [Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs] and said, ‘Listen, sure, but we also understand that GBV is a very structural issue, and so, we would like to help the government understand CSOs because there are things that they're not going to be able to understand as well as we do.’ The CEO noted that she didn’t know if the hesitancy was towards LEGABIBO or CSOs in general, but there had been a reluctance by the new government [to engage]. If the hesitancy was towards LEGABIBO, it would be ironic because it was the president who, as a lawyer, had represented the organisation in [LEGABIBO’s] registration case, so it’s not like he doesn’t know LEGABIBO exists.

The FFM team summarised that the government is not proactive in helping the LGBT+ community, but it doesn’t go out of its way to cause them harm. CEO agreed. The FFM team asked what type of discrimination and violence LGBT+ people experience, CEO thought these questions were always going to go unanswered because the research isn't there. Nobody views research as something worthy of investment. More often than not, we have to do our lobbying to get research passed. Rather than speak to [actual data or statistics], CEO explained that unfortunately she could only speak to the normative things that inform how [LGBT+] people are seen in the country. There's almost this tension that's happening at the moment where Botswana is under the impression that homosexuality is a European import, almost like a consequence of colonialism. However, at the same time – and CEO thought this was happening generally across the continent – there’s a need almost for decoloniality and embracing who we are as Africans. But then the clash comes here because homosexuality precedes colonialism.

The CEO noted that what’s been interesting is that when we go into the more remote areas, the grandmothers and the grandfathers are a lot more receptive of trans and lesbianism and gayness, more than, say, somebody in Gaborone. CEO thought this was because they're able to make a linkage between our inherent history as people and the knowledge that has always persisted amongst Africans, that homosexuality has always existed. It’s not like we invented this thing. There are parts of the country that you can go to, and on the markings on the wall, you can see that it's visibly 2 women or visibly 2 men. And Health and wellness officer ore – if you sit with adults in a rural area, enough stories will come up about how trans people back in the day used to be rainmakers and revered and honoured, as opposed to [being ostracised].

CEO noted that her retort has always been that what has been imported is inhumanity, because as Africans, we've always been understanding. There's never been this ostracism that happens and we've never been defined by our differences. She thought the country was still grappling with [LGBT+ people] being seen as a Western import. But the country is also having almost an existential personality crisis: who are we? Because again, if we're going to say that we want to embrace more of our culture, that means a lot of things that have come as a consequence of colonialism then have to be rubbished and that means throwing away capitalism, and nobody's going to throw that away.

The FFM team asked if LEGABIBO collects data on types of discrimination faced by LGBT+ people who come to report cases. How does society manifest its discrimination, or is there acceptance in some cases? CEO explained that there is a standard template form that people fill out. We try to make it clear to people that we’re trying to document very specific kinds of cases, because what does happen is that sometimes, for example, we've had a married couple come to see us, a heterosexual couple, even though we are a human rights organisation with our primary focus on LGBT. They came in genuinely wanting to report an incidence of marital rape between the 2 of them, so we reported it. But that doesn't do anything for the numbers that we need for the advocacy and the policy changes that [LGBT+ people] need as a community.

The CEO thought [the question of discrimination] was also tied very closely to the absence of requisite legislation around hate crime and hate speech. There has been a much greater prevalence of hate speech. You see it on social media. If an effeminate man, for example, has pink nails and eyelashes, the comments are absolutely horrendous to the extent of, ‘We should kill you. You’re not even going to make it to hell.’ CEO thought there was also a scary religious fundamentalism creeping into the country and contributing to what we're seeing within the community. Now you have people who were allies or activists calling themselves former gays and repenting, saying, ‘What possessed me for being lesbian for so long? I'm straight now, guys’.

The CEO added that there’s quite a lot [of discrimination – unclear, source did not clarify], so it's hard for us to have the numbers in terms of the reporting. But [it occurs at] very different levels [depending on location]. No [2 places are] the same. For example, when we were doing our research, it was interesting that a place like Letlhakane [unclear, source did not clarify], which is synonymous with mining, was documenting higher incidences of violence. [Gay] miners, who tend to be in the closet, so to speak, when they weren’t working were forcing themselves onto young gay men in the region. And you see that kind of context isn't something that you're going to necessarily experience a lot of [primarily] because there's no mining town per se.

The CEO continued that there are different nuances in different regions, but she thought that a lot of it [possibly violence or discrimination] is formed by the patriarchal nature of society. Society is deeply patriarchal and the country is deeply violent as well. Unlike our neighbouring countries, it's not that we've been on the brink of a civil war, because we haven't had political killings. People assume it's peaceful, but if you also look at the political history of this country, people are deeply suppressed. There was a time when you couldn’t speak candidly because there'd be dire consequences. So it's patriarchal, inherently violent, and it's cultural nuances that contribute to that. [It’s also] culture without nuance, that culture where people just assume that because you're a man, it means you must be in a suit and you must do this. If you're a woman, you must have 6 kids by the time you're 30. CEO observed that she was considered an alien for being 30 without a kid. The FFM team noted that such expectations would cause stress. CEO agreed.

The FFM team asked what problems LGBT+ people experience. Are there differences between the experiences of different groups within the LGBT+ community, for example, trans people, who tend to be more exposed (because of their profiles)? Did CEO have a sense of the scale of the problems? CEO observed that we can never speak about violence without recognising the intersectionality of violence. A person’s identity or social identity is always going to be informed by their gender, race, class, etc. CEO thought that for lesbians, for example, the fact that they are women already disenfranchises them because of gender equities or equality. Adding a layer of being [LGBT+] says to society that they don’t want to be with a man, and [society thinks], ‘How dare you?’ because that's what women are meant to do, to procreate. The churches say that, society says that, traditional leaders say that, and the solution to that is to fix it. In this country, things are fixed through violence, so that’s how we [end up with] corrective rape. It’s somebody saying, ‘I don't like the fact that you don't want to be with me, so I'm going to fix it for you.’ CEO noted that she did not have numbers but that she could confidently say there are at least 6 incidences [of corrective rape] nationally every month. The FFM team asked whether this was based on news media reports, CEO confirmed that it was, but added that sometimes in a focus group discussion, somebody describes something without using [the term ‘corrective rape’] and you have to deduce it. If someone says, ‘I’m going to rape you because you're a lesbian,’ then unless you know that it's corrective rape, you're just going to think that you got raped because you're a lesbian. CEO thought it was also an issue of language and that the language had not evolved. For marital rape, men still don't think it's a crime to rape their wives because legally it's not [marital rape is not sanctioned within the law]. But many times, they had sat there listening to women say they had sex last night even though they didn’t want to. [Yet] it would be very rare for a woman to wake up and say she had been maritally raped.

The CEO thought that the [issue for] lesbians would be the compounded notion of being a woman and the multiple identities that intersect with that. For bisexual people, [society’s] response would be that they were confused. They are belittled quite a lot, or thought of as selfish, or thought to have an insatiable desire almost like they can’t help themselves. [Society thinks] they don’t even know whether they want a man or a woman and this is viewed very negatively, as if they are so [greedy] that they want everything.

The CEO noted that it would be difficult for her to speak about gay men from a personal perspective because, as men, they tend to be the focus of everything. Even when it comes to healthcare interventions, they're the ones consistently catered for through condoms and programmes. But she thought there was also a masculinity crisis amongst gay men, because if someone in Botswana was asked who they thought was gay, they would choose the most feminine [man] they could think of because in people’s perceptions, that’s what being gay is. If someone were to mention the most macho, the tallest, the buffest man in the world and say he was gay, nobody would be able to compute that because of the notions of masculinity associated with that. CEO noted that this is quite prevalent in schools, where we're witnessing incidences of young boys being bullied on the basis of their sexuality. Other boys are going to beat up the more effeminate, quiet boy on the basis of him being perceived to be gay. Again, the patriarchal [culture] won't allow the boy to stand up and say why he is bullied, because he wouldn’t want to be thought of as fragile.

The FFM team asked whether a person could be openly gay or lesbian in Botswana and live safely. CEO noted that a person can be openly gay or lesbian, but she thought safety was often a comparative thing. For example, in South Africa, [LGBT+] protections are constitutional, and they've done absolutely everything right [legally] speaking. Yet in South Africa, one in 3 women are raped, so it’s hard to say. The FFM team asked whether the one in 3 was women generally, CEO confirmed yes. She noted that gay people in Botswana don’t wake up in the morning with the fear of not returning to their home that evening. But CEO thought it was necessary to [rethink] use of that metric of whether it's safe or not. A woman [could have to] severely conform. For example, if a lesbian woman wants to dress in her preferred way, her work will compel her to dress in a certain way so that she’s perceived to be heterosexual to avoid the violence associated with being perceived to be a butch lesbian, because men see butch lesbians as a threat to their own masculinity. CEO noted that she wasn’t sure that there had [ever] been a hate crime on the basis of sexual orientation in Botswana, but that she stood to be corrected on that. However, she thought there were nuances [in the treatment of LGBT+ people] that were worthy of greater interrogation, and that if such research was undertaken seriously, people would be quite shocked by what came up.

The FFM team summarised that on the surface, Botswana appeared to be a more tolerant environment [for LGBT+ people] than its peers. CEO agreed. The FFM team asked whether there had been any mob violence or lynchings of LGBT+ people, CEO observed that there had been an incident maybe 3 or 4 years ago in which a visibly openly gay man in Gaborone had tried to get in a taxi or another mode of transport and had been stoned by quite a number of people, which caused a spectacle. She noted that this is the irony of society, because if you’re waiting for a bus and you scream that your phone has been stolen, the community will rally around you because there’s a belief in mob justice. However, nobody supported the gay man or came to his aid because there was a rationale that he deserved what happened to him. This was why research was always going to be important. CEO noted that her strong suspicion was that these things are happening, but that they continue to be undocumented because nobody's asking the questions, nobody's funding the research. Physical violence should not be used as a metric for whether violence is happening because there are cultural things, systemic nuances, gender biases, all kinds of things that fuel violence as we know it now.

The FFM team summarised that physical violence was only one manifestation but there were also psychological and cultural practices and expectations that shrink the space people can exist in if they don’t conform to heterosexual [norms]. CEO noted that she agreed 100%. Even the inability to report cases to the police would make an interesting study. The FFM team asked whether the police have no sexual orientation or gender identity category in their record keeping. CEO noted that they do not but that it is something LEGABIBO should embark on. It would be really interesting to see on average how many LGBT identifying people walk into the police station to report a crime. The FFM team asked whether CEO had come across a case in which an LGBT+ person who reported a crime had received some sort of response, whether positive or negative. CEO noted that she didn’t have numbers but that LEGABIBO have a current case of a gender non-conforming person who was consistently verbally harassed by their neighbour. This escalated [and turned] physical and the victim in question [strongly believed] that the violence was rooted in their sexuality, so they came to us. We’re not a legal firm and although we can do strategic litigation, as an organisation we don't litigate per se. The victim had gone to the police a number of times and when they got there, they would either be dismissed or told to come back later. Through our network and coCEOection with the Office of the Ombudsman, we reached out to the Ombudsman, and they advised that the survivor should go back and get the number and name [of the officer they reported the incident to]. Once you report a crime, the officer dealing with the incident must give you a response or take further action within 2 weeks. As we suspected, 2 weeks [passed] and the issue is now with the Ombudsman. We’re looking to sue the Commissioner of Police for negligence. That kind of case doesn't happen every day for us. It’s only that this person felt a lot more comfortable coming to us. The FFM team asked whether that was the only example of a person coming to LEGABIBO to pursue a case after they’ve not had much help from the police, CEO noted that it was.

The FFM team asked whether there were other cases where LGBT+ people had been to the police, CEO explained that LGBT+ people do not feel comfortable going to the police. She noted that even as somebody with a number of privileges, she herself does not feel comfortable going to the police. She thought that was by design. The FFM team asked whether this was a general thing or to do with being LGBT+, or being a woman, or anything else. CEO explained that it’s not very encouraging to go, and that [the issue] is the nuances. As an example of nuances, the CEO noted that in order to vote, people need to show their ID. For trans people, because of the gender marker issue, their ID might not reflect who they are as a person, which also speaks to issues of democracy. As another example, CEO observed that an activist who is visibly trans had mentioned how, during Covid, she would have rather sat at home and died than gone to the hospital because she was unsure which ward they were going to put her in.

The CEO continued that even with the police, she strongly suspected that the fear, particularly for trans and intersex people, would be what would happen if things escalated. For example, if a trans person or intersex person was arrested, which cell would they be put in? If an intersex person got into a brawl, which hospital bed would they be put in? Those kinds of nuances aren't clear [just from looking at the person]. It’s not even clear with someone whose gender marker resonates with their gender expression. CEO noted that she’s a woman and her sexuality would precede her only in certain circumstances because otherwise people would ordinarily perceive her as being heterosexual, whereas she is not. She thought there was a privilege in being able to do that, to be perceived as something, whereas fundamentally you're not. Trans and intersex people don't have that privilege.

On the issue of civil society support for the LGBT+ community, the FFM team asked whether there were other groups who provide support in various ways. CEO noted that the fact there are only 2 million people in Botswana is both a good thing and a bad thing. Collaborative efforts are quite easy to do, and LEGABIBO does quite a lot of work with BGBVC [Botswana Gender-Based Violence Support and Prevention Centre] and Women Against Rape in Maun. On the intersectionality of violence as it's experienced by [LGBT+] people, she thought there was yet to be that kind of collaboration so that all of the CSOs could speak about sexual assault and rape. She thought there had never been a convening [specifically] to discuss sexual violence as it pertains to [LGBT+ people]; rather, the title would just be sexual violence and then they would speak about it. The CSOs are there and the energy is there, but quite a lot of CSOs are in a very tricky place because of funding and geopolitics.

The CEO added that LEGABIBO is like an umbrella organisation. A lot of grassroots [organisations] have emanated from us because they want to focus on their area of expertise in a way that we aren't always able to. For example, Botswana Trans Initiative focuses purely on trans and intersex issues. They've been able to foster really interesting relationships with the government and the police in terms of bringing them in for training, etc. We also have Black Queer DocX, which is more centred on bisexual and lesbian women, and they approach things from a feminist perspective. The FFM team asked whether Black Queer DocX focuses on advocacy and research, CEO confirmed that they do. The FFM team asked whether there are CSOs that provide counselling and safe spaces, CEO noted that there is Tebelopele, an [HIV] testing partner. There’s a GBV aspect to their screening because if you come in for a test and you have a black eye, they’re legally compelled to ask how you got it. They just recently celebrated 25 years combatting HIV in the country.

The CEO added that although she doesn’t say a lot of great things about her country, she thought the fight against the HIV was really phenomenal. Botswana had been exemplary in its fight and she thought this was because of the understanding that things are intersectional. It wasn’t a case of targeting a specific group. It was everybody, including sexual minorities. The FFM team asked whether that ecosystem created with NGOs (non-governmental organisations) and government which had formed to address HIV/AIDS has persisted and is moving to other human rights issues such as the LGBT+ situation. CEO noted that she wished the government saw it that way, but she remained hopeful.

The FFM team asked whether LGBT+ people can live together openly as a couple. CEO observed that she grew up having an aunt whose lifelong housemate was a woman. It took getting older to realise that they weren’t just really good friends. CEO thought it was not strictly illegal in a sense, but was more a question of whether the couple could sign a lease and pay the rent. In Kenya, there have been instances where people have been forced out of their homes for cohabiting. CEO noted she had never heard of an instance [in Botswana] where people of the same gender had been [forced] out of their home for cohabiting. The FFM team asked whether this was the case in cities only, CEO thought it was mostly in cosmopolitan areas, and noted that she couldn’t imagine [cohabiting] happening in Maun, for example. She could see a white couple living together in Maun but not a black couple, although she didn’t think cohabitation was criminalised. The FFM team asked how society treats same-sex cohabitation, CEO thought women would be thought of as roommates and the situation [viewed] as being cute. For 2 men, people would think they were really close. The FFM team asked what would happen if people knew they were in a relationship, CEO thought derogatory terms would be used. She noted that she had been out with her girlfriend before in a very public place and comments were made but they weren't kicked out. The waiters made very derogatory remarks about them that were not nice. CEO noted that this was why she wanted to [push back against the idea that] if there's no physical violence, it doesn't mean that violence doesn't exist at all, because name-calling is a psychological thing that can really affect someone. Nobody would classify it as violence, and the police themselves would ask, ‘Did she hit you though?’ It's almost like we have to wait for something to happen.

The FFM team summarised that a same-sex couple cohabiting openly may face harassment and get remarks, but physical violence would not happen often.

CEO agreed.

The FFM team asked whether it would be possible for an LGBT+ person to move and relocate around the country, CEO thought it would be quite possible. She noted that she was actually glad now that the decriminalisation of same-sex activity in Botswana took as long as it did and that the government said Botswana was not ready because that compelled LEGABIBO to do the research so that we could counter the court's arguments. In the early ’90s, the position was that fairness was a weird, strange thing, and then there was [the HIV crisis]. CEO noted she had definitely seen the evolution over time and thought it was fully attributable to advocacy and to research and to movement-building and all these things that now are severely underfunded. There was a moment in time when it genuinely felt like we were on the verge of acceptance because we had infiltrated every crevice of the country, from speaking to traditional leaders and humanising it. Sometimes when you say to somebody, ‘How would you feel if your neighbour was gay?’ it’s quite easy to be indifferent. But it's a different question when you say, ‘How would you feel if your grandson was gay?’ That humanises the question. In the level of work and the advocacy that was being done over the years, it was very little about whether or not you have a vagina or penis; it was about acceptance, just being accepting, and that phrase of Ubuntu about recognising neutral humanity amongst people.

CEO continued that this was why she is so angry at this [US] administration, because they've set us back years. She noted that she had a strong feeling that, for example, if you'd asked somebody how they felt if their neighbour was gay in 1998 versus today, [the answers would be] star Health and wellness officer y different. What we're witnessing now is more, ‘Well, as long as it doesn't affect me.’

The CEO added that we also can't underestimate the impact of the anti-gender movements that we see creeping in through East Africa in particular. She noted that she was glad that Botswana had protected its legal wins so there’d be no legal regression. But when you look at countries like Zambia, for example, who have it in their Constitution that they're a Christian nation, you can easily see how that would be ripe ground for that kind of rhetoric, and with first ladies, people are getting quite creative now. First ladies are being invited for conferences to be taught about family. This is a religious fundamentalist theory and it's coming in at warp speed. CEO noted that she worried about that.

The FFM noted that underlying the previous question was the implication that there are different tolerances in different parts of the country. Asked whether it would be fair to say that there are, CEO noted that [there are differences even between] religious stakeholders themselves. The only religious faction that has categorically said they have an issue is the Evangelical Fellowship of Botswana, but you have the Botswana Council of Churches, which is more like the umbrella for all the churches, and the former leader of Botswana Council of Churches is a huge ally of [LGBT+] people and the community. He has performed many unions abroad for same-sex couples. We were actually just with him 2 weeks ago. He was marching in solidarity with us. The FFM team asked whether this was at Pride, CEO confirmed that it was. She noted that he's never shied away from categorically saying these are God's people and that God preaches love, not discrimination. So there are those nuances as well, where there are some people that are using biblical texts to preach for love and for humanity. It's just that those minute, few who happen to be a lot louder than the positives [church groups] that are debunking the work. The FFM team asked whether it was Botswana Council of Churches that is generally an ally and has been tolerant, and if there are other Christian groups more fundamentalist in nature who are less welcoming. CEO agreed. She observed that it’s worthy of applause for the Council of Churches to categorically stand with an organisation like ours on the question of human rights and love, but [more broadly, religious stakeholders are] a mixed bag for sure.

The FFM team asked if there was anything to add, particularly in relation to GBV, CEO explained that she would introduce LEGABIBO’s healthcare officer, in particular because she deals with a lot of the programming around gender-based violence and is the person who clients predominantly meet first when LEGABIBO receives them.

The HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER joined the meeting.

The FFM team asked what the role of health and wellness officer at LEGABIBO involves, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER explained that she is a healthcare officer and assists the health and wellness manager with programming to help provision for the [LGBT+] community, specifically provision of health services in terms of HIV programming cycles. We are currently trying to move to programming for incidents for the community, so non-communicable disease, because our main focus for the longest time has been HIV.

The FFM team asked what laws there are to protect women against GBV. HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER explained that in Botswana there are different forms of violence. For the population we serve, which is the [LGBT+] community, one of the forms of violence that people face is rape [as well as] physical assaults and murder. We don’t serve kids below the age of 18 so we can’t speak on defilement, but across Botswana there’s been a rise in defilement cases as a form of violence against children. The FFM team asked who the main perpetrators of GBV are, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICET noted that physical assault [is committed by] family members. Most cases of rape are correctional rape, and most [are committed by] community members trying to correct someone's gender identity, and then there are cases from the community due to how someone identifies. The FFM team asked whether family members meant partners or the wider family, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted family from brothers and sisters to your intimate partner, so there is also intimate partner violence in the [LGBT+] community. This is usually physical assault.

The FFM team asked whether HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER had a sense of numbers. How many cases had LEGABIBO dealt with? HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted that they would go back to their database and share [the information]. A lot people are not comfortable sharing lived experiences like that. They are slow in terms of reporting to the police. There are other service providers that come to LEGABIBO seeking help but [survivors] would say that they don’t want to go to the police and report the matter with the police because they’re not comfortable being assisted by a police officer or a social worker. The FFM team asked why they are uncomfortable going to the police, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted [that there are] issues of discrimination and stigma. It’s because our service providers in Botswana aren’t queer-friendly in respect of how people identify. It's from the lived experiences of our clientele, who say, ‘I tried going to the police to report the matter but I was shunned because I'm currently dating a female. They mocked my relationship status to ask how I could date a female and why I was thinking like a male,’ something like that. The FFM team asked whether people had tried going to the police, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER confirmed that they had tried. The FFM team asked whether the police had responded, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted that [those who tried going to the police had met with] resistance. The FFM team asked whether the police ever help or sometimes help, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER observed that they do help sometimes, one out of 5 [times]. The statistic is very low because [so few [unclear, sourced did not clarify] provide queer-friendly services. But as an organisation, we are trying by all means to capacitate service providers.

The FFM team asked whether LEGABIBO also works with other service providers such as health services. HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted that they work with nurses, social workers, the police, the dikgosi (traditional chiefs) and district commissioners. The FFM team asked whether LEGABIBO goes out and provides training and guidance, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER confirmed that they do. The FFM team asked whether that was a rolling programme, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER explained that it depends on the programme that they are currently aligning to, and that it depends on the funding. The FFM team noted that they had understood from [CEO] that funding is a problem at the moment. HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER observed that funding has been very, very scarce with regard to the [LGBT+] organisations. The FFM team asked whether that had particularly been an issue this year [2025] because of US funding being paused, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER confirmed this.

The FFM team summarised that LEGABIBO would share their numbers and that the [scale of GBV] was hard to gauge. People don’t often go to the police and when they do, the police often don’t help. HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER agreed. The FFM team asked whether LGBT+ people are able to get healthcare, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted that they can’t. That’s why LEGABIBO is there as an organisation. We have a clinic to offer healthcare services for them because they're not comfortable being seen and accessing health services outside community-based organisations because of the issues stated. The FFM team asked whether this was because if LGBT+ people went to a healthcare facility they might get ridiculed, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER confirmed that it was. The FFM team asked whether this would be at an individual level rather than a government policy to discriminate, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted that it’s [at an] individual level. The FFM team asked whether they bring their own values to the workplace, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER confirmed this. The FFM team asked whether LEGABIBO also trained healthcare workers. If so, did they think it made any difference? Did they see any signs of more acceptance? HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted that they had conducted training for healthcare workers this year. They had conducted sensitisation training for healthcare workers and other service providers such as police officers and soldiers. They went around the country. Some of our community members feel like there was an impact, so there has been something somewhat different in terms of the provision of services from the service providers.

The FFM team asked whether there were NGOs besides LEGABIBO providing support in this sphere. HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted that there are many organisations. We have BONELA and BTI [Botswana Trans Initiative]. We also have Men for Health. In terms of psychosocial support services, there is BOFWA [Botswana Family Welfare Association] and BGBVC, which is at the forefront of providing psychosocial services and safe shelter for everyone, regardless of how they identify.

The FFM team asked whether there had been any changes in the GBV situation over time. Was the situation getting better or worse? HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted that it’s getting worse by the minute. The FFM team asked whether there was more violence, or whether people were reporting more because of campaigns to raise awareness about gender-based violence. HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER observed that it's because there's been a rise in violence and the law is not doing anything to hold people accountable. It’s taking a long time to litigate. If you were assaulted today, the litigation process of the case would be [concluded] after about 3 years. The FFM team asked whether people were becoming more violent, or whether [the change was occurring] because they could do things and not be held to account. HEALTH AND WELLNESS noted that it’s because you can do something [today] and get bailed tomorrow. The bail laws are really lenient to perpetrators. You could kill someone today and then tomorrow you’d be out on bail. The FFM team noted that they had heard that a Bail Act was introduced last year. Had it improved things? HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted that the other thing is that laws were being passed but were not being implemented, so you could have a bail law passed by Parliament but not effectively put into place.

The FFM team asked whether there are quite strong anti-GBV laws to protect women, but implementation is the problem. HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER confirmed this. The FFM team sked why she thought the laws were not being implemented, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted that this was a big question and suggested asking the police and social workers why the laws are not being implemented because they are the ones who are supposed to [be responsible for] the implementation process.

The FFM team asked whether these levels of violence are countrywide, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER confirmed that they are. She noted that there is underreporting of cases in remote, rural locations. If you’re in a group setting and having a conversation, for example, with LBQ [lesbian, bisexual and queer] women around mental health or GBV, someone will say they’ve been assaulted before but they didn’t go to report it. The FFM team asked whether that meant there is better reporting in bigger places like Gaborone, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER noted that there is, in the towns and cities. The FFM team asked whether people feel more confident that they can get services and support in the towns and cities, HEALTH AND WELLNESS OFFICER confirmed this.

Annex T - Interview with Pink Triangle LGBTQ Support Group

Date 25 July 2025
LocationOnline – Microsoft Teams
Attendees GG – Pink Triangle LGBTQ Support Group; 2 HO Officials

Lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people)

The FFM team ask GG for background about herself and work. GG explained that they are a human rights activist in Maun [Ngamiland, Botswana] focusing on LGBT[+] persons. They had been doing this since 2018 but begun working for [Lesbian, Gays and Bisexuals of Botswana] LEGABIBO in 2020. Had worked as a human rights activist with different organisations – currently with Safe Place International (SPI), an international organisation whose founder is in California [USA], the Executive Director in Greece, Director of Operations in India, and Global Director in Cape Town, South Africa. There are different country directors in Kenya, Uganda, Greece and Spain. GG is the country director for Botswana. The FFM team noted that GG was linked to the Pink Triangle LGBTQ Support Group (PT) and asked about this. GG noted PT is a personal project, but SPI is their job. PT is a LGBT[+] support group [operating] in [Maun]. GG is trying to register it [with the government], they do not have a website yet only a Facebook page that they are trying to revamp.

GG continued that currently they are using their life as an example that [LGBT+ people] are here in real life [be]cause for [a] long time [they have] been told and taught that being queer is just a western thing, it does not exist in Botswana, we are just copying [what’s on] the TV. So, GG holds sensitization workshops, capacitation trainings [to empower or equip people], campaigns to raise awareness on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (SOGIE).
