[This is] because [Batswana] have [been taught] that there are only 2 sexes - being female and male. Intersex [people] and [people of same-sex sexual orientations are] not really recognised. We have [been told] that being heterosexual is the only way to go. So, GG has different workshops teaching people [about] SOGIE.

GG continued that they have a programme for family interventions. When they receive a case that [a LGBT+ person] has been disowned by their family, we step in to try and talk to and teach their family that what this [LGBT+] person is doing [being gay, lesbian or trans], [is] not the worst [thing as] seen [by the family], [it is] just [the person] expressing who they are. So we try to get families to group counselling [sessions], teaching them and exposing them to more queer people and queer lives so that they can finally understand who they live with.

GG added we have another programme called ‘Sexuality and Spirituality’ where we engage with religious leaders of [different] congregations and have Bible studies with them, sit down, talk about being queer. [We] have queer people [coming into this] space, to sit down with pastors, bishops, [and] read the Bible together. [We] try to show them that it's OK to be queer [and] still worship God or Allah.

GG continued [w]e also train health professionals [which GG was doing the following week] on SOGIE. We have a lot of cases where LGBT+ people resort to backstreet health measures because they're being stigmatised and discriminated when they get to [a] health post. Instead of [LGBT+ people] being assisted when they get to the clinics, instead of [being] given medication, they [are] told what they're doing is demonic. So we train [healthcare professionals to understand] that being LGBT+ does not mean that you are an evil person as people perceive it.

GG [summarised that] generally my job is raising visibility on being queer, putting themselves out there. They [also] capacitate different heads of villages, train[ing] traditional leaders because that you cannot get in [a] village and do something without [the] chief knowing. So, we sit down [with] chiefs, train them [and] call different LGBT+ people to come [and] share their lives, their life stories, and how they wish they [could] be supported by the audience [traditional chiefs].

GG added [w]e also trained police officers because that they don't even record intimate partner violence (IPV) cases [between LGBT+ couples] that come to them as GBV or IPV. They just take them as a fight between 2 women that were just fighting or caught drunk. [The police] omit [to document] that this was a couple that came in and one person beat the other person. So we are also capacitating [the police], training them to [understand about GBV / IPV between LGBT+ people and that these are also violent cases that need us to stand up and [take] act[ion] on. The FFM team asked if the police were not documenting these cases correctly because the people involved were LGBT+ or because it was GBV. GG noted it’s [because they are] LGBT[+] cases. The FFM team clarified that the police don’t record the cases because they are LGBT+ individuals. GG agreed. [The police] don't record [the incident as GBV / IPV] because it's from LGBT[+] couples. GG added that when you ask [the police] why [they do] not document [cases] as [IPV] or GBV because this person was hitting the other one because they feel like they have an upper hand in the relationship, the response is always [that it was] just 2 men [fighting], men fight all the time, that is not something that we can waste our resources on. GG continued, we are trying to [stop] th[e] unnecessary omission or stigma or discrimination just because the relationship is not hetero by teaching [the police] and capacitating them, having [training sessions] on a quarterly basis as much as [our] funds allow. GG [had] been trying to make sure that each quarter [they] have one training [session] with different police officers. [PT/SPI] cannot afford to [do the training] monthly as the [Maun] district is big and we are trying to capacitate every single police officer, but funds do not allow that to happen. The FFM team asked if GG tries to train police officers at different stations in the district on a quarterly basis. GG explained that they don’t train each [police] station, but take representatives from each police station - for example 3 from one station, 3 from another - then bring them to one [place] because we want all stations to have someone that is capacitated, to [being able to] step in and help [in LGBT+] cases.

The FFM team asked if raising awareness and talking to different elements of society is making a difference? Are people receptive and responsive to these conversations you are having? GG stated yes. Before February [2025] - before the unnecessary executive orders that happened in US [which cut USAID] - we were [making] beautiful progress. We [had] adults voluntarily reaching out to us, to me, saying, ‘Can I be part of the P flag?’ ‘Can I be part of the movement to also help this and this and this? Because I realised that my niece is giving me [the] sense that they might be gay’ or ‘I realised that me violating people that are different from me was not OK’. Even the police [have engaged], GG noted that [they have] now a good number of police officers on their speed dial that I know if I'm not in town or if I hear I about a case of violence or assault [against a LGBT+ person they can] call [a] specific police officer [and] they will handle [the] case well till they see the end of it.

GG added that we have a number of lawyers [who can assist]. They also [know] a number of nurses and doctors if we need any health assistance and we are not sure if the people that are on duty are homophobic. There's a good number of people that we can call. [It is the same with the traditional leaders, same with religious leaders [we know people who we can call on to assist]. But after [the US] executive orders we have seen those numbers declining and we had seen some of [these people] questioning if supporting the [LGBT+] movement and being there for queer people is worth it because if [the US] – where [some people think] being LGBT+ comes from – is saying [being LGBT+] is not allowed, how would we allow it in Africa? GG noted that [people think this] even if we say [being LGBT+] does not originate in [the US], we are here in Botswana, we are [a]live, I found out that I'm gay before watch[ing] television, I found out that I'm gay when I knew America only [as a place] on a map, [before] knowing what [was] going on there. So now, with the AIDS card, [people] are relating it to Trump not condoning [people] as being gay. The FFM team clarified that the executive orders GG referred to were the US administration’s decision to cut USAID, specifically programmes supporting gender identity, and the accompanying rhetoric about gender rights? GG agreed.

The FFM team asked GG for an overview of how LGBT+ people are treated generally in Botswana and in Maun specifically. GG as [SPI] country director, they could talk about the [situation] [nationally]. Generally, if compared to South Africa, GG [thought the situation in Botswana] [is] similar. The only difference is that Botswana is not [as] openly violent as South Africa where you can be killed for being queer. In Botswana families will disown you, we get LGBT[+] people on a daily basis being disowned by their families. On a daily basis [LGBT+ people] get fired from their jobs, right after their supervisors or their bosses have found out about their sexuality. On a daily basis, [LGBT+ people] get chased out from churches. The minute that sexuality is disclosed, [people] in Botswana would choose not to physically violate you, but emotionally they will. Financially [people] will cut you off and from jobs or the support that you might get.

GG continued [the issue] that happen[s] most in [Maun] district is [that there are] a lot of forced marriages. [When a LGBT+ person] share[s] with [their] family that [they] are queer or [a woman/girl] give signs [of] masculine presenting – [they] get into soccer, play mostly with the boys – [they] get into a forced marriage, they [have] even [been] cases of child marriage. [A]fter [the] decriminalisation [of same sex sexual relations] in 2019, the defence mechanism that most families [have] is that [if the] teenage [girl] show[s] signs of being masculine [their family] get[s] them married to someone that is older. [These girls] don't even have time now to say ‘I would [like to] date a woman’ because [they’re] already married to [a] man. We are trying to fight child marriage cases time and again, same with forced marriages.

GG further noted on collective rape, we have queer people and kids [whose] mothers give consent and permission to uncles to sexually assault them in the name of correcting their sexuality. And when you talk to family members the excuse is, ‘This girl says she's lesbian just because she never tasted what a man is.’ They don’t care about consent, when you say [to the family], ‘But you violated them and this is defilement’. The fact that they're under 18 and [the family] gave an old man permission to have sex with [the girl] goes against all laws in Botswana. [The families] will find ways to hide behind culture. They hide [the girls/women] from our organisation, it is only when GG/PT/SPI do village canvassing, [travelling] around small villages in Maun [for a month or 2] when we [find out] a 15-year old [girl] is pregnant. When you follow up the case, not only is it defilement [sex with a minor] but it is corrective rape because [the girl] came out to their family that they're lesbian or that they're bisexual. [The family] were trying to give [the girl] a ‘taste’ of what a man is like. That is how LGBT[+] people are mostly treated in Botswana.

The FFM team noted that GG referred to girls who were lesbians but asked if it is different for boys who gay. Were they, for example, forced into marriages too? GG said, yes. For gay men, yes, they are also forced into marriage. The only difference is that they're forced to marriage when they're adults - when they're 20 and upwards. For [girls/lesbians] it's different because they get forced into child marriages, but for gay [men] they get forced into marriages [when they are older]. For trans people, their identity is invalidated and not appreciated at all. They [are] forced to identify as something that they're not just because they [are] told that no one can be trans. If you were born female bodied, of course you are a woman. They don't have room for being nonbinary, for transitioning to the other sex. A trans woman [will not be allowed to do roles traditionally done by women]. [Families] force [them] to do the [roles] that are supposed to be done by men.

The FFM team asked if GG had specific examples and numbers of these incidents of abuse and discrimination against LGBT+ people? GG [needed to] refer to their [organisation’s] database [for accurate numbers] but [estimated] that only 2% of people [who] are queer in Botswana are living freely [openly], and that is because of the privileges that they receive from their families. Either you're from a progressive family or you stay in a city - if you stay in Gaborone – [then] you have a higher chance of living a good life. But if you stay in the north of Botswana where you live in villages you have [a] high chance of not fully being yourself or not being allowed to live your full truth because on a daily basis they [family / community] will repeatedly remind you that what you're doing is not allowed. When a person goes to university in cities [then] comes back home to the village and tells [their family] about [their] sexuality, the [family’s] first [response] will always be, ‘You learned that in school, which is why you are not going back there. You learnt that in university, instead of them teaching you good things, they are teaching you to have sex with different people, with wrong people.’

The FFM team asked if GG had personally dealt with or had any number of cases they had assisted. GG noted that they would have to consult their database, with cases they had assisted going back to 2022. But yes, personally they've dealt with cases like that. GG was one of the cases, disowned by their family, and their sexuality and identity blamed on their education. GG was also a victim of not being given medical assistance at [a] clinic when [staff] found out about their sexuality.

The FFM team noted that GG had referred to 2% of LGBT+ people living openly. Is that something based on cases you're aware of or a number you have estimated? GG it's based on the update that we had [in November 2024] at the national LGBT[+] conference. We shared statistics, the percentages were based on that. The FFM team asked where the conference was held and who organised. GG noted it was in Gaborone organised by LEGABIBO.

The FFM team asked if GG had any numbers on the number of openly LGBT+ people in Botswana? GG did not know but said they could try and call other LGBT+ organisations to [find out], maybe we can get a rough number from the members that we each have as organisations.

The FFM team noted that there was a pride event in Gaborone in June 2025. Was there also a Pride event in other towns, for example Maun or Francistown? GG said no, [Pride] only happens in Gaborone. That's where [LGBT+ people] sort of feel safe because our families are not [there] – most of our families are in villages. The only Pride things that GG had done in Maun was a small movie and a games night where attendance was restricted. You have to have a RSVP because most people here are not ‘out’ [with] with their families. So [Pride] mostly happens [in] Gaborone.

The FFM team asked if a LGBTI+ person can get protection from the police? GG noted that we had a march on Saturday [12 July 2025] against IPV and GBV, and stigma and discrimination [against] LGBT[+] persons. We had protection from the police. If you talk to [the police] in Maun it's sort of possible to get protection because we have formed [a] partnership with the station commander. We have sat down with him and agreed that [if] we communicate in time he will always release some of his staff to assist [us] when needed for any activities that we do. That helps in making [Maun] safe for everyone in it.

The FFM team clarified, how easy is it to get protection from the police, for example, if an LGBT+ person suffers violence, harassment, or, in an extreme case, corrective rape. GG noted it's a 70-30 thing: 70% [of LGBT+ people seeking help from the police] are likely to find homophobic people there, homophobic officers on duty [who] blame [the violence/harassment] on [the LGBT+ person]. Then there is a 30% chance they might go [when there are police] that we have trained on handling LGBT+ matters and they'll get their case assisted like any other case. But if [the victim is] forced to get a restraining order, it will mean the case would have to be documented [in] the same way that you'd record a complaint from a person in a heteronormative relationship because we have Legal Aid Botswana [LAB], [which] provides free lawyers to everyone that cannot afford private law firms. The FFM team confirmed that LGBT+ people can also access LAB? GG, noted yes.

The FFM team noted that GG had 70% of LGBT+ people might not find a police officer who was helpful? GG, agreed. The FFM team asked what happens in those circumstances if someone goes into a police station, finds a police officer who is not pro LGBT rights? Will that case not be recorded or will not be given any protection? GG noted that most of [these LGBT+ people] give up and [do not] seek justice for what happened to them. [Those people who] know of our organisation [PT/SPI] and the work that we do end up coming to our office or calling for help. Then we step in and follow up the case till we make sure that they get justice. [But] if they don't know of the work we do and they don't have our contact [details], they end up giving up and never reporting. We still have cases of LGBT[+] people that say they don't trust police officers and they don't feel safe about reporting [incidents to the police]. So, they stay at home and [accept] the violence [they have experienced or] retaliate[d] [against] the people violating them because they feel the justice system has failed them.

The FFM team asked if GG had dealt with cases where a LGBT+ person came for help and they went to the police, the perpetrator was arrested and, sometimes, prosecuted? GG noted the only punishment that [a police officer] would probably get from not fully helping a client [a LGBT+ person] [would be] a suspension and a warning letter. But all of the cases brought to us we always make sure they get the assistance that they need. So we don't have any that we did an active referral, and we failed it.

The FFM team clarified that the police investigate and there is some sort sanction for the perpetrator. GG noted [that once a LGBT+ person / woman] lets us [PT/SPI] know that they were not assisted [by the police] we make sure that we get involved in that case fully from the beginning. [Finding out if] the investigation [is] still ongoing.[asking the] station commander [to tell] the [responsible] officer to always keep us [i]n the loop and if there [are] any developments [in] the case and update the [GG/SPI] because it is no longer [only the police’s] case now because [they] failed the client at the beginning.

The FFM team asked if the protection that the police provide is effective? GG noted that it is, but they do not give detail[ed] protection like in other countries where a police officer check[s] in on you at your [home]. The only thing that we can get them [to provide is] a restraining order against [the perpetrator] and getting [the LGBT+ person] to a safe house. [T]he safe houses that we use are [provided by] Women Against Rape (WAR) and our safe house that we opened on 27 March 2025. But the safe house that we have been using [is provided by] WAR. If we cannot get a restraining order, we need to get [the LGBT+ person] to a place of safety as soon as possible. Our first choice has always been [WAR’s] safe house [for women only].

The FFM team noted that the police have established gender-based violence (GBV) branch, which was present at the police station in Maun. Has that made any difference to how the LGBT+ population is treated and is able to get protection from the police? GG noted that yes, it has. Now instead of walking into the public section [of the police station] to report their cases, [LGBT+ women] go straight to the gender unit and report [there]. The FFM team clarified if the GBV unit and reporting place was in a separate, screened off area in the Maun station (than the desk for other crime reports). GG noted that, yes, [the GBV branch] have their own office.

The FFM team asked if GG had any numbers of LGBT+ cases were reported and how many were prosecuted? GG noted that for all the numbers [statistics] the FFM team had asked for, GG needed to call the person they work with and [other LGBT+ organisations] so that they can give solid numbers and not only give numbers from my organisation [but] all the organisations that assist LGBT[+] persons.

The FFM team asked how easy is it for a LGBT+ person to get legal aid? GG noted that it's as it is [for] everyone. All you have to do is report your case [to LAB], go through a screening process [to] show that you are not financially [able] to get a private [lawyer]. [T]hen after that has been established, your case goes ahead. The only discrimination that you might be unlucky [enough to experience] is if the person that is helping you [is] homophobic. But for people that GG has referred to LAB in Maun [no-one] had call[ed] back to say [they didn’t] want to follow up [the] case because [they were] ill-treated [by the lawyer], they all went on with their cases.

The FFM team summarised the government's position towards to LGBT+ people: it is not (actively) to discriminate against them, but there may be individuals in healthcare or in the police who are homophobic? GG thought the government also have a hand in fuelling the homophobia that is in all government offices. [That is] because the forms that we have [to complete] in Botswana [only refer to] female and male, intersex [is not] included. But [if a healthcare worker is going] to assist me in a hospital [or] clinic [they] only pay attention to [my sex] - the fact that I am female bodied - and overlook that I'm dating another person [who] is female bodied [they are] not going to fully assist me.

GG continued, so our request [of the government is for] forms showing both sex and gender. [If] a trans man [goes to a government office but the official only] pay[s] attention to the fact that [they are] female-bodied and overlook[s] that [they are] taking Testosterone as part of gender-affirming hormone therapy] which means there are a lot of changes in [their] body. So, the help that [an official is] going to give [the person is] for someone [who is female bodied and] only has oestrogen very active in their body overlooking that now testosterone is also active, that [the person is] taking [testosterone] shots on a monthly basis. So, we have always thought our government is fuelling that [discrimination or lack of acceptance of people’s identities], turning a blind eye to any request to make forms inclusive of everyone. For example, the Marriage Act has no provision where it says people of the same sex cannot get married, but the district commissioners tell us that they cannot wed [people] of the same sex because they have not got anything [in writing] from the [government], something from Parliament, that will say you can go ahead and marry these people. The Marriage Act does not say you cannot marry same-sex people, it is a grey area. Most of our statues are just grey areas on what to be done and what not to be done.

The FFM team summarised: the government is not actively discriminating against LGBT+ people but it is not going out of its way to help or change things to be inclusive and support them. There are grey areas in the law, such as the Marriage Act, which applies to hetero-normal people but not same-sex couples. GG agreed. The FFM team also noted that same-sex sexual relations had been decriminalised in a court case in 2019 and that LEGABIBO had successfully brought a court to case against the government to allow it to register as an NGO in 2016. Both were positive steps. GG – acknowledged this.

The FFM team asked if there are any other civil society groups that operate in Maun to support the LGBT+ population? GG noted that it is only them because LEGABIBO recently closed their office after the foreign aid cuts. GG makes sure not to get overwhelmed with implementing [support] and [training] in the district by keeping all stakeholders active and involved in cases that they do and in the work that they do.

The FFM team asked if there were safe spaces for LGBT+ population in Maun? GG, noted yes, the safe houses that we and WAR have. The FFM team asked if GG’s safe house was supported by Pink Triangle, GG said yes.

The FFM team asked if there were places where LGBT+ person can socialise in Maun? GG, noted yes. There [are a] number of restaurants and bars [owned / run by] people we have [been] trained [by PT/SPI] and some are beneficiaries of our SPI programme. So they are open to queer people and make sure that everyone that [goes is welcome]. They use the rainbow design [to indicate they are LGBT+ friendly]. There's one that's written ‘Open for everyone, but mostly if you are queer’. There are menus with rainbow designs to show that there are [LGBT+] allies. So we have a number of restaurants that have benefited from the SPI [programme] - they continue to be a good space for [LGBT+ people]. We [SPI] have also train[ed] managers and staff at hotels.

The FFM team summarised that despite there being discrimination and harassment, there are also spaces in Maun where an LGBT+ person can go to socialise and be accepted? GG said yes.

The FFM team asked how many people can stay at the Pink Triangle safe house. GG noted that it is small, the maximum number that can be accommodated is 12 - but right now we [have] 15 - because it's only a 3-bedroom house. And we have a micro grant from SFI of only USD1,000. The FFM team asked how long can people stay there and if it was for both men and women? GG noted it's for everyone [male bodied and female bodied]. The plan for the safe houses [is to] give [a person] shelter for a maximum of 6 months. But [during this time] we try to get [the person] jobs, we try to come up with all possible and different ways to empower [them] so that [they] can get to be independent because [the reason] most people come to the shelter is because they lost their jobs. Some of them have been disowned by their families, so they don't have financial support to cover the rents. So, we bring in different people, [to provide advice on] different business aspects for inspiring entrepreneurs, [support] on how total to write business ideas, how to apply for small loans, how to write proposals to fund their passion projects so they can finally, be out and about, and [support] themselves. So far there isn’t anyone we have failed get independent in the 6 months.

The FFM team asked how long has the safe house and support process been operating and how many people have you helped? GG – we have been operating [only] since March 2025 and we are currently assisting 15 people [who stay at the safe house]. [There are also people] that come in during the day for Wi-Fi and [other support] they can find [at the house]. [As of] [l]ast week, [we had helped] 210 people. [They] are still in the closet [not open about their SOGIE and] still stay with their families. So they would come in for therapy sessions, training on how to write [business] proposals, to access Wi-Fi [to do] free online courses or the online courses that we are paying for them.

The FFM team summarised the Pink Triangle safe house has been open since March 2025, and provides training, access to education, healthcare, and psychosocial counselling? GG agreed. We provide psychosocial support [and] psychological support with counsellors from WAR and a [counsellor] from the Red Cross. We also have one private doctor [who] comes in once [every] 2 weeks for group counselling and we have a psychologist that is on call, who works with Letsholathebe II Memorial Hospital.

The FFM team asked if there are other staff members in your team? GG noted we are a team of 5 volunteers. [There is a team member] managing the shelter. She is a social worker by profession. The [PT] board chair [helps with] empowerment – for example finding different proposals to help empower people. There are 2 [working] on health needs and 2 on community health work, HIV testing and counselling. Most of the ‘general’ work is me. [We] [u]s[e] our personal qualifications or exposure in the [LGBT+] movement to try and serve the people.

The FFM team asked if all the team are volunteers, does the money for project (safe house and support to LGBT+ people) come from grants provided by Safe Places International? GG noted yes, it's our only source of money. We [have a] grant [from] them this year in March [running until] March [2026]. It's a [one year] year micro grant and most of the funds we have only covers the rent. Most of the things we [have] are donations from stakeholders in the village [Maun].

The FFM team asked if an openly LGBT+ couple are able to together in Botswana and in particular Maun. GG most of the time it is choosing to sacrifice your relationship with your family, to be with your partner. Or if the other person is out and their family has accepted them, and then the[ir] [partner] [can be] more out. People that cohabitate or stay with their partners [are] renting their own spaces and for most of them their family members don't know [they are in a same-sex] couple – [the family] they're just friends. GG continued, using myself as an example, I [can] stay with my [female partner] because my family disowned me in 2020, Maun is not [her] hometown - she comes from the south of Botswana and [her family] don't know that she's queer, she has not [come out] back home - and I have my own place. So [the] way to stay with your [partner] if you [are] queer is if you have your own place. If you don't have your own place, [you cannot live with your partner] unless you sacrifice your relation[ship] with your family.

The FFM team asked, if a person has the means to rent a place, what the societal view is of a LGBT+ couple living together. GG noted that back in 2018/2019, [people] were shunning [LGBT+ people / same-sex couples] and we [would] not risk letting people know that we are a couple. We'll let people know that we're just roommates, housemates, sharing bills not a couple. [Since then with] the work that we have been doing in Maun, we have seen good adjustment [by people generally] and we have got exposure to people who are [now] OK and are tolerant [of LGBT+ people / couples]. For example, my landlord is OK with my sexuality and knowing that I have a [female partner]. My previous landlord was OK as well and I know a number of people that are renting, and their landlords know they are gay and have no problem with that.

GG continued, so it's a progressive thing, but we have people [who have had] homophobic landlords, and they're forced to move out and go somewhere else. So, there's a good share of people that don't want [LGBT+ people] in their [properties], who would prefer not to give [them] a place if they found out [their SOGIE. There is also a] good number of people that will not care that [a person is] gay long as [they are] paying rent, long as [they] are respecting the rules of their place.

The FFM team checked that the situation described was in Maun. GG, confirmed that it was. The FFM team asked if the situation was different in cities like Gaborone or Francistown. GG noted that in the city it is fine whether you're gay or not – [people there] don't care [as] long as you pay [rent]. Also, city life is so busy [landlords] barely care about what you're doing and what you're not doing, you can get in a place and start renting a place without meeting your landlord - all you have to do is you receive a lease agreement. You exchange the document, dealing with xx of this number and the ID number is this, and you sign [and] e-mail the lease agreement, meet [the landlord] over a zoom call or over a phone call, find the keys and that's it. [People in Gaborone] don’t get to meet [their landlords] and sit down with them as compared to the village. [In the village] you have to meet with the landlord, sit down with them, listen to them – to the rules for their house, the rules for their yard and what time you have to be back and what you can and cannot do.

The FFM team clarified that when GG referred to city, they meant Gaborone? GG noted that they [were] specifically referring to Gaborone because although Francistown is the second city, it is also culturally and traditionally ‘saturated’, there are a lot of cultures that do not condone being queer and are very big on child and forced marriages. So, this freedom you can mostly find it in Gaborone and a few surrounding areas of Gaborone.

The FFM team asked if it is possible for a LGBT+ person to access services such as healthcare, education (other public services), if they were to move from one area to another, for example, from Gaborone to Maun. GG, noted yes, they can. Botswana is big on the right to education for everyone. For accommodation, the way to get this is keeping your sexuality private, show up as an apparently ‘normal’ straight human being and make sure they don't get to know that you are queer or you're gay. As for health, unfortunately, there's no way you can withhold your sexual orientation / gender identity because health workers will eventually ask if you are sexually active [and if you have a partner]. So, you are forced to disclose and share this with them, but LGBT+ people can get services. But it is not as easy as it is for heterosexual people. So GG summed up for:

  • education, it's a green light
  • accommodation LGBT+ people have to be smart with it, don't just show up and [be open about their sexual orientation / gender identity] if [they] desperately need accommodation because there is a high chance [of coming across] homophobic landlords
  • health – there are occasions a LGBT+ person won’t get assisted once they reveal their sexuality

The FFM team clarified that with regard to healthcare, the negative experience / discrimination is because of the views / values of the individual healthcare worker not because of institutional discrimination. GG agreed. The FFM team clarified if GG’s comments with regard to healthcare were about Maun or nationally? GG noted they were talking about nationally. The FFM team further clarified, within the country is Gaborone the most tolerant, Maun less so and in small villages it is very difficult for LGBT+ people. GG agreed.

The FFM team asked if it is the same for employment – do LGBT+ people face discrimination? GG, there is a lot of discrimination on the employment side, [but the] people [who] suffer [most] are the trans community. [Employers see an] ID telling [them] that [a trans woman is] male-bodied, but [the person sitting before them [is p]utting on a dress or makeup. So those [trans people] are really feeling the ‘heat’ when it comes to employment. [Employers would think], ‘I would not have my company be associated with people like you or things like you’ ([we’ve reached a point where trans people] as things now). If you ask [employers] about [what is the] dress code, they don't have anything solid to [say why the trans person’s] dress code is against [the company’s policy - why the trans woman is not conforming] but on [a] personal basis they will choose not to hire [the trans person], saying it will tarnish the company’s image. For [LGB+ people], if you identify with your sex, if you are cisgendered, it's easy for you to get a job. The only risk is after some time [the employer] find[s] out about your sexuality.

The FFM team clarified, if a LGBT+ person – a lesbian – is open about their sexual orientation, they may it difficult to get a job, or if a person is discreet about their sexual orientation but this becomes known they may risk losing their job. GG agreed. Yes, if you are discreet and later [the] employer finds out you have a greater chance of losing your job.

The FFM team asked in all these areas of potential discrimination how often this happens and how many people are involved – are there statistics? GG, as already mentioned they will need to gather together the statistics after the meeting. But off the top of my head for June, I have received emergency requests from about 10 people that lost their jobs [after] their supervisor or bosses learning about their sexuality. The FFM team asked clarified if that was in Maun only. GG noted, no, different parts of Botswana. Those are people that are the alumni of the leadership course provided by SPI, not general queer people.

The FFM team asked if the attitudes of employers change with different types of job or in different industries? GG noted yes. We have not [had] any complaint[s] from private law firms or someone saying the government did not hire me because I identify as queer. We have nurses that are LGBT+. We have lawyers that are LGBT+. We have police officers that are LGBT+. We have a lot of LGBT+ people that are soldiers, and none of them has ever filed a complaint during our training saying, ‘I was ill-treated because I'm masculine presenting’. [The] big problem [is in] the private sector. GG [speculated] in the private sector, let's say I'm in HR [human resources], [there is a] high chance of me being a best friend with the boss or sharing with the boss people [information about who they met] and not really following the [company’s employment] rule[s]. But in the private sector we have a lot [of complaints], shops, companies, restaurants, bars, tourism.

The FFM team asked about the treatment of soldiers, does the government say that it will recruit people who are openly gay? GG noted [the government] put[s] out an [advert] and memo for the whole country. GG thought that every year [the government] recruit[s] people and the requirements are to be fit, not have any chronic illness[es], to be a certain height, a certain weight [but there is] nothing [about how you identify], nothing [about] where you come from, nothing singling out anyone. So that's the reason why LGBT+ people run to be soldiers or police officers, because the qualifications are basically fitness. The FFM team asked if anyone can be openly gay in the army? GG thought yes.

The FFM team asked if gay men and lesbians are treated differently, is gender an issue? GG, yes, they are different. Lesbians are very vulnerable to corrective rape. Feminine presenting gay men are very vulnerable to random assaults, physical assaults. For trans people, [they are most] vulnerable to unemployment because of how they present themselves. And for bisexual people, [they] are vulnerable to all of [these issues] because they assaulted in marriages because they're attracted to the other sex, when they get to healthcare providers they'll called it upon themselves because they're dating 2 different people, why not stick to one sex? Because there is a stereotype that [bisexual people] spread HIV or [sexually transmitted diseases] STIs. These are the top issues that GG had seen reflect[ed] in different groups as they come [to PT / SPI]. [So] corrective rape is mostly for lesbians, physical assaults for feminine gay men and unemployment or retrenchment from jobs for trans people. It is very difficult for a transgender person to get a job compared to any other [LGBT+] group.

The FFM team asked are transgender individuals also vulnerable to physical assault and violence? GG noted that they are. Which is why, for example, if I'm born and bred in Maun, the best way for me to live my life and be safe is [to] relocate to a different place and be trans there because people won't know that I was born male. They're only going to see the female version of me. That way I'm not prone to any violence or abuse as compared to if I am fully transitioning and in Maun. So always safe thing to do is relocate into a different place.

The FFM team asked if relocation within the country is possible, are there any barriers? GG, thought no [problem]. Within the country it is easy, if you have means to fund your life, you have a place to live and you manage to get a job.

The FFM team asked besides Pink Triangle, LEGABIBO and BONELA, are you aware of other organisations, NGOs, that help out and provide any form of support - counselling, financial, healthcare - to LGBT+ people? GG noted, yes, there is Botswana Trans Initiative and Success Capital [GG provided contact details at each organisation].

The FFM team asked since the same-sex law was decriminalised in 2019, has there been a noticeable change in attitudes towards LGBT+ people? GG funnily enough, we feel like the decriminalisation has put us in danger. Now if you are little diverse, our parents associate this with being gay. Before the change of law they ignored it, they did not care. Now they have been exposed to new terms, now you can be lesbian or gay. The parents used to think a same sex couple were just best friends. Also, we did not have [the] pressure of ‘coming out’. Now, after the decriminalisation, parents are questioning everything, you are forced to explain yourself. They see you putting on any pants [trousers] that you bought, they say, ‘So now you're also a lesbian?’, ‘Now you're also gay because you're a man and you're doing your hair?’. Parents / people before the decriminalisation were just ignorant, [they] even had a traditional term if you were male bodied [but] feminine presenting that explains you are only comfortable around women [but] [acknowledged] that you are a man. They didn't know anything about being gay. So, the decriminalisation legally was a good win, but in practice it was a gun to our heads because now we are forced to come out, explain everything we do, why we are different, where we are diverse.

[NB GG did not provide the UKHO FFM with statistics subsequent to the meeting.]

Annex U - Interview with the Botswana Police Service

Date 11 July 2025
LocationBotswana Police Service, Zambezi Towers, Gaborone
Attendees 6 BPS senior officials; 3 HO officials

Women and gender-based violence (GBV)

OFFICIALS explained that Botswana Police Service (BPS) had prepared a brief to share the FFM team on the gender-based violence situation (GBV) in Botswana:

‘Botswana Police Service is mandated to ensure the safety and security of the people of Botswana and the residents of Botswana by section 6 of the Botswana Police Act, Chapter 21:01. The mandate of the Botswana police is to prevent and detect crime, repress internal disturbances, maintain security and public tranquillity, apprehend offenders and bring them to justice, and to enforce all written laws with which it is directly charged to generally maintain peace. Therefore, as a result, the Botswana Police Service has prioritised the fight against gender-based violence in its policing agenda. Maybe there's a need for us to inform you about the staff complement of the Botswana Police Service, or the BPS. I’ll keep on referring to it as the BPS. The country of Botswana is policed by 5 divisions, and from the 5 divisions, 17 districts, 84 police stations and 384 police posts.

‘Over the years, the BPS has continually employed various measures and interventions to ensure prompt response to GBV reports, safety of parties involved and protection of the vulnerable. I wish to state that a surge in GBV-related reports and child abuse noted over the years the advent of Covid-19, escalating statistics on GBV were reported. That is, during the Covid era, we recorded an increase in the number of GBV cases. There was a very sharp increase in the number of GBV-related offences during the lockdowns imposed from April 2020 as well as offences against children. This has not only raised awareness on the prevalence of GBV issues, but also served as an urgent demand for a change in the BPS responsiveness towards combatting GBV and child-related offences.

‘As a result, BPS found it imperative to establish a Branch dedicated to dealing with cases of GBV. So in April 2021, the Gender and Child Protection Branch was established as a strategic initiative towards efficient and effective tackling of these crimes. The mandate of the branch is to provide investigative support in cases of GBV and crimes involving children in all environments they are in, including offences which are facilitated by the use of the Internet. The formation of this branch was necessitated by a number of factors, such as the prevalence of GBV-related offences and also compliance with international and regional instruments and protocols, such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the [UN] Convention on the Rights of the Child, the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child and the [UN] Convention on Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women. Furthermore, recommendations from various studies and reports – inter alia, the 2012 GBV study [The Gender based violence indicators study], the 2018 relationship study [Botswana National Relationship Study] and the 2004 CRC reports placed a demand on the police for specialised and focused services, specifically tailored on GBV victims and vulnerable groups such as children. Since its inception, the branch has been working progressively towards improving response and handling of GBV cases, integration of child-friendly policing concepts to our processes, strengthening partnerships for a seamless and comprehensive service, improving the experience of victims on reporting cases and ensuring that police officers are equipped with the necessary training to respond to GBV and all crimes against children.

‘We do have some achievements that we would like to share with you that were made after the establishment of the branch itself. We have seen improved access to services. We have the GBV toll-free number [0800 600 144] where victims can call from the comfort of their homes at any time. We also have created safer spaces for reporting. Furthermore, we make case follow-ups from social media platforms. There there's also the integration and child-friendly policing concept. The BPS established victim- and child-friendly spaces as a measure to eliminate disparities in accessing of justice for all victims, including key populations and those in vulnerable situations. We have 8 child-friendly centres across the country. These centres were developed to strengthen child-friendly and age-sensitive procedures for children in contact with the law. The objective of establishing these facilities was to create a justice system which is more aligned with children's specific and development needs and to facilitate child participation. This is a step in the right direction to attain improved access to justice. The BPS has also developed a set of guiding principles aimed at ensuring that officers are committed to integrating GBV into their work and are adequately skilled to do so. We have also developed the standard operating procedures [SOPs] for the reception, interviewing and referral of cases involving children at police stations. These are the tools that deal with GBV and child-related cases to ensure that interventions are well-coordinated, comprehensive and synchronised.

‘In term of training or capacity of police officers, the BPS has developed some training programmes in achieving best evidence-based practice in interviewing children. Officers have been and continue to be capacitated with appropriate competencies and skills for preventing acts of violence and providing the needed care to survivors of violence and abuse. Hence developments brought by the organisation facilitated effective and comprehensive provision of medical and psychological care to GBV survivors and children exposed to any form of abuse or harm. In order to protect victims, we also have the virtual juvenile courts. The BPS collaborated with the Ministry of Justice and Correctional Services and they have adopted video teleconferencing. Equipment is fitted in the child-friendly centres to enable virtual hearings in children’s cases. The new model is being heralded as a ground breaking, making court more accessible and convenient for the children. The BPS in its efforts has a strategic approach for promoting gender equality across all sectors and levels of policy-making, development and organisational practices. This is to ensure the integration of the gender perspective into the design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of all the policies, programmes and processes within the BPS.

In terms of prevention, the BPS mission is to provide professional policing services and partnership with the community. This was formulated in the quest to bring the community on board to assist in policing and prioritising prevention. So we have got the promotion of community-led prevention programmes or strategies. There are also programmes geared towards empowerment of men, as we believe that men are the agents of change. There is also use of science and technology in GBV investigations. Furthermore it is important to coordinate and cooperate with partners, therefore the BPS continues to collaborate with key stakeholders in the fight against GBV and child abuse.

‘The BPS has also benefited from development partners such as UNICEF, SADC [Southern African Development Community] Debswana, who continuously support our efforts in providing quality and comprehensive services for all victims of GBV, including children. Future efforts to improve our operational efficiencies include promoting community-led prevention programmes, enhancing reporting and support systems, and prioritising the establishment of the GBV one-stop service centre. We're also developing the caring for the carers programme to support officers that are involved in the investigation of GBV and child involved offences. We are also going to expand the victim- and child-friendly spaces that we already have, and lastly integrate the restorative and reformative approach to policing.

‘I think I've touched on a lot of issues, but in conclusion, we are saying that through all these efforts, it is evident that the BPS continuously aligns to the country's obligations to international and regional instruments and protocols to ensure compliance and enhance community-led policing programmes and deployment of science and technology and intelligence-led policy initiatives that will over the years yield the desired outcomes of a safe and secure Botswana free from GBV and violence against children’.

[OFFICIALS joined the meeting.]

The FFM team noted that OFFICIALS mentioned there are 12,200 or so police officers. How many women and men are in the police force? How is it split? OFFICIALS explained that there were around 30% women. He thought that number had grown now because in [recent] intakes, they’d been recruiting around 50:50 [men: women], so he expected it to be around 35%.

The FFM team asked whether all police officers receive training that includes gender-sensitive or GBV training. OFFICIALS explained that yes, all police officers are trained on gender-sensitive approaches to policing. There are a select few officers who are then deployed to the Gender and Child Protection Branch, and those officers are given even more specialised training and investigative tools to deal with GBV as a whole. That includes human trafficking and child protection issues. But all police officers are trained to adequately be able to provide assistance should there be an issue of GBV.

The FFM team asked how big the Gender and Child Protection Branch (GCPB) is. How many people are in it and what are their functions? Does it provide training? OFFICIALS explained that The Gender and Child protection Branch has officers across all the 84 police stations in the country. The FFM team asked whether this is all the main towns and not every post, but most of the stations. OFFICIALS confirmed yes, all of the big stations. The FFM team asked for clarification as to whether it is all stations. OFFICIALS noted that it is all of the 84 police stations. OFFICIALS added that it’s a fairly new branch, every year the branch is getting a manpower boost to increase the number of officers within each and every police station.

The FFM team asked whether they are actively recruiting to that unit. Did they intend to expand it? OFFICIALS noted yes, recruiting to the branch.

The FFM team asked whether these officers receive and investigate GBV cases. Are they investigatory officers, what is their role exactly? OFFICIALS explained that they receive, investigate and provide referrals [of GBV cases], and look at the safety measures that are needed for the victims, like shelters in cases where you can't take the victim back to the same environment that they come from. The FFM team asked whether, when OFFICIALS mentioned referrals, that is from other police officers or from other organisations. OFFICIALS explained that it is other institutions like healthcare, or the social workers that the person might need the services of. The FFM team asked whether this meant the officers have a mixed role, a variety of roles. OFFICIALS confirmed that that officers are from different professional backgrounds such as social work, psychology, investigations, early child development, counselling, etc.

The FFM team asked whether the GBV branch operates the SOPs and also trains other officers in GBV. OFFICIALS confirmed yes. OFFICIALS added that GCPB is responsible for cascading all of its training, all the specific techniques that are needed to attend to GBV cases, to all police officers, so that at any point in time when somebody comes with an issue, they'll be attended to.

The FFM team asked whether a victim coming to the station could therefore be attended to soon. OFFICIALS confirmed that she could. The FFM team asked whether, if a woman comes in and says, ‘I’ve been abused by my partner,’ she can access the station and she’ll be directed to them. OFFICIALS confirmed yes.

The FFM team noted that the police mentioned the 8 child-friendly spaces. Are these only for children, or can women access them as well? OFFICIALS explained that they are for children. These are child-friendly police stations. The police are realising that to take a child and expect them to be interviewed in a regular police station with uniformed police officers is not conducive for a child, so they have strategically identified residential houses that have been turned into police stations for children, but they look very much like houses. And if you get a chance to see them, we'll actually take you to one of them so that you can see it. It's just a house resembling a home with televisions, play areas, toys etc, to help the child relax when they are being interviewed, and the police officers deployed there do not put on uniform.

OFFICIALS added that we have shelters for other GBV victims. The FFM team asked for confirmation that they have shelters. OFFICIALS noted that they have – well, not the government, they are owned by NGOs and the police refers victims to them for safety. The FFM team asked whether these were the NGO shelters referred to earlier. OFFICIALS confirmed that they were.

The FFM team asked whether there is a separate process when the police handle cases where adult women have experienced GBV, and what is that process? OFFICIALS explained that adults are generally attended in normal police stations but in what are called victim-friendly spaces. The police haven’t always had them; they’re a new development. All the new police stations that are being built come with victim-friendly spaces. But the thing they feel is more important is the knowledge within the police officers themselves in terms of what the victim needs, in terms of privacy, in terms of proper risk assessment. That’s why they concentrate on the police officers, so that even if there's no space to hold an interview, they realise that the victim still needs privacy. So even if there's no office, the victim can be taken aside somewhere and they’ll still be able to have a private space where they can be interviewed.

The FFM team summarised that victim-friendly spaces don't exist in many stations or posts yet, but the training is that you should take the person aside and allow them to explain the situation. OFFICIALS agreed, adding that they should also be given privacy.

The FFM team noted that some sources they had spoken to had said that’s not always the case that victims get privacy to report their case. Sources have also said that it could be quite traumatic or difficult to explain your circumstances, maybe because of stigma or fear. So is there space to do that in police stations, and the process is to do that? OFFICIALS noted that it’s possible that some victims may not have been afforded privacy because many of these victim friendly efforts are a new development. However, the BPS is doing its best to close the gaps. A lot of effort is put into training police officers to understand victim centred approaches so as to provide sensitive handling and response to GBV. OFFICIALS explained that he wouldn't be surprised if at one or 2 stations there could be a situation where somebody may not have been given the right treatment, but in general, police officers are trained to understand that if somebody – anybody – comes into a police station and needs to be attended to, they will be afforded the necessary assistance.

OFFICIALS added the issue of affording victims privacy dates back to 2001. Police officers have been instructed to afford [victims] the privacy that they need. So if a rape victim comes to the office, they'll not be interviewed in a Community Service Centres (CSC) where there are lots of complainants. They will be taken out of the CSC to a safe private room, so they are not interviewed in the presence of other complainants. This has been in place since 2001. But we can’t dispute that someone could say, ‘I was interviewed in the presence of so many officers.’ The other arrangement that we practise is for female victims to be interviewed by female police officers so that they are comfortable. But sometimes a rape victim might feel more comfortable to be interviewed by a different gender and if that aids the case, they are afforded that choice.

The FFM team asked whether every station has male and female officers. OFFICIALS noted yes. She added that there are more female than male officers deployed in the GCPB, to deal with such issues surrounding cases of GBV.

The FFM team asked how many officers there are typically in a station. How big are the 84 stations, and what populations do they usually serve? OFFICIALS explained that the number of police officers is determined by the size of the policing area as well as the crime situation. He noted that as he said earlier, the ratio of female to male officers is around 35:65.

The FFM team asked whether some of the police posts are quite small. Is there a ratio for the size of a community that has access to a police post? As it’s quite a big country with a small population, is it difficult in some places to get access to the police sometimes? OFFICIALS thought accessibility to police services is quite good in Botswana. Even the smallest villages would have access to at least a Police Post. The FFM team asked whether that would be one or 2 officers. OFFICIALS confirmed that it would, and explained that even in posts, they try as much as possible to have the representation of both female and male officers.

OFFICIALS added that there are also customary courts, and that at every customary court, there’s a police office. Customary courts are in almost every village.

The FFM team asked what the police department’s relationship with the customary court is, and how closely they work with each other. OFFICIALS explained that they work closely because there are some cases that are handled by the customary court, and the police officers take those cases to the court. In some instances, the police are housed at the customary court; they have an officer at the customary court in the same building where their offices are. The FFM team asked what the title of that officer would be, OFFICIALS explained that because it’s a police post, the person would be a Post Commander.

The FFM team asked whether, under the dual legal system, it is possible for a case to jump from the customary courts to the non-customary (statutory or common law) courts. OFFICIALS explained that the customary courts have 2 responsibilities: they try criminal cases as well as civil cases, the same as a magistrate. The FFM team asked whether this is under the Penal Code. OFFICIALS explained that this is determined according to seriousness. Serious cases are taken to the higher courts and less serious cases are taken to the customary courts. Generally speaking, GBV cases go to the Magistrates’ courts.

The FFM team asked whether the victim has a choice, or is it mandatory for them to first go to the customary court and then to the civil court? OFFICIALS explained that the victim doesn’t decide; the determination is made on the basis of the nature of the case that’s been reported.

The FFM team asked whether the police officer would decide. OFFICIALS confirmed that the prosecution would decide. The prosecution decides where the case goes. In terms of GBV, those cases don’t go to the customary courts.

OFFICIALS added that normally, the police officers take cases to the customary courts. In higher courts Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) takes charge. A police officer may be delegated responsibility to prosecute at Magistrate’s Court by DPP.

The FFM team asked whether there is a national database of reported crimes and ongoing investigations that all police stations and posts can access. If someone commits a crime in Francistown and then comes to Gaborone, do the police [in Gaborone] know about it and can they find those records? OFFICIALS explained that they have the CCRS, the Crime and Criminal Recording System. However, the Gender and Child Protection Branch has also developed their database which they use to record GBV and child involved offences. There’s a lot of other communications that is shared between police stations on criminals including digital platforms on criminal/wanted person particularly those that are on the run thus increasing police capability to catch criminals.

OFFICIALS asked to provide more information about ‘wanted’ communications, etc.

OFFICIALS explained that normally, when the police investigate, they circulate via safe links by the station, using our systems, our radio communications, or publish on the police Facebook page. The FFM team asked whether the first method OFFICIALS mentioned was electronic communication by e-mail and then the Facebook page. OFFICIALS confirmed this.

The FFM team asked whether there was, however, no database as such. OFFICIALS explained that in addition to the CCRS and the manual recording in the registers, there is an office at police headquarters responsible for the collation of statistics. On a quarterly basis, they do the crime returns and that is done online. We also have the strategy department and monitoring branch, which produces the annual reports. So that's where you get all the statistics for all reported cases. The FFM team asked whether this means individual stations collate their cases and then submit them to the central branch, who collate for the whole country. OFFICIALS confirmed yes, exactly. OFFICIALS added that, for example, if you file at the central police station in Gaborone, then it’s in an automated data centre and you can find it in that database. OFFICIALS noted that they do [therefore] have a database.

The FFM team noted that part of the reason they were asking about a database was because everyone they had spoken to had mentioned the case of the murder of a woman at the University of Botswana 2 weeks ago by her former partner, and it was documented in the newspapers that he was subject to a restraining order. A magistrate was quite critical that despite the restraining order, the perpetrator had been able to find his former partner and kill her. A source had suggested to the FFM team that the restraining order may have been issued in Francistown, but the murder took place in Gaborone. So was there not communication between the police in the 2 cities? Is this a just a sensational example or is it representative of police handling of GBV cases more generally? OFFICIALS observed that normally the problem where the victim has a restraining order is that [they] apply for it themselves [via the courts]. They are issued with the restraining order and then they have to disclose it to the police. The problem will be that they tend to obtain it themselves, and most of the time the police might not be aware of it. The FFM team asked for clarification as to whether the police do not know about restraining orders. OFFICIALS confirmed that this was the case in some instances.

The FFM team asked whether the victim therefore has to go to the police and say, ‘There’s a restraining order’? OFFICIALS noted that we have to realise that the issue of restraining orders is outside the police because the police are not necessarily involved in getting the restraining order. The FFM team asked whether this is because it’s a court order. OFFICIALS confirmed that it is.

OFFICIALS observed that the social environment in the country, however, is such that a lot of people will still go and get a restraining order against another person but then later make the first request for the same person to come over, forgetting completely about the restraining order, and where the police did not know anything about this, we may end up seeing a serious situation like this when people have been together this whole time. Also, in many cases, men are the primary providers for the family. Sometimes, because of that, transactions end up being done after the restraining order has been issued, between the very person who took out the restraining order and the perpetrator, without the police knowledge.

The FFM team asked whether there are any plans to strengthen that system, for example through the use of electronic tagging. RB explained that there is a plan to start a pilot. But the police role in this instance is enforcement. So if there is a court order, they enforce it; the actual policies should be from the Ministry of Justice. The Ministry of Justice mentioned that there is a proposal, even though they are not sure how effective that proposal will be, to tag criminals [who are subject to] restraining orders.

The FFM noted that there has been talk about a Sex Offenders Bill. Is a sex offenders register something that exists already? OFFICIALS explained that the register is almost there, making it easy to connect the other stakeholders involved: the police, the judiciary and immigration at the border so that whenever somebody leaves the country, they can just check in the system if it's a sex offender or whatever is in the register. OFFICIALS thought that before the end of this year [2025], that should be functional.

The FFM team asked whether that requires the bill to become law, OFFICIALS explained no, it has been passed but there were a few sections that have just been amended. OFFICIALS added that manual registration is in place, it’s just that the electronic system needs to be in place so everything can be connected. The FFM team asked whether he/she expected that to be this year, OFFICIALS confirmed that he/she did.

OFFICIALS explained that a process is underway to digitalise most of the government’s systems. One of them is the Sex Offenders Registry. There have been a couple of visits to countries like Estonia, who are also assisting with the project to help digitalise all of the government’s services. With digitalised systems, there would be integrated electronic records for everything, including records like the police were talking about. OFFICIALS noted that he was very hopeful they would have something up and running by the end of this year [2025].

OFFICIALS added that the starting point, which the president said should be a priority, is a digital ID. We have ID cards and these just need converting to digital IDs, and then we'll have what we call a single source of truth from the IDs, and that will include the Sex Offenders Registry and all the other government systems and so on.

The FFM team asked whether the police document (record) reported GBV crimes. OFFICIALS confirmed that yes, they are documented. Every year, the police compile reports.

The FFM team asked whether these crimes are broken down into types of GBV. OFFICIALS confirmed that yes, in terms of GBV, they are categorised. There is: rape, common assault, assault occasioning actual bodily harm, murder, unlawful wounding, defilement of person under the age of 18, cruel punishment of children etc. Those are the offences we have categorised, and that’s GBV.

The FFM team asked whether the numbers have changed. OFFICIALS observed that the recent GBV statistics indicate an increase in GBV statistics. This, however, does not in itself indicate an increase in GBV crime. Factors that could explain this trend include increased reporting resulting from increased awareness creation. Another possible reason is the improvement in the handling of GBV victims thus leading to victims generally feeling safer within the police stations. Therefore, generally speaking, the numbers are going up, but this doesn’t necessarily indicate a worsening crime situation.

The FFM team asked whether the police as an organisation have been campaigning on GBV. OFFICIALS observed that they are campaigning with everything they have. For example, there is an organisation called the Organisation of First Ladies of Africa. All of our first ladies belong to that organisation – the previous one and the current one – and they've been targeting GBV. The police work with the First Lady together with other stakeholders across the country, and generally what we see is that as soon as we have been doing a campaign in a certain place, the reporting goes up. The FFM team asked whether the BPS itself campaigns, too, OFFICIALS confirmed that yes, they have intensive campaigns that are specific to GBV coming up. In November every year, there's an annual 16 days of activism against GBV, where it’s just the BPS. There's also an annual 60-days of action on Crime and Road Safety Campaign coded Operation Pabalesego where GBV is among the targeted crimes. Both operations are held across the country.

OFFICIALS explained that there are many other efforts. The police collaborate with village leadership in what they call Pitso where they call all stakeholders to come and talk about GBV. He further explained that they just had a Commissioner’s Run against GBV in March, and many others yet come.

OFFICIALS noted that BPS also conducts operations with neighbouring countries, operations that are co-ordinated: Operation Thunder, Operation Basadi – an operation that was led by police officers in the region. These operations target specific offences such as human trafficking, drug trafficking, GBV related offences and so on.

The FFM team asked whether regional campaigns are held annually or just every so often. OFFICIALS observed that these are held annually in some cases more than once a year.

The FFM team asked, turning back to the statistics, whether the police also keep records of the number of arrests for GBV-related incidents. And if the police are also prosecuting, do they keep records of the number of prosecutions? OFFICIALS observed that they do, because in the investigation cycle, all activities such as report, arrest, bail, investigation, and trial are documented. The FFM team asked whether that data is available for the FFM team to see, OFFICIALS confirmed that it is.

The FFM team noted that there is published data from 2021, and the courts published data, too, that shows Botswana had a high number of reported incidents of rape but very low prosecution and disposal rates. What was the view of the police as to why there is this attrition from reporting to disposal?

OFFICIALS observed that what you realise is there has always been a problem. It's a general problem; it's not specific to rape cases. It's an issue of just the general justice system in BWA. Conversion of cases from report to prosecution takes a bit long. But it's across all the cases, it’s not specific to rape cases. Now we are trying to move to electronic courts because most of our courts are still manual [paper-based]. If everything is being captured manually, it's tedious, so it takes a bit of time. So what we are trying to do is that process of digitalisation of everything, which includes the court system itself, so that even with the records, it makes the process more efficient. Then justice will be served, on time.

The FFM team noted that in the UK, the reported number of prosecutions for rape is also low. It’s the process of justice. You have a report but that doesn't mean it's credible. You have to investigate, and maybe the person withdraws their case. Is that similar here? Maybe the evidence is not strong enough? Are there weaknesses in the process? OFFICIALS noted that there are different kinds of rape: gang rape, stranger rape, date rape. So depending on the type of rape that has been committed the difficulty of detection varies. For example if it's stranger rape, it's not going to be easy to arrest the perpetrator. It will take time looking for the perpetrator, unless they’re habitual offenders. For example, in the recent past the Forensic Science Laboratory was able to link old rape cases with the offenders though DNA analysis. In all cases of rape, samples or specimens are taken to the lab, which are analysed to help detect the perpetrator.

OFFICIALS added that, in the UK, the age of defilement is 16. In BW it is under 18. The FFM team asked whether he meant the age of consent, OFFICIALS confirmed that he did. He explained that, due to the higher age of consent in Botswana (18) as compared to the UK (16), the number of persons that experience defilement (statutory rape) will generally look higher in Botswana thus inflating the crime statistics in Botswana.

OFFICIALS observed that there are multiple reasons: there’s that, and besides, justice continues to take quite a bit of time and through that time, you lose a lot of information because things aren’t digitalised, etc. But there are many other situations. There are a lot of cases that are withdrawn. As the police, we’ve taken a stance to say that we will not withdraw any GBV cases. But they can still be withdrawn at the magistrate level in court, and I think these withdrawals are poverty-related. So there are many reasons that play into it. And it’s not specific to GBV, it’s across the board. The FFM team asked whether it is correct that if someone comes to a police station with a GBV complaint, before it goes to court or the police decide to send it to court, the person cannot withdraw it, the police will not let them withdraw it. OFFICIALS confirmed that, only for GBV, that is correct.

The FFM team asked for clarification that the only time a GBV case can be withdrawn is when it moves from the hands of the police to the courts. OFFICIALS confirmed this. OFFICIALS added that there was a general observation that cases were being reconciled at family level so that the cases would be withdrawn. So the police made a decision to disallow withdrawal of GBV cases at investigation (police) level and register all GBV cases with the courts.

OFFICIALS observed that in respect of the speedy delivery of justice, BW is actually collaborating now with the UK. They extended an invitation to us. When Lord Collins [of Highbury, former undersecretary in the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office who had various roles including the UK’s Special Representative on Preventing Sexual Violence in Conflict] was here at the beginning of the year, we met with the President because the UK also had a similar problem. Just after Covid, there was a backlog of cases. So they extended an invitation to us to go to the UK and have conversations with them on how we can actually speed up the process of justice. It’s something that we are working on. It's not really specific to GBV cases, it’s all [criminal] cases.

The FFM team thanked OFFICIALS and asked whether the statistics will show that some of these GBV cases are prosecuted and lead to sentencing, and that people end up in prison for their crimes. The OFFICIALS confirmed this.

[NB the BPS did not supply the requested statistics in follow up correspondence.]

The FFM team noted that one point that had been mentioned to them was bail, and that sometimes bail is issued to perpetrators of crimes in GBV cases who then commit further crimes while out on bail. How often is bail issued and what are the criteria? Did the police have any comments about crimes committed while on bail, and is that something they track? OFFICIALS noted that the issue of bail is a big concern for all residents of BW. Citizens generally praise the police for arrests in GBV offences however they complain that unfortunately following the arrest, the perpetrators are then let out on bail. According to Botswana laws, one is presumed innocent until found guilty in court, hence the reason why bail is given whilst awaiting trial. This unfortunately leads to a lot of reoffending in GBV. The issue is being discussed in many platforms in attempts to find a lasting resolution. Furthermore, the Bail Act 2024 has also narrowed the existing gaps.

The FFM team asked what the criteria are for bail to be granted. OFFICIALS noted that there’s the Bail Act now.

OFFICIALS explained that with GBV, it depends on the seriousness of the offence. If it’s common assault, normally the police would arrest [the suspect] and detain them for 48 hours, then they’d release them on what’s called police bail. For serious offences, they might be held until [the case was heard before a] court. In the past, there used to be that problem of bail being granted. Now there’s a new Bail Act, which is [tougher]. It passed last year [2024]. He explained that the act is specifically a Bail Act and there was no such Act before.

The FFM team asked whether the act provides clearer guidelines on when to provide bail, OFFICIALS confirmed that it does and that they should be followed before the accused can be released. All necessary process should be followed involving the victim and the [police] station commander of the area, and any other person who is involved in the matter should also be involved. The FFM team asked whether that is likely to have an impact on bail, or has already had an impact, OFFICIALS noted that it has, because the accused in the University of Botswana case has been refused [bail]. Even the relatives were involved. The FFM team asked for clarification as to whether the suspect in that case had been arrested and bail refused. OFFICIALS confirmed that he continues to be remanded in prison and that stakeholders were called to come and show why he should or should not be bailed, in accordance with the new Bail Act.

OFFICIALS observed that on paper, as a country, there are lots of efforts to try and fix all these problems. However, in terms of effectiveness in cascading new initiatives such as this one [the use of bail], we have a challenge as a country because of resource limitations. The way the Bail Act is set, we shouldn't really see a lot of people being granted bail.

The FFM team observed that in terms of resourcing do the police have the equipment and the facilities they need to do their job? OFFICIALS noted that we can never say we have enough resources, but we do. OFFICIALS observed that the government puts a lot of resources into supporting the police to do their work.

Lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, intersex people and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+ people)

The FFM team explained that the second group they are interested in is LGBT+ people. They noted that they understood that, in effect, same-sex sex is no longer illegal. But what is the police stance towards this community? If a LGBT+ person was assaulted by another Motswana how would the police react? OFFICIALS noted that it’s simple: an assault is an assault. Currently, there's a task force within the police that has been tasked to work with the Global Fund to develop curriculum to sensitize police officers on human rights approaches specifically to improve police capacity on dealing with Key populations. That’s because it's one thing to say an assault is an assault, but in practice, sometimes you will find some differences in the sense that we are from different cultures as much as we may be trained. Sometimes the culture comes into effect.
