Botswana is many years behind western countries, therefore our understanding of some issues is still limited, but we are doing the best we can as a country to bring ourselves up to speed. We are aware we've got some gay communities in the country, and they are entitled to support just like anyone else who [approaches the police]. I do think that they still have challenges just because of our own personal and cultural beliefs, and because we’re still not used to these differences. But in terms of where the law stands, everybody has the same entitlements. OFFICIALS observed that the police are non-discriminatory. OFFICIALS noted that the enlistment into the BPS is non-discriminatory and hence gay people have equal opportunities to be employed within the organisation.

The FFM team asked whether there is more acceptance of LGBT+ people in the cities than in rural areas. Are they able to move around? And if they had any issue, would the police help? OFFICIALS noted that he did not know of any situation in which anybody had been attacked because they are gay, but that he could not say it had never happened. In cities, people understand better about different sexual orientations, but in a smaller villages, they may not understand these differences as well. Even so, he doubted that it would ever reach the point of a person being attacked.

The FFM team asked whether there were any examples of the police having been asked for assistance by an openly LGBT+ person. OFFICIALS asked if the FFM team meant a case in which [male partners] had had a misunderstanding. The FFM team explained that they meant, for example, where a gay man had been attacked and had come to the police saying, ‘I've been assaulted because I'm gay.’ OFFICIALS and OFFICIALS noted that they could had not had such a case. OFFICIALS added that where they state that they are partners, they do come: ‘I had gone away for 2 days and my boyfriend beat me because he’s cheating on me with this other one.’ They do come but we cases are opened as with any other demographics.

The FFM team asked whether this meant cases are not treated as LGBT+ cases, but are treated in the same way as other cases. OFFICIALS confirmed this. OFFICIALS added that they do not disaggregate data on LGBT+ [people] but that they may need start doing so because international conventions require it. OFFICIALS noted that [the phrase used in Botswana laws] is ‘any person’.

Witchcraft and traditional practices

The FFM team asked whether crimes relating to witchcraft, traditional practices or female genital mutilation (FGM) have been reported to the police, maybe in the north, near the borders with Zimbabwe and Angola?

OFFICIALS noted that there are no [reports of] mutilations [FGM] in BWA. OFFICIALS noted: definitely not [FGM]. OFFICIALS agreed – not in our country. OFFICIALS explained that if [FGM] happens here, we’re not aware of it. There’s definitely no case reported to the police.

The FFM team asked whether there are instances of witchcraft/ritual killing. OFFICIALS explained that there are only 3 sections in the Witchcraft Act. OFFICIALS explained that calling someone a witch is an offence. OFFICIALS observed that regarding ritual killing, she didn’t know whether it's a perception by Batswana because at times, maybe the person will be reported as missing, then they'll later be found dead, maybe in the bush with some body parts missing. The assumption by the Batswana might be that it’s a ritual killing, whereas [it might have been] scavengers. The FFM team asked whether OFFICIALS meant animals. OFFICIALS confirmed that she did.

The FFM team asked whether it would be unusual for body parts to go missing. OFFICIALS observed that it is not completely unusual for body parts to go missing. This, however, in many cases is attributed to other factors such as anger by the perpetrator, scavengers, etc., rather than ritual killings.

[NB the BPS did not provide the UKHO FFM with statistics subsequent to the meeting.]

Annex V - Fact finding mission terms of reference

Purpose

To obtain information about the situation and treatment of women, particularly those faced gender-based violence (GBV), and LGBT+ people; availability of protection and scope to relocate.

Terms of Reference (ToR)

  • Demography
    • size of subsets of female population such as ethnic minority groups
    • size of LGBT+ population, specifically L and B women
  • Legal context
    • positive / negative laws protecting women / LGBT+ people
    • other (policy) measures taken by the government to support women / LGBT+ people
  • Social, economic and political rights and attitudes
    • societal and family attitudes including towards lone women
    • economic participation
    • political participation
    • single women
  • Prevalence of violence / discrimination
    • type of GBV/discrimination including LGBT+ people
    • levels of GBV/discrimination, including official statistics, surveys and studies, and reports to the police / state
    • profile of victims – age, gender, location, education, socio-economic background
  • Criminal justice system
    • size and distribution of police including GBV/LGBT+ specialist units
    • training and guidance for police and judiciary on GBV / LGBT+ rights
    • numbers of reported crimes, arrests and prosecutions from GBV against women / LGBT+ people
    • number and distribution of courts, including GBV / LGBT+ specialist courts
    • numbers of cases heard and outcomes
    • legal aid – availability and accessibility
  • Assistance available to women/LGBT+ people
    • state agencies
    • civil society - number and location of organisations
    • nature of support services provided including
      • financial
      • legal aid
      • counselling
      • shelter
      • safe social spaces
  • Freedom of movement taking into account:
    • legal / physical barriers
    • access / availability of
      • accommodation
      • education
      • healthcare
      • employment
    • circumstances of single women

Annex W - Fact-finding mission introductory note

The following note was provided to all sources before and/or at each meeting:

UK Home Office Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) to Botswana, 6 to 17 July 2025

Aim of mission

The purpose of the FFM is to obtain information about gender-based violence (GBV) and the treatment of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+) (with a focus on lesbian and bisexual women).

We would like to meet with you to fill gaps in our knowledge on these subjects.

The fact-finding mission team is made up of 3 Officials from the UK Home Office’s Country Policy and Information Team (CPIT): [redacted].

About the Home Office and CPIT

The Home Office is the UK government department responsible for immigration and asylum. CPIT’s role within the Home Office is to collate information about countries which is used to support Officials (and immigration judges) involved in asylum and human rights decision-making in the UK. Many of CPIT’s country reports are published on the UK government’s website.

More information about CPIT’s range of products, including reports of other FFMs, can be found on GOV.UK.

Format of the FFM

During our visit we intend to meet a range of sources who can provide an informed view on the issues of interest listed below.

The FFM team will take notes of the meetings. These notes may be included a report made publicly available on the GOV.UK website and used in litigation proceedings.

However, we will not publish any information you provide if you do not consent to this. If you prefer that the information is not made publicly available, this will be respected.

We will provide you with an opportunity to review and amend the meeting notes to ensure they are an accurate reflection of our discussions. We will also ask you how you wish to be cited. If you prefer not to be named personally you can choose to be identified in more general terms. Examples include by the name of your organisation or department (‘an Official from the Department of Health’, ‘representative of a NGO’), or by your occupation (an ‘academic’ or ‘journalist’).

Areas of interest

These include:

  • Demography of women / LGBT+ people
  • legal rights
  • societal and family attitudes
  • types of gender-based violence (GBV) and discrimination
  • prevalence of GBV and discrimination
  • the criminal justice system and state protection
  • civil society support and assistance
  • freedom of movement

For further information contact: [redacted]

July 2025

Research methodology

The country of origin information (COI) in this note has been carefully selected in accordance with the general principles of COI research as set out in the Common EU [European Union] Guidelines for Processing Country of Origin Information (COI), April 2008, and the Austrian Centre for Country of Origin and Asylum Research and Documentation’s (ACCORD), Researching Country Origin Information – Training Manual, 2024. Namely, taking into account the COI’s relevance, reliability, accuracy, balance, currency, transparency and traceability.

Sources and the information they provide are carefully considered before inclusion. Factors relevant to the assessment of the reliability of sources and information include:

  • the motivation, purpose, knowledge and experience of the source
  • how the information was obtained, including specific methodologies used
  • the currency and detail of information
  • whether the COI is consistent with and/or corroborated by other sources

Commentary may be provided on source(s) and information to help readers understand the meaning and limits of the COI.

Wherever possible, multiple sourcing is used and the COI compared to ensure that it is accurate and balanced, and provides a comprehensive and up-to-date picture of the issues relevant to this note at the time of publication.

The inclusion of a source is not, however, an endorsement of it or any view(s) expressed.

Each piece of information is referenced in a footnote.

Full details of all sources cited and consulted in compiling the note are listed alphabetically in the bibliography.

Terms of Reference

The ‘Terms of Reference’ (ToR) provides a broad outline of the issues relevant to the scope of this note and forms the basis for the country information.

The following topics were identified prior to drafting as relevant and on which research was undertaken:

  • Legal context (considering laws that protect and/or discriminate constitution, criminal, penal and civil codes) applicable to
    • general anti-discrimination provisions
    • specific to women and girls in political, economic, social, cultural, civil or any other field
    • government statements
    • government departments, policies, and programmes
  • Societal attitude - cultural and family status and attitudes, including attitudes of religious groups, and representation and discourse in media.
  • Domestic and public violence against women (from state and non-state. Violence may take many forms including sexual, such as rape, honour crimes, and harassment (particularly in the workplace) child marriage, FGM. For each:
    • nature of violence and perpetrators
    • prevalence, including variations amongst particular groups.
  • State protection.
    • security services and judiciary, size, composition, capability and effectiveness, including specific units or groups with the remit to assist women or particularly vulnerable groups.
    • attitudes of security forces and judiciary to women
    • accessibility to protection and justice
    • enforcement - arrest and detentions, prosecutions, and convictions
    • assistance and support - witness protection, shelters and other support, and compensation
  • Civil society assistance
    • legal advice and support
    • financial
    • accommodation, shelters, helplines
  • Freedom of movement
    • geography
    • legal freedoms/restrictions
    • safety of movement
